Those whom he desired. Not volunteers or the qualified, but those he wanted. “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). If you belong to Christ, that is why — not that you searched harder or something in you recommended itself. He wanted you, with nothing behind it but his own good pleasure, which is why nothing can get behind it and undo it.

And they came. Half the doctrine in four words. His wanting produces their coming; the call isn’t an offer left on the table but a summons that creates its answer, as the same voice once said “Let there be light.”

Twelve. No one in Israel heard that number innocently: twelve sons of Jacob, twelve tribes, twelve stones on the high priest’s breastpiece. Ten tribes had been lost for seven centuries, and the prophets promised their regathering. Jesus preaches no sermon about restoring Israel. He appoints twelve men, and every Jew watching understands the claim: this is Israel beginning again, around him (cf. Matthew 19:28).

To be with him. The first purpose isn’t what we expect — not to be trained, deployed or made useful, but to be with him. These men will spend three years mostly watching: him praying before dawn, handling a hostile room, tired and interrupted, touching a leper, eating with the wrong people. Almost none of it will feel like ministry. All of it is the training.

Then sent. The second purpose, and the order never reverses: sent men are with-him men first. When a church or Christian swaps them, the work hollows out from inside. That diagnoses a common Christian tiredness — not too much work, but too much work fed from too little Christ: a rota, a group, an argument to win online, and months without an unhurried hour with him. The cure is v. 14: go back and be with him. A test: when did you last spend an unhurried hour with him?

Do Christians have this authority today? Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe they do, and practise deliverance ministry. But this authority was given to the Twelve when Jesus sent them out, among the signs that marked the apostles (2 Corinthians 12:12). The New Testament letters never tell believers to cast out demons; they tell them to “Resist the devil” (James 4:7), put on God’s armour (Ephesians 6:10–18), and pray. The devil is real and still works, but Christ has bound the strong man (3:27), and the believer fights with the word, prayer and the fellowship of the church.

For those who can no longer do much. The elderly, ill, housebound: the first calling on every disciple is one no illness can revoke. You are called to be with him, and you can do that from a bed.
verseByVerse.note: “Apostle” means one who is sent.

parallels.desc: the Twelve and the twelve tribes

verseByVerse.quote: He appointed the twelve: Simon (to whom he gave the name Peter); James the son of Zebedee and John the brother of James (to whom he gave the name Boanerges, that is, Sons of Thunder); Andrew, and Philip, and Bartholomew, and Matthew, and Thomas, and James the son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus, and Simon the Zealot,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mark lists the Twelve: Simon renamed Peter, James and John the “Sons of Thunder,” Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus and Simon the Zealot. Jesus chose flawed, ordinary and even opposed men, named them for what grace would make them, and united them in himself — a picture of the church.

Peter. Not a nickname but a verdict in advance: “Peter” sounds like the Greek for rock (cf. Matthew 16:18). Simon was anything but — impulsive, loud, three years from swearing he had never met Jesus. Jesus names him for what grace will make him. That is how he speaks to his people (cf. John 1:42).

Sons of Thunder. A name with a smile and an edge. Thunder is loud, sudden and does no work, and Mark shows why they earned it: they wanted to call down fire on a village (Luke 9:54) and asked privately for the two best seats in the kingdom (10:35–40). Jesus knew their temperament when he chose them, named it, and appointed them anyway. He isn’t recruiting finished men.

Andrew. There first (John 1:40–42), spending his whole New Testament career bringing people to Jesus and disappearing — his brother, a boy with bread and fish, some Greeks. Never at the head of a list, never minding. If your service is small and no one attaches your name to it, Andrew is your man.

The quiet middle. Several of Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus say little or nothing in the New Testament. No sermon of Thaddaeus survives (he is probably the “Judas the son of James” of Luke’s lists), not one line of James son of Alphaeus. Known to history as names in a list — and their names are in the foundations of the city of God (Revelation 21:14). If it troubles you that your life will leave no trace, look at the middle of this list.

Matthew and Simon. Matthew, the tax collector of chapter 2. And Simon the Zealot: “Zealot” points to burning zeal for Israel and the law, very likely the nationalist mood that wanted Rome driven out by force and counted a Jew collecting Rome’s money a traitor. In any other year, Simon’s ambition would have been to kill a man like Matthew. Here they share a list, roads, a common purse and fields to sleep in for three years. Nothing in the politics of the day could reconcile them; only the man in the middle did.

That is the church. From its first day: people with nothing in common but Christ, which turns out to be more than everything they had against each other. A test: is there someone in your church you would never otherwise have chosen? Thank God for them — it is working.
verseByVerse.note: Peter means “rock.” Thaddaeus is probably the “Judas the son of James” of Luke’s lists.

verseByVerse.quote: and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list ends: “and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him.” Jesus knowingly chose the man who would betray him, yet Judas was fully responsible — and his story warns against hidden, unrepented sin while showing that the fear of being a Judas is not itself the mark of one.

The floor gives way. A plain, unhurried list, and then this. Every Gospel list of the Twelve ends here, with a clause about the betrayal; no one could say the name afterwards without saying what he did.

Called with the rest. Appointed on the mountain, called by name, one of “those whom he desired” (v. 13), present for three years at every private explanation. Sent out with the others to preach and cast out demons (6:7, 13), with no hint his mission failed or that anyone suspected him. When Jesus said one of them would betray him, no one looked at Judas; each asked, “Is it I?” (14:19).

Did Jesus know? Yes: “Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him” (John 6:64). Choosing Judas wasn’t a regretted error. Nor was Judas a puppet. Mark holds both: “the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed!” (14:21). It was written, and he did it and answers for it.

For the betrayed. If you have been betrayed by someone close: your Lord chose his traitor with eyes open, kept him at his table, washed his feet, and called him friend in the garden. He wasn’t caught out. Nothing done to you has caught him out either.

Could I fall away like Judas? The question that keeps sensitive people awake. Judas was never a believer who lost his salvation; he was near Christ without ever being in Christ, and John names the mechanism: as keeper of the money bag “he used to help himself to what was put into it” (John 12:6). The rot was private, ordinary and financial, running for years under an unblemished public record. He didn’t fall in one night; he arrived at that night. So no, you can’t be snatched from the Father’s hand (John 10:28–29). But don’t use that to skip the examination; use it as the reason you can bear to make it.

Remorse or repentance. The test isn’t whether you have sinned badly — Peter denied him with oaths that same week and was restored on a beach. It is what you do afterwards. Judas felt remorse, threw the money into the temple, and went out to a rope. Peter wept and came back. Remorse looks at itself and despairs; repentance turns to Christ and lives.

If you fear you are a Judas. That fear isn’t the mark of a Judas. Judas sat through the warning at the supper and reached for the bread. Go to Christ with the thing you are afraid of — the one move Judas never made, always open to him.
verseByVerse.note: “Iscariot” is often taken to mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea, but that is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went home, and the crowd gathered again, so that they could not even eat. And when his family heard it, they went out to seize him, for they were saying, "He is out of his mind."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Back home, the crowd is so great they can’t even eat, and Jesus’ family set out to seize him, saying, “He is out of his mind.” Even those closest to Jesus misunderstood him; faithfulness to God may look like madness to family, and the Lord who bore that wound stayed tender toward them.

No time to eat. Back to the house in Capernaum, and it starts again. Not that they couldn’t rest or talk — they couldn’t eat. The Son of God missed meals because of the volume of human need at the door. The household had been chaotic, exhausting and loud for weeks.

To seize him. Word reaches Nazareth twenty-five miles away — crowds, missed meals, clashes with authorities, a delegation coming from Jerusalem — and his family comes. The verb is strong, the one used of the mob arresting him in the garden (14:46). They mean to take him home by force before he embarrasses the family further or gets himself killed. Their diagnosis, reported without softening: “He is out of his mind.”

His mother among them. Verse 31 says who came, and the first name is his mother — Mary, who heard the angel, said “let it be to me according to your word,” was told her son would be called Son of the Most High, and treasured the shepherds’ words (Luke 1:26–38; 2:19). Here she is on the road with her other sons to take this one home. She wasn’t a woman of flawless, finished faith above ordinary disciples’ confusion. She was a real disciple, and like every real disciple she had to grow. His brothers were further back: “not even his brothers believed in him” (John 7:5).

Where her story goes. An encouragement, not a scandal. The Mary outside the crowd here stands at the cross when most of the Twelve have run (John 19:25) and prays in the upper room after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). She moved from outside to inside, from misunderstanding to worship — the journey this passage defines as belonging to the true family. If your coming to Christ has been uneven, with long stretches of not understanding him, you are in his mother’s company.

When your family thinks you have gone too far. If your own family say your faith has become excessive, unhealthy, that someone should have a word — your Lord felt that wound first, from those who knew him best. He didn’t harden against them or let it turn him from his Father’s will, and he stayed tender while he did it. By the end his brother James writes to the church as “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (James 1:1), and his mother is in the prayer meeting. A test: are you staying both faithful and tender with family who misunderstand you? Pray for them today.
verseByVerse.note: “His family” means his relatives.

parallels.desc: even his brothers did not believe

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribes who came down from Jerusalem were saying, "He is possessed by Beelzebul," and "by the prince of demons he casts out the demons."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Scribes from Jerusalem declare that Jesus is possessed by Beelzebul and casts out demons by the prince of demons. Unable to deny his miracles, they attribute God’s power to Satan — showing that there are only three real verdicts on Jesus, and that hearts set against him will build a theology to justify it.

An official delegation. Not local critics but professionals from the capital, sent ninety miles to assess him. (“Came down” is how one always spoke of leaving Jerusalem, which was “up” whatever the map said.)

They couldn’t deny the miracles. It is often assumed his opponents thought the miracles tricks. They didn’t. The people best placed to expose a fraud, with every professional motive, concede the events and dispute only the power behind them. In Galilee the evidence wasn’t in question; the explanation was.

Beelzebul. Behind the name stands Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron whom King Ahaziah consulted (2 Kings 1:2); by Jesus’ day it was a title for the prince of demons (cf. v. 23). So the charge is as bad as it gets: not mistaken, not even a fraud, but that the power visibly at work in him is hell’s, and that he is occupied by it.

Three verdicts. Mark sets two accusations side by side: his family says he is mad; the theologians say he is evil. Between them they cover the ground people have covered ever since, because there have only ever been three verdicts on Jesus, and the third is costly. He is deluded, or dangerous, or what he says he is. What has never been on the menu is the comfortable modern option of a wise, gentle teacher everyone can admire. No one who met him thought that. They loved him or wanted him dead. A test: which verdict has your life actually given?

The problem wasn’t evidence. These scribes had the best religious education in the world and the Scriptures largely by memory. They walked ninety miles, stood in the room, watched God’s power set people free with their own eyes — and wrote it up as demonic. When a heart has decided, it builds a theology to house the decision, and the better educated, the better the theology. That is why Jesus answers with logic first and mercy second — and why the warning that follows is the most frightening thing he ever said.
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan (v. 23).

verseByVerse.quote: And he called them to him and said to them in parables, "How can Satan cast out Satan? If a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand. And if a house is divided against itself, that house will not be able to stand. And if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but is coming to an end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls his accusers to him and shows by parables that Satan cannot cast out Satan: a divided kingdom or house cannot stand, and if Satan were fighting himself he would be finished. Jesus answers slander with patient reasoning, and his argument proves his power is not Satan’s — yet argument alone changes no heart.

He called them closer. They have just accused him of being possessed by the devil, and he invites them in. Not shouted across the room or dismissed behind their backs — he calls the men who slandered him into conversation.

He reasons. “How can Satan cast out Satan?” Faced with the most serious accusation in the Gospel, Jesus answers with cold logic, not outrage. There is a place for argument in defending the faith, and the Lord uses it.

Three airtight steps. A divided kingdom can’t stand — everyone in that room knew Israel had split after Solomon and never recovered, and they lived after Rome’s own civil wars. A divided house can’t stand — anyone who has watched a family tear apart over money or a grievance knows it. And if Satan has risen against himself, “he cannot stand, but is coming to an end.” The trap closes: their theory requires the devil to be expelling his own troops from his captives, in public, successfully. If true, their theory has just announced the end of the kingdom of darkness — exactly what they came to deny. Either the exorcisms aren’t from Satan, or Satan is finished.

Take what is true seriously. Jesus doesn’t deny a devil, a kingdom of darkness, or organised opposition. He concedes the framework and shows it won’t bear their weight. That is how a Christian should argue: take what is right in a view seriously, and press the part that fails.

Argument changes no heart. More searching: an unanswerable argument changed no one in that room. Jesus won completely, and the scribes went home unmoved. Remember that when you burn to win an argument about the faith with someone you love. Argument can clear an obstacle and is worth making well; it has never, on its own, changed a heart. That is the Spirit’s work — the very Person these men are about to be warned against resisting. A test: are you praying for that person as much as you are arguing with them?

verseByVerse.quote: But no one can enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man. Then indeed he may plunder his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can plunder a strong man’s house without first binding the strong man. Jesus isn’t Satan’s agent but the stronger one who has come to tie him up and carry off his captives — and he bound Satan by letting himself be bound and crucified.

On the attack. Jesus stops defending and, with one picture, turns the accusation inside out: a house, a strong owner, goods secure inside, and someone who wants them.

The goods are people. He concedes much: there is a strong man, the house has been securely held, the goods really are his by conquest. The picture takes the kingdom of darkness seriously. And the goods are people — every possessed man in Galilee, every soul on the beach, every reader before Christ came for them: inventory in a strong man’s house.

Which man is Jesus? They said he was the owner’s agent. But no one breaks into a house he owns or carries off goods already his. Jesus is in the house not as servant but as the thief, and the owner is on the floor with his hands tied.

Binding first. You can’t walk off with a strong man’s property while he stands. So every deliverance in this Gospel isn’t a skirmish but a removal van: furniture carried out of a house whose owner has been dealt with. The New Testament keeps the picture: God “has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Colossians 1:13) — a word for moving property (cf. Isaiah 49:24–25).

When was the strong man bound? The strangest and best turn in the faith: by a stronger man who let himself be bound first. In a garden, soldiers tied Jesus’ hands, and he didn’t resist. They led him bound to a high priest, to a governor, and fastened him to a cross with arms open and immovable — the posture of a man who can plunder nothing. And that was Satan’s binding: God “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him” (Colossians 2:15); “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). The strongest man who ever lived let the owner tie him up and died — and that is how the ropes went onto the other wrists.

Stolen goods. If you are in Christ, understand what you are. Not a volunteer who signed up, but stolen goods. You were in that house; the owner had every claim on you; you had no way out. Someone broke in and carried you out over his shoulder, and the price of the raid was his life. A test: do you live as one still under the old owner’s fear, or as one carried out?

parallels.desc: the prey taken from the mighty

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, I say to you, all sins will be forgiven the children of man, and whatever blasphemies they utter, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin"— for they were saying, "He has an unclean spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus declares that all sins and blasphemies will be forgiven, except blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which is eternal sin — because they were saying he had an unclean spirit. God’s forgiveness is vast enough to cover every sin; the only unforgivable sin is the settled, informed rejection that calls the Spirit’s work evil — and anyone afraid they have committed it has not.

The widest promise first. “Truly” is “amen,” Jesus putting his own authority behind a statement — and what he puts it behind is this: all sins and every blasphemy. Not most, not the respectable ones. Things said in rage, in a hospital corridor at three in the morning, years of mocking him, words you wouldn’t repeat to anyone — all forgivable. Don’t hurry past it. The most sweeping sentence about mercy Jesus ever spoke was spoken to men who had just called the Holy Spirit a devil.

The one exception. “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin.” And Mark at once says what it refers to: “for they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit’” (v. 30). He anchors it in what was happening in that room. Men watched God’s Spirit set people free before their eyes; they couldn’t deny it; and with full knowledge they called it the work of hell. That is the sin: not doubt, confusion or a hasty word, but the settled, informed decision to look at the light and name it darkness — and to keep saying so. “They were saying” it: not a slip, but a position maintained.

Have I committed it? Many tender Christians read this at night and can’t sleep. Plainly: if you are afraid you have committed the unforgivable sin, you haven’t. That isn’t a comforting fiction. The sin is the terminal hardening of a heart against the Spirit — so calcified that it sees God at work and calls it the devil without a tremor. Fear of this sin requires that you want to be forgiven, that you care what God thinks of you, that being cut off from him horrifies you. That doesn’t come from a hardened heart. Hardened hearts don’t lie awake over their standing with God; they sleep very well. The scribes went home untroubled. Your distress is evidence of a conscience still alive under the Spirit’s hand, and the Spirit doesn’t trouble someone he has abandoned. The hardness that commits this sin doesn’t tremble; it calculates.

A test you can run tonight. Can you honestly say you want Christ — that if he would have you, you would come? Then come; he has never turned away anyone who did. “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37), with no clause excepting people afraid they have gone too far.

Why it is unforgivable. Because it is unrepented, and unrepented because the one committing it has no wish to repent or be forgiven. Someone who wants pardon is by definition not there. Your fear isn’t your danger. It may well be the Spirit’s own work in you, drawing you to the only place where fear is answered.

verseByVerse.quote: And his mother and his brothers came, and standing outside they sent to him and called him. And a crowd was sitting around him, and they said to him, "Your mother and your brothers are outside, seeking you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ mother and brothers arrive, stand outside, and send in to call him, while the crowd sits around him. Being near Jesus — even by family, upbringing or church involvement — is not the same as belonging to him; yet his family later came in, and no one is beyond his reach.

They arrive. Mark has built to this since v. 21: the family set out to seize him; the Jerusalem delegation accused him; the strong-man argument and the terrible warning were given. Into that room comes a message from the door: your mother and brothers are outside.

Outside, sending in. The house is packed with people on the floor close enough to touch him, and his own mother is on the pavement sending a message. They don’t come in; they send for him, as you do when you expect to be obeyed — family authority, a mother and grown brothers requiring the eldest to come out. And v. 21 says what they intend when he does.

Who were these brothers? The plain reading is that they were sons of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus. Matthew names them and mentions sisters (Matthew 13:55–56; cf. Mark 6:3); John says “not even his brothers believed in him” (John 7:5); Acts sets them beside Mary but apart from the apostles (Acts 1:14). Two other views arose in the early church to protect belief in Mary’s perpetual virginity: that they were Joseph’s sons by an earlier marriage, or cousins. Scripture says neither, and Matthew says Joseph “knew her not until she had given birth to a son” (Matthew 1:25), which most naturally implies they afterward lived as husband and wife. The more likely reading is that these were Jesus’ younger brothers.

Proximity is not belonging. Here is the chapter’s geography in one sentence. You can be his mother and be outside. You can have carried him, fed him, known him better than anyone alive, and be in the street while strangers sit at his feet. That isn’t really about Mary. It is about anyone whose link to Christ is nearness rather than surrender: raised in it, related to it, married into it, employed by it, on the rota, known by name — and functionally outside, sending messages in, wanting Christ to come out and fit into a life organised without him.

A test. Without panic, but without dodging: am I in the room or at the door? Not “Have I been around this a long time?” — the family had been around him thirty years. Have I sat down before him as one who wants what he says more than I want him manageable?

They came in. Real hope, because Mary doesn’t stay outside. The woman on the pavement in Capernaum is at the cross when the disciples have scattered (John 19:25) and in the prayer meeting after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). The brothers who don’t yet believe will include James, who writes as “a servant… of the Lord Jesus Christ,” and Jude. No one in that street is beyond the reach of the man in that house. It took a resurrection, but they came in.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, "Who are my mother and my brothers?" And looking about at those who sat around him, he said, "Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Looking around at those sitting with him, Jesus says, “Here are my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of God, he is my brother and sister and mother.” Jesus doesn’t reject his natural family but announces a new family: all who come to him in faith and obedience belong to him as closely as kin.

Not a snub. “Who are my mother and my brothers?” is a question asked in order to be answered, and the answer is among the most extraordinary things he ever said about ordinary people.

He looked around. Mark keeps giving us Jesus’ eyes. In v. 5 he looked round at hard men with anger and grief. Here he looks round a floor full of nobodies — fishermen, a reformed tax collector, a former Zealot, whoever got in that morning — face by face, taking his time, before he speaks.

Not demoting his mother. He said it while his mother stood in the street, but not at her expense; the New Testament forbids that reading. He honoured her from the cross, arranging her care with almost his last breath (John 19:26–27), and he condemned using religion to escape duty to parents (7:11–13). This isn’t the demotion of the natural family but the announcement of a second one.

Whoever. No pedigree — not descent from Abraham, education, record, family or reputation. Whoever.

Does the will of God. Not admires it or believes correct things about it — the demons had the doctrine right and were no relation of his. This is the chapter’s dividing line, drawn at the door: not what you can recite, but whether you have come in and sat down under his word. Lest that become a performance to earn, Jesus defined the work: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent” (John 6:29).

Brother and sister and mother. Not followers or servants, but the closest words the language has. And “sister,” in a room where a rabbi’s disciples were men — no accident.

For the family-less. Some reading this had a father never satisfied; some have a family gone quiet since they became Christians — the empty seat at Christmas, the brother who doesn’t call; some have no one left alive who remembers them as a child. To all of them the Lord looks round a room and says: here. These are mine, and so are you. Not a support group, but a family with a Father, a firstborn brother “not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11), and a household you will still belong to when every other name on your family tree is forgotten.

Your mismatched congregation. So the awkward church you sit among on Sunday isn’t a social arrangement you could improve by finding people more like yourself. It is your family, given by Christ, who named them before you did. A test: who in your church family do you need to treat as a brother or sister this week?

The man who said it. Called mad by his family and demonic by the theologians the same afternoon, soon to be deserted by every man in that room, he went to the cross to make a family out of people who had none — so a room of strangers on a dirt floor could be looked at, one face at a time, by the Son of God, and called his mother and his brothers.

3.theology:
Two of the most-asked questions in Mark sit in this chapter, and both deserve a straight answer.

Was Jesus's anger sinful? No — and v. 5 shows how to tell, because it gives the anger and the grief in one breath. He looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart. Sinful anger wants the other person diminished and would be quietly disappointed by their repentance; righteous anger grieves, wants the wrong put right and the wrongdoer restored, and would be glad to be made unnecessary. Be angry and do not sin (Eph. 4:26) is a command with a boundary, not a contradiction.

What is the unforgivable sin? Mark answers it himself in v. 30 and the answer is anchored, not abstract: for they were saying, He has an unclean spirit. It is the settled, informed, deliberate attribution of the Holy Spirit's unmistakable work to Satan by men who have seen it with their own eyes and chosen their verdict. It is not a slip, a doubt, or a season of confusion. And the pastoral corollary is firm: the person terrified of having committed it has not, because the fear itself requires a conscience still responsive to the Spirit, and that is precisely what this sin destroys. The hardness that commits it does not tremble; it calculates.
3.examples:
The chapter's two great alliances are worth setting side by side, because they explain a great deal about churches.

Then: Pharisees and Herodians — strict separatists and worldly courtiers, men who despised each other on religion, politics and money — in a room together within minutes, agreeing perfectly on one thing: how to destroy him. Nothing on earth unites people like a shared hatred of the light. Pilate and Herod became friends the day Jesus was sent back and forth between them (Luke 23:12).

And then: Matthew the tax collector and Simon the Zealot on the same list of twelve, walking the same roads for three years. In any other year of the world, Simon's politics would have called for a knife in Matthew's ribs. Nothing reconciled them except the man in the middle.

Now: both are still in operation. A congregation can be welded together by what it is against, and it will feel like unity and it will not be. Or it can be a collection of people with nothing whatever in common except Christ — which is more than everything they had against each other. If your church contains people you would never otherwise have chosen, that is not a defect to be managed. It is the evidence.

4.title: Seed, Soil, and the Sleeping Lord
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, and the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land. <sup>2</sup>And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them: <sup>3</sup>“Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. <sup>4</sup>And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it. <sup>5</sup>Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. <sup>6</sup>And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away. <sup>7</sup>Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain. <sup>8</sup>And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.” <sup>9</sup>And he said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>10</sup>And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. <sup>11</sup>And he said to them, “To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, <sup>12</sup>so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven.” <sup>13</sup>And he said to them, “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? <sup>14</sup>The sower sows the word. <sup>15</sup>And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them. <sup>16</sup>And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. <sup>17</sup>And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away. <sup>18</sup>And others are the ones sown among thorns. They are those who hear the word, <sup>19</sup>but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. <sup>20</sup>But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.” <sup>21</sup>And he said to them, “Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? <sup>22</sup>For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. <sup>23</sup>If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.” <sup>24</sup>And he said to them, “Pay attention to what you hear: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. <sup>25</sup>For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away.” <sup>26</sup>And he said, “The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. <sup>27</sup>He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. <sup>28</sup>The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. <sup>29</sup>But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.” <sup>30</sup>And he said, “With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it? <sup>31</sup>It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, <sup>32</sup>yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade.” <sup>33</sup>With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. <sup>34</sup>He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything. <sup>35</sup>On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, “Let us go across to the other side.” <sup>36</sup>And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him. <sup>37</sup>And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. <sup>38</sup>But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” <sup>39</sup>And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, “Peace! Be still!” And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm. <sup>40</sup>He said to them, “Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?” <sup>41</sup>And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is Mark's great block of teaching, and it is built to answer one question the previous chapter forced: if Jesus really is the King, why does this look so small and go so badly? The professionals have called him demonic, his family thinks he is unwell, and the kingdom of God at this point consists of a preacher in a borrowed boat and twelve unimpressive men.

The answer comes in seed. A sower broadcasts across ground he cannot see into, and three-quarters of it appears wasted — and the harvest is still thirty, sixty, a hundredfold, when a Galilean farmer expected five or ten (vv. 3–20). A man scatters seed and goes to bed, and it grows while he sleeps and he does not know how (vv. 26–29). The smallest speck in the garden becomes the largest plant in it, with room in its branches for the birds of the air — which in Ezekiel and Daniel means the nations (vv. 30–32).

Then the teaching stops and the test begins. He says let us go across, and the crossing nearly kills them. The chapter that has been about hearing the word ends with the word spoken to a hurricane, and with a question left deliberately unanswered: Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–25 — The Sower and the Purpose of Parables
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The pulpit (vv. 1–2). The crowd is so large that Jesus pushes a boat out a few yards and preaches from the water, with the people banked up the shore. The setting is itself a picture: one voice, one seed, going out over a great many different kinds of ground.

The parable (vv. 3–9). A sower walks a field and the seed lands in four places — a trodden path, a shelf of rock under thin soil, a patch of thorn roots, and open ground. Three losses and one harvest so large it would have made a Galilean farmer laugh.

Why parables at all (vv. 10–12). The hardest paragraph in the chapter, and Jesus does not soften it. He quotes Isaiah's commission to a nation that had already shut its eyes, and says the stories both shelter the seeker and confirm the scorner.

The explanation (vv. 13–20). The only parable Jesus takes apart line by line in this Gospel. Four soils, four fates, and the third one is the one most of us are living in.

The lamp and the measure (vv. 21–25). The hiding is temporary — a lamp goes under a basket for a moment, not for a life. And what you do with what you have heard determines what you will be given next.
verseByVerse.theology:
Verses 11–12 are the hardest words in the chapter, and they should not be smoothed over. Matthew's version says Jesus speaks in parables because people do not see (Matt. 13:13); Mark's says he speaks so that they may not see, lest they should turn and be forgiven. Read flatly, that sounds as though the Lord veils truth deliberately to stop people repenting.

Three things dissolve the difficulty. First, the words are a direct quotation of Isaiah 6:9–10 — God's charge to a prophet sent to a nation that had already, for generations, shut its own eyes. This is not fresh cruelty; it is the settled judgement of God on hardened refusal. Second, the so that carries the weight of fulfilment as much as bare purpose: the parables come to a people who have chosen blindness and confirm the choice, which is how God deals with those who insist — he gives them over to the dark they preferred (cf. Rom. 1:24). Third, and decisively, the door is never bolted. Those around him with the twelve understood nothing either. The difference between them and the outsiders is one thing only: they asked.

So the same parable is judgement and mercy at once. It hardens the scornful and shelters the seeker — hiding the truth from the mouth that would only spit on it, while keeping it within arm's reach of anyone who will turn and ask.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a farmer broadcasting seed by hand across ground he has not sorted in advance, some of it landing where it has no chance at all.

Now: every faithful preacher, parent and friend who keeps sowing without being able to see the soil. The sower in the parable does not test the ground first, and he is not blamed for the path, the rock or the thorns. That is a real relief for anyone who has taught a class for years, or raised children in the faith, and cannot see a harvest. Your job was the sowing.

And a hundredfold is not a rounded-up figure. Ordinary yields in that country ran five- or tenfold, and a farmer who got thirty would have talked about it for the rest of his life. Jesus names thirty as the lowest of the three good outcomes. Three-quarters of the field appears to fail, and the harvest is still absurd. Whatever the losses look like from where you are standing, the ledger at the end is not in doubt.

verseByVerse.quote: Again he began to teach beside the sea. And a very large crowd gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, and the whole crowd was beside the sea on the land. And he was teaching them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus teaches a huge crowd from a boat by the lake, teaching them many things in parables. His parables are not simple illustrations but stories that draw hearers in and make them ask where they stand before God’s word.

A boat for a pulpit. The crowd is too big for the shore, so Jesus sits in the boat he had kept ready (3:9) and is pushed out a few yards. Sitting was the teacher’s posture. The ground near Capernaum rises from the water in a natural curve, and the water carries sound; a man in a boat can be heard by thousands on the slope without shouting. He uses the shape of his Father’s world as a sound system.

The setting is the sermon. One voice from one point, going out over a vast crowd — farmers and fishermen, Pharisees listening for errors, mothers with children pulling at them, people who walked from Judea and people who wandered down because of the commotion. One seed; many kinds of ground.

Mostly teaching. “Again he began to teach.” We remember the miracles; Mark records that most of the Lord’s time went on teaching — what he was doing when the roof came in (2:2), and here.

What a parable does. Not a children’s illustration, nor a code with a decoder ring. The word covers proverbs, riddles and comparisons, and all of them make you work. A plain statement — people respond differently to God’s word — is easy to agree with and forget; you can nod without a flicker of self-suspicion. But give someone a field with four kinds of ground, and he walks round its edge wondering which patch he stands on. He must enter the story to understand it, and once inside, it has him. Nathan didn’t open with “You are the man”; he told of a poor man’s ewe lamb and let David pass sentence on himself (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

Expect to be handled. Read this chapter expecting the same treatment. Jesus isn’t giving information about four kinds of hearer. He is walking you into a field and asking where you are standing.
verseByVerse.note: Teaching from a boat let the whole crowd on the shore see and hear him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus commands, “Listen!” and tells of a sower whose seed falls partly on the path, where birds eat it at once. God’s word is sown widely and generously, and the first danger is a heart so hardened by routine that the word never gets in.

Listen. His first word is a command, and the parable ends, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (v. 9). A story bracketed by warnings about how you receive it.

How sowing was done. Not neat drills. A Galilean farmer carried seed in a fold of his cloak or a bag and threw it in a wide arc across the whole field; often the ploughing came after, turning the scattered seed in. Fields were unfenced: paths crossed them, limestone lay a few inches down in places, last year’s thorn roots waited at the edges. The sower isn’t careless; he can’t see what is six inches under any given yard.

A first comfort. For anyone who has taught, preached, raised children in the faith, or spoken of Christ to a friend and seen nothing happen: you aren’t asked to survey the soil first. You couldn’t; you can’t see into another person. Sow. Results were never your assignment.

The path. Not bad ground but ground walked on so often it set like a floor. No one decided to make it hard; traffic did — the same feet, day after day, until nothing could get in. And the birds came at once. The seed doesn’t even fail slowly; it lies in plain view and is gone before the sower reaches the end of the row. Verse 15 names the birds (see there).

The soil no one worries about being. That is its danger. The rocky hearer has a crisis; the thorny hearer feels the squeeze. The path feels nothing. The word arrives, lies there, is carried off, and he goes home to lunch undisturbed and slightly bored. A test: when did a sermon last stay with you past lunch?
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed falls on rocky ground with little soil; it springs up quickly but withers in the sun because it has no root. Quick enthusiasm is no measure of real faith; what matters is the hidden root that holds when hard times come.

Rock under the surface. Not stones scattered through soil, but a shelf of limestone a few inches down with a thin skin of earth on top. From above it looks like the rest of the field.

The best performer at first. “Immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil.” It came up fast because the soil was shallow: warmth collects over rock, the seed can’t go down, so everything goes up. The fastest, greenest growth in the field is the growth that will die. Anyone twenty years in church has seen it: the new convert whose enthusiasm makes everyone else feel lukewarm, at everything, telling everyone — and gone in three years, with no one sure when they stopped coming. Early growth told you nothing.

The same sun. The sun isn’t the enemy; it ripens the harvest in the good soil of the same field. The heat that kills one plant matures another, and the difference is underground. That reframes hard seasons: trouble is the weather in which real growth is finished and shallow growth exposed. The same bereavement, diagnosis or humiliating years will make one believer and break another, and the difference was decided before the heat came.

No root. Not attacked or argued out of it — withered from underneath, where no one was looking. So the question isn’t how green you look this month but what is happening in the dark. Roots grow in private and in boring stretches: the unimpressive half-hour with a Bible on a wet Tuesday; prayers that feel like talking to the ceiling; Sundays attended when you would rather not; doctrine understood before you need it. None of it shows; that is the point.

A test. If the heat came this year — the illness, the redundancy, public embarrassment for being a Christian — what exactly would you draw on? If the answer is a feeling from a conference, you have been told in advance, kindly, while there is time to dig (see also on vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed falls among thorns, which grow up with it and choke it, so it yields no grain. The word can be slowly crowded out by other living, growing concerns, leaving a life that looks green but bears no fruit.

Thorns you can’t see. At sowing the thorns aren’t visible: what is in the ground is a root system, last season’s bushes cut or burned off at the surface, dormant, the earth above looking as good as anywhere. Then the rains come and both grow at once — not a thorn field with a little wheat, but wheat and thorns coming up together, drawing on the same water, light and few inches of earth (cf. Jeremiah 4:3).

Choked. A violent verb, related to the one used of the pigs drowning (5:13) and a man seizing a debtor by the throat (Matthew 18:28) — violent, though silent. No moment of decision; no one digs up the wheat. It is simply crowded, shaded and starved by things that are also alive and also using the ground.

No grain. The outcome that should stop us. The plant is still there — green, standing, in leaf. Walk past in June and you would say it was doing fine. It simply never produces anything. Verse 19 names the thorns, and they are not what we expect (see there). A test: what in your life is green but bearing nothing?

verseByVerse.quote: And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold." And he said, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Other seed falls on good soil and yields thirty, sixty and a hundredfold; and Jesus calls whoever has ears to hear. Despite many losses, God’s word produces an astonishing harvest, and true hearing is a gift to be sought from Christ.

Good soil receives. The good soil does nothing to become good; it doesn’t clear its own stones or grub out its thorn roots. It receives what falls and lets it go down. The parable isn’t asking you to manufacture your own fertility; the field is worked on, not self-improving.

Slow, not dead. “Growing up and increasing” — Mark alone gives the process, the quiet answer to the shallow soil. That plant sprang up at once; this one takes its time. Fast isn’t the same as fruitful, and slow isn’t the same as dead.

A ludicrous harvest. An ordinary yield in that country was perhaps fivefold to tenfold, from which next year’s seed came. Thirtyfold would be talked about for life. Jesus names thirty as the worst of his good outcomes, then sixty, then a hundred, which ordinary farming doesn’t produce (cf. Genesis 26:12). Do the sum: three-quarters of the field looks a total loss — seed to birds, seed withered, seed strangled — and the harvest still fills every barn and leaves the farmer laughing in the yard.

For discouraged disciples. It was a live question for the Twelve. It looked as though this was going badly: the professionals called him demonic, his family thought him mad, the crowds wanted healings, and the kingdom was a preacher in a borrowed boat and a dozen unimpressive men. Jesus tells them what the accounts will say at the end, and it isn’t close. Hold that when your own field looks mostly loss — children not walking with God, years of teaching that seemed to change no one, a smaller church. The losses are real and honestly named. They aren’t the story. God, who supplies seed to the sower, will multiply it and increase the harvest (2 Corinthians 9:10).

Ears to hear. A refrain that sounds again over the seven churches in Revelation. Everyone on that beach had ears; that is why it is a warning. The hearing that saves isn’t the hearing the whole crowd was already doing. Physical hearing is universal; spiritual hearing is a gift, and whoever wants it has only to ask the one in the boat. Ask him for it today.
verseByVerse.note: A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. And he said to them, "To you has been given the secret of the kingdom of God, but for those outside everything is in parables, so that they may indeed see but not perceive, and may indeed hear but not understand, lest they should turn and be forgiven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the crowd has gone, those around Jesus with the Twelve ask about the parables, and he says the secret of the kingdom has been given to them, but to outsiders everything is in parables, so that seeing they don’t perceive, “lest they should turn and be forgiven.” Parables both reveal and judge: to hardened hearts they confirm refusal, but to anyone who stays and asks, Christ gladly explains.

They stayed. The beach empties, and a smaller group stays to ask what he meant. That is the hinge of the passage. The insiders aren’t insiders because they understood — v. 13 shows they understood nothing. They are insiders because when the sermon ended they didn’t go home. They stayed and asked.

A secret given. The word is “mystery,” which in the Bible never means a puzzle for the clever but something God kept hidden and has now disclosed. It is “given” — by one Giver. No one works it out. And in Mark the secret is a Person: the kingdom has arrived in a carpenter from Nazareth who is going to a cross.

Does Jesus speak in parables to stop people repenting? It sounds so, and the difficulty shouldn’t be smoothed over. Three things resolve it. First, the words are Isaiah 6:9–10, God’s commission to a prophet sent to a nation that had shut its own eyes for generations; the preaching would now confirm them in it. Not fresh cruelty, but God’s settled judgment on hardened refusal — the passage the New Testament uses again and again to explain unbelief (Matthew 13:14–15; John 12:40; Acts 28:26–27). Second, “so that” is the language of fulfilment as much as of bare purpose: this happens, and Isaiah’s word comes true — what Paul calls God giving people over to what they have chosen (Romans 1:24, 26, 28). Third, decisively, the door is never bolted. The proof sits in the room: those given the secret understood nothing thirty seconds earlier. What separated them from the crowd walking home was that they asked. “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find” (Matthew 7:7).

Judgment and mercy together. To someone who has already decided, a parable is one more story to shrug at, and every shrug sets the ground harder. To someone troubled by it, it is a door left open, a truth kept just out of reach so that he must come and ask, and the asking is the beginning of everything.

A test. This chapter has been strange in places. Did you notice, and go and ask him? Or did you find it obscure and get on with your day? Those who stayed on the beach didn’t have better minds. They had a habit of not leaving.
verseByVerse.note: A “secret” (mystery) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables? The sower sows the word. And these are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear, Satan immediately comes and takes away the word that is sown in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gently rebukes the disciples’ lack of understanding and explains: the sower sows the word, and the path stands for those from whom Satan immediately takes it away. God works through his ordinary spoken word, and Satan actively snatches it from hearts hardened by familiarity — but God can break up hard ground.

A rebuke while explaining. “Do you not understand this parable? How then will you understand all the parables?” There is a sigh in it, and Mark records it. But it is said in the middle of explaining, not as a refusal. A mercy for slow disciples — all of us. The men with him three years were consistently baffled, and worse in chapter 8. He keeps teaching people who aren’t quick.

The seed is the word. Not a general religious influence, experience or mood, but a message in sentences that can be spoken and heard. So the kingdom comes by an ordinary means anyone can use: “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17); we are born again “through the living and abiding word of God” (1 Peter 1:23). An unremarkable sermon in a half-empty building on a wet Sunday isn’t a low-grade activity. It is the sowing.

Satan takes it. Jesus names a person, not a process. The word doesn’t merely evaporate; someone comes and takes it — “the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:4). “Immediately”: not a slow leak but at once — in the car park, on the walk home, in the first conversation afterwards. “Takes away”: a theft, not a verdict on the word, removed before it could get in. So sitting through a sermon and remembering none of it by lunch isn’t always a neutral lapse of concentration. Something can be at work in it.

How hearts harden. No one chose the path; traffic made it — the same feet over the same ground until it set like a floor. That is how a heart hardens: not by a decision to reject God, but by years of the same routines, until the gospel is just a sound you have heard before.

The path needn’t plough itself. If you have started to find it dull, take that seriously and take it to God tonight in exactly those words. He has never refused someone who asked him to break up his hard ground: “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26).

parallels.desc: the god of this world has blinded the minds

verseByVerse.quote: And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who, when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. And they have no root in themselves, but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately they fall away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rocky ground stands for those who receive the word immediately with joy but have no root in themselves, and fall away when trouble or persecution comes because of the word. Joy at hearing the gospel is good, but faith that never takes root in the heart will not survive its cost.

Nothing wrong with the joy. This soil frightens sensitive people and is often misread. Jesus doesn’t criticise the gladness; real conversion is glad, as the man who found treasure in a field went “in his joy” and sold all he had (Matthew 13:44). The problem isn’t that they were happy, but that happiness was all there was.

No root in themselves. The diagnosis is in the last two words. Not no root in the church or in good teaching — no root in themselves. Something was never internalised. The faith was held at the level of atmosphere — music, friendships, the feeling in the room, an admired preacher — and never went down into the private ground no one sees.

For a while. Which is why it takes time to tell. This soil looks like good soil, better at first, and keeps looking fine for a season — perhaps two years.

On account of the word. Not trouble in general, but trouble that comes because of the faith itself: friendships that cool once you are known as a Christian, the joke at work you are now on the wrong side of, the family grown careful with you, the promotion that goes elsewhere — and in much of the world far worse. This is the soil that discovers Christianity is expensive after assuming it was free. “Fall away” is “are tripped up,” the root of the offence the cross gives (1 Corinthians 1:23). Fast in, fast up, fast out.

Were these true believers who lost their salvation? Arminian Christians read the parable that way: the rocky soil received the word with joy, so it must have been real faith, later lost (cf. Hebrews 6:4–6). But Jesus says they “have no root in themselves”; something was missing from the start. The joy was real, but it wasn’t the life of a new heart. “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19). The more likely reading is that the fruitless soils describe profession without possession. A true believer may stumble and struggle, but the word that has truly taken root goes on to bear fruit.

A test. Ask it while the weather is fine: what are you doing this month that will still hold you in ten years? Roots go down in unglamorous places — opening the Bible on Tuesday with no appetite and reading anyway; understanding a doctrine before the diagnosis comes; praying when it feels like the ceiling; belonging to a church rather than attending one, so others know you well enough to hold you. None of it shows an inch of growth. That is what makes it root.

You can ask the Farmer. Rocky ground in a field can do nothing about the rock. You can. You are the one soil in the story able to go to the Farmer and say, “There is something hard underneath me, and I can’t shift it.” Ask him now, in an ordinary week. That prayer has never been declined.

verseByVerse.quote: And others are the ones sown among thorns. They are those who hear the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches and the desires for other things enter in and choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The thorny ground stands for those who hear the word, but the cares of the world, the deceitfulness of riches and desires for other things come in and choke it, so it bears no fruit. The great danger for comfortable Christians is not gross sin but ordinary worries, money and wants crowding out God’s word.

Not sins. The soil that describes most Christians in a comfortable country, and its three weeds aren’t adultery, theft or blasphemy, but worry, money and ordinary wanting. That is why it can’t be diagnosed by examining your conduct.

The cares of the world. The ordinary word for anxiety, the one Peter uses: “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). The mortgage, the scan result, the struggling child, frail parents and the decisions coming, the news checked six times a day about disasters you can’t affect. Most are duties, not sins — and they strangle the word, because worry isn’t passive. It takes the time and mental room hearing God needs, even while you sleep.

The deceitfulness of riches. Not riches, but the lie money tells: a little more will make you safe. It is told as loudly to the man with little as to the man with much, which is why this weed grows in every income bracket. Wealth isn’t evil; it is dishonest company, promising a security it has never delivered to anyone (cf. 1 Timothy 6:9–10).

Desires for other things. The most devastating phrase, because so casual; Jesus doesn’t bother naming them. The extension, the bike, the holiday researched every evening, the series everyone watches, the hobby that has become what you think about while others talk. None of it wrong — the whole point of this soil, and why it is so hard to see from inside.

Let in. “Enter in and choke the word.” Nothing was pushed out; things were let in, one reasonable thing at a time, until the word was crowded to the edge of a life it once centred. Not dead or renounced — standing, green, leafy, and bare at harvest.

Is this hearer a Christian at all? Some teach that he is a carnal Christian, saved but fruitless and unrewarded (cf. 1 Corinthians 3:15). But in the parable only the good soil yields a harvest, and Jesus says, “Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matthew 7:19). The more likely reading is that a life that bears nothing at the harvest shows a faith that never truly lived. A believer may go through seasons of little fruit and be pruned (John 15:2); but the word truly received doesn’t stay barren for good.

Two harder questions. Don’t ask, “Is there anything bad in my life?” There may be nothing. Ask: what has been crowded out? Name what used to happen and has quietly stopped — praying, reading, hospitality, the conversation about Christ you haven’t had in a year, not by refusal but for lack of room. And: where does the overflow go? When your week has a spare hour and your mind a spare half-hour, where do they go, automatically? Whatever answers that is what is growing in your field.

Cut them, by name. The only thing that works with thorns isn’t feeling bad about them but cutting them — one at a time, with a name attached. The specific anxiety, handed over in specific words. The specific spending, stopped. The specific evening, given back. Unglamorous, and the whole job. Pick one this week.

verseByVerse.quote: But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good soil stands for those who hear the word, accept it, and bear fruit — thirty, sixty or a hundredfold. True hearing welcomes God’s word with its authority and bears fruit as the result, not the price, of receiving it; and every fruitful believer, whatever the yield, is good soil.

Three verbs, in order. Hear, accept, bear fruit. The path heard too; hearing is where everyone starts and three of four stop.

Accept. The verb that separates this soil: to welcome, take in as your own, as you receive a guest rather than a leaflet. The rocky ground “received” the word too, with an ordinary verb; here it is the warmer one — the difference between taking a letter at the door and opening it, reading it, and doing what it says. Accepting isn’t agreeing the sermon was true; everyone agreed God should be obeyed. It is letting the word in with authority, allowing it to contradict you and change Monday. A test: what has God’s word contradicted in you lately, and did you let it?

Fruit is the result, not the price. The order matters pastorally and is constantly reversed. No plant produces grain by straining to. It receives light, water and soil, and fruit is what comes out. “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me” (John 15:4). That answers a way of life that exhausts sincere Christians: trying to squeeze fruit from themselves and concluding they are failures. You aren’t asked to manufacture; you are asked to receive, keep receiving, and let it go down.

Thirty counts. The kindness easy to miss: the yields differ, and all three are good soil. Jesus could have said a hundredfold and stopped. He put thirty in the same category. The thirtyfold Christian isn’t second-class; a farmer with thirty would be the talk of the village.

Don’t measure against another’s field. Some believers are given health, gifts, years and opportunity, and their lives are visibly fruitful. Some are ill, poor, obscure or worn down, and what they produce is thirty — a marriage held together, a few people prayed for by name for decades, a faith kept in a hard place where no one applauded. Both are in this verse, sown by the same hand, and the barn doesn’t sort them. What God asks of a field isn’t that it be the best, but honest ground taking in what falls — and the Sower who scattered seed across your life knew what was under the surface, and threw it anyway.

parallels.desc: whoever abides in me bears much fruit

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Is a lamp brought in to be put under a basket, or under a bed, and not on a stand? For nothing is hidden except to be made manifest; nor is anything secret except to come to light. If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A lamp isn’t lit to be hidden under a basket or bed but set on a stand; nothing is hidden except to be revealed. God’s present concealment of the truth about Jesus is temporary and for the sake of its full revealing — and so is his hidden work in our lives.

A question a child could answer. After a paragraph about seeing and not perceiving, Jesus picks up a household object. The lamp is a small clay dish of oil with a wick; the basket a grain measure; the bed a low pallet. The question is faintly comic: no one lights a lamp to hide it — you would put it out and save the oil.

Hiding for the sake of showing. It answers the worry of vv. 10–12. If parables conceal, has God gone into hiding things? No. Concealment in God’s kingdom is always temporary and for a later revealing. A lamp goes under a basket for a moment while carried across a room; it doesn’t live there. “Nothing is hidden except to be made manifest” — not that hidden things sometimes come out, but that the whole purpose of the hiding is the showing.

In this Gospel. Jesus silences demons, hushes the healed, tells disciples to say nothing — then dies in public outside a city wall in the busiest week of the year, and a Roman officer says aloud what no one was allowed to say (15:39). The secret was always going to be shouted. It was protected until it could be understood, as you shield a flame with your hand while carrying it — not wanting the room dark but lit.

What God is doing in the dark. A comfort for parts of your life that make no sense yet — situations prayed over for years with nothing to show. This verse doesn’t promise an explanation next Tuesday. It promises that the darkness isn’t the point. “For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known” (1 Corinthians 13:12).

Our secrets too. The same saying has a searching side: “Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed” (Luke 12:2). The Christian’s comfort is that the things he most dreads coming to light were dealt with at the cross before they were ever brought up. A test: is there something you are hiding that you need to bring to Christ now, rather than wait for it to come to light?
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of oil with a wick; the “basket” was a grain measure.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Pay attention to what you hear: with the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and still more will be added to you. For to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warns, “Pay attention to what you hear,” for the measure you use will be measured to you and more added; to the one who has, more will be given, and from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken. Hearing God is something we do well or badly: obeying what we hear enlarges our capacity to receive more, while ignoring it hardens us.

Listening is something you do. Luke has it, “Take care then how you hear” (Luke 8:18). The chapter’s point arrives as a command: listening isn’t passive, succeeded or failed at by accident, but something done well or badly, and answered for.

Your own container — and more. A market-stall image: you bring your own vessel to be filled, and what you take home depends on its size; bring a thimble and you carry a thimbleful, however generous the merchant (cf. Matthew 7:2). Then Jesus breaks the picture: “and still more will be added to you.” This merchant heaps it over. God’s arrangement isn’t strict reciprocity but generosity that outruns the vessel.

Not money but capacity. “To the one who has, more will be given” sounds like the worst thing about the world — the rich get richer. But Jesus isn’t describing money. He is describing spiritual capacity, and there it is simply how understanding works. What you take in and act on enlarges the vessel you bring next time; what you hear and shelve doesn’t stay neutral but quietly shrinks your capacity to hear. You know this from ordinary life: learn a little music and you hear more in the next piece; learn a little of a language and you hear words where there was only noise. Use expands the organ; disuse shrinks it. A truth heard and never obeyed doesn’t wait patiently to be obeyed later; it hardens, and next time it is easier to ignore. That is the path of v. 15 from the inside: ground made hard by traffic.

A test. Think of the last clear thing God said to you through Scripture or a sermon — not the last interesting thing, but the last thing you knew you were meant to do: the conversation, the habit to stop, the person to forgive, the money to give. Did you do it? If yes, expect more; the promise isn’t stingy. If no, understand what is at stake: not that God is annoyed, but that the next word will be fainter, and the one after fainter still, until you sit through the very words that once moved you and feel nothing.

The container that grows. “Pay attention to what you hear” isn’t a call for concentration but for obedience, because obedience is the only container that ever gets bigger.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–41 — The Growing Seed, the Mustard Seed, and the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The seed that grows while you sleep (vv. 26–29). A parable found only in Mark, and it is the most relaxing thing in the chapter. A man scatters seed and then goes to bed, gets up, goes to bed, gets up — and the seed grows, and he knows not how. The growth is not his doing and never was.

The mustard seed (vv. 30–32). The proverbially smallest thing in the garden becomes the largest plant in it, with branches enough for birds to nest in. Spoken to twelve unimpressive men whose movement looked like nothing at all.

As they were able to hear it (vv. 33–34). Mark tells us the teaching was calibrated: parables to the crowd, everything explained in private to the disciples. God gives truth at the rate a person can take it.

The storm (vv. 35–41). And then the chapter stops talking about the word and puts them in a boat. It was his idea to cross. The storm was not an interruption of obedience but the road it went down. He is asleep on a cushion; they are bailing; and the question they ask at the end — who then is this? — is the question the whole Gospel has been walking toward.
verseByVerse.theology:
The stilling of the storm is not a nature miracle among others; it is a disclosure of who is in the boat, and the disciples' own Scriptures gave them the answer to their question the moment they asked it.

In the Old Testament, mastery of the sea belongs to God and to nobody else. You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Ps. 89:9). He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Ps. 107:29) — in a psalm about sailors at their wits' end who cried to the LORD in their trouble. It was God who shut in the sea with doors and said thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed (Job 38:8–11). To the ancient mind the sea was chaos itself, the one thing no king could command.

So who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? has exactly one possible answer, and it should have frightened them more than the weather did.

And hold the two halves of the scene together, because the chapter will not let you have one without the other. He was asleep because he was exhausted — a real man, worn out, on a boat cushion, so tired that a storm did not wake him. And he silenced the sea with a word. Fully man in his exhaustion, fully God in his voice, in the same four feet of a fishing boat.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: experienced fishermen, on their own lake, in their own boat, bailing with their hands and certain they were about to die — while the Lord of wind and wave slept four feet away.

Now: the same accusation, in the same words, from every believer in a storm — do you not care? And it is worth noticing that Mark preserved the accusation. The Gospel does not tidy up the prayer of frightened men into something more reverent. There is a place in Scripture for saying exactly that to God, and the Psalms are full of it: Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? (Ps. 44:23).

Two things follow. First, he answered the panicked prayer before he corrected the panic — the storm was stilled, and then the question about faith was asked. He is not waiting for you to pray well before he acts. Second, their fear did not end when the danger did; Mark says they were filled with great fear after the calm. They were more frightened of the man in the boat than of the wind. That is not a failure. That is the beginning of knowing who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. The earth produces by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom is like seed a man scatters: he sleeps and rises, and the seed grows by itself, he doesn’t know how — blade, ear, full grain — until harvest. God, not us, makes his kingdom grow; we are to sow faithfully, rest in his power, accept growth by stages, and expect the appointed harvest.

Mark’s own parable. Only Mark records it, and it is the most restful thing in the chapter. A man sows — and then, the surprise, does nothing.

He sleeps and rises. The rhythm of an unremarkable life: bed, up, bed, up. No watching the field at night, no digging up seed to see how it is doing. “The seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how.” He doesn’t control it — he doesn’t even understand it — and his ignorance doesn’t slow the crop by a day.

Spoken to the unqualified. Twelve men just handed a mission they were plainly unqualified for, soon to be sent out two by two with no money. Everything in them will want to know how it works and whether they are doing it right. Jesus tells them: you scatter, then you sleep. The power was never in the sower. Not a licence for laziness — the man still sows and comes with a sickle at the end — but release from a burden no one was asked to carry. You can’t make a seed germinate, argue someone into the kingdom, engineer revival, or force growth in your own soul. “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6).

Then go to bed. Do your sowing honestly and generously — the conversation, the teaching, years with your children, the invitation, the faithful ordinary Sunday. Then go to bed. Actually go to bed. The anxious sleeplessness that passes for spiritual seriousness isn’t in this parable, and the crop doesn’t depend on it. A test: what are you losing sleep over that belongs to God to grow?

By itself. “The earth produces by itself” — literally, automatically. Not without God; this pictures how God works. But without the farmer.

Stages. “First the blade, then the ear, then the full grain.” The tenderest line for anyone worried about their own slowness or another’s. Stages can’t be skipped or hurried. A blade isn’t a failed ear; it is what a healthy plant looks like in April. God isn’t disappointed with a young Christian for not being an old one, and he isn’t finished with an old one either (cf. James 5:7).

The harvest is fixed. “He puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come” echoes Joel: “Put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe” (Joel 3:13), a text about the final judgment. So this isn’t merely about patience. The harvest is fixed, coming when the grain is ripe. The long, quiet middle of history, where the kingdom looks small and slow and nothing seems to happen, isn’t drift. It is growing season, and the man with the sickle knows the day.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records this parable of the seed growing by itself.

parallels.desc: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe
the farmer waits for the precious fruit

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "With what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it?
