It is like a grain of mustard seed, which, when sown on the ground, is the smallest of all the seeds on earth, yet when it is sown it grows up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the air can make nests in its shade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom of God is like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, which grows larger than all garden plants so that birds nest in its shade. The kingdom begins tiny and unimpressive in Jesus and his followers but will grow to shelter the nations — so small beginnings are no measure of God’s work.

Comically small. He asks the question aloud, as a teacher does to make the class lean in, and the answer is deliberately small. The mustard seed was the proverb for tininess, as we say “a grain of sand”; the rabbis used it so.

The smallest of all seeds? An objection sometimes raised: other seeds are smaller. Jesus isn’t lecturing on botany or making a claim about the world’s seed catalogue. He uses the everyday proverb of his hearers, about the seeds a Galilean farmer handled, as we say the sun rises without being wrong about astronomy. What matters is the size in the hand: a speck you could lose in the creases of your palm.

Eight feet in a season. Black mustard there grows eight or ten feet in a season — tall enough to ride through, woody enough to hold weight. Nothing in the seed announces it.

Who was listening. Twelve men and a few others on a beach in a provincial district of an occupied country, following a village carpenter whose family thinks him unwell and whose national leadership has ruled him demonic. Rome has legions and roads and an emperor. This has a boat. And Jesus says the kingdom of God is that speck in your hand.

Birds are the nations. The last clause is a deliberate echo every Jew would catch. In Ezekiel, God plants a sprig on Israel’s mountain and it becomes a noble cedar: “under it will dwell every kind of bird; in the shade of its branches birds of every sort will nest” (Ezekiel 17:23). In Daniel, the great tree sheltering beasts and birds is a world empire (Daniel 4:12). The birds are the nations: a kingdom big enough for the peoples of the earth to live in.

From speck to shade. At one end, a speck, a dozen men, a borrowed boat, a preacher three years from execution; at the other, shade for the world. The distance is covered not by strategy, numbers or weather but by the nature of the seed. Small isn’t weak, slow isn’t failing, and only in the hand does a mustard seed look like nothing.

For the discouraged. If the part of the kingdom you can see is discouragingly small — an ageing congregation, a Sunday school class of four, the one believer in a family, years of prayer for someone who hasn’t moved an inch — you aren’t looking at the tree. You are looking at the seed, and you were never given the ability to tell the difference by looking. Two thousand years on, the speck has branches on every continent, people of every language nest in its shade, and the seed hasn’t finished growing. Keep sowing.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man.

verseByVerse.quote: With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear it. He did not speak to them without a parable, but privately to his own disciples he explained everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus spoke the word in many parables “as they were able to hear it,” and explained everything privately to his disciples. Christ teaches tenderly at the pace people can bear, and he explains his word to those who stay close and keep asking.

As they were able to hear. One of the kindest sentences in the Gospel. He measured what he said not to what he could have said, nor to what was true — all of it was — but to what they could bear. He does it to the end: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). The Son of God, with everything worth knowing, holds things back out of tenderness for the capacity of the people before him.

For your own slowness. There is a way of reading the Bible that turns into anxiety — the sense that you should have grasped more by now, that others see what you don’t. He isn’t withholding out of displeasure. He gives at the rate a person can receive, and that rate isn’t a judgment on you. A field gets the blade before the ear, and the farmer isn’t disappointed in April.

For how you treat others. If the Lord calibrated what he said, so should we. There is a zeal that unloads everything it knows onto a new believer, a struggling one, or someone just bereaved — every doctrine, every hard edge — and calls it faithfulness. It isn’t; it is failing to notice who is in the room. Say what they can hear. There will be more Tuesdays. A test: who do you need to speak to more gently this week?

Explained everything. Two audiences, two levels, and the difference again isn’t intelligence but nearness. The explanation happens privately, to those who stayed. The crowd got the story; those who didn’t go home got the meaning. He didn’t leave his own people with a riddle; the door into the private room was never locked.

Stay behind and ask. The plainest lesson from the plainest verse: the difference between a Christian who understands his Bible and one who doesn’t is rarely ability and very often this — one keeps coming back to Christ with the bits he didn’t follow, and the other closes the book. Stay behind. Ask. He explains everything to the people who do.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day, when evening had come, he said to them, "Let us go across to the other side." And leaving the crowd, they took him with them in the boat, just as he was. And other boats were with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That evening Jesus tells the disciples to cross to the other side of the lake, and they take him in the boat “just as he was,” with other boats alongside. The storm they meet comes not from disobedience but in the course of following Jesus’ own command.

His idea. “Let us go across to the other side.” Fix this now, because it changes how the storm is read: going onto the lake was his idea. They weren’t running away, taking a shortcut, or making a poor decision he then had to rescue. He said cross, and they crossed, and the storm that nearly killed them met them in the middle of doing exactly what he told them.

Not every storm is a wrong turn. Much Christian thinking assumes the opposite: when trouble comes, we search backwards for the wrong turn — what did I miss, where did I disobey, is this because I stopped praying? Sometimes there is a wrong turn, and it should be found. But this boat was in this storm because Jesus put it there; obedience was the route in. Job didn’t suffer for drifting; the book opens insisting he was blameless. Paul was in God’s will on the ship that broke up under him (Acts 27). Your storm may not be evidence of anything gone wrong. It may simply be what the other side costs. A test: are you blaming yourself for a storm that came through obedience?

Just as he was. A small detail only an eyewitness gives. No going ashore, no meal, no change of clothes. He had sat in that boat teaching since morning, and they pushed off with him still in it, exhausted where he sat. Keep it in mind when you find him asleep in v. 38.

Other boats. Mark alone records it. The storm didn’t fall on one boat; others were out in the dark with no one aboard who could still a wave. Mark says nothing more, and the silence is its own comfort: when the calm came, it came over the whole lake. Some who benefited most from the miracle may never have known who did it. Some of what God does in answer to the church’s frightened praying spills far past the church and is never traced back.

verseByVerse.quote: And a great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling. But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. And they woke him and said to him, "Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A violent storm swamps the boat while Jesus sleeps on a cushion in the stern, and the terrified disciples wake him: “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?” Jesus is truly human — exhausted enough to sleep through a storm — and he welcomes even our panicked, accusing prayers when we bring them to him.

A real squall. The word is a hurricane-like squall that hits without warning. The lake lies nearly seven hundred feet below sea level in a bowl, with the Golan heights rising steeply to the east and gullies running to the water; cold air pours down onto warm air over the lake, and glass can turn to breaking waves in minutes. Waves broke over the side, one after another, and the boat was going down.

Professionals afraid. At least four of these men had fished this lake since boyhood. Their terror isn’t amateurs’ panic. When men like that conclude they are about to drown, they are almost certainly right.

Asleep on the cushion. Three details no one would invent: the stern, the cushion, the sleep. The stern had a small raised deck; the cushion may have been the helmsman’s, perhaps a ballast sandbag used as a pillow — “the cushion,” as a man remembers the exact object.

The Son of God was tired. One of the great windows on who Jesus is. He sleeps because he is worn out, taken off “just as he was” after a day’s teaching. Properly, physically tired — the tiredness that won’t wake for a hurricane and cold water breaking over you. He was hungry (11:12), thirsty (John 19:28), wept at a grave (John 11:35). Whatever else the incarnation means, it means there is a man in that boat, and he is exhausted. And more than exhaustion: he can sleep in a storm on a lake he made. “In peace I will both lie down and sleep; for you alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8).

An accusation. “Do you not care that we are perishing?” isn’t a prayer request but an accusation, and Mark doesn’t tidy it up. They don’t ask him to do anything. That is what fear does: it goes past the danger and attacks God’s character. The real terror in the boat wasn’t the water but the sudden conviction that the one in charge had gone quiet and might not be bothered.

Scripture keeps such prayers. If you have prayed like that — in a hospital corridor or at two in the morning, words you would be ashamed to repeat in church — notice that Scripture preserves this sentence, and is full of its kind: “Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever!” (Psalm 44:23); “How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). He would rather have it shouted at him from four feet away than have you drown politely at the other end of the boat. They got one thing right amid everything wrong: when they were sure they were dying, they went to him. Go to him with yours.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden violent storms are common. The cushion was probably the helmsman’s seat or a sandbag in the stern.

parallels.desc: the sleeping prophet in the storm
awake! why are you sleeping, O Lord?

verseByVerse.quote: And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea, "Peace! Be still!" And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus wakes, rebukes the wind and tells the sea, “Peace! Be still!”; the wind stops and there is a great calm. Jesus commands creation with the authority Scripture gives to God alone — and at the cross he went into the storm of judgment for us rather than silencing it.

No preparation. He doesn’t take the helm, tell them to bail harder, or pray for deliverance. He wakes in a swamped boat and speaks to the weather as though it had been misbehaving.

Rebuked, muzzled. “Rebuked” is the word used when he rebuked the unclean spirit in the synagogue (1:25); he addresses a storm as he addresses a demon, a hostile thing with no business there. “Peace! Be still!” is gentler in English. The second word means, literally, “be muzzled,” the same verb he threw at the demon (1:25). The sea is told to shut its mouth and stay shut.

Only God commands the sea. To Israel the sea was no beauty spot; it was chaos, the old enemy that swallows men. Only one Person in their Scriptures gave it orders: “You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them” (Psalm 89:9); “He made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed” (Psalm 107:29); “Thus far shall you come, and no farther, and here shall your proud waves be stayed” (Job 38:11). And here is a carpenter in a fishing boat, wet through, speaking to a storm in the dark.

Instantly flat. Wind doesn’t stop; it drops away, and the sea runs on for hours — the swell outlives the storm. Here there is no interval: wind gone, water flat, as if the lake had never moved. Mark sets the two “greats” side by side: a great windstorm (v. 37), a great calm, one sentence between.

He speaks to it. The difference between him and every other help you have had: everything else works with the situation — manages it, mitigates it, gets you through. He speaks to it. The gap between him and us isn’t one of degree. A test: what storm in your life have you only been managing, instead of bringing to the One who can speak to it?

The storm he didn’t silence. Set this beside the cross. On a hill outside Jerusalem the sky goes black at noon for three hours, a man cries that God has forsaken him, and he dies (15:33–37). That day no one rebuked the storm. He went into it and let it break over him with nothing held back; it wasn’t muzzled and didn’t stop until it had finished with him. The voice that could silence anything said nothing — so that when storms come for you, they come as weather and not as wrath.

parallels.desc: you rule the raging of the sea
he made the storm be still

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?" And they were filled with great fear and said to one another, "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks, “Why are you so afraid? Have you still no faith?” and the disciples, filled with great fear, ask one another, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” Jesus rescues before he rebukes; real faith trusts him in the crisis; and the right answer to their question is that the one in the boat is the Lord of creation himself.

Rescue first. It sounds hard, but look at the order. He stilled the storm and then asked the question. He didn’t sit up and require better praying before he would act. He dealt with the water because they needed it dealt with, and only afterwards turned to what was wrong inside the boat. Remember that next time you are ashamed of how badly you prayed in a crisis. He isn’t waiting for you to pray well.

Afraid of the wrong thing. He isn’t asking why they were frightened of a hurricane — any sane person is. The word is timid, cowardly, and the issue is the object of their fear: every reason to fear the lake, none to fear it with him aboard. The rebuke isn’t “you felt something” but “you forgot who was in the boat.”

Still no faith. “Still” is the sad word. They had seen a leper cleansed, a paralytic walk, a withered hand restored, demons obey him in public. What they hadn’t done was take any of it into the one place it would cost them something — where they thought they were dying. That is a familiar distance: between what you believe on Sunday and what you can lay hold of at three in the morning. Faith is tested not by whether you can affirm a doctrine, but whether it is load-bearing when the water comes over the side. A test: which truth about Christ do you need to lean your full weight on this week?

A greater fear. The strangest thing in the chapter: the danger is over, the lake like glass, and they are more frightened than in the storm — “they feared a great fear.” They had feared drowning; now they fear the man dripping wet four feet away. That isn’t a failure of faith but the beginning of understanding. When you realise what has been sharing your boat all afternoon, terror isn’t unreasonable. Isaiah saw the Lord and said, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5). Peter, after another miracle on this lake, said, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (Luke 5:8). The fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins.

Who then is this? They ask each other in the dark and don’t answer. Mark leaves it hanging, because the whole Gospel is the answer, completed when a Roman soldier says it at the cross (15:39). But their own Scriptures had already answered: there is one name in the Old Testament who stills the sea, and no second candidate (Psalm 65:7; Job 38:8–11).

Who was in the boat. The man asleep on the helmsman’s cushion, so worn out by a day’s preaching that a hurricane couldn’t wake him, is the One who said “Thus far shall you come, and no farther” to the ocean before there was a man alive to see it. Not a good teacher who happened to be useful in an emergency, but the Lord of wind and sea, tired out in the stern, having chosen to be there in a body he took so that he could sleep, thirst, bleed and die for the men bailing water round his feet.

parallels.desc: who stills the roaring of the seas

4.theology:
Why parables? Verses 11–12 are the hardest words in the chapter and they should not be softened. Matthew says Jesus speaks in parables because people do not see (Matt. 13:13); Mark says so that they may not see, lest they should turn and be forgiven. Three things resolve it. The words are a quotation of Isaiah 6:9–10, God's charge to a prophet sent to a nation that had already shut its eyes for generations — settled judgement on hardened refusal, not fresh cruelty. The so that carries fulfilment as much as bare purpose: the parables meet a people who have chosen blindness and confirm the choice, which is how God deals with those who insist (cf. Rom. 1:24). And the door is never bolted — those around him with the twelve understood nothing either, and the one thing that separated them from the crowd walking home was that they stayed and asked.

Who is in the boat? In the Old Testament, command of the sea belongs to God alone: you rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, you still them (Ps. 89:9); he made the storm be still, and the waves of the sea were hushed (Ps. 107:29); thus far shall you come, and no farther (Job 38:11). So the disciples' closing question has exactly one possible answer. And Mark holds the two natures within four feet of each other: asleep from sheer exhaustion on the helmsman's cushion, and muzzling a hurricane with a word.
4.examples:
The four soils are not four historical types but four live possibilities in any congregation on any Sunday, and the third is the one that describes most Christians in a comfortable country.

The path was not made hard by a decision; it was made hard by traffic — the same feet over the same ground until nothing could get in. That is how hearts harden in real life: not by rejecting God but by hearing about him so often that the sound becomes familiar.

The rocky ground grows fastest, and grows fastest because the soil is shallow. The heat that kills it is the same sun that ripens the harvest in the next furrow. Roots are grown in private, in the boring stretches, and the test is simple: if the trial came this year, what exactly would you be drawing on?

The thorns are not sins. Jesus names them — cares, riches, and the desires for other things. Worry, money, and the ordinary wanting of ordinary stuff. This soil cannot be diagnosed by examining your conduct, because there may be nothing in it to confess. It is diagnosed by what has quietly stopped: the praying, the reading, the conversation about Christ you have not had in a year — not refused, just crowded out.

And the good soil yields thirty, sixty, or a hundred — and all three are good soil. Jesus put thirty in the same category as a hundred. Some believers are given health and years and visible fruitfulness; some produce a marriage held together and a few names prayed for over decades in a hard place where nobody applauded. Both are in verse 20, and the barn does not sort them.

5.title: Legion, Daughter, and the Hand That Takes Hold
5.text: <sup>1</sup>They came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gerasenes. <sup>2</sup>And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit. <sup>3</sup>He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain, <sup>4</sup>for he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. No one had the strength to subdue him. <sup>5</sup>Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones. <sup>6</sup>And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. <sup>7</sup>And crying out with a loud voice, he said, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.” <sup>8</sup>For he was saying to him, “Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!” <sup>9</sup>And Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” He replied, “My name is Legion, for we are many.” <sup>10</sup>And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country. <sup>11</sup>Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, <sup>12</sup>and they begged him, saying, “Send us to the pigs; let us enter them.” <sup>13</sup>So he gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea. <sup>14</sup>The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. And people came to see what it was that had happened. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. <sup>16</sup>And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. <sup>17</sup>And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region. <sup>18</sup>As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him. <sup>19</sup>And he did not permit him but said to him, “Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.” <sup>20</sup>And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled. <sup>21</sup>And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered about him, and he was beside the sea. <sup>22</sup>Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing him, he fell at his feet <sup>23</sup>and implored him earnestly, saying, “My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live.” <sup>24</sup>And he went with him. And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him. <sup>25</sup>And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, <sup>26</sup>and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse. <sup>27</sup>She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. <sup>28</sup>For she said, “If I touch even his garments, I will be made well.” <sup>29</sup>And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease. <sup>30</sup>And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned about in the crowd and said, “Who touched my garments?” <sup>31</sup>And his disciples said to him, “You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, ‘Who touched me?’” <sup>32</sup>And he looked around to see who had done it. <sup>33</sup>But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. <sup>34</sup>And he said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.” <sup>35</sup>While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler’s house some who said, “Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?” <sup>36</sup>But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, “Do not fear, only believe.” <sup>37</sup>And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John the brother of James. <sup>38</sup>They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly. <sup>39</sup>And when he had entered, he said to them, “Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping.” <sup>40</sup>And they laughed at him. But he put them all outside and took the child’s father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was. <sup>41</sup>Taking her by the hand he said to her, “Talitha cumi,” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, arise.” <sup>42</sup>And immediately the girl got up and began walking (for she was twelve years of age), and they were immediately overcome with amazement. <sup>43</sup>And he strictly charged them that no one should know this, and told them to give her something to eat.
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is three impossible cases in a row, and the arrangement is deliberate. A man no one could restrain, a woman no one could cure, and a child who has already died — the whole range of human helplessness, met in one day and a boat ride.

It is also a chapter about uncleanness, and a modern reader misses most of it without knowing that. Under the Law three things defiled by contact: a grave, a discharge of blood, and a pig. Mark has put all three in one chapter. Jesus lands in a graveyard among pigs to save a man who lives in the tombs; an untouchable woman takes hold of his clothes in a crowd; and he ends the day taking a corpse by the hand. Every one of those contacts should have made him unclean under the system he himself gave. Every one of them runs the other way instead.

The two halves are held together by twelve years — the length of the woman's suffering and the whole life of Jairus's daughter — and by one word. The father calls the girl his little daughter; Jesus calls the destitute, unclean woman in the street Daughter, the only time in the Gospels he addresses a woman that way. The chapter opens with a man nobody could chain and closes with a girl being handed something to eat.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The landing (vv. 1–5). The storm of chapter 4 was crossed to reach this beach, and the welcoming party is one man out of the tombs — chained, unchainable, screaming night and day, cutting himself with stones. Mark spends five verses establishing that this case is beyond every remedy human beings had.

The encounter (vv. 6–10). He runs and falls at Jesus's feet, and the voice that comes out of him tries to put Jesus under oath. Asked its name, it answers with the word for a Roman army: Legion.

The pigs (vv. 11–13). The demons beg to be sent into a herd, and are permitted — and the herd goes over the cliff. What they intended for the man is acted out on the hillside for everyone to see.

The town's verdict (vv. 14–17). The neighbours arrive, find the man dressed and talking sense, and are frightened. They do not ask Jesus to stay and do more. They ask him to leave, and he goes.

The commission (vv. 18–20). The one man who wants to come is told no — and given a district instead of a boat. He becomes the first missionary to the Gentiles, and his whole training was what had happened to him.
verseByVerse.theology:
This chapter turns on ceremonial uncleanness, and a modern reader misses most of its force without knowing that. Under the Law, three things made a person unclean by contact: a corpse or a grave (Num. 19:11–16), a discharge of blood (Lev. 15:25–27), and a pig (Lev. 11:7). Mark has put all three in one chapter, and the man in this scene is standing in all of them at once — living among tombs, on a hillside where pigs are grazing, in Gentile country.

The whole logic of the purity system ran one way: uncleanness is contagious and holiness is not. Touch a corpse and you are defiled; the corpse does not become clean. Which is why what happens next in this chapter is so startling. A woman whose bleeding has made her untouchable for twelve years puts her hand on Jesus, and she is healed rather than he defiled. He takes a dead girl by the hand, and she gets up. The current runs backwards.

That is not Jesus ignoring the Law. It is the Law's purpose arriving. The system taught Israel for centuries that sin and death spread and cleanness does not — so that when a man walked into Israel whose holiness was catching, they would know exactly what they were looking at. He is the one clean thing in the world that cannot be contaminated, and everything he touches is what changes.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a Gentile town given a neighbour back — sane, dressed, sitting down — and a hillside of dead livestock, and it grieves the livestock and asks the Healer to go.

Now: the same trade is still on offer, and it is not usually made by wicked people. It is made by people who have counted the cost of Christ disrupting an arrangement that works — the business practice, the relationship, the private habit, the plans — and quietly concluded they would rather keep the pigs. Nobody in that town denied the miracle. They simply decided it was too expensive.

And note what he does when they ask. He does not argue, and he does not stay. He gets into the boat. That is one of the most sobering sentences in the Gospel: Jesus goes where he is asked to go, including away.

But he does not leave them without a witness. The man they had chained and could not hold is left behind in the district with nothing to offer but what had been done to him — and by chapter 7 the crowds on that side of the lake will come out to meet Jesus. One restored man, telling one town, and the ground was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: They came to the other side of the sea, to the country of the Gerasenes. And when Jesus had stepped out of the boat, immediately there met him out of the tombs a man with an unclean spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus crosses into the Gentile country of the Gerasenes, and as he steps out of the boat a man with an unclean spirit comes at him from the tombs. Jesus went through a storm and into pagan territory for one man everyone had given up on — and he goes there to confront evil head-on.

The crossing was for him. The last chapter ended with a hurricane and a filling boat, and this is the shore they were crossing to. Jesus said, “Let us go across,” and the other side held one person who needed him. If the price was a night that nearly killed twelve sailors, he paid it — for a man his own town had abandoned.

Gentile ground. The Decapolis region, ten Greek cities east and south of the lake: pagan territory with pig farms on the hills. The first time in this Gospel Jesus leaves Jewish land, and he goes to fight.

Gerasa, Gadara or Gergesa? A reader with a map will notice: Gerasa was some thirty miles from the lake, too far for a herd to run into the sea. Matthew names the Gadarenes (Gadara, about six miles off); some manuscripts read Gergesenes. The likeliest answer is that Gergesa — modern Kursi, right on the eastern shore where the hills drop steeply to the water — is the spot, and Gerasa and Gadara were the well-known cities whose districts reached down to it. Each writer named the region by the city his readers knew, as one might say a village lies in greater London. The steep bank is still there.

One man or two? Matthew says two men (Matthew 8:28); Mark and Luke tell of one. No contradiction: Mark and Luke follow the one who spoke, begged to go with Jesus, and was sent home to tell his story; neither says there was only one.

Living among the dead. “Immediately” — one foot on the beach and the man is coming down at them out of the rocks. The limestone hills there are full of cave tombs, some big enough to stand in. That is his address. And “unclean”: a grave defiled anyone near it for seven days (Numbers 19:16). He lives inside permanent uncleanness — outside the town, worship, and every category people use to order the living — and the town knows it and no one has come to get him.

Does demon possession happen today? The New Testament treats it as real, and nothing says it ended with the apostles; missionaries in places of open idolatry have often met things they could only describe this way. But Scripture also distinguishes the possessed from the sick (1:32–34), and most suffering of mind and body has ordinary causes and needs ordinary care. Two errors are to be avoided: seeing demons behind every illness, and denying that the devil works at all. A Christian, indwelt by the Spirit, cannot be possessed; and what drives out evil is not a technique but Christ, sought in prayer and in his word.

Who is stronger? On one side of the beach, a man from the tombs, unclean, unreachable, owned by something that hates him; on the other, a man stepping out of a boat, wet through, who has just slept through a hurricane. The next twenty verses answer which is stronger. A test: who is the person you have quietly written off as beyond reach? Jesus crossed a storm for such a man.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Gergesenes, some Gadarenes. The region lay on the east side of the lake, Gentile country. Tombs were unclean places.

verseByVerse.quote: He lived among the tombs. And no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain, for he had often been bound with shackles and chains, but he wrenched the chains apart, and he broke the shackles in pieces. No one had the strength to subdue him. Night and day among the tombs and on the mountains he was always crying out and cutting himself with stones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man lives among the tombs; no chains could hold him, no one could subdue him, and night and day he screams and cuts himself with stones. The man is utterly beyond human help, and the evil in him aims at his destruction — the kind of person Jesus deliberately came to find.

Past help. Three verses of description before a word is spoken, every clause establishing that this man was past help. He “lived among the tombs” — not hid there occasionally; the dead were his company.

No one anymore. “No one could bind him anymore.” They had tried, repeatedly; there had been a time when the town still attempted something, and it had stopped. Chains torn apart, shackles smashed — Mark, who has this from Peter, describes it like physical evidence. “No one had the strength to subdue him” — the word for taming an animal. They had come to trying to tame a man, and failed at that too. Restraint failed, confinement failed; he was written off, for years.

Screaming night and day. Not a fit that came and went; night and day on the hills, where the sound carried down. The district went to sleep hearing him.

Cutting himself. This lands hardest on a modern reader and must be handled gently, because many know exactly what it describes. First, what it shows about the power in him: everything the demons do aims at his destruction. They have taken him out of home, town, company, clothing and his own mind, and now use his own hands against his own body. That is the enemy’s settled programme wherever given room: not pleasure or power but ruin, worked where possible through the victim’s own hands. The pigs will act it out for all to see (v. 13).

If you hurt yourself, or love someone who does. Take the whole of this carefully. The verse isn’t here to give you a diagnosis, and it would be wrong to read every case of self-harm as possession; Scripture plainly distinguishes the demonised from the ill (1:32–34), and pain, shame and illness explain most of what people do to themselves. Go to a doctor; that is an ordinary mercy from God, not a failure of faith. What the passage does tell you is the direction the story runs. The man whom no one could hold or help is soon sitting quietly, dressed, talking, in his right mind, with the marks of the stones still on his arms. And the One who restored him didn’t flinch at meeting him at his worst — screaming, bleeding, out of control, in a graveyard (cf. Isaiah 65:4). He came to that beach on purpose. Bring the worst to him; he isn’t repelled by it.

parallels.desc: who sit in tombs, who eat pig’s flesh

verseByVerse.quote: And when he saw Jesus from afar, he ran and fell down before him. And crying out with a loud voice, he said, "What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing Jesus from afar, the man runs and falls before him, and the demon cries out, “What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me.” Evil knows exactly who Jesus is and that it is defeated; correct words about him without love are worthless, and the demons can only plead.

He ran. Across broken ground, from a distance, to get to Jesus — then down on his face. Who did the running? Mark doesn’t say, and probably it can’t be separated: a man who has wanted help for years and never reached it, and a power that must come because it can do nothing else before the Son of God. Both arrive at the same feet. The posture is worship, though not willing — a rehearsal of the day when “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10).

Flawless theology, no good. “Son of the Most High God” — “God Most High” is a name for God often on Gentile lips in the Old Testament, Melchizedek’s name for him (Genesis 14:18–20) and Nebuchadnezzar’s. On the pagan side of the lake even the demons use the local vocabulary, correctly. And it does them no good (cf. James 2:19). You can have the doctrine right, use the right name, take the right posture, and be no nearer salvation. The difference between this cry and a Christian’s isn’t accuracy; this one means “keep away from me.” A test: when you speak rightly about Jesus, do you mean “come near” or “keep away”?

A demon attempting exorcism. “I adjure you by God” — to put someone under oath was the professional exorcist’s standard technique: name a higher power and bind the spirit by it. So the demon tries the exorcist’s own tools on the Exorcist, invoking God to stop the Son of God — the last resort of something that understood in three seconds it was completely outmatched. It doesn’t work for a moment.

Before the time. “Do not torment me.” Matthew gives the full sentence: “Have you come here to torment us before the time?” (Matthew 8:29). They know there is a time, what is fixed for them, and who fixed it; their only argument is about the schedule. The kingdom of darkness here isn’t confidently opposing Christ. It is a defeated thing negotiating for a delay.

If evil frightens you. No shame in that. But notice who is on the ground and who is standing. The demons in Mark are never once calm before Jesus. They shout, beg, bargain and go. He hasn’t yet had to raise his voice.
verseByVerse.note: “Most High God” is a title often used by or to Gentiles.

parallels.desc: even the demons believe — and shudder

verseByVerse.quote: For he was saying to him, "Come out of the man, you unclean spirit!" And Jesus asked him, "What is your name?" He replied, "My name is Legion, for we are many." And he begged him earnestly not to send them out of the country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus has commanded the unclean spirit to come out; he asks its name, and it answers “Legion, for we are many,” begging not to be sent out of the country. Jesus has absolute authority over even the most overwhelming evil, and he exposes and names what has been destroying a person before freeing him.

A command already given. Mark steps back to tell us what was already happening: the exchange of v. 7 answered a command Jesus had given — “Come out of the man.” The screaming and bargaining are what a thing does on its way out. No ritual, formula, or higher name invoked — exactly what every ancient exorcist needed and what the demon had just tried on him. Jesus doesn’t appeal to an authority. He is one.

Why ask its name? The only time in the Gospels Jesus asks a demon its name, and he doesn’t need the information. Two things are being done. For the man: everything done to him happened in the dark, unnamed, for years. The thing that owned him is made to identify itself aloud, before witnesses, before it is thrown out. What was destroying you is made to say what it is. And for the record: Mark wants readers to grasp the scale, and only the enemy can supply the figure.

Legion. The word lands like a boot. A legion was a Roman unit of several thousand soldiers — not a metaphor in that district but what had marched up their road. A legion arrives, occupies, stays; it can’t be resisted or negotiated with. That is the word these spirits choose, and it describes what they had done to this man: moved in, taken possession, held territory. And it explains why nothing worked. The town had been trying to chain a man. The man was a garrison.

Two occupations. Mark sets them side by side: the one everyone could see — soldiers on the road, taxes to Caesar — and the one no one could do anything about. Jesus walks up the beach and evicts the second with a sentence; he will deal with the first in his own way and at his own cost, when Rome nails him to a post outside Jerusalem and finds it can’t hold him either.

Begging. The strongest power in the district reduced to asking, as again in v. 12; Luke says they feared being sent “into the abyss” (Luke 8:31). As the man on the ground heard it: he had been held by thousands, he was worth a storm and a crossing to the One who came for him, and the thousands spent the whole conversation pleading. A test: what in your life feels like an occupying army? It is no match for him; bring it to him by name.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman legion numbered several thousand soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a great herd of pigs was feeding there on the hillside, and they begged him, saying, "Send us to the pigs; let us enter them." So he gave them permission. And the unclean spirits came out and entered the pigs; and the herd, numbering about two thousand, rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The demons beg to be sent into a herd of pigs; Jesus permits it, and about two thousand pigs rush down the steep bank and drown. Evil’s aim is always destruction, shown here for all to see; and one person restored is worth more than any amount of property.

Somebody’s livelihood. No Jewish district would keep two thousand pigs, unclean under the law (Leviticus 11:7). This is Gentile country, and the pigs are someone’s business.

Permission. “Send us to the pigs.” Begging again. The Legion can go nowhere and do nothing without permission — which tells you how much of what happens in this world is unsupervised: nothing. “So he gave them permission” — five words that raise the chapter’s hard questions. Two thousand animals over a cliff, and a reader who cares about justice and a ruined business may ask what this was for. Three things answer it without pretending the loss didn’t happen.

The demons did it. He permitted; they drove the herd. And in permitting, he let their intention show itself in the open. For five verses we have been told what they did to a man — tombs, chains, screaming, stones. Now the district watches what that programme looks like unhindered: everything it enters goes straight over the edge and into the water. The pigs are the man’s story acted out in seconds on a hillside, so no one has to take Mark’s word for it.

Heaven’s arithmetic. One tormented man restored — mind, clothes, family, town — and sent out as a herald of mercy is worth more than any number of animals. “Of how much more value is a man than a sheep!” (Matthew 12:12) — and than a pig. God’s care for animals is real: he feeds the ravens, counts the sparrows, and the righteous have regard for their beasts (Proverbs 12:10). But set against each other, there is no contest.

The town’s reaction settles it. Offered a neighbour raised from a living death and a hillside of dead livestock, they will grieve the livestock and ask the Healer to leave (v. 17).

A test. The question isn’t about pigs. Some would still rather keep their herd than lose their sins. The cost of Christ is always visible and countable — the money, the relationship, the ambition, the private arrangement that works. What he gives is a person in his right mind, which never appears in the accounts until later. The town did the sum on the day and came out against him. How often have you done the same sum, over something far less than two thousand pigs?
verseByVerse.note: Pigs were unclean animals under the law; a herd of two thousand shows this was Gentile country.

verseByVerse.quote: The herdsmen fled and told it in the city and in the country. And people came to see what it was that had happened. And they came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man, the one who had had the legion, sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The herdsmen spread the news, the people come out, and they find the formerly possessed man sitting, clothed and in his right mind — and they are afraid. Christ can completely and instantly restore a person everyone had given up on, but encountering such power can frighten people rather than draw them.

The news spreads. Of course the herdsmen ran; two thousand animals lay at the bottom of a cliff. They told it in town and country, and within the hour the whole district knew and came out.

His old name. They “saw the demon-possessed man” — still his name in that town; the only way anyone knew to refer to him.

Three lovely details. “Sitting there” — the one people skip. He hasn’t sat down in years; whatever was in him never let him be still. Now he sits quietly in the middle of the town, “at the feet of Jesus,” Luke adds (Luke 8:35), the posture of a disciple. “Clothed” — he had been naked; someone has given him a garment, and his dignity returns with his mind. “In his right mind” — one word, meaning sound-minded, self-possessed. He is here; he can hold a conversation, hear his own thoughts for the first time in years.

No process. No gradual rehabilitation or years of careful work. He came down from the rocks screaming and is sitting on the ground in a borrowed coat, listening. That is what Christ does with a case everyone else has closed.

For those praying for the unreachable. The addict, the person not in their right mind, the family member no one knows how to help: this town had concluded nothing could be done. They were right about their own resources and wrong about the possibilities, and the difference arrived by boat. Keep praying.

Afraid. The turn no one expects: not relieved or delighted for him, but afraid — the fear that filled the boat after the storm (4:41), fear of a power you can’t classify or control. Awe before God isn’t wicked in itself. What this town does with it next is another matter.

verseByVerse.quote: And those who had seen it described to them what had happened to the demon-possessed man and to the pigs. And they began to beg Jesus to depart from their region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the eyewitnesses tell what happened to the man and the pigs, the people beg Jesus to leave their region. People can know the facts about Jesus and still reject him because he costs too much — and he will not force himself on those who send him away.

The man and the pigs. The eyewitnesses report both items in one account, and the town weighs them up.

The third begging. The demons begged not to be sent away, then to go into the pigs; now the people beg for what the demons wanted — for Jesus to go somewhere else. One of the most sobering verses in the Gospel. No one disputes what happened or calls it a trick. They have facts, eyewitnesses, and their neighbour in his right mind before them. Their considered, unanimous request is that the man who did it get back in his boat.

Why? Mark doesn’t say, and needn’t. They had watched a hillside of assets go into the water and understood something many admirers of Jesus never grasp: he isn’t safe, and he doesn’t stay within the budget. A man who could do that to a herd might do it to anything. Better the misery you have priced than the mercy you can’t. So they chose the graveyard they knew — and the choice isn’t exotic. It is the most ordinary transaction in the world.

A test. What in your life is currently more expensive to lose than Christ is to have? Not in theory — in fact: the relationship he wouldn’t sanction, how you make your money, the evening habit, the ten-year plan never put in his hands. Everyone has an answer, and the test is what you do when he walks up the beach and touches it.

He goes. The most frightening thing here, stated without comment: “as he was getting into the boat.” No argument or second attempt, no sermon on the shore about what they threw away. They asked him to leave, and he left. He doesn’t force himself on a town that has counted the cost and declined. “Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone” (Hosea 4:17) — the most terrifying kind of answered prayer.

But not without a witness. Don’t close the account there, because he doesn’t. He leaves the district the one thing it can’t chain, cut or drive away: a man with a story.

verseByVerse.quote: As he was getting into the boat, the man who had been possessed with demons begged him that he might be with him. And he did not permit him but said to him, "Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you." And he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis how much Jesus had done for him, and everyone marveled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Jesus leaves, the healed man begs to go with him, but Jesus sends him home to tell his friends how much the Lord has done for him and how he has had mercy on him; he proclaims throughout the Decapolis what Jesus had done. Sometimes Christ’s no to our best request is a commission, and every believer, however new, can tell what Jesus has done for them.

To be with him. The fourth and last begging, and a prayer any Christian recognises: he wants to go with Jesus. “That he might be with him” is the exact phrase of the Twelve’s appointing — “so that they might be with him” (3:14). He asks to be a disciple in the strictest sense: the best request in the chapter, from the only person on that beach who has understood anything.

No. “He did not permit him.” One of Mark’s hardest sentences: he permitted the demons; he didn’t permit the man. The finest prayer on that shore, asking for nothing but Jesus himself, was answered no. If you have prayed the best prayer you know and been refused, you are in good company. Paul asked three times for his thorn to go and was told no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Jesus asked in the garden that the cup pass, and it didn’t (14:36). A no from Christ isn’t a sign you asked badly or he stopped caring. Sometimes it is a redeployment.

Why is this man told to tell, when others are told to keep silent? Others were told to say nothing (1:44; 5:43). But he lived in Gentile country, where there was no crowd waiting for a Jewish Messiah to lead a revolt and where Jesus wouldn’t be staying. The danger that made silence wise in Galilee didn’t apply. And he was to tell what the Lord had done for him, not to proclaim a title.

Home, the hardest field. Not a place in the boat but a district; not nearness but a commission. Home, to the town that chained him, the neighbours who heard him screaming for years and did nothing, the family that gave up. The hardest mission field on earth: people who knew you before and can’t be impressed by a stranger’s testimony because they were there — which is exactly why they can’t argue with it. A test: who at home needs to hear what Christ has done for you?

One qualification. No theological education, no years with Jesus, no Scriptures at hand — only what happened to him: “how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.” If you think you aren’t equipped to say anything about Christ, this man is the answer, and he had been out of his mind that morning.

The Lord is Jesus. Catch what he did with his instructions. Jesus said, tell what the Lord has done. He went and told “how much Jesus had done for him.” He made the substitution himself, a Christian of ten minutes in a pagan district — and had already grasped that the man on the beach and the Lord God of Israel weren’t two subjects. His first sermon was better than the disciples’ theology.

Ten cities. “Everyone marveled.” When Jesus returns to the Decapolis (7:31), crowds come and bring him their sick. The town that begged him to leave got him back, because the man they couldn’t chain wouldn’t stop talking.
verseByVerse.note: The Decapolis was a league of about ten Greek cities, mostly east of the Jordan.

parallels.desc: Jesus later returns to the Decapolis

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–43 — Jairus’s Daughter and the Woman with the Bleeding
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The father (vv. 21–24). A synagogue ruler — a man of standing, from the very institution that has been building a case against Jesus — comes through the crowd and goes down on his face. His twelve-year-old is dying. Jesus goes with him, and there is not one word of negotiation.

The interruption (vv. 25–34). On the way, a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years, ruined by doctors' fees, ceremonially untouchable, gets close enough to take hold of his clothes from behind. She is healed instantly — and then Jesus stops the entire procession to find her. Jairus stands and watches while his daughter dies.

The news (vv. 35–36). Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further? — and Jesus overhears the sentence and speaks over the top of it: Do not fear, only believe.

The house (vv. 37–43). Professional mourners in full cry, and a man who says the child is sleeping, and a room that laughs at him. He puts them all out, takes a dead girl by the hand, and says two words in the language a mother would have used.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mark has interleaved these two stories deliberately — his habitual sandwich — and the links are not decoration. Both turn on twelve years: the girl's whole life, and the length of the woman's suffering. The year that family received a daughter is the year this woman's life began to come apart. Both are called daughter — the one by her father, the other by Jesus. Both are healed by touch: she takes hold of his garment, he takes hold of her hand. And the same Greek verb, sōzō, runs through both — made well, and saved, are the same word.

Set side by side, they say one thing between them. The woman had exhausted every human resource over twelve years; the father had run out of time in an afternoon. Slow ruin and sudden catastrophe, and the same answer to both.

And the interruption is the point of the arrangement. From where Jairus is standing, the delay is fatal — Jesus stops to talk to a woman who is already healed, and while he talks, a child dies. But the delay is what Jairus is given to watch. He hears a desperate woman told your faith has made you well before he hears the words your daughter is dead. God's delays are not always the absence of an answer. Sometimes they are the school in which faith is taught the thing it is about to need.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a woman who had tried everything else and everyone else, coming from behind, in a crowd, hoping to take what she needed without being seen.

Now: everybody who comes to Christ as a last resort, after the money, the specialists and the years have all run out — and finds that the last resort was the first and only real one all along. She had no right to be in that crowd and she knew it; her condition made her contagious under the Law, and every person she brushed against on the way through was defiled by her. She came anyway.

And notice that Jesus was not content to heal her anonymously. He stopped everything, in public, and drew her out — not to shame her, since she had done nothing wrong, but because he wanted more for her than a cure. She got a conversation, a word about her faith, a blessing of peace, and a name: Daughter, the only time in the Gospels he calls a woman that. She came for a healing and went away with a relationship. He always gives more than was asked, and it is never the part you were focused on.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus had crossed again in the boat to the other side, a great crowd gathered about him, and he was beside the sea. Then came one of the rulers of the synagogue, Jairus by name, and seeing him, he fell at his feet and implored him earnestly, saying, "My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay your hands on her, so that she may be made well and live." And he went with him. And a great crowd followed him and thronged about him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Back across the lake, Jairus, a synagogue ruler, falls at Jesus’ feet begging him to come and lay hands on his dying little daughter, and Jesus goes with him at once. Desperate need humbles even the respectable, and Jesus responds immediately to faith, though often more largely than we ask.

A man who shouldn’t be there. Back on the Jewish shore, a crowd waiting. Mark names Jairus, which he rarely does, probably because he was known in the church afterward — someone people could go and ask.

The establishment. A synagogue ruler wasn’t a preacher but the senior layman who ran it — appointed readers, kept the building, held the town’s respect. And the establishment has already met to plan Jesus’ destruction (3:6), and Jerusalem scribes have declared him possessed (3:22). Every professional instinct and social pressure in his life points away from this beach.

On his face. “He fell at his feet” — before everyone, a dignitary in the sand before a preacher his colleagues had written off. Desperation stripped his standing, and he didn’t try to hold on to it. That is what a dying child does: burns away everything you worried about the week before. And there is a hidden mercy in it — the grief destroying him got him to the only place where help was. A test: what has your pain pushed you toward — Christ, or away?

My little daughter. A diminutive, a father’s word. She is twelve (v. 42), nearly a woman in that world and still his little girl.

A method in mind. “Come and lay your hands on her.” He assumes Jesus must be present and touch her. He will learn that isn’t the limit of it, and that the coming delay isn’t the disaster it looks. Most of us pray with the mechanism specified: this way, by this date, through this means. God isn’t offended — he didn’t correct Jairus. He simply means to answer more largely than the request was framed.

And he went. The gospel in miniature. No conditions, no questions about whether Jairus had been at the meeting in chapter 3, no lecture about coming sooner. Jesus goes where desperate faith brings him, at once.

The crowd as obstacle. They press in on all sides; a man with a dying child at home now moves at the pace of a mob through a village street. Every step is slower than it should be — and it is about to stop altogether.
verseByVerse.note: A ruler of the synagogue organised its services and cared for its building.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the crowd is a woman who has had a discharge of blood for twelve years, suffered much under many doctors, spent everything, and only grown worse. She was not only ill but excluded, impoverished and hopeless — and Mark tells her story honestly for everyone who has tried everything and grown worse.

The clock stops. Like a novelist, Mark freezes the journey and turns the camera elsewhere, leaving a man with a dying daughter standing in the street.

Twelve years. Built in deliberately: Jairus’s daughter is twelve (v. 42). The year that family received a child was the year this woman’s life began to fall apart. One household counting birthdays; another woman counting the same years and losing everything.

More than a medical problem. Under the law, a woman with chronic bleeding was ceremonially unclean as long as it lasted (Leviticus 15:25–27), and the uncleanness spread: anything she sat on, anyone who touched her bed. In practice she couldn’t enter the temple courts or worship with the congregation, couldn’t be touched without defiling the other person, and if married, twelve years had almost certainly ended the marriage. Twelve years untouched: no embrace, no hand on the shoulder, no worship, no place at anyone’s table. Whatever the bleeding did to her body, the loneliness did worse.

Suffered under doctors. Mark’s word is strong. Ancient remedies for this were degrading and often painful; the Talmud preserves a list, including carrying the ash of an ostrich egg in a linen rag and drinking wine mixed with gum and alum. Twelve years of that, each new man with a new theory. Luke the doctor tells the same history and can’t quite phrase it so bluntly (Luke 8:43).

Everything spent. Whatever she had is gone. Not just ill but destitute, in the way that leaves a person feeling foolish — she paid for it all herself, one hopeful appointment at a time.

Worse. “No better but rather grew worse.” Not merely that nothing worked, but that twelve years of effort, money, hope and humiliation left her further down than she started. If you have a chronic illness or a chronic anything — a marriage every attempt has made colder, a child who has moved further away with each intervention, a besetting sin you have fought with every weapon and are visibly losing to — this verse is in your Bible on purpose. Mark takes two verses to say she had tried everything and was worse, and doesn’t hurry past it. Then he tells you what she heard. A test: have you brought your long, unresolved trouble to Christ, or only to every other help?
verseByVerse.note: A woman with a flow of blood was ritually unclean and made others unclean by touch; twelve years meant twelve years of exclusion.

parallels.desc: a woman with a discharge of blood

verseByVerse.quote: She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. For she said, "If I touch even his garments, I will be made well." And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having heard about Jesus, the woman comes up behind him in the crowd and touches his garment, believing she will be made well; at once her bleeding stops and she feels herself healed. Even small, fearful, muddled faith that reaches out to Christ receives his power — and his holiness, unlike our uncleanness, is what spreads.

She had heard. That is all she has — not a meeting or a personal promise, just what people are saying, taken seriously enough to act on. Faith often begins no more than this: “faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17).

From behind. She can’t come face on. To approach openly would mean explaining in a crowded street what was wrong with her, and admitting she had no business in that crowd. That is the real risk, not embarrassment: under Leviticus 15 her uncleanness passed by contact. Everyone she pushed past was defiled, unknowing. If recognised, it would be a riot. She came anyway. Think what twelve years of being untouchable does to a person, then think what it took to walk into a crowd.

The fringe. Matthew and Luke specify the fringe, the tassel every Jewish man wore at the corner of his cloak to remember God’s commandments (Numbers 15:38–39). The furthest, lowest, trailing edge of him; she doesn’t reach for his hand.

Muddled faith, not refused. “If I touch even his garments, I will be made well.” We hear her talk herself into it, and her theology is imperfect, almost superstitious, as though the power were in the cloth. Jesus doesn’t correct that, and never in this Gospel refuses someone for a poor grasp of how it works. What saved her wasn’t the accuracy of her understanding. It was that she put out her hand. A test: are you waiting to understand everything before you reach for him?

The current ran backwards. “Immediately the flow of blood dried up” — twelve years, stopped mid-street. And every law of uncleanness ran one way: the unclean contaminates the clean, never the reverse. Touch a corpse and you are defiled; the corpse isn’t raised. So it had worked for fifteen centuries. By every rule she was taught, she should have made him unclean. Instead she was made clean. The contagion went backwards. That isn’t Jesus breaking the law but its purpose arriving: Israel had been taught for centuries that sin and death spread and holiness doesn’t, so that when a man came whose holiness was catching, they would know what they were looking at.

She felt it. “She felt in her body that she was healed.” Twelve years, and she felt it stop.

parallels.desc: touching the fringe of his garment

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him, immediately turned about in the crowd and said, "Who touched my garments?" And his disciples said to him, "You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, 'Who touched me?'" And he looked around to see who had done it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus, aware that power has gone out from him, turns and asks, “Who touched my garments?”; his disciples point out that the whole crowd is pressing on him, but he keeps looking for the one who did it. Healing is personal and costly to Christ, and many brush against him while only faith truly takes hold of him — and he wants to meet that person face to face.

Not leaked power. “Perceiving in himself that power had gone out from him” could be read as though healing were a charge that leaked out unawares. Two things rule that out. He asks the question at all and “looked around to see who had done it”; a power simply draining away wouldn’t go looking for anyone. And he will say, “your faith has made you well,” not “my cloak has.” It wasn’t mechanical or a transaction completed without him noticing; it was personal from both ends. Mark describes its cost: something went out of him. God in the flesh, and the giving isn’t free even to him — which is why, at the end, the giving will take everything (cf. Luke 6:19).

Did Jesus not know who had touched him? His question wasn’t for his own information but to draw her out, as God asked Adam, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). Even so, Mark doesn’t hide that in his earthly life the Son accepted real human limits; he says the day of his return is known only to the Father (13:32). He is fully God and truly man, and he wanted her face to face.

Pressing versus taking hold. The disciples are exasperated: “You see the crowd pressing around you, and yet you say, ‘Who touched me?’” Fair enough — everyone in that street had touched him. But they missed the distinction the Gospel turns on. The crowd pressed against him; one woman took hold of him. Contact isn’t faith. Hundreds of hands were on Jesus that afternoon and exactly one received anything.

A test. It is possible to spend a lifetime in the press — in the building, the congregation, the family, brushing against him week after week — and never reach for him on your own account. The jostlers went home as they came; the woman went home well. Have you ever actually taken hold of him for yourself?

He won’t leave it anonymous. She had what she came for; she could have slipped away cured, and no one would know. To her, being found out was the worst thing that could happen. Jesus refuses to leave it there — and is willing to hold up a dying child’s rescue to do so. He has something for her she didn’t think to ask for, worth the delay.

verseByVerse.quote: But the woman, knowing what had happened to her, came in fear and trembling and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. And he said to her, "Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trembling, the woman comes, falls before him, and tells him the whole truth; Jesus says, “Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.” Christ wants not just to heal us secretly but to receive us openly; he welcomes the outcast into his family and gives lasting wholeness to those who come to him.

Fear and trembling. She could have stayed silent; the crowd was huge, the question unanswerable, the disciples had all but told him to drop it. She came forward, shaking, expecting to be exposed as the woman who had made half the street unclean and rebuked for taking what she had no right to take.

The whole truth. Not a summary: the twelve years, the doctors, the money, the marriage if there was one, why she came from behind, what she had hoped — the entire humiliating history, aloud, in a public street, to a man she had just met. That is confession, and why we avoid it: not the general admission that we are sinners, but the whole truth in particular words to the One entitled to hear it. And nothing was owed; she was already healed. He draws her out not because the cure was incomplete but because he won’t have a relationship with her that consists of her taking something from behind and running away. A test: is there something you have taken from him without ever telling him the whole truth?

Daughter. The reason he stopped the procession. The only woman Jesus addresses as “Daughter” in the Gospels. Nobody’s anything for twelve years — untouchable, unwelcome in worship, a name spoken in lowered voices — and his first word gives her a place in a family. And Jairus stands three feet away with his own daughter dying, while Jesus calls a destitute, unclean, middle-aged woman no one would look at twice by the same name.

Your faith. He locates the power rightly: not the fringe, technique, crowd or her boldness, but faith — small, frightened, muddled, reaching from behind. That is all it has ever taken. Faith saves not because it is impressive but because of whom it takes hold of.

Does this mean that enough faith guarantees healing? No. Faith is the hand that reaches; Christ is the one who heals, and he heals as he wills. Paul prayed three times for his thorn to be taken away and was told, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9), and he left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). A believer who isn’t healed hasn’t necessarily failed to believe. Faith trusts Christ whether he heals now or raises us whole at the last.

Peace and permanence. “Go in peace” — behind it the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, everything in its place, the whole person put right. She came for a body and leaves with a life. “Be healed of your disease” settles her for good. After twelve years she might have spent her life waiting for it to start again; he tells her aloud that it is over. And into the silence after that sentence, the messengers arrive from Jairus’s house.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking, there came from the ruler's house some who said, "Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?" But overhearing what they said, Jesus said to the ruler of the synagogue, "Do not fear, only believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Messengers arrive to say Jairus’s daughter is dead and there is no need to trouble the Teacher further; Jesus overhears and tells Jairus, “Do not fear, only believe.” Jesus overrides the world’s settled verdict on death and calls us to keep trusting him when things look hopeless — and his delays, though costly, are never accidents.

Merciless timing. “While he was still speaking.” The word of the woman’s peace is barely out when the men from the house arrive, and Jairus, standing through the whole delay, hears what he has dreaded for ten minutes.

The world’s philosophy of death. Two sentences, kindly meant. “Your daughter is dead” — a fact; the mourners are already at the house and will laugh at any other suggestion. “Why trouble the Teacher any further?” — the conclusion, and the sentence to look at hard. “Teacher” is their estimate of him and the reason for their advice: a teacher is fine at a sickbed and useless at a grave. Their theology isn’t hostile, just too small, and it produces the most reasonable pastoral advice in the world: stop praying about this one.

Still given gently. That advice is still given, in that tone, by people trying to be kind: the marriage is over, stop praying; he is seventy-eight and hardened, leave it; that door is closed. Always based on a true fact and an inadequate estimate of Christ. A test: what have you stopped praying for because someone kindly told you it was finished?

Did Jairus’s daughter die before or after he came to Jesus? Matthew has Jairus say at the start that his daughter “has just died” (Matthew 9:18). Matthew tells the story briefly and gives its outcome from the beginning; Mark and Luke tell it in sequence, with the messengers arriving on the way. Both are true accounts of the same event, told at different lengths.

The cost of the delay. Had Jesus not stopped for the woman, he would have reached the house in time. From where Jairus stood, the interruption killed his daughter — a stranger’s twelve-year complaint that could have waited an hour. That is one of the hardest things about how God works: his delays are real, cost real people real things, and aren’t accidents.

Speaking over it. “Overhearing what they said” — the word can mean he heard it and refused to let it stand. He doesn’t let the message settle. “Do not fear, only believe” are commands, not comfort: not “don’t worry, it will be fine,” but what to do with the next ten minutes. Stop the fear that is already running. Go on believing — keep doing what you did when you fell in the sand; nothing has changed about who I am. “Only” is the tender word: he doesn’t ask Jairus to feel confident, produce an emotion he lacks, or understand why the woman came first. Just this one thing.

What the delay was for. Jairus had just watched, at point-blank range, a hopeless twelve-year case healed by a touch, heard her called Daughter, and told to go in peace. He didn’t know it, but he was given the last lesson he would need in the ten minutes before he needed it. God’s delays aren’t always the absence of an answer. Sometimes they are the school.

verseByVerse.quote: And he allowed no one to follow him except Peter and James and John the brother of James. They came to the house of the ruler of the synagogue, and Jesus saw a commotion, people weeping and wailing loudly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus lets only Peter, James and John come with him to Jairus’s house, where he sees the loud commotion of mourning. Jesus begins training his closest disciples here, and he looks with compassion on grief rather than brushing it aside.

The crowd left behind. Whatever happens in that house won’t be a public demonstration. The great press of people that followed from the shore is left in the street.

The inner three. The first time Mark takes these three apart, not the last: they are on the mountain at the transfiguration (9:2) and taken deeper into Gethsemane (14:33). An education, and notice the syllabus. The men who will watch him in glory and in agony are first taken to watch him in a dead child’s bedroom. And one of them told the story to Mark years later, with the furniture still in it.

The commotion. An uproar — what the house sounded like from the street. Mourning there was loud, immediate and professional. Even the poorest family was expected to hire flute players and a wailing woman; a man of Jairus’s standing would have had a houseful, and Matthew mentions the flute players (Matthew 9:23). They came fast, for burial was the same day in that climate, and their job was to make grief audible. Nothing false about the family’s sorrow, nothing contemptible about the mourners; that is how a village buried its children. But it settles one thing beyond dispute: the professionals had already arrived. No one sends for the mourners while there is a pulse.

He saw it. Before he says anything, “Jesus saw a commotion.” He doesn’t push through or shout over it. He stands in the doorway of a house full of the loudest sound people make, and looks. He will stand at another grave and weep (John 11:35), knowing he is about to empty it. The knowledge that he can undo death has never made him indifferent to it. He isn’t embarrassed by grief and doesn’t hurry anyone through it — worth knowing if you are in a house like this one, or have been. A test: do you hurry grieving people along, or stand with them as he did?
verseByVerse.note: Peter, James and John were the inner three, with Jesus again at the transfiguration and in Gethsemane. Hired mourners were customary at a death.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered, he said to them, "Why are you making a commotion and weeping? The child is not dead but sleeping." And they laughed at him. But he put them all outside and took the child's father and mother and those who were with him and went in where the child was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells the mourners, “The child is not dead but sleeping,” and they laugh at him; he puts them all out and takes the parents and his three disciples in to the child. For Jesus, death is like sleep — something he will wake people from — and he brings the grieving close to see his power, though the world mocks it.

Was she really dead? This sentence has been seized on for two centuries: she was never really dead — a coma, a faint, a lucky misdiagnosis — so this is no resurrection. The reading collapses when you look. Everyone present was certain she had died: the messengers reported it as fact, and the house was full of professional mourners in full cry. Those people made their living recognising death; they laughed at Jesus precisely because they knew a corpse when they saw one. And Luke the physician says plainly what happened when Jesus spoke: “her spirit returned” (Luke 8:55).

What “sleeping” means. Not a second opinion on her pulse, but his settled way of speaking of the death of those he means to raise. Of Lazarus, four days in the tomb, he said, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep,” and when the disciples took it literally, “Lazarus has died” (John 11:11–14). Paul uses the word for Christians in the grave: “those who have fallen asleep,” and Christ “the firstfruits” of them (1 Thessalonians 4:13–14; 1 Corinthians 15:20). So it isn’t a smaller claim than resurrection but a far larger one. To the mourners death was the end of the sentence; to the One in the doorway it was as temporary as a night’s sleep, and waking this child would cost no more effort than a parent leaning over a bed in the morning. He doesn’t deny she died. He announces that death, in his presence, has become something you get up from. A test: how do you speak of believers who have died — as gone, or as asleep in Jesus?
