None of it feels like betrayal. All of it is what this verse is about.

Of him will the Son of Man also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.

And here is the answer, and it is a straight reciprocity: shame now, shame then.

Do not soften it, but do understand what it is measuring. He is not threatening people for a failure of nerve in a hard moment — the man whose preaching lies behind this sentence had failed exactly that, in a courtyard, three times, with oaths, and was forgiven on a beach and made the leader of the church. Settled shame is not the same as a moment of cowardice, and the difference is what you do afterwards.

What he is describing is a life in which he was quietly kept out of sight because the cost of being known with him was judged too high.

And now look at the picture in the last clause, because everything turns on it.

Consider who is speaking. A Galilean carpenter, standing on a road near a pagan shrine, in an occupied province, with a few dozen people around him, twelve of whom have just proved they do not understand a word. He has told them he is going to be arrested by the leadership of his own nation and executed.

And he says: when I come in the glory of my Father, with the holy angels.

That is Daniel's vision, and he has already told them he is that figure — one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, given dominion and glory and a kingdom, and all peoples serving him (Dan. 7:13–14).

So the whole question of shame is finally a question of timing. There is a case for being embarrassed by him now: he is a provincial nobody with a crucifixion in front of him, and the world's opinion of him has not improved much since. And there is a day coming when the sky opens and the Son of Man arrives in his Father's glory with the armies of heaven, and every one of the people you were afraid of is looking at him.

Nobody will be ashamed of him then. The only question is whether you were ashamed of him now, when it cost something — and whether, on that day, the one thing you want is to hear him say your name in front of the holy angels and not look away.
verseByVerse.note: “Adulterous” is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God.

8.theology:
Two feedings, not one story told twice. Jesus makes the disciples recite both with the figures (vv. 19–20): five loaves, five thousand, twelve baskets; seven loaves, four thousand, seven baskets. Twelve baskets for Israel, one for each tribe; seven for the nations, the number of fullness. And some of them have come from far away is how Scripture speaks of the Gentiles coming in (Isa. 60:4; Eph. 2:13).

Why no sign? Not because evidence is illegitimate — he had given a great deal and would give more. What he refuses is a miracle produced on demand as the price of belief, from men who have already shown what they do with the evidence they have. If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead (Luke 16:31) — which proved exactly right, since somebody did, and the men who got the report first paid soldiers to say the body was stolen (Matt. 28:12–13).

After three days. Mark's phrase (v. 31; 9:31; 10:34) against Matthew's and Luke's on the third day is not a discrepancy but the Jewish reckoning, in which any part of a day counts as a day. Scripture settles it: the chief priests recall this prediction as After three days I will rise and in the same breath ask Pilate for a guard until the third day (Matt. 27:63–64).

Get behind me, Satan. Not a verdict on Peter — Jesus takes him up the mountain in the next chapter and restores him on a beach at the end. It names the source of the objection. This shall never happen to you (Matt. 16:22) is a kingdom without a cross, which is the wilderness offer (1:13) returning through the mouth of a friend, and it will come a third time from passers-by at the foot of the cross — save yourself, and come down (15:30).
8.examples:
Then: a crowd in Galilee hearing take up his cross in a country where the governor Varus had crucified two thousand men within living memory. Nobody heard a metaphor. They had watched condemned men carry the crossbeam out through the streets, stripped and jeered at, walking in one direction only.

Now: we have worn the phrase smooth and made a cross into a difficulty — a hard marriage, an illness, a colleague. That is not what it meant. A man carrying a cross was not a man with a burden; he was a man already condemned, publicly, on his way out of his own life.

And deny himself is the verb used of Peter in the courtyard: I do not know the man, he is nothing to do with me. That is what you are asked to say about yourself — not self-hatred, and not going without sugar, but the removal of the self from the throne, so that what do I want? stops being the question that decides. Name the specific matter this week where that is in play. If you cannot name one, the denial is theoretical.

And the third word is what keeps this from being grim heroism: follow me. You are not asked to carry a cross into the dark alone. You are asked to walk behind somebody whose back you can see, who is going first, and who within months will carry an actual beam up an actual road.

One more, from v. 38. He does not say whoever denies me — he says ashamed, which is not a decision or a moment but a temperature. Very few Christians in a comfortable country face a moment of denial. What we face is a thousand small pressures toward silence, each with a respectable name: the sentence not said when the conversation turned, the qualifying phrase offered up to buy distance (I'm not one of those Christians), the belief not mentioned to a colleague in four years. None of it feels like betrayal. All of it is what the verse is about.

9.title: Glory on the Mountain, Failure in the Valley

And he was transfigured before them, <sup>3</sup>and his clothes became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them. <sup>4</sup>And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus. <sup>5</sup>And Peter said to Jesus, “Rabbi, it is good that we are here. It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. <sup>45</sup>And if your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, <sup>48</sup>‘where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.’ <sup>49</sup>For everyone will be salted with fire. <sup>50</sup>Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”
9.overview:
Mark puts the brightest and the bleakest scenes in his Gospel back to back, and the join is the point.

Six days after telling his disciples he must be killed, Jesus takes three of them up a mountain and stops holding the veil in place. Moses and Elijah stand with him and — Luke tells us — discuss his exodus, which he is about to accomplish at Jerusalem. Peter, terrified, offers to build shelters. A cloud comes down and the Father says the only thing he commands in this Gospel: listen to him. Then the light goes, and they see Jesus only.

And they walk down into a shouting crowd, an argument with the scribes, nine defeated colleagues, and a boy convulsing on the ground. The father has been watching this since the child was small, has pulled him out of fires and out of water, and has just been let down by the disciples — which is where the if you can in his prayer came from. Out of him comes the most honest sentence anybody says to Jesus in the Gospels.

The rest of the chapter is a road and a house. Jesus tells them a second time that he will be handed over and killed; they do not understand and are afraid to ask; and they fill the silence by arguing about which of them is the greatest. So he sits down, picks up a child, and redefines greatness — then warns them, in the most violent language he ever uses, about tripping up the little ones and about keeping anything that is taking them to Gehenna. The chapter ends: be at peace with one another.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — The Transfiguration and the Failure in the Valley
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The mountain (vv. 2–8). Six days after telling them he must be killed, Jesus takes three men up a high mountain and, for a few minutes, stops holding the veil in place. Moses and Elijah stand with him. Peter, terrified, starts talking. A cloud comes down, and a voice says the one thing heaven has ever commanded about him: listen to him.

The descent (vv. 9–13). Coming down, he tells them to keep it quiet until the resurrection — and they go on down the hill privately trying to work out what rising from the dead could possibly mean.

The valley (vv. 14–29). And at the bottom: a crowd, an argument, scribes pressing their advantage, nine defeated disciples, and a father whose son has been convulsing since childhood and who has just watched the professionals fail. Out of his mouth comes the most honest sentence anybody says to Jesus in the Gospels.

Mark has put the brightest and the bleakest scenes in his book back to back on purpose. The glory on the mountain is real. The failure in the valley is real. And the same Christ is in both.
verseByVerse.theology:
What actually happened on the mountain? The word is metamorphōthē — he was transformed, changed in form. And the point is not that something was added to Jesus but that something was, for a moment, no longer withheld.

Set it beside Moses. When Moses came down Sinai his face shone (Ex. 34:29–35), and he had to veil it — but that light was borrowed, reflected off a glory he had stood near, and it faded, which Paul says is exactly why he veiled it (2 Cor. 3:13). Here the light comes out from inside. His clothes go white because of what is underneath them.

So this is not a miracle done to Jesus. It is a brief withdrawal of the ordinariness he had been wearing since Bethlehem — three men allowed to see, for a few minutes, what was true of him every day they had walked beside him without noticing.

And why these two men? Moses is the Law and Elijah the Prophets; between them they are the whole Old Testament, standing on that mountain not to be admired alongside Jesus but to attend on him. Luke tells us what they were discussing: his departure — the word is exodus — which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). Moses, who led the first one out of Egypt, is talking about the greater one with the man who will lead it, and the road out runs through a cross.

Then they are gone, and Mark writes the sentence the whole scene exists for: they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: three men who had seen the glory of God on a mountaintop, walking down into a shouting crowd, a public argument, and nine colleagues who had just failed in front of everybody.

Now: the come-down is the most ordinary experience in the Christian life, and Mark has built the chapter to prepare you for it. The conference ends. The retreat finishes. The Sunday that lifted you is followed by a Monday. And what is waiting at the bottom of the hill is usually not glory but a mess — the same marriage, the same diagnosis, the same argument, the same failure.

Two things to take from how Mark has arranged this. First, the mountain is not the point. Peter wanted to build shelters and stay, and he was told to come down and listen. The vision was given so that three men could go into the valley knowing who was walking beside them.

Second, Jesus goes down. He does not stay in the light. He walks into the shouting, asks what the argument is about, and takes charge of it — and the boy he lifts up off the ground is lifted by the same hands that had shone on the mountain.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God after it has come with power.

This verse has troubled readers for centuries, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a shrug, because at first glance it looks like a promise that failed. Every person standing there has been dead for nearly two thousand years. Did Jesus say the kingdom would arrive in their lifetime, and was he wrong?

No — and the answer is largely a matter of reading the next sentence.

Mark's own arrangement points to the Transfiguration. The very next words are and after six days, and then three of the men standing there are taken up a mountain and see the Son of God in unveiled glory. Mark almost never gives precise intervals; he gives one here. Some standing here will see it — and six days later, three of them did.

Two things confirm the reading. Peter himself, writing about that mountain years later, says exactly this: we were eyewitnesses of his majesty... we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain, and he introduces it as evidence of the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Pet. 1:16–18). Peter took the Transfiguration to be a preview of the kingdom in power, and he was standing there when this promise was made.

And the wording fits: some standing here. Not all of them, not most — a few. Three went up that mountain.

Other answers have been offered by serious people, and they are not foolish. Some take it of the resurrection, some of Pentecost, some of the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. There is truth in the instinct behind all of them: the kingdom comes in power in stages, and the Transfiguration is a preview of what the resurrection accomplishes and the Spirit applies. But Mark's after six days is not decoration, and it is the strongest signal in the text.

Now take the pastoral point, because there is one and it outlasts the debate.

Think about when this promise was made. Six days earlier Jesus had told them he would be rejected, killed, and raised — and Peter had tried to talk him out of it, and been called Satan for it, and the whole company had been told to take up a cross.

Into that, he promises that some of them will see the kingdom before they die. And then, within a week, he keeps it.

That is worth holding on to when the promises of God feel like a long way off and you have been told to expect a cross. He is not vague about timing because he is unsure. He gave three exhausted, frightened men a sight of the end of the story to carry them through the middle of it — and one of them was still writing about it as an old man facing his own execution.

verseByVerse.quote: And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James and John, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, and his clothes became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And after six days. Mark rarely dates anything, and he dates this. Six days after Caesarea Philippi — six days after Peter's confession, the first plain word about the cross, and the hardest rebuke in the Gospel.

And any Jew reading it would hear a second thing. When Moses went up Sinai, the glory of the LORD dwelt on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. And on the seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud (Ex. 24:16). Six days of waiting, then the voice out of the cloud. Mark is telling you what kind of scene this is before it starts.

Jesus took with him Peter and James and John. The three again — the same three who were in the room when the little girl was raised (5:37), and the same three who will be taken further into the garden at Gethsemane (14:33).

That is the syllabus, and it is worth naming. The men chosen to see him in glory are the men chosen to see him in agony. Neither sight is complete without the other, and the Lord does not give the first without eventually requiring the second.

And led them up a high mountain by themselves. Mark does not name it. Tradition says Tabor; Hermon is nearer to Caesarea Philippi and is genuinely high, nine thousand feet, snow on it much of the year. Either way, the point is the isolation: up, and away, and alone.

And he was transfigured before them.

The word is metamorphōthē — transformed, changed in form.

And the crucial thing to grasp is that nothing was added. This is not a miracle performed on Jesus, as though heaven had turned a light on him. It is a withdrawal — for a few minutes, the ordinariness he had worn since Bethlehem stopped being held in place.

Paul uses the language of transformation for what happens to Christians: be transformed by the renewal of your mind (Rom. 12:2), and we all... are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Cor. 3:18). What broke out of him on that mountain is what is being worked into us, slowly, all our lives.

And his clothes became radiant, intensely white, as no one on earth could bleach them.

Mark reaches for the only comparison a fisherman had and admits it will not do. The word for bleaching is the technical term for the fuller's trade — the man who cleaned and whitened cloth, the best whitener anyone in that village knew. And Mark says: not like that. Nothing on earth does this.

Notice that it is the clothes he describes. Matthew adds that his face shone like the sun (Matt. 17:2); Mark keeps his eye where a frightened man's eye would go, on the garment in front of him, and tells you that the light was coming through it from underneath.

Set it beside Moses, because Mark expects you to. When Moses came down Sinai his face shone — and he had to put a veil over it (Ex. 34:29–35). But that light was borrowed. He had stood near a glory and carried some of it away, and it faded, which Paul says is exactly why he covered it (2 Cor. 3:13).

Here the veil is the flesh, and the glory is inside it.

Which means that for three men, for a few minutes, the arrangement of the incarnation was reversed. They had walked beside this man for months — eaten with him, watched him sleep in a boat, seen him tired — and the whole time, this was what was underneath.
verseByVerse.note: The mountain is unnamed; tradition says Tabor, but Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi, is also suggested. A fuller bleached and whitened cloth.

verseByVerse.quote: And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And there appeared to them Elijah with Moses, and they were talking with Jesus.

Two men, dead for centuries, standing on a mountainside in Galilee, in conversation.

Take the fact itself before the symbolism, because it is easy to move to the meaning and miss what is being said about death. Moses died on Nebo and God buried him (Deut. 34:5–6). Elijah went up in a whirlwind and did not die at all (2 Kgs. 2:11). Both of them are here, alive, recognisable, and busy. Whatever happens to the people of God when they leave this world, it is not extinction and it is not sleep in the sense of unconsciousness. They are alive to God, and they have things to discuss.

Why these two?

Moses is the Law and Elijah the Prophets — the two halves of the Hebrew Bible as any Jew would name them, and the pair Malachi names in his closing verses (Mal. 4:4–5). Between them they are the whole Old Testament, standing on that mountain.

And they have not come to be admired alongside Jesus. They have come to attend on him — which is exactly what Peter is about to get wrong.

There is more. Both of these men had their own mountain, and it was the same one. Moses asked to see God's glory and was hidden in a cleft of the rock on Sinai while the glory passed by (Ex. 33:18–23). Elijah, fleeing for his life, came to Horeb — the same mountain — and stood at the mouth of a cave while the LORD passed by (1 Kgs. 19:8–13). The two men in all Scripture who had asked to see the glory of God and been given a glimpse of it are standing here, on another mountain, looking straight at it.

They asked to see. Now they see, and it has a face and a name and is going to Jerusalem to die.

And they were talking with Jesus. Mark leaves the conversation unreported. Luke does not: they spoke of his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem (Luke 9:31).

The word Luke uses is exodus.

Sit with that for a moment. Moses led the first exodus — the blood on the doorposts, the sea opened, a nation walked out of slavery. And here he is, discussing the greater one with the man who will lead it, and this exodus will be accomplished not by a sea but by a cross, and the blood will not be a lamb's.

Six days ago Peter tried to talk Jesus out of the cross. Now the Law and the Prophets appear in glory and talk about nothing else.
verseByVerse.note: Moses and Elijah stand for the Law and the Prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to Jesus, "Rabbi, it is good that we are here. Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah." For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Peter said to Jesus, Rabbi, it is good that we are here.

He is not wrong about that. It is good that they are there, and there is nothing to criticise in the gladness.

But then he keeps going.

Let us make three tents, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.

The word is skēnai — booths, shelters of branches. And it is very likely he has the Feast of Tabernacles in mind, when Israel lived in leafy shelters for a week to remember the wilderness, and which the prophets had made a picture of the age to come, when God would dwell with his people at last (Zech. 14:16–19).

So Peter is thinking: this is it. The glory has come, the great ones have arrived, the age of God dwelling with men is beginning. Let us set up and stay.

Three things are wrong with it, and they are all instructive.

He wants to stay. Six days ago he heard that the Son of Man must suffer and be killed, and he objected. Now he is on a mountain full of light and his instinct is to make the moment permanent. It is the same instinct in a nicer form: anything but the road down.

He wants to build something. Faced with the unveiled glory of God, his impulse is to get busy — to organise, to construct, to be useful. There is something in a certain kind of religious temperament that cannot simply stand still and behold, and must be doing.

And he makes it three. One for you, one for Moses, one for Elijah. Equal accommodation, equal honour. It is the kindest possible mistake and it is still a mistake, and the voice from the cloud is about to correct precisely that.

It is worth noticing that Peter's error is not disbelief. He is being warm, reverent, hospitable and enthusiastic. He is also arranging the Son of God as one of three, and that is a thing people still do — Jesus placed respectfully in a line of great teachers, given his own shelter, honoured among the founders. He fits nowhere in such a row.

For he did not know what to say, for they were terrified.

And here is Mark's editorial note, and it is one of the most human sentences in the Gospel — and remember whose memory this is. Peter is the source. This is a man, thirty years later, telling the church: I had no idea what to say, so I said something.

He was terrified. He is standing in the presence of undisguised glory, and the silence was unbearable, and words came out.

Which is worth taking to heart, because it is one of our most reliable failures. In the presence of something too large — real glory, real grief, real suffering — the impulse is to fill the space. Job's friends were faultless for seven days while they said nothing, and ruined it the moment they opened their mouths. At a graveside, at a hospital bed, in the presence of God himself, the pressure to produce a sentence is enormous and it is almost always better resisted.

Be still, and know that I am God (Ps. 46:10). Peter could not be still, and Mark did not hide it.
verseByVerse.note: The tents may recall the Feast of Booths.

verseByVerse.quote: And a cloud overshadowed them, and a voice came out of the cloud, "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a cloud overshadowed them.

The cloud is not weather. Any reader of the Old Testament knows this cloud: it went before Israel in the wilderness, settled on Sinai, filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter, and came down on Solomon's temple so that the priests could not stand to minister (Ex. 40:34–35; 1 Kgs. 8:10–11). It is the visible sign that God himself has come down — what the rabbis called the Shekinah, the dwelling.

And the verb Mark uses, overshadowed, is the very word the angel used to Mary: the power of the Most High will overshadow you (Luke 1:35).

So Peter, who wanted to build three shelters, is enveloped in the real one. God does not need his branches. He has brought his own dwelling, and it has covered them.

And a voice came out of the cloud, This is my beloved Son.

The second of only two times in this Gospel that the Father speaks aloud, and the words are almost the same as the first. At the Jordan: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (1:11) — said to Jesus, in the second person, at the start.

Here it is This is — third person, addressed to the three men standing there. The same testimony, turned outward. God is telling somebody else who this is.

And consider the timing. It comes six days after the Son announced that he was going to be rejected and killed. The Father's public endorsement is given precisely at the point where the plan looks like failure — as if to say: this is the one I love, and this road he has just described is the road I sent him down.

Listen to him.

Three words, and they are the only command God the Father gives in the whole Gospel of Mark. Everything the Almighty has to say to these men, at the height of the greatest vision they will ever be given, is: listen to him.

Take the measure of that. Not build for him, which is what Peter proposed. Not feel something, which is what the moment was producing. Not stay here. Listen.

And listen to him about what? About the last thing he said, which they had refused to accept. The command is aimed at the argument at Caesarea Philippi. Peter had corrected him; heaven says, in effect, do not correct him — hear him.

There is also an echo underneath it that Moses would have recognised, since he is standing there. Moses had promised: The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among you... it is to him you shall listen (Deut. 18:15). The voice from the cloud is telling three Jewish fishermen that the promise has arrived.

Which is the plainest practical word in the chapter, and it is not complicated. Whatever else God wants from you, this is what he has said out loud: listen to his Son. Not to your instincts about what the Christian life ought to look like. Not to the version of Jesus you find manageable. To him — including the parts you would rather he had not said.

And suddenly, looking around, they no longer saw anyone with them but Jesus only.

The cloud lifts. Moses is gone. Elijah is gone. The light is gone.

And Mark writes the sentence the whole scene exists for: Jesus only.

The Law has done its work and stepped back. The Prophets have done theirs and stepped back. Everything Israel had been given for fifteen hundred years was pointing at this man, and when he is fully in view the pointers are not needed.

So the vision ends, and what is left standing on that mountain is what was there before it started and will be there after every vision any Christian ever has: an ordinary-looking man from Nazareth, who is the Son of God, and no one else — and he is enough.
verseByVerse.note: The cloud recalls the cloud of God’s presence at Sinai and over the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: it is to him you shall listen

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were coming down the mountain, he charged them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. So they kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were coming down the mountain. That is a sentence worth pausing on before its content. They came down. Peter wanted to stay; the shelters were never built; and within a paragraph the three of them are back in a shouting crowd.

Nobody lives on the mountain. The vision is given for the valley.

He charged them to tell no one what they had seen, until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.

The silence again — but this is the first time in Mark that the ban has an expiry date, and that changes it entirely.

Everything so far has been tell no one, full stop. Now it is tell no one until. The lid is coming off; there is a date; and the date is the resurrection.

Which tells you what the secret was always for. It was never permanent concealment. It was timing — the truth about him kept back until there was a cross and an empty tomb to define it, because a glorious Christ preached without a crucified one produces exactly the kind of Messiah Peter had in mind six days ago.

And it explains why they had to be silent about the mountain in particular. Imagine those three going down and telling the other nine, and the crowds, what they had seen. The movement would have become unmanageable within a week, and the story they told would have been the wrong story, because it would have had no cross in it.

So they kept the matter to themselves. They obeyed — and for once in this Gospel the disciples obey an instruction to be quiet, which nobody else in Mark manages.

Questioning what this rising from the dead might mean.

And here is a sentence that ought to reassure every slow Christian.

These are the three. They have just watched the Son of God shining, heard the voice of the Father, and seen two dead prophets alive on a mountainside — and they walk down the hill arguing quietly among themselves about what he could possibly mean by rising from the dead.

It is not that they disbelieved in resurrection as such; any Pharisee-taught Jew believed in a general resurrection at the last day. What they could not fit together was a Messiah who dies and then, individually, in the middle of history, gets up. There was no category for it. Nobody expected it. They had heard the words twice now — at Caesarea Philippi and again on this hillside — and the words would not go in.

Which is quietly one of the strongest arguments that the resurrection was not invented. Men do not fabricate a story they were manifestly not expecting, had no framework for, and did not understand when it was explained to them in advance. Mark records their bafflement without embarrassment, because it is what happened.

And take the comfort in it. You may have read a passage of Scripture many times and still not have it. That is not necessarily unbelief. Sometimes it is simply that the thing is bigger than the categories you have, and it will not fit until something happens that makes room for it. For these three, that something was an empty tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, "Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?" And he said to them, "Elijah does come first to restore all things. And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt? But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they asked him, Why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?

They have just seen Elijah. That is what prompts the question, and it is a real one.

The scribes taught it from the last page of the Old Testament: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes (Mal. 4:5). Elijah comes first, then the Day. So if Elijah has only just now appeared on a mountaintop to three men in private — where does that leave the timetable? And more sharply: if you are the Messiah, where was the forerunner?

There is probably an objection buried in the question too, of the kind the scribes were no doubt already making: you cannot be the Christ, because Elijah has not come.

Elijah does come first to restore all things. He grants the doctrine. The scribes are right about the sequence.

And how is it written of the Son of Man that he should suffer many things and be treated with contempt?

Then, in the middle of answering, he turns a question back on them — and it is the more important one.

He is asking: since you are so attentive to what is written about Elijah, what have you done with what is written about the Son of Man? Where is that in your scheme?

And it is worth asking where it is written, because he assumes they know. Isaiah 53: he was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows... he was pierced for our transgressions. Psalm 22: all who see me mock me... they have pierced my hands and feet. Psalm 118, Zechariah 12 and 13, Daniel 9.

It was all there. It had been read aloud in every synagogue in the country for centuries. And a whole nation had built a Messiah out of the conquering passages and quietly stepped over the suffering ones.

That is a permanent temptation and not an ancient one. We assemble a picture of God from the verses we like and treat the rest as background noise — the promises without the warnings, the comfort without the cost, the Jesus who accepts without the Jesus who commands. Jesus's question is the corrective, and it is uncomfortable precisely because it appeals to Scripture they already had.

But I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased, as it is written of him.

The forerunner has already been and gone, and they missed him — because he did not look like Elijah returned in fire. He looked like a man in camel's hair by a river, and he ended in a cell, and his head was carried into a banquet on a dish because a girl danced well (6:14–29).

Matthew makes the identification explicit: they did not recognize him... Then the disciples understood that he was speaking to them of John the Baptist (Matt. 17:12–13). And the angel had said it before John was born: he would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah (Luke 1:17).

Now see what Jesus has actually done with this exchange, because it is not a lesson in prophetic chronology.

He has said: the forerunner came, and they killed him. And in the same breath he has asked what is written about the Son of Man suffering and being treated with contempt.

The pattern of the herald is the pattern of the King. They did to John whatever they pleased; they will do to me whatever they please. He is walking down that mountain, six days after the first passion prediction, with the glory barely faded off him, telling three men that the road runs the same way it ran for John.
verseByVerse.note: Elijah, in Jesus’ words, is John the Baptist.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the disciples, they saw a great crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them. And immediately all the crowd, when they saw him, were greatly amazed and ran up to him and greeted him. And he asked them, "What are you arguing about with them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they came to the disciples, they saw a great crowd around them, and scribes arguing with them.

Mark's cut is deliberate and brutal. The previous verse has them on the mountainside with the light barely gone. This one has them at the bottom, walking into noise.

Painters have felt it for centuries — Raphael's last work puts the transfigured Christ in the upper half of the canvas and this scene in the lower, the convulsing boy and the pointing hands, because the two belong in one frame.

Look at what is in the frame. A great crowd — so this is public. Scribes arguing with them — and these are the professional opponents, who have found the disciples in a failure and are pressing it in front of everybody.

Nine men are standing there having promised something and not delivered it, with a sick child on the ground and their critics in full voice.

That is what was waiting at the bottom of the hill.

And it is worth saying plainly, because it is such a common experience: the come-down is not a sign that the mountain was false. Peter, James and John had genuinely seen the glory of God only a short time before. It did not exempt them from walking into a shouting match. The conference ends, the retreat finishes, the Sunday that lifted you is followed by a Monday in which nothing has changed and something has probably got worse. That is not evidence that God was not on the mountain. It is the shape of the Christian life, and Mark has arranged his Gospel to prepare you for it.

And immediately all the crowd, when they saw him, were greatly amazed and ran up to him and greeted him.

The whole crowd turns. Mark's word for their reaction is strong — utterly astonished, thrown — and it is the same root used of the women at the empty tomb (16:5–6).

Why so startled? Mark does not say. Some have wondered whether something of the mountain was still on him, as it was on Moses coming down Sinai. It may simply be the shock of his arrival at the exact moment of a public humiliation. Either way, the effect is instant: the argument stops and everybody runs.

And he asked them, What are you arguing about with them?

And with one question he takes possession of the scene.

Notice what he does not do. He does not go straight to the boy, though a child is convulsing on the ground. He does not upbraid the nine in front of the crowd. He asks what the argument is about — and by asking, he moves himself into the middle of it, and the scribes are now arguing with him.

He steps between his failed disciples and the men attacking them, and that is the first act of the rescue. Whatever he has to say to the nine, he will say inside a house, privately, at the end (v. 28).

verseByVerse.quote: And someone from the crowd answered him, "Teacher, I brought my son to you, for he has a spirit that makes him mute. And whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid. So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And someone from the crowd answered him.

Not the scribes, though the question was addressed to them. Not the disciples. A man in the crowd — Mark leaves him almost anonymous, because that is all he is until he opens his mouth.

He is the only person present who is not interested in the argument.

Teacher, I brought my son to you.

Three things in that little sentence.

Teacher — the smallest title in the chapter. He has no theology of who Jesus is; the crowd's estimate is all he has.

I brought my son — he has done the one thing available to him. He has carried the boy here.

To you — and this is the ache under everything he says. He came looking for Jesus, and Jesus was up a mountain, and he got the disciples instead.

For he has a spirit that makes him mute.

The boy cannot speak. He has never told his father what it is like.

And whenever it seizes him, it throws him down, and he foams and grinds his teeth and becomes rigid.

Now the father describes it, and the detail is unbearable because it is a father's detail. He has watched this many times. He knows the sequence: the seizure, the fall, the foam, the teeth, and then the stiffening, the body going rigid and spent.

Two things need saying here with care.

First, the symptoms are those of severe epilepsy, and Mark knows it. Matthew even uses the ordinary word for it (Matt. 17:15). Scripture is perfectly capable of distinguishing illness from demonic affliction and routinely does (1:32–34, where the sick and the demonised are listed separately). What is described here is a specific case in which the two are bound together, and Jesus addresses the spirit because that is what is there.

It does not follow — and it must not be made to follow — that seizures, mental illness or disability are generally to be treated as possession. That inference has done immense harm to suffering people, and the Bible does not license it. If your child has epilepsy, this passage is not a diagnosis. Take them to a doctor, which is an ordinary mercy of God.

Second, what this passage is for is the father. This is a man who has spent years watching his child thrown to the ground. He has never had a conversation with him. He has lifted him off floors, cleaned him up, and lived with the sound of it — and the next verses will tell us it has been happening since the boy was small, and that fire and water have nearly taken him more than once.

If you are caring for a child who cannot be fixed, this man is in your Bible on purpose, and Jesus is about to give him a great deal of time.

So I asked your disciples to cast it out, and they were not able.

The last clause is said quietly and it is the hinge of everything that follows.

There is no accusation in it — he does not say they refused, or did it badly. He simply reports the fact, and the fact has done its damage. He came to the church and the church could not help him, and in two verses' time you will hear exactly what that has cost his faith.

verseByVerse.quote: And he answered them, "O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
O faithless generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you?

This is the sharpest thing Jesus says in the whole Gospel, and it needs handling carefully, because a hasty reading turns it into impatience with a suffering father, which it is not.

Who is he talking to? Mark says he answered them — plural, and the address is to a generation, not a man. It takes in the nine who failed, the scribes who were arguing, and the crowd who came to watch. It is not aimed at the father, who has just been described as bringing his son and asking for help. He is the one person there doing the right thing.

And what is the tone? Not irritation at inconvenience. The phrase how long am I to bear with you is Old Testament language, and it is God's language — the LORD in the wilderness saying how long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs? (Num. 14:11). It is the grief of a God who has done everything and been believed by almost nobody.

So this is the voice from the mountain, unveiled so recently, now standing in a valley looking at what unbelief has made of his own disciples.

And there is something else in it, which is easy to miss and worth naming: how long am I to be with you? He is not going to be with them much longer, and he knows it. Six days ago he told them so. There is a shadow of the cross in the sentence — a man measuring the time he has left against the slowness of the people he is leaving it with.

Now notice what comes next, because it is the whole character of Christ in four words.

Bring him to me.

The rebuke ends and the rescue begins in the same breath. He does not say: come back when you have more faith. He does not dismiss the crowd, or refuse to act in an atmosphere of unbelief, or make the healing conditional on an improvement in the general standard.

He says: bring him here.

That is the sentence to take away. He is genuinely grieved by faithlessness — he says so, and hard. And the very next thing he does is call the boy over.

Which is worth knowing if you have ever hesitated to bring something to God because you were ashamed of the state of your faith when you brought it. This chapter contains a hard word about unbelief and an immediate invitation, and they are spoken by the same voice in the same breath. The rebuke is real. It is not a refusal.

parallels.desc: a perverse generation, children in whom is no faithfulness

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the boy to him. And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed the boy, and he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. And Jesus asked his father, "How long has this been happening to him?" And he said, "From childhood. And it has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him. But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they brought the boy to him. And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed the boy.

The presence of Jesus provokes it. It has been like this since chapter 1 — nothing unclean can be near him and stay quiet.

And there is a hard mercy in the timing, though it will not have felt like it to the father. The worst seizure the boy has, he has in front of Jesus. What had been happening in fields and houses where nobody could help is now happening in the one place where something can be done about it.

And he fell on the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. Mark does not look away, and neither should we. This is a child on the ground in front of a crowd.

And Jesus asked his father, How long has this been happening to him?

Now stop, because this question is the most surprising thing in the passage.

There is a boy convulsing on the ground at his feet. Jesus can deal with this in a sentence — he has silenced a legion and a hurricane with fewer words than this. And he turns to the father and asks a question about the case history.

He does not need the information. So what is the question for?

It is for the father. Nobody has asked this man anything. He has spent years carrying this alone; he has just been let down in front of a crowd; and the Son of God stops the whole scene and asks him how long it has been going on.

That is pastoral care of a kind most of us never manage. Faced with a crisis, we go straight to the problem. He goes to the person, and lets him talk, and the talking is part of the healing that is about to happen.

And he said, From childhood.

Two words, and there is a life in them. Not a recent illness. Not something that came on last year. From when he was small — so this father has never known his son well. He has never heard his voice; he has never had a normal day.

And it has often cast him into fire and into water, to destroy him.

And now he tells the rest, because he has been asked. The open cooking fire in the floor of a village house. The well. The lake. Every hearth and every water jar in that man's life has been a threat for years, and he has pulled his son out of them often.

Which means this father has not slept properly in a decade. He cannot leave the boy alone. He has lived at the pitch of a man expecting a catastrophe at any moment, because he has already had several.

And he understands what he is dealing with: to destroy him. He is not describing bad luck. There is an intention behind it, and he has watched it working.

But if you can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.

And there is the sentence, and it should be read slowly, because it is the honest condition of a great many people.

If you can. He did not arrive with that clause. He came looking for the man everyone said could heal — and he found nine of his followers who could not, and a public argument about it, and now the doubt has got in through the crack their failure made.

That is worth naming for what it is. The disciples' failure damaged this man's faith in Christ. He is hedging in front of Jesus because of what happened while Jesus was up a mountain.

And it still works exactly that way. People's confidence in the Lord is regularly damaged by his people — the church that let them down, the Christian who wronged them, the prayer meeting that promised and produced nothing, the leader who fell. They come to Christ afterwards with an if you can that was not there before.

Have compassion on us. Not on him — on us. He has been ill for both of them.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "'If you can'! All things are possible for one who believes." Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, "I believe; help my unbelief!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus said to him, If you can! All things are possible for one who believes.

He picks up the man's own two words and hands them back.

The Greek is abrupt — Jesus quotes the phrase and leaves it hanging, and the ESV's exclamation mark is right. If you can! It is not mockery. It is a man seizing on the one word in the sentence that does not belong there, and refusing to let it pass.

Because the if is in the wrong place. The father has attached it to Jesus's ability, and there is nothing wrong with Jesus's ability. He has just come down from a mountain where the Father called him his beloved Son.

All things are possible for one who believes.

And here a note of caution is needed, because this sentence has been made to say something cruel that it does not say.

It is not a formula: believe hard enough and you will get what you want. That doctrine has crushed a great many suffering people, who have been told that a diagnosis stands because their faith was insufficient, and it is not what is being taught here. Read on: the boy is healed by a father who says out loud that he does not have enough faith.

What Jesus is doing is moving the man's if from one place to another. The question was never whether Christ can. The question is whether this man will take hold of him. Faith is not a force that makes things happen; faith is empty hands held out to someone who has everything.

Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, I believe; help my unbelief!

And there it is — the most honest sentence anybody speaks to Jesus in the Gospels, torn out of a man in a crisis.

Mark says he cried out. This is not a considered theological formulation. It is a shout, from a man on his knees beside a convulsing child, with a crowd watching.

Take the two halves separately, because both are extraordinary.

I believe. He will not deny the faith he has. It is real. It is what brought him here, bringing his son to the one who might help.

Help my unbelief. And he will not pretend it is more than it is. He has just heard all things are possible for one who believes, and instead of manufacturing a confidence he does not feel, he tells the truth: there is unbelief in me, and I cannot get rid of it, and I am asking you to deal with that too.

He does not ask for stronger faith so that he can then qualify. He asks Christ to help the very thing that disqualifies him.

That is the prayer, and it is the reason this verse has been the lifeline of honest Christians for two thousand years. Because most of us are not in one state or the other. We believe and we doubt, in the same hour, about the same thing. We can affirm every article of the creed and lie awake unable to feel a word of it.

And the great temptation is to sort yourself out before you come — to work up the required confidence and then pray, as though faith were the entry fee.

This man did the opposite. He brought both halves and dumped them at Christ's feet.

And look what happens next: the boy is healed.

That is the answer to the prayer and the vindication of it. Jesus does not say come back when you are sure. He does not require pure, unmixed trust before he acts. He meets the faith that is there, trembling and shot through with doubt, and does the very thing the man's doubt said he could not do.

So if your faith this morning is a mess — if you believe and cannot feel it, or feel it and cannot hold it — do not wait until it improves. Say this man's sentence. It is in the Bible because God intends it to be prayed, and the boy got up.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records the father’s cry.

parallels.desc: without faith it is impossible to please him

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together, he rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, "You mute and deaf spirit, I command you, come out of him and never enter him again." And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out, and the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, "He is dead." But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when Jesus saw that a crowd came running together.

He notices the crowd swelling and acts because of it — which almost certainly means he wants this over before it becomes a spectacle. He has been avoiding this all Gospel: the healing that turns into a show. He deals with it now, quickly.

He rebuked the unclean spirit, saying to it, You mute and deaf spirit.

He names it precisely. The father said the boy could not speak; Jesus adds deaf. And there is a grim appropriateness in it: the thing has shut the child in, sealing off both the way words come out and the way they get in.

I command you, come out of him and never enter him again.

Two things in the sentence, and the second is the one to notice.

I command you. First person, no invocation, no formula, no appeal to a higher name. This is not what the exorcists of that world did, and it is not what the disciples had done. He speaks in his own authority.

And never enter him again. Nowhere else in the Gospels does Jesus add this clause. Why here?

Because the father has just told him it has been happening from childhood, and because this is a boy who has been thrown into fires and into water for years, and the fear in that household is not only that it might happen but that it will keep happening. Jesus is not simply ending an episode. He is closing the door and telling the father it is closed.

He does not merely relieve; he settles. Which is what he did for the woman with the bleeding — be healed of your disease (5:34), a word of permanence for someone who would otherwise have spent every morning of the rest of her life waiting for it to come back.

And after crying out and convulsing him terribly, it came out. It does not go quietly. The last thing it does on the way out is hurt him as much as it can. Whatever else is true of the powers of darkness in this Gospel, they are malicious to the final second and they always obey.

And the boy was like a corpse, so that most of them said, he is dead.

The crowd's verdict, and they may well have thought it reasonable. He is lying still, white, not breathing that anyone can see. Most of the people there conclude that the healer has killed him.

Imagine the father in that half-minute. He has just prayed the truest prayer of his life, and his son is lying on the ground looking dead.

There is something here about the way God sometimes works, and it is worth having: the moment before deliverance can look exactly like the disaster you feared. The corpse comes before the rising. Israel was never more trapped than with the sea in front and the chariots behind.

But Jesus took him by the hand and lifted him up, and he arose.

And now look at the vocabulary, because it reads like a resurrection.

Took him by the hand — the same gesture as with Peter's mother-in-law (1:31) and with the dead girl in Jairus's house, where he said Talitha cumi (5:41). Lifted him up — ēgeiren, the verb used of Christ himself being raised. And he arose — anestē, the verb behind resurrection.

Mark could have written and the boy got up. He wrote the two words the church would use for Easter.

And he wrote them in the same chapter as the Transfiguration, a few verses after a promise of rising from the dead that nobody in the party understood (vv. 9–10).

So here, in a valley, in front of a crowd that has already pronounced him dead, the Son of Man reaches down and takes a boy's hand and raises him — a small, dusty rehearsal of what he is walking to Jerusalem to do for the world. He does not shout it. He simply takes hold of a child that everybody has given up on, and stands him on his feet.

parallels.desc: he took her by the hand

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately, "Why could we not cast it out?" And he said to them, "This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had entered the house, his disciples asked him privately, Why could we not cast it out?

Notice first where the conversation happens. Indoors, afterwards, in private.

He never humiliated them in the valley. The scribes were arguing, the crowd was watching, nine men had failed publicly — and Jesus took over the situation, healed the boy, and said nothing to them about it until the door was shut.

That is worth copying by anyone who has to correct anybody. The correction is real and it is coming; it is not delivered in front of an audience.

And their question is a fair one. Why could we not? They are not making excuses. They have done this before — they were given authority over unclean spirits (3:15) and they had gone out two by two and cast out many (6:13). They are not amateurs, and they know something has gone wrong that they cannot account for.

And he said to them, This kind cannot be driven out by anything but prayer.

Notice what the answer is not.

It is not a technique. He does not say they used the wrong formula, or commanded too weakly, or should have laid hands on him, or needed a different name. There is no method being withheld.

It is not more authority, either. They had all the authority they needed; he had given it to them and never withdrawn it.

It is prayer — and here you have to see that he is not prescribing a step they omitted on the day. He is diagnosing a life.

If prayer were a component of the procedure, the failure would be a slip. But that reading collapses immediately, because Jesus himself does not pray in this passage. He arrives, asks a question, speaks a sentence, and it is done. What he does not do here is what he does very early, while it is still dark, in a desolate place (1:35) and all night on a mountain before choosing the Twelve (Luke 6:12) and in Gethsemane until he sweats.

So prayer here means the posture of a whole life — the settled, daily, unspectacular dependence out of which authority actually operates.

And now the diagnosis becomes uncomfortably clear. These men had succeeded before. They had come back from that mission delighted, and demons had obeyed them. And somewhere between that success and this valley, the authority had quietly become a possession — something they had, something that worked, a capacity they carried about with them rather than a gift held moment by moment from the hand of the one who gave it.

They did not stop believing. They stopped depending. And the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the inside, until a day comes when the thing does not work.

This failure is not a first-century problem. Every generation of the church faces the same drift: the forms of spiritual ministry deployed without the ongoing communion that gives them any power at all. It is entirely possible to preach, counsel, lead, teach and serve on accumulated competence — and to be, in the valley, exactly where these nine were.

The test is simple enough to apply. How much of what you do for God this week will have been prayed about beforehand? Not prayed over in the sense of a sentence before you start. Prayed about, as a man who knows he can do nothing.

Some manuscripts add and fasting. The oldest and best manuscripts do not have it, and it was probably added by copyists from the church’s own practice. Jesus’ point is dependence on God in prayer. Fasting is good, and Jesus expected his disciples to fast (Matt 6:16–18), but it is not the secret here.

Apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5) is not an exaggeration and it is not a rebuke. It is a description, and the nine in that valley had just proved it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “and fasting.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 30–50 — The Second Prediction and the Argument on the Road
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The second telling (vv. 30–32). Walking quietly through Galilee, avoiding notice, Jesus tells them again that he will be delivered up, killed, and rise. Mark adds a devastating detail: they did not understand, and were afraid to ask.

The argument (vv. 33–37). And what they were talking about instead comes out at Capernaum. He asks what they were discussing on the road, and they go silent — because they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. His answer is to sit down, state the rule (last of all and servant of all), and then pick up a child and hold him.

The complaint (vv. 38–41). John, apparently thinking this a good moment, reports that they stopped a man casting out demons in Jesus's name because he was not one of them. He is told to leave him alone — and that a cup of water given to a disciple will not be forgotten.

The warnings (vv. 42–50). Then the hardest words in the Gospel: a millstone for anyone who trips up a little one, and a hand, a foot and an eye better lost than kept.

The whole section hangs together. Men who have just been told about a cross are arguing about rank, policing the boundaries of their group, and in serious danger of tripping up people smaller than themselves — and it ends with be at peace with one another.
verseByVerse.theology:
"The one who is not against us is for us" (v. 40) seems to collide head-on with whoever is not with me is against me (Matt. 12:30; Luke 11:23), and a reader who notices it deserves an answer.

They are not answering the same question, and that is the whole key. Here the subject is a fellow worker — a man casting out demons in Jesus's name, plainly on Christ's side, who simply does not belong to the disciples' circle; and the lesson is generosity: do not treat an ally as an enemy merely because he is not of your party. There the subject is Christ himself, and the men in view are Pharisees who had just called his works the devil's — open opponents; and the lesson is that toward Jesus there is no neutral ground.

So the two sayings guard two different errors. Toward other Christians serving under a different banner from ours we are far too quick to say against us, and Jesus says: not so — if he is for me, he is for you. Toward the Lord himself we would love to imagine a comfortable middle ground of the undecided, and Jesus says there is none. Read together they are not a contradiction but a pair of fences: be generous about the boundaries of the movement, and uncompromising about the claims of the King.

And a word about the verses your Bible skips. A reader with a King James Bible will find the refrain of v. 48, about the undying worm and the unquenched fire, three times over, at verses 44, 46 and 48. Modern Bibles print it once, at v. 48, and leave 44 and 46 as footnotes. Those two repetitions are a copyist's echo of v. 48 and are not in the earliest manuscripts. Nothing is lost. The sentence stands once, in full force, exactly where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah 66:24.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: twelve men arguing on a road about which of them was the greatest, on the road after being told that their Master would be handed over and killed.

Now: the same argument, conducted with better manners. It runs under a great deal of church life — who was consulted, who was thanked from the front, whose name went on it, who got asked to do the thing you were not asked to do. Nobody says I am the greatest. Everybody knows exactly where they stand in the room.

And notice how Mark exposes it: they kept silent. They would not tell him. Which is the surest sign of all that they already knew it was wrong — you do not go quiet about a conversation you are comfortable with.

Then watch what Jesus does with it, because he does not abolish ambition; he reverses its direction. If anyone would be first — the wanting is allowed to stand — he must be last of all and servant of all. Not last of some. Not servant of the deserving. Of all.

And then he picks up a child, who in that world had no legal standing, no money, no influence and nothing whatever to offer in return — and says that receiving one such is receiving him. The test of greatness in the kingdom is not how you treat the people who can advance you. It is how you treat the ones who cannot do a thing for you, when nobody is watching.

verseByVerse.quote: They went on from there and passed through Galilee. And he did not want anyone to know, for he was teaching his disciples, saying to them, "The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise." But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They went on from there and passed through Galilee. And he did not want anyone to know.

He is travelling incognito through his own province — the region where his ministry began, where the crowds first came, where he could not enter a town openly a few chapters ago.

The public phase is ending. From here the Gospel narrows: less crowd, more instruction, and the road turns toward Jerusalem. What he has left to do is with these twelve men, and there is not much time.

For he was teaching his disciples. That is why he wants privacy. The teaching now is not for the multitude.

The Son of Man is going to be delivered into the hands of men.

The second passion prediction, and it is not a repeat — there is a new word in it, and it is the darkest in the sentence.

Delivered is paradidotai — handed over, given up, betrayed. It is the word used of Judas throughout this Gospel, and of the chief priests handing Jesus to Pilate, and of Pilate handing him to the soldiers. It runs through the passion narrative like a thread.

And here it is in the present tense and, more strikingly, in a form that does not say who is doing it. Somebody hands him over. Judas will, and the priests will, and Pilate will — and behind all of them, Paul says, it was God: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom. 8:32).

Into the hands of men. Not into the hands of Rome, or of the Sanhedrin, or of his enemies. Men. Humanity in general — which is where the reader is standing.

And they will kill him. And when he is killed, after three days he will rise.

Flat, unadorned, and with the resurrection attached again, as it was the first time. He has never once mentioned the death without the rising.

But they did not understand the saying, and were afraid to ask him.

And Mark, as usual, tells the truth about his own leaders.

Two failures, and the second is worse than the first.

They did not understand. That is forgivable and by now familiar. It is the second time they have heard this, and it still will not go in.

And were afraid to ask him. That is not ignorance. That is a choice.

Why afraid? Perhaps because of what happened last time somebody raised it — Peter took him aside about this exact subject and was called Satan, and nine men saw it. Perhaps for a more ordinary reason: they suspected they would not like the answer.

And that is a very recognisable state, and it is worth being honest about it. There are questions Christians decline to ask God. Not because they cannot be asked — Scripture is full of people asking far bolder ones — but because we half-know the answer, and the answer would require something.

The passage you skip. The subject you never bring into prayer. The area of your life you have quietly agreed with yourself not to discuss with him. It is not doubt; doubt at least engages. It is avoidance, and the men in this verse invented nothing new.

And look what they do with the silence. They do not ask him about the cross — and then they fill the rest of the walk with an argument about which of them is the most important. The unasked question leaves a space, and something always moves into it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Capernaum. And when he was in the house he asked them, "What were you discussing on the way?" But they kept silent, for on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest. And he sat down and called the twelve. And he said to them, "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they came to Capernaum. And when he was in the house he asked them, What were you discussing on the way?

He waits until they are indoors. Whatever he heard on the road, he says nothing about it until the door is shut — the same restraint he showed with the nine after the failure in the valley.

And the question is gentle. He does not accuse. He asks.

But they kept silent.

Three of the most eloquent words in the chapter.

They will not tell him. And the silence is a confession, because you do not go quiet about a conversation you are comfortable with. They had been perfectly happy to have it among themselves on the road; asked to repeat it in front of him, not one of the twelve can get the sentence out.

That is a test worth borrowing, and it is uncomfortably effective. Would you be willing to repeat, out loud, to Christ, the last conversation you had about somebody else? Not the words only — the tone, and the reason you said it. Most of us have a category of speech that dies instantly in his presence, and the dying is the verdict.

For on the way they had argued with one another about who was the greatest.

Mark supplies what they would not, and note the placement, because it is the whole indictment. This is the same road. He has just told them, for the second time, that he is going to be handed over and killed. And the conversation among the men walking behind him was about rank.

Note also that it was an argument. Not a passing thought. They discussed it at length, and there were positions, and cases were made.

Before that is treated as a first-century absurdity, be honest about how familiar it is. Nobody in a church says I am the greatest. But the argument runs anyway, silently and constantly — who was consulted and who was not, who got thanked from the front, whose name is on it, who was asked to do the thing you were not asked to do, who is regarded as sound. It can be conducted entirely without words and everybody in the room knows the standings.

And he sat down and called the twelve. Sitting is the posture of a teacher. What follows is not an aside; it is a lesson, deliberately staged.

If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all.

And now the sentence, and the first thing to notice is what it does not do.

It does not condemn the desire. If anyone would be first — the wanting is allowed to stand. Jesus does not tell them that ambition is wicked and they should have none. He tells them where the front of the queue actually is.

He reverses the direction rather than removing the drive. You want to be first? Here is the road: go to the back, and serve.

And the two absolutes at the end are what make it impossible to soften. Last of all — not last of some, not modest about your position, but bottom. Servant of all — the word is diakonos, the man who waited at table, and there is no qualifying clause. Not servant of the deserving, the grateful, the promising, or the people who might one day be useful. Of all.

Which turns the whole thing from an attitude into something measurable, because service of that kind can be looked up in a diary. It is easy to feel humble. It is not possible to be a servant in the abstract.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a child and put him in the midst of them, and taking him in his arms, he said to them, "Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he took a child and put him in the midst of them.

Having said it, he shows it. There is a child in that house — perhaps a child of the household, in a house that may well be Peter's — and Jesus goes and gets him and stands him in the middle of the room, in the space the twelve have made by sitting round.

The argument was about who takes the highest place. He puts a child in the centre of it.

And it is important to know what a child meant in that world, because we have sentimentalised this scene beyond recognition. We think of innocence, wonder, trust. That is not what a first-century adult saw. A child had no legal standing, no property, no voice, no rights to speak of. Children were loved — of course they were — but they were nobodies. They could not advance you, defend you, repay you or add anything to your position.

So the object lesson is not be innocent like this. It is: here is a person who can do absolutely nothing for you.

And taking him in his arms.

Mark alone records this, and he records it twice: here, and when he takes the children in his arms and blesses them in chapter 10 (10:16).

Peter remembered it. That is why it is here. He is telling the church in Rome, thirty years later: while he was explaining greatness to us, he was holding a child.

And the picture is worth staying with. Twelve grown men who have been arguing about rank, sitting in a circle, and the Lord of glory in the middle of them with a small child in his arms.

Whoever receives one such child in my name receives me.

Receives is the word for welcoming a guest — taking someone in, giving them your attention and your table.

So the standard is set, and it is exact. Not whoever loves children. Whoever receives — takes trouble over, makes room for, welcomes as a guest — one who has nothing to give in return.

And whoever receives me, receives not me but him who sent me.

And then the chain, and it goes further than anyone would expect: the child, then Christ, then the Father.

Which means the greatness of an act is not measured by the significance of the person you did it for. It is measured by who is standing behind them.

So here is the test, and it is more searching than a general resolution to be humble. How do you treat the people who cannot do a thing for you? The person at church nobody seeks out. The elderly relative whose conversation goes in circles. The junior colleague. The child in your own house at the end of a day when you have nothing left. The one whose gratitude you will never hear about and whose name will not be mentioned when the work is described.

Everybody is attentive to the people who matter to their position. The kingdom's ranking is worked out entirely on the others — and Jesus says that when you welcome one of them in his name, you have welcomed him, and behind him, God.
verseByVerse.note: Children had little status in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: John said to him, "Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us." But Jesus said, "Do not stop him, for no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me. For the one who is not against us is for us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John said to him, Teacher, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he was not following us.

The timing is superb and John cannot possibly have intended it. Jesus has just held up a child and said that receiving a nobody in his name is receiving him — and John's contribution is to report an occasion when they stopped somebody acting in that name.

It is the only time John speaks alone in this Gospel, and he seems to expect approval. He is a Son of Thunder, after all (3:17), and this is exactly the sort of thing thunder does.

Look carefully at the reason he gives, because he states it with perfect and damning clarity: because he was not following us.

Not because he was not following you. The man plainly was — he was casting out demons in Jesus's name and, we should note, succeeding, which is more than the nine had managed in the valley.

The objection is to his membership, not his master. He was not in the group.

And that is the whole of sectarianism in one clause, then and now. There is a way of caring about the kingdom that has quietly become caring about our part of it — where the first question asked about a man's ministry is not is Christ being preached? but whose is he? It flourishes among people who are entirely orthodox and entirely sincere, and it produces the strange spectacle of Christians relieved rather than glad when good work is done by somebody outside their circle.

But Jesus said, Do not stop him.

Flat, immediate, no discussion.

For no one who does a mighty work in my name will be able soon afterward to speak evil of me.

The reasoning is practical rather than sentimental. A man who has just seen the name of Jesus work is not about to start slandering it. Whatever is deficient in his understanding, and whatever his affiliation, he is not on the other side, and the evidence is what happened.

For the one who is not against us is for us.

Now the saying that has troubled readers, because Jesus elsewhere says the opposite: whoever is not with me is against me (Matt. 12:30; Luke 11:23). Set side by side they look like contradictions — here neutrality counts in a man's favour, there it counts against him.

They are answering different questions, and that is the key.

Here the subject is a fellow worker. A man casting out demons in Jesus's name, plainly on Christ's side, who simply does not belong to the disciples' circle. The lesson is generosity: do not treat an ally as an enemy because he is not of your party.

There the subject is Christ himself, and the men in view are Pharisees who had just called his works the devil's — open opponents. The lesson is that toward Jesus there is no neutral ground and no fence to sit on.

So the two sayings guard two opposite errors, and both errors are alive. Toward other Christians who serve under a different banner from ours, we are far too quick to say against us — and Jesus says: if he is for me, he is for you. Toward the Lord himself, we would very much like a comfortable middle ground of the undecided — and Jesus says there is none. A heart not with him is already against him.

Read together they are not a contradiction but a pair of fences: be generous about the boundaries of the movement, and uncompromising about the claims of the King.

parallels.desc: whoever is not with me is against me

verseByVerse.quote: For truly, I say to you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For truly, I say to you, whoever gives you a cup of water to drink because you belong to Christ will by no means lose his reward.

The truly is the amen-formula, and he keeps it for things he wants underlined. He has just used it nowhere in this passage; he uses it here, for a cup of water.

And the placing is deliberate. He has spent three verses widening the boundary — do not stop the man outside your circle — and now he goes further and widens it to the smallest imaginable act.

A cup of water. Consider what he could have chosen. He has just spoken of casting out demons. He could have said: whoever preaches, whoever heals, whoever gives up his home.

He says a drink of water. In a hot country it costs nothing; the well is there and everybody has a cup. It is the least thing one human being can do for another and still be said to have done something. There is no expense, no skill, no risk, and nobody will ever hear about it.

And it will not be forgotten.

Because you belong to Christ. That is the qualifying clause, and it is the whole of it. Not because the giver was impressive, or the act large, or the motive perfectly pure. Because of whose the recipient was.
