The value of the act is not in the water. It is in the name attached to the person handed the cup — which is exactly what he said two verses earlier about the child. Receive a nobody in my name, and you have received me. Hand a disciple a drink because he is mine, and it goes on the account.

Will by no means lose his reward. The double negative in the Greek is emphatic: it is not going to be lost. Not overlooked, not mislaid, not too small to register.

Which is worth having if the service you are able to give is very small and entirely unnoticed. Most Christian work is. It is meals cooked, lifts given, chairs put out, a message sent to somebody having a bad week, an hour spent with a person nobody else has time for, prayer for people who never learn they were prayed for.

None of it will be described from a platform. All of it is on a list.

And he will read the list out one day, and the people named will not recognise their own lives in it: Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? — as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me (Matt. 25:37–40).

The King of glory keeps a record of cups of water. That is the sort of King he is.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin.

The tone changes completely, and the change is deliberate. He has just promised a reward for the smallest kindness done to one of his people. Now he states what happens at the other end.

Who are the little ones? The child is still in the room — he is holding him, or has just set him down — so children are certainly not excluded. But the qualifying phrase is who believe in me, which points wider: the small, the new, the fragile, the ones whose faith is genuine and not yet strong. The recent convert. The person hanging on by their fingernails. Anyone whose grip on Christ could be loosened by what you do.

Causes... to sin is one word in Greek, skandalisē — to trip up, to put a stumbling block in someone's path. It covers more than teaching them error. It is anything you do that makes it harder for a weak believer to keep walking.

It would be better for him if a great millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.

And now the most violent image Jesus ever uses about anybody.

Get the picture right. This is not the small hand-mill a woman turned in her kitchen. It is a great millstone — the upper stone of a village mill, the one an animal walked in circles to turn. It is a slab of rock weighing hundreds of pounds. One man could not lift it.

And it is to be hung round the neck, and the man dropped into the sea. There is no coming up. Ever. He does not float; he is not found.

Then hear the comparison, which is the actual sentence: it would be better for him. Jesus is saying that a violent, hopeless, irrecoverable death would be the preferable outcome — that being drowned like that is the lucky version of what is coming to a man who trips up one of his little ones.

He does not speak like this about doubters, or the confused, or the openly immoral, or even his enemies. He speaks like this about people who damage the faith of the small.

Which makes this the most solemn verse in the New Testament for anybody with influence over somebody weaker — and that is a great many of us.

It is a word for parents, whose children's picture of God is being assembled largely out of what they see at home, and whose faith can be quietly ruined by a father who is one man on Sunday and another on Tuesday.

It is a word for anyone who teaches or leads in a church, and for anyone whose conduct is watched by a younger Christian who thinks well of them.

And it is a word about ordinary talk. You do not need to preach heresy to trip somebody up. It is done with a cynical remark about a fellow believer in front of a new convert; with the running commentary on the church's failings that a fragile person overhears; with the joke that makes something holy look small.

The father in the valley had his faith damaged by disciples who let him down, and he arrived at Christ saying if you can. Somebody put that clause in his mouth.

So it is worth asking, without panic and without evasion: who is watching me who is weaker than I am, and is anything I do making it harder for them? He weighed the answer against a millstone.
verseByVerse.note: The millstone is the heavy upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey.

verseByVerse.quote: And if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life crippled than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire. And if your foot causes you to sin, cut it off. It is better for you to enter life lame than with two feet to be thrown into hell. And if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out. It is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than with two eyes to be thrown into hell, 'where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
And if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off.

Having warned them about tripping up other people, he turns to the far more likely danger, which is yourself. And the same verb runs through: it is the skandalizō of verse 42. What trips others up may be your influence; what trips you up is nearer to hand.

Three examples, in a deliberate order — hand, foot, eye. What you do, where you go, what you look at. Between them they cover most of the ways a person is ruined.

Is he asking for literal self-mutilation? No, and the reason is not squeamishness — it is that it would not work. Chapter 7 settled this: nothing outside a man defiles him; the trouble comes from within, out of the heart (7:21). A man with one hand can still covet, and a blind man can still lust. Amputate everything and the heart is untouched. That is precisely why the church has never taken this literally, and why the few who have were pitied rather than admired.

But do not let that soften it into nothing. This is hyperbole in the service of deadly seriousness, and the seriousness is the point: there is nothing in your life so valuable that it is worth keeping if it is taking you to hell. A hand is not a luxury. Nor is an eye. He deliberately chose things you cannot spare.

It is better for you to enter life crippled. And notice the word: life. He calls the kingdom life, and the alternative, three times over, hell. Those are the only two categories in this paragraph.

So make it concrete, because vagueness here is how the passage gets neutralised.

The hand is what you do. The foot is where you go — the house, the road home past a particular door, the company you keep because it is easier than explaining. The eye is what you look at, and in our generation that is almost entirely one object, which is in your pocket and lit up at midnight.

And the surgery Jesus describes is not moderation; it is removal. Not be more careful with it — cut it off. Which in practice means the ruthless, concrete, slightly embarrassing measure: the app deleted rather than managed, the phone that does not come upstairs, the account closed, the friendship stepped back from, the route changed, the arrangement told to another Christian so that it can be asked about. Every one of those feels disproportionate. That is the feeling of amputation, and it is exactly the feeling he is describing.

Than with two hands to go to hell, to the unquenchable fire.

The word rendered hell three times here is Gehenna, and it is a real place with an address.

It is the Valley of Hinnom, a ravine running along the south side of Jerusalem. There, in the darkest days of the kingdom, apostate Israel burned its own children alive in sacrifice to Molech — Ahaz did it and Manasseh did it (2 Chr. 28:3; 33:6), and Josiah defiled the place so that it could never be used that way again (2 Kgs. 23:10). Jeremiah called it the Valley of Slaughter (Jer. 7:31–32).

So Jesus takes a real, stinking, smouldering valley that every one of his hearers could have walked to in half an hour, and makes it his picture of final judgement: the place fit only for what is utterly rejected.

Where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.

And the closing line is not his own invention. It is a quotation of the last verse of Isaiah (Isa. 66:24), which pictures the corpses of those who rebelled against God — and the two images together say one terrible thing. The worm does not finish its work; the fire does not go out. This ruin does not end.

Take one plain observation about the man saying it. Nobody in the Bible speaks about hell as often or as vividly as Jesus does. The tenderest person who ever lived — who held a child while he taught, who groaned over a deaf man, who thought about a raised girl's breakfast — is the one who will not let this subject alone. It cannot be dismissed as the harshness of the Old Testament or the invention of a later church. It is on the lips of the Saviour, and he says it three times in six verses because he means his people not to go there.

Does this teach that punishment is conscious and unending? Some evangelicals hold that the lost will finally be destroyed and cease to exist, and they note that the line comes from Isaiah 66:24, where the worm and fire consume the dead bodies of the rebels. But in Jesus’ use the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched; it is the punishment, not its victims, that ends nowhere. He sets eternal punishment beside eternal life (Matt 25:46), and Revelation says the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever (Rev 14:11). The more likely reading is that the punishment is conscious and unending. It is meant to drive us to the one who bore judgment for all who come to him.

And a note on the verses your Bible skips. A reader with a King James Bible will find this refrain three times, at verses 44, 46 and 48; here the numbers run 43, 45, 47, 48. Those two repetitions are a copyist's echo of v. 48 and are not in the earliest manuscripts, which is why modern Bibles drop them to a footnote. Nothing has been lost or removed: the sentence stands once, in full force, exactly where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verses 44 and 46, repeating verse 48. “Hell” renders Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched

verseByVerse.quote: For everyone will be salted with fire. Salt is good, but if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again? Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For everyone will be salted with fire.

One of the strangest sentences in Mark, and commentators have puzzled over it for centuries. But its two key words are the way in.

Fire is the last word of the previous paragraph, where it meant judgement — unquenchable, in Gehenna.

Salt comes from somewhere else entirely: you shall season all your grain offerings with salt. You shall not let the salt of the covenant with your God be missing (Lev. 2:13). Salt was rubbed into every sacrifice laid on the altar. It was the covenant seasoning.

So the saying holds two destinies in one breath, and the same element does opposite things to them. The unrepentant meet the fire that consumes. The disciple — who has just been told to cut off hand and foot rather than perish — meets the fire that purifies: the costly, cleansing fire of a life laid on the altar as an offering.

Everyone will meet fire. The only question is which kind, and Peter says the same thing when he writes to Christians under persecution: do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, and the tested faith is more precious than gold that perishes though it is tested by fire (1 Pet. 4:12; 1:7).

Other readings have been offered: that every believer will be tested by fire (1 Cor 3:13); that disciples are to be offered to God like sacrifices seasoned with salt (Lev 2:13; Rom 12:1); or that the wicked will be preserved, as salt preserves, in the fire of judgment. The reading given here keeps the link with the fire of v. 48 and the salt of the sacrifices, and is the more likely: everyone meets God’s fire, either as judgment or as the refining of a life given to him.

Salt is good.

And now the tone gentles, and the chapter comes in to land.

Salt in that world did two things. It preserved — the only thing standing between a household and rotten meat. And it seasoned — it made food taste like something. Both are pictures of what a disciple is meant to be: the thing that stops the rot and the thing that gives savour.

But if the salt has lost its saltiness, how will you make it salty again?

The salt of that region was not pure sodium; it was scraped from the shores of the Dead Sea, full of other minerals, and the salt could genuinely leach out and leave a white powder that looked identical and did nothing. You could not restore it. You threw it out.

And that is the sober question sitting under the sentence: a Christian who has quietly lost the thing that made him different is not obviously distinguishable from one who has not. He looks the same. He is in the same place on Sunday. He simply no longer preserves anything or gives any flavour to anything, and there is no procedure for putting it back.

Have salt in yourselves, and be at peace with one another.

And there is the last line of the chapter, and everything in the second half has been walking toward it.

Remember what these men have done in these last days. They failed in a valley and had to be rescued in front of a crowd. They were told about the cross and were afraid to ask what it meant. They argued on the road about which of them was the greatest, and then would not admit it. And John stopped a man doing good work because he was not one of their party.

To that group, Jesus says: be at peace with one another.

Notice the order, because it is the whole of Christian ethics in one sentence. Have salt in yourselves comes first — the inward reality, the ruthlessness with your own hand and foot and eye, the thing that actually makes you different. And be at peace with one another follows from it. Peace in a church is not produced by managing personalities. It is what happens when a group of people have each dealt honestly with themselves.

And it is worth seeing where that leaves the argument they started the day with. Twelve men wanted to know which of them was the greatest. He held a child, told them to go to the back and serve everybody, warned them what happens to a man who trips up one of the little ones, told them to cut off whatever is taking them down — and then said: now be at peace with each other.

He is going to Jerusalem to make that peace at his own expense. Within weeks they will be arguing about rank again (10:35–41). And on the night he is handed over, he will get up from the table, take a towel, and wash the feet of every one of them.
verseByVerse.note: Salt was added to every sacrifice. Salt from the Dead Sea could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

parallels.desc: with all your offerings you shall offer salt
let your speech be seasoned with salt

9.theology:
What happened on the mountain? The word is metamorphōthē — transformed. And nothing was added; something was, for a moment, no longer withheld. Set it beside Moses, whose face shone coming down Sinai and had to be veiled (Ex. 34:29–35) — but that light was borrowed and fading, which Paul says is why he covered it (2 Cor. 3:13). Here the light comes from inside; the clothes go white because of what is underneath them. Three men were allowed to see, for a few minutes, what was true of him every day they had walked beside him without noticing.

Who will not taste death? (v. 1) Mark's own arrangement answers it: the very next words are and after six days, and Mark almost never gives intervals. Some standing there would see the kingdom come with power — and six days later, three of them did. Peter confirms the reading himself, citing that mountain as evidence of the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ (2 Pet. 1:16–18). Serious readers have argued for the resurrection, Pentecost, or AD 70, and the instinct behind those is right — the kingdom comes in power by stages — but after six days is not decoration.

Why could the disciples not cast it out? (v. 29) Not a technique, and not a shortage of authority — he had given it and never withdrawn it. Prayer here is not a step they omitted on the day but the posture of a whole life. They had succeeded before; somewhere between that success and this valley the authority had become a possession rather than a gift held moment by moment. They did not stop believing. They stopped depending — and the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the inside until the day it does not work.

And the verses your Bible skips. A King James Bible has the refrain of v. 48, about the worm that does not die, three times, at vv. 44, 46 and 48. Those two repetitions are a copyist's echo of v. 48 and are absent from the earliest manuscripts, which is why modern Bibles footnote them. Nothing is lost: the sentence stands once, in full force, where Jesus quoted it from Isaiah 66:24.
9.examples:
Then: a father who had watched his son thrown to the ground since childhood, pulled him out of fires and out of water, never heard him speak — and who came looking for Jesus, found the disciples instead, and watched them fail in front of a crowd.

Now: the if you can in his prayer was not there when he set out. The disciples' failure damaged his faith in Christ. That still happens exactly the same way: the church that let someone down, the Christian who wronged them, the leader who fell, the prayer meeting that promised and produced nothing. People come to Christ afterwards with a clause in their mouth that somebody else put there — which is worth remembering by anyone whose conduct is watched by a weaker believer, and it is why v. 42 talks about millstones.

And then watch what the man does with the little he has. I believe; help my unbelief! — a shout, not a formulation, from a man on his knees beside a convulsing child. He will not deny the faith he has, and he will not pretend it is more than it is. He asks Christ to deal with the very thing that disqualifies him.

Most of us are not in one state or the other. We believe and doubt in the same hour about the same thing, and the great temptation is to sort ourselves out before we come — to work up the required confidence and then pray, as though faith were the entry fee. This man brought both halves and dumped them at Christ's feet.

And the boy was healed. That is the answer to the prayer and the vindication of it. Jesus does not say come back when you are sure. He meets the faith that is there, trembling and shot through with doubt, and does the very thing the man's doubt said he could not do. So if your faith this morning is a mess, do not wait for it to improve. Say this man's sentence. It is in the Bible to be prayed.

10.title: The Road, the Ransom, and the Beggar Who Followed
10.text: <sup>1</sup>And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds gathered to him again. And again, as was his custom, he taught them. <sup>2</sup>And Pharisees came up and in order to test him asked, “Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?” <sup>3</sup>He answered them, “What did Moses command you?” <sup>4</sup>They said, “Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away.” <sup>5</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment. <sup>6</sup>But from the beginning of creation, ‘God made them male and female.’ <sup>7</sup>‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, <sup>8</sup>and the two shall become one flesh.’ So they are no longer two but one flesh. <sup>9</sup>What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” <sup>10</sup>And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter. <sup>11</sup>And he said to them, “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, <sup>12</sup>and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.” <sup>13</sup>And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. <sup>14</sup>But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, “Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God. <sup>15</sup>Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.” <sup>16</sup>And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them. <sup>17</sup>And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” <sup>18</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone. <sup>19</sup>You know the commandments: ‘Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.’” <sup>20</sup>And he said to him, “Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, “You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>22</sup>Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. <sup>23</sup>And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, “How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!” <sup>24</sup>And the disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! <sup>25</sup>It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup>And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, “Then who can be saved?” <sup>27</sup>Jesus looked at them and said, “With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.” <sup>28</sup>Peter began to say to him, “See, we have left everything and followed you.” <sup>29</sup>Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, <sup>30</sup>who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. <sup>31</sup>But many who are first will be last, and the last first.” <sup>32</sup>And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him, <sup>33</sup>saying, “See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. <sup>34</sup>And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise.” <sup>35</sup>And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.” <sup>36</sup>And he said to them, “What do you want me to do for you?” <sup>37</sup>And they said to him, “Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.” <sup>38</sup>Jesus said to them, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” <sup>39</sup>And they said to him, “We are able.” And Jesus said to them, “The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, <sup>40</sup>but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared.” <sup>41</sup>And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. <sup>42</sup>And Jesus called them to him and said to them, “You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. <sup>43</sup>But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, <sup>44</sup>and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. <sup>45</sup>For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” <sup>46</sup>And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. <sup>47</sup>And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>48</sup>And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, “Son of David, have mercy on me!” <sup>49</sup>And Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” And they called the blind man, saying to him, “Take heart. Get up; he is calling you.” <sup>50</sup>And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus. <sup>51</sup>And Jesus said to him, “What do you want me to do for you?” And the blind man said to him, “Rabbi, let me recover my sight.” <sup>52</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Go your way; your faith has made you well.” And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
10.overview:
Chapter 10 takes the three things people build their lives out of — marriage, children, money — and hands them, one after another, to a man walking to Jerusalem to die.

The Pharisees open with the question that cost John the Baptist his head, and Jesus refuses to argue about grounds for divorce. He goes behind Moses to Genesis: male and female, one flesh, what therefore God has joined together, let not man separate. Then parents bring children and the disciples turn them away, and Jesus is indignant — the only time in Mark that word is used of him, and it is aimed at his own men. Then a rich man runs, kneels, asks the best question in the Gospel, is looked at and loved by the Son of God — and goes home, because there was one thing he would not give.

The second half is a road. Jesus walks ahead with a set face while the twelve follow amazed and the crowd follows afraid, and he tells them for the third time exactly what is waiting: handed over, condemned, given to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed, raised. James and John's response is to ask for the two best seats — and out of that squabble comes the summit of the Gospel: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

Then Jericho, and a blind beggar who shouts a messianic title none of the disciples has used, is told to be quiet, shouts louder, throws away the only thing he owns, and follows Jesus up the road. The chapter opened with a rich man who would not follow and closes with a beggar who did.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–31 — Divorce, Children, and the Danger of Riches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The trap (vv. 1–12). He crosses into Herod's jurisdiction, and the Pharisees immediately ask him about divorce — the question that cost John the Baptist his head. Jesus refuses to argue about grounds and goes behind Moses to Genesis: male and female, one flesh, joined by God.

The children (vv. 13–16). Parents bring their children to be touched, the disciples turn them away as an interruption, and Jesus is indignant — the only time in Mark that word is used of him, and it is aimed at his own men. Then he picks the children up and blesses them.

The rich man (vv. 17–22). A man runs, kneels, and asks the best question in the Gospel. Jesus looks at him and loves him, and asks for the one thing he will not give. He goes away sorrowful, and Mark does not soften the ending.

The impossibility (vv. 23–31). A camel through a needle's eye, disciples asking then who can be saved?, and the only answer there has ever been — with man it is impossible, but not with God.

Three subjects, and one thread running under them: marriage, children, money. The three things people build their lives out of, handled one after another by a man walking to Jerusalem to die.
verseByVerse.theology:
Divorce, and what Mark leaves out. A reader with Matthew open will notice that Mark's version is starker. Matthew twice records an exception — except for sexual immorality (Matt. 5:32; 19:9) — and Mark records none, while adding, for his Roman readers, the case of a wife who divorces her husband.

That is not a contradiction but a difference of purpose. Mark gives the principle in its unguarded, creation-order form, the way a thing is stated when you want its full weight felt. Matthew, writing where the rabbis argued endlessly over grounds, records the one qualification Jesus actually allowed. Paul adds a second — the believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is not enslaved (1 Cor. 7:15). So the Reformed churches have long recognised two grounds on which the bond may be broken and the innocent party freed: adultery and desertion, and no others.

Mark's silence is not a denial. It is a refusal to lead with the exception — because the moment the exception becomes the headline, hardness of heart starts hunting for a way in. Jesus will not begin where the Pharisees wanted to begin, with the escape clause. He begins with the joining that God himself performs.

And "Why do you call me good?" (v. 18) is not Jesus denying that he is good or that he is God — and note that he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light. The young man has tossed off Good Teacher as easy flattery. Jesus stops him: do you know what you are saying? Goodness in the full sense belongs to God alone. So either you should not have called me good — or, if the word is right, you must reckon with who I am. It is not a denial of his deity but a door held open to it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man who ran, knelt, asked the right question, had kept the commandments since boyhood, was looked at and loved by the Son of God — and went home.

Now: he is the most alarming figure in the Gospel precisely because there is nothing wrong with him. He is not a Pharisee, not a hypocrite, not hostile. He is sincere, moral, eager and respectful, and he is the one person in Mark who meets Jesus, is loved by him, and walks away.

And notice what stopped him. Not an argument. Not doubt. One thing he would not hand over.

So the question the passage actually asks is not am I a good person? — he was, by every visible measure. It is: what is the one thing? What would you be unable to say yes to, if Christ named it tonight? For this man it was money, and Jesus went straight to it, because a rival throne is always specific.

The test is not hypothetical either. Most people know the answer within a few seconds and then spend a while explaining why that particular thing is different. He went away sorrowful, which means he knew exactly what he was refusing. Mark records no second visit.

verseByVerse.quote: And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan, and crowds gathered to him again. And again, as was his custom, he taught them. And Pharisees came up and in order to test him asked, "Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he left there and went to the region of Judea and beyond the Jordan.

Galilee is finished. He will not come back, and everything from here runs toward Jerusalem.

Note where he goes: beyond the Jordan — Perea, the eastern strip. And that matters for what happens next, because Perea, like Galilee, was ruled by Herod Antipas.

Which is to say: he has just walked into the jurisdiction of the man who beheaded John the Baptist, and the very next thing he is asked about is divorce.

And crowds gathered to him again. And again, as was his custom, he taught them. Mark says again twice. The pattern of the whole ministry in one sentence: they came, and he taught.

And Pharisees came up and in order to test him.

Mark tells us the motive first, as he did in chapter 8. This is not enquiry.

Asked, Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?

Now understand what a loaded question this was, because on the surface it looks academic and it is nothing of the kind.

First, it was politically lethal. John the Baptist had told Herod Antipas that his marriage to his brother's wife was unlawful, and it had cost him his freedom and then his head (6:17–29). Herod's fortress was in this very region. If Jesus answers strictly, there is every chance of a repeat — and the men asking know it.

Second, it was a live rabbinic dispute, and everyone knew the sides. Moses had permitted a man to divorce his wife if he found in her some indecency (Deut. 24:1), and the whole argument turned on that phrase. The school of Shammai held it meant unfaithfulness and nothing else. The school of Hillel held it could mean almost anything — the rabbis' own examples include spoiling a dish, and one teacher allowed a man to divorce his wife if he found someone prettier.

So the question is designed to make him take sides in a controversy where every answer loses somebody.

And third — and this is the part we feel least — it is a question asked entirely from the man's side. Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife? In that world the initiative was almost always his alone; a woman put away had no property, no standing, and very little future. The Pharisees are debating the limits of a man's freedom to dispose of a person.

Nobody in that conversation has mentioned the wife.

Jesus is about to.
verseByVerse.note: “Beyond the Jordan” is Perea, the land east of the river, ruled by Herod Antipas — who had imprisoned John for his marriage. Rabbis debated the grounds for divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, "What did Moses command you?" They said, "Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away." And Jesus said to them, "Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He answered them, What did Moses command you?

He answers a question with a question, and the question is a trap of its own, because the verb is precise.

He asks what Moses commanded.

They said, Moses allowed a man to write a certificate of divorce and to send her away.

And they hear it, and correct him without realising they have conceded the whole argument. Allowed, they say. Not commanded. Permitted.

They are right, and they have just handed him the case. There is no commandment in the Law of Moses that anyone should divorce anybody. What Deuteronomy 24 does is regulate a practice already going on — and if you read it carefully, the regulation is protective. The certificate was the woman's document. It was written proof that she had been released and was not an adulteress, without which she could be accused, destitute, for the rest of her life. Moses was not opening a door; he was limiting the damage on the other side of one already open.

And Jesus said to them, Because of your hardness of heart he wrote you this commandment.

And there is the verdict.

Hardness of heart — the phrase Mark used of the Pharisees in the synagogue (3:5), and close to what he has said twice now of the disciples themselves (6:52; 8:17): a heart that has thickened until it cannot feel.

So the legislation exists because of a defect in the people it was given to. It is not a description of what God wants. It is a piece of damage limitation for a world in which men will put their wives out whether or not it is permitted, and the law steps in to see that at least she leaves with a paper in her hand.

Notice also the pronoun, which is very sharp: he wrote you this commandment. Not us. Not Israel. You. The concession was granted to people like you, for hardness like yours, and you have turned it into an entitlement and come here asking how far it extends.

This is worth having as a way of reading Scripture, because it is a distinction we constantly lose. There is a difference between what God permits and what God intends. The Bible regulates polygamy, slavery, warfare and divorce; it does not commend any of them, and in every case the regulation is a restraint on a fallen practice, not a blueprint. To read a concession as an endorsement is exactly the mistake being made in this conversation.

And there is a searching application in it. The question is this allowed? is very often the wrong question, and it is nearly always asked by somebody who has already decided what they want. A man who genuinely wants to please God does not begin by establishing the outer boundary of what he can get away with. That is the Hillel question, and Jesus will not answer it.

He goes back further than Moses instead, to a garden.
verseByVerse.note: A certificate of divorce freed a woman to remarry.

verseByVerse.quote: But from the beginning of creation, 'God made them male and female.' 'Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh.' So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But from the beginning of creation.

That is the move, and it is the most important thing in the passage. Asked about Deuteronomy, he goes to Genesis. Asked about the rules for ending a marriage, he goes to what a marriage is.

And notice the authority he treats Genesis with. He quotes two verses from Genesis 1 and 2 as settling the question — as God's own word about how human beings were made — and he treats the creation account as the deeper and earlier thing, behind and above the Mosaic regulation.

God made them male and female. Genesis 1:27. Marriage is not a human invention that societies happen to have adopted and may therefore adapt. It is built into the way people were made, before any law, before any culture, before the fall.

Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife. Genesis 2:24, and there are two verbs in it worth separating.

Leave — a public, decisive break with the strongest tie a person has had up to that point. Marriage begins with a departure, and a marriage in which one party has never actually left home, emotionally or practically, will feel the fault line for decades.

Hold fast — the Hebrew behind it means to be glued or welded, and it is used of a man clinging to God himself (Deut. 10:20). It is not a mood. It is a decision that is renewed and does not depend on how the week has gone.

And the two shall become one flesh. So they are no longer two but one flesh.

Jesus adds the last clause himself; it is his comment on the text. And it is a statement of fact rather than an ideal to be aimed at. Something has actually happened. Two people have been made into a single unit, and the union is real whatever either of them feels about it on a given morning.

Which is why the ending of a marriage is never merely administrative. You cannot separate one flesh without tearing something, and everyone who has been through it knows this in their body long before they can say it.

What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.

And here is the sentence, and the weight of it is in the two agents.

God has joined. That is the claim, and it is enormous. The joining is not done by the couple, or the officiant, or the registrar, or the guests. God does it. Which means that in every genuine marriage — including yours, including marriages between people who have never given him a thought — there is a divine act, and the two people are dealing with something they did not make.

Let not man separate. Man did not do the joining, and man is therefore not competent to do the undoing.

So take the plain practical word for anyone currently married, because this verse is not primarily about ending marriages; it is about how you regard the one you are in.

You are not in an arrangement that continues as long as it works. You are in something God did. And that changes what to do on the bad days — the year that is going wrong, the stretch where you feel nothing, the point at which the thought first arrives that you might have made a mistake. The question in that hour is not is this still working? It is: what did God join, and what am I doing to keep it?

Marriages are rarely separated by a decision. They are separated by a thousand small permissions — the conversation not had, the resentment kept, the friendship at work that becomes the place you are understood. Let not man separate is a command about all of that, and it is addressed to the man in the mirror.

parallels.desc: male and female he created them

verseByVerse.quote: And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter. And he said to them, "Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her, and if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in the house the disciples asked him again about this matter.

The pattern of this Gospel once more: a public statement, then a private question, and the men who get the fuller answer are the ones who ask.

And notice that they ask again. Whatever he said outside, they want it gone over. The teaching had clearly landed as something startling, and it is worth remembering that: the disciples were as taken aback as anyone. Matthew records what they said in the house — if such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry (Matt. 19:10). These were not men who found this easy.

Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her.

Two things in that sentence would have startled a first-century Jewish ear.

First, the act itself is named as adultery. Under the rabbinic system, a properly executed divorce ended the marriage, and a man who then remarried had done nothing wrong; the certificate had cleared him. Jesus says the certificate does not touch what God joined.

Second — and this is the astonishing part — the wrong is done against her.

In Jewish law, adultery was understood as an offence against a husband: a man could not commit adultery against his own wife, because she was, in the legal sense, the injured party's property rather than the injured party. Jesus says the woman is the one sinned against.

Take the measure of that in a conversation which began with men debating the limits of a man's freedom to dispose of a person. Nobody in verse 2 mentioned the wife. Jesus puts her at the centre of the sentence and names her as the one who has been wronged.

Wherever the gospel has gone, that has followed. The elevation of women in the societies Christianity touched is not a modern correction applied to an embarrassing text; it starts here, in a house in Perea, with a rabbi telling twelve men that a discarded wife has been sinned against.

And if she divorces her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.

And now a clause found only in Mark, and it tells you who he is writing for.

Under Jewish law a woman could not normally initiate a divorce at all. Under Roman law she could, and did — it was common among the propertied classes, and Herodias herself had done it (6:17). Mark is writing to the church at Rome, where the women in his congregation had legal options no woman in Galilee had, and he includes the sentence that applies to them.

It is a small thing and it says something large: the standard is the same in both directions. There is no double standard here, no allowance for the husband that is denied the wife. What God joined, neither party may separate.

Is there then no ground at all for divorce? Mark gives the principle without qualification, but he is not the only witness. Matthew records the exception, except for sexual immorality (Matt 19:9), and Paul adds desertion by an unbelieving spouse: the brother or sister is not enslaved (1 Cor 7:15). Some Christians hold that there are no grounds at all, only separation; others allow divorce for many reasons. The more likely reading is that adultery and desertion are real grounds, and that in those cases the innocent party is free to remarry. That is not a list of loopholes; even then reconciliation is better where it is possible.

What of those who divorced on other grounds and remarried? The sin is real and should be confessed. But a second marriage, once made, is a marriage, and the answer is not to break it, which would add another sin (cf. Deut 24:1–4). Christ forgives the repentant, and they are to live faithfully where they now are.

And a word must be said plainly to the reader who is already divorced, perhaps remarried, and reading these hard sentences with a sinking heart — because this is a passage people live inside rather than merely study.

The standard has not moved, and it would be no kindness to pretend it has; a church that lowers it to seem gentle has only made grace unnecessary. But hear this clearly. There is no sin named here that the blood of Christ does not cover, and no marriage so broken — by your fault, another's, or the tangle of both — that grace cannot make something new of what remains.

The gospel does not meet you in the marriage you should have had. It meets you in the life you actually have, and it meets you there with a Saviour who came to give his life as a ransom for many (v. 45) — the divorced among them. Whatever your history, the same command stands for today and the same mercy stands under it: repent where you must, receive what he freely gives, and walk forward forgiven.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish law did not allow a wife to divorce her husband, but Roman law did; Mark’s wording covers both.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them, and the disciples rebuked them. But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, "Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were bringing children to him that he might touch them.

Parents, presumably — Luke's word suggests some were infants (Luke 18:15). It was ordinary in that world to bring a child to a respected rabbi for a blessing, and that is all these people are asking. Put your hand on him.

And the disciples rebuked them.

The verb is strong — the same one used of Jesus rebuking demons and Peter rebuking Jesus. They did not gently discourage. They told them off.

And their reasoning was almost certainly sound by any ordinary measure. The Master is on the road to Jerusalem. He has been teaching all day, he has just handled a hostile delegation on divorce, he is tired, and there is a queue of adults with real questions. Children are not a priority. Somebody has to manage the diary.

It is worth noticing that this is the second time in two chapters the disciples have tried to control access to Jesus — they stopped a man casting out demons because he was not one of them (9:38), and now they are turning away parents with babies. There is something in religious people that gravitates toward the door.

But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant.

Mark alone records this, and it is a remarkable word.

Mark uses the same word of the ten when they are furious with James and John later in this chapter (v. 41). This is not mild disapproval. Jesus was angry — and he was angry with his own disciples, and the cause was that children were being kept away from him.

Hold both halves of that. The Son of God, days from the cross, becomes visibly angry because somebody turned away a queue of toddlers.

So if you have ever wondered whether the small and unimpressive matter to Christ, this verse settles it in the strongest terms available. What made him angry was not the interruption. It was the gatekeeping.

Let the children come to me; do not hinder them.

Two commands, and the second is the one to sit with. Do not hinder. The word is the one used in Acts when the Ethiopian asks what prevents me from being baptised? (Acts 8:36).

And it is worth asking who hinders children now, because it is rarely done deliberately. It is done by treating them as a distraction to be managed until they are old enough to matter — the church that has no room for them, the family in which faith is discussed but never with them, the parent who is too tired at bedtime and always will be. Nobody rebukes anybody. The children simply do not get brought.

For to such belongs the kingdom of God.

Note the wording carefully: to such, not to these. He is not saying that children are automatically in and adults are not. He is saying the kingdom belongs to people of this kind — and the next verse will say what kind that is.

Does this passage support baptizing infants? Many Christians think so. They read do not hinder them as a word about bringing children into the covenant community and giving them its sign. But no one is baptized here. Jesus blesses the children; he does not baptize them, and the point he draws is about receiving the kingdom like a child (v. 15), with empty hands. The more likely reading is that baptism belongs to those who have come to faith, while the children of believers are brought to Christ in prayer and teaching from the start.

And what of children who die young? Scripture gives no age of accountability and no formula. Some believe that all who die in infancy are saved, others only the children of believers; the safest course is to say no more than Scripture says. But it gives good ground for hope: David expected to go to his son (2 Sam 12:23), and the one who took children in his arms is the Judge who will do right (Gen 18:25).
verseByVerse.note: Children had little status in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it." And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I say to you, whoever does not receive the kingdom of God like a child shall not enter it.

The amen-formula again, for something he wants underlined. And it is stated negatively, which makes it a condition rather than a compliment: no one enters any other way.

So what is it about a child?

Not innocence. Let us be honest, since Scripture is: children are not morally blank. Anyone who has raised one knows that selfishness needs no teaching, and David says he was brought forth in iniquity (Ps. 51:5). Jesus is not proposing that we return to a purity that never existed.

Not simplicity of mind either, as though faith required us to stop thinking. This is the same Lord who told a scribe to love God with all his mind.

It is dependence. A small child in that world owned nothing, earned nothing, and could contribute nothing. He did not negotiate for his dinner; he was fed. He did not qualify for his place in the family; he was born into it. Everything he had came to him as a gift from somebody bigger, and he took it without embarrassment.

That is how the kingdom is received, and it is the exact opposite of how everything else in life is acquired.

Which is why this is so hard for competent adults. Every other sphere rewards the self-sufficient — the person who earns it, manages it, deserves it, brings something to the table. Here, the qualities that recommend you everywhere else are the disqualifying ones. Receive is the only verb on offer.

And it explains what happens next in the chapter. A child comes with empty hands and is welcomed. A rich man comes with full ones and cannot get in.

And he took them in his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.

He does not merely permit them. He picks them up.

The verb is that rare one again — enagkalisamenos, to fold in the arms — and it occurs twice in the whole New Testament, both in Mark: here and in chapter 9, where he set a child in the middle of the argument about greatness (9:36).

Peter remembered it both times. And this is a fisherman in Rome, decades later, telling a church that when the Lord of glory dealt with children he did not pat them on the head. He gathered them up.

The parents had asked for a touch. He gave them an embrace and a blessing, one child at a time, on a road going up to Jerusalem, while grown men stood by wishing he would get on.

And then he laid his hands on them — the same hands that had taken a dead girl by the hand (5:41) and lifted a convulsing boy off the ground (9:27), and which would within weeks be nailed down and unable to hold anybody at all.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him and asked him, "Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" And Jesus said to him, "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as he was setting out on his journey, a man ran up and knelt before him.

Everything about the approach is right, and Mark makes sure you notice.

He ran. A grown man of standing — Matthew tells us he was young, Luke that he was a ruler — running down a public road. In that culture men of position did not run; it was undignified. He does not care.

He knelt. In the dirt, in front of an itinerant teacher, in public.

Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?

And the question is the best question anybody asks in this Gospel. Nobody else asks it. The Pharisees ask about divorce law and signs from heaven; the disciples ask about seats and greatness; this man asks how to be saved.

So hold the whole picture before the verse turns hard, because the point of this passage is nearly always missed by making him a villain. He is not one. He is eager, humble, urgent, morally serious, and asking the right thing. If he walked into your church you would thank God for him.

One phrase in his question is worth marking, though, because it is the crack in it: what must I do to inherit? An inheritance is precisely the thing nobody does anything for. You receive it because of who you are in the family. He has used the language of gift and attached it to the language of achievement, and he does not notice.

The child two verses ago received. This man wants to know the price.

And Jesus said to him, Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.

This has been seized on for centuries as though Jesus were denying that he is good, or denying that he is God. He is doing neither — and notice that he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it.

He holds it up to the light.

Good Teacher was not a normal form of address; the rabbis did not use it. It is flattery — warm, sincere, and cheap, the kind of compliment a man pays to a respected figure on his way to asking a favour.

And Jesus stops him: do you know what you have just said? Goodness in the full and final sense belongs to God and to nobody else.

Which leaves exactly two possibilities, and the man never works out which one he is in. Either you should not have called me good — in which case you have come running and kneeling to the wrong person. Or the word is right, and you must reckon with who is standing in front of you.

It is not a denial of his deity. It is a door held open to it. He came asking what he must do, and the deeper question — the one he never reaches — is who is this?

And there is a hard little test in it for the way we talk about Jesus. It is possible to say very warm things about him and mean very little — to call him wonderful, loving, good, the greatest teacher who ever lived — and to be paying a compliment rather than making a confession. He is quite capable of stopping a man mid-sentence and asking whether he knows what he is saying.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says he was young, Luke that he was a ruler. Jesus does not deny his goodness; he asks the man to think about what he is saying.

verseByVerse.quote: You know the commandments: 'Do not murder, Do not commit adultery, Do not steal, Do not bear false witness, Do not defraud, Honor your father and mother.'" And he said to him, "Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You know the commandments.

He begins where the man began. The question was what must I do, so Jesus goes to the law — not because keeping it is how anyone is saved, but because it is the mirror the man needs to look into.

And he lists them, and the list is worth examining, because two things about it are odd.

First, they are all from the second table. Do not murder, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, defraud, honour your father and mother — every one concerns how you treat other people. Not one of the first four commandments is mentioned: no other gods, no idols, the name, the Sabbath.

That is deliberate, and it is a trap set with great gentleness. The man's problem is going to turn out to be a first-table problem — a rival god — and Jesus recites only the commandments the man can pass, and waits.

Second, one item on the list is not one of the Ten. Do not defraud is not from Exodus 20. It appears in the Law elsewhere — you shall not oppress your neighbor or rob him; the wages of a hired worker shall not remain with you all night (Lev. 19:13) — and it is about withholding what is owed, particularly to a labourer.

Jesus has slipped it in among the Ten, and it is the one commandment on that list that a wealthy landowner in first-century Palestine would have been most likely to break, and least likely to notice himself breaking. It is the sin of the account book, not the bedroom.

He is being probed, kindly, at the exact point of his danger, and he does not feel a thing.

And he said to him, Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.

Two things to say about that answer, and they pull in opposite directions.

It is not contested. Jesus does not say no you have not. There is no rebuke here, no exposure of secret vice. Mark's next sentence is that Jesus looked at him and loved him. Taken as most men would take such a claim — that he had been an upright, observant, decent man since boyhood — it appears to have been true.

And it is the most self-condemning sentence in the chapter. Because a man who has genuinely understood any commandment does not talk like this. All these I have kept is not the language of someone who has looked into the law and seen his own face. It is the language of a man who has treated it as a checklist and is now waiting to be told the remaining item.

Note also what he dropped. He called Jesus Good Teacher in verse 17; here he says simply Teacher. Something in the first exchange registered.

And notice what he still assumes, because it is the reason he cannot be helped yet: he thinks something is missing that can be added. He has the impression that the account is nearly complete and one more entry will balance it.

What he is about to be shown is not an additional item. It is that the whole account belongs to somebody else.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus lists the commandments about one’s neighbour; “do not defraud” is not one of the Ten in so many words; it may stand for the tenth, against coveting (cf. Lev 19:13).

parallels.desc: the second table of the Ten Commandments

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, "You lack one thing: go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me." Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus, looking at him, loved him.

Mark alone records this, and it is one of the tenderest half-sentences in the Bible.

The verb for looking means to fix the eyes on somebody — a deliberate, held gaze, not a glance. And then: he loved him. It is the only place in this Gospel where we are told that Jesus loved a particular individual.

Take that before anything else, because everything hard that follows must be read inside it. The words about to be said are not said coldly. They are the words of a man who has looked at this eager, moral, self-deceived young person and been moved with love for him.

You lack one thing.

Which must have been a relief for about two seconds. He came asking what was still outstanding, and here it is — a single item.

And then the item.

Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.

Is this required of every Christian? No, and the Gospels themselves settle it. Peter kept his house in Capernaum. Zacchaeus gave away half, and was told salvation had come to his house that day (Luke 19:8–9). Joseph of Arimathea was rich and remained so, and it was his money that bought the tomb. Jesus does not issue this command to anybody else in the New Testament.

It is not a universal rule. It is a scalpel, and it goes to one man's one thing.

Because notice what the demand actually does. It exposes a first-table problem with a second-table instruction. The man had passed the whole list about neighbours; Jesus now finds out, in one sentence, whether he has any other gods — and the answer comes back immediately.

And see the shape of the offer, because it is not asceticism. Jesus does not tell him to be poorer. He tells him to trade: give away treasure on earth and receive treasure in heaven, which is the better end of any bargain ever offered to a human being. And then the real prize, which is not the treasure at all — come, follow me. He is being invited to join the Twelve.

This is the only person in Mark called personally by Jesus who says no.

Disheartened by the saying, he went away sorrowful.

Mark's first word means his face fell — the same root used of a darkening sky. You can see it happen.

And then he goes. Slowly, we may imagine, but he goes.

And here is the thing that should stop us: the sorrow is real. He is not angry, not scoffing, not arguing. He knows exactly what he is refusing and he refuses it anyway, and he is miserable about it. There is such a thing as sorrow that is not repentance — grief over the cost of obedience that never actually obeys — and this man is its portrait.

For he had great possessions. Mark gives the reason last, flat, without comment. And there is a bitter irony in the phrasing, because it is exactly the wrong way round. He did not have great possessions. They had him.

And notice what Jesus does not do. He does not call after him. He does not soften the terms, offer a smaller figure, or suggest they discuss it over a meal. The Son of God, who loved this man, watched him walk away and let him go.

That is what love looks like when it will not lie to you. A love that lowered the price would have been the crueller thing — it would have sent him home comfortable, with his idol intact, thinking himself safe.

Mark records no second visit. The saddest verse in the Gospel is a man walking down a road with everything he came for still in his hands.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark notes that Jesus looked at him and loved him.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, "How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!" And the disciples were amazed at his words. But Jesus said to them again, "Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God! It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus looked around and said to his disciples. He watches the man go, and then turns to the twelve. What follows is not aimed at the departing figure; it is for the men staying.

How difficult it will be for those who have wealth to enter the kingdom of God!

And the disciples were amazed at his words.

To understand why they were staggered, you have to know what they had been taught. In the Old Testament, prosperity is repeatedly a sign of God's favour — Abraham, Job, Solomon. The popular theology of the day drew the obvious conclusion: a rich man is a blessed man, and his wealth is the evidence.

And there is a practical version of the same logic. A rich man can afford to be generous, keep the law scrupulously, endow a synagogue, give alms. He has the leisure to be devout. If anyone was going to make it, surely he was.

Jesus has just said the opposite, and the ground moves under them.

But Jesus said to them again, Children, how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God!

He says it a second time, and the second time he takes the qualification off.

Read it carefully. Verse 23 was about the wealthy. Verse 24 is about everybody: how difficult it is to enter the kingdom of God. Full stop. The rich man's case is not a special category — it is the general human case with the difficulty made visible.

And notice the word he begins with: Children. It is affectionate, and it is the only time he uses it in Mark. He is about to say the hardest thing in the chapter, and he opens it the way a father does.

It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.

The largest animal anyone in Palestine handled, and the smallest hole anyone in Palestine used.

And it is meant to be impossible. Two attempts to soften it have circulated for centuries and both should be laid aside.

The first says the Needle's Eye was a small gate in the Jerusalem wall through which a camel could squeeze if it knelt and was unloaded. There is no evidence such a gate existed; the story appears first in the eleventh century, and it turns the saying into a piece of encouraging advice — with a bit of humility and less baggage you can just about manage it — which is precisely the opposite of the point.

The second suggests the word should be cable rather than camel, since the Greek words are similar. The manuscripts do not support it, and it would not help: a ship's rope will not go through a needle either.

He meant impossible. The disciples' reaction in the next verse proves they heard it that way, and Jesus does not correct them.

And before this is filed under other people's problems, be honest about who is reading. Anyone with a home, a change of clothes, food that is not in question this week, and medical care within reach is, by every measure the world has ever known and by most measures it knows now, rich. This is not a passage about bankers. It is the camel and the needle, and we are the camel.
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration. The idea of a gate called “the Eye of the Needle” is a much later invention.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, "Then who can be saved?" Jesus looked at them and said, "With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were exceedingly astonished, and said to him, Then who can be saved?

Exceedingly astonished — stronger than the amazed of verse 24; the second saying has hit harder than the first.

And their question is exactly the right one, which is worth saying because the disciples so often get things wrong. Here they reason perfectly. If the man with every visible advantage — money, morality, eagerness, a clean record from boyhood — cannot get in, then nobody can.

They have understood that the difficulty is not a matter of degree. It is not that the rich have further to walk. It is that the door will not admit anyone under their own power.

And notice that the question is not academic. These are men who have left everything, and Peter will say so in two verses. If wealth cannot buy entry, neither can renunciation, and they have just worked that out.

Jesus looked at them.

Mark keeps showing us the eyes of Jesus in this chapter. He looked at the rich man and loved him (v. 21). He looked around at the disciples (v. 23). Now he fixes his gaze on them again before he answers, because what is coming is the most important sentence in the passage and he wants them looking back.

With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.

And there is the gospel, in a sentence, in answer to a question about salvation.

Take the first half seriously, because we habitually take it as an exaggeration. With man it is impossible. Not difficult. Not unlikely without help. Not achievable by the exceptionally devout. Impossible — with the same total force as the camel and the needle.

No one has ever saved himself, contributed to it, met God halfway, or made himself a better prospect. Not the rich man with his clean record, not Peter with his abandoned boat, not you.

That is why the disciples' question has only one possible answer, and it is not the poor, or the humble, or those who try hardest. The answer is: nobody — unless God does it.

But not with God. And there is the turn, and it is the whole of Christianity. The impossibility is real and it is total, and it is God's to solve, and he has solved it.

Which quietly demolishes the most popular religious sentence in the English language — that God helps those who help themselves. It is not in the Bible and it is the exact reverse of this verse. God saves those who cannot help themselves, which is everybody.

And notice how this is going to be accomplished, because it is not left in the air. The man saying it is on the road to Jerusalem, and in eighteen verses he will say why: to give his life as a ransom for many (v. 45). The impossibility is not overcome by a change in the requirements. It is overcome by a death.

So if you have ever looked honestly at yourself and concluded that you have no business being in the kingdom of God, you have understood verse 27 better than most. That is the correct assessment, and Jesus made it first, and then said the four words that answer it: but not with God.

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: Peter began to say to him, "See, we have left everything and followed you." Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions, and in the age to come eternal life. But many who are first will be last, and the last first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter began to say to him, See, we have left everything and followed you.

Mark's began to say is delicate, and possibly a kindness — as though Peter started the sentence and thought better of finishing it.

And it is Peter all over: honest, blurted, and not quite what it should be. The rich man has just failed to leave everything. Peter has watched him go, heard about the camel, heard that it is impossible, and what comes out is: we did, though.

There is a real question underneath — Matthew records it plainly: what then will we have? (Matt. 19:27) — and it is not an entirely unworthy one. These men had left boats, nets, a business, a home, a family. It cost them something real.

But it is the wrong question two verses after with man it is impossible. He is doing arithmetic again.

And look what Jesus does with it. He does not rebuke him. He answers generously, at length, with an amen-formula on the front.

There is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel.

The list is specific and it is the list of everything a man in that world had: his property, his siblings, his parents, his children, his land. And the qualifying phrase is not incidental — for my sake and for the gospel. Loss as such is not commended. Christians are not called to abandon families as a spiritual achievement; what is in view is what following him costs when it costs something.

Who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands.

And here is the promise, and it is stranger and better than it looks, because he repeats the list.

Note two things about the repetition. It is a hundredfold — the extravagant number from the parable of the sower (4:8, 20), the yield that made no agricultural sense. And it is now, in this time, not only in heaven.

So what is he promising? Not that a man who gives up a house will be given a hundred houses. He is promising the church.

Leave your family for Christ and you are given families — a hundred homes where you are welcome, a hundred mothers, brothers, sisters. That is not poetry; it is what actually happened. Paul greets a woman in Rome as his mother, who has been a mother to me as well (Rom. 16:13). The New Testament church is a network of houses and tables belonging to people who were not related to each other.

And it is still true, and it is one of the few promises of Christ that can be tested this month. The believer with no family who is never alone at Christmas. The convert cut off by his relatives who has more people praying for him than he can count. If your church is not that for somebody, this verse is an indictment before it is a comfort.

One item in the list is missing from the first list, and it is deliberate: with persecutions.

He puts it in the middle of the blessings, unemphasised, as one of the things received. Nobody left persecutions behind; everybody is given them. It is the most honest recruitment sentence ever spoken, and it is the reason this promise cannot be mistaken for a prosperity scheme. The hundredfold arrives with trouble attached, in the same parcel.

But many who are first will be last, and the last first.

And the last word is a warning aimed straight at the man who said we have left everything.

The kingdom's order is not a league table with the earliest and most sacrificial at the top. Peter is being told, gently, that having left the most does not put you first — and by the end of this same chapter James and John will have asked for the top two seats, and the ten will be furious, and the whole company will need to be told again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–52 — The Road to Jerusalem, the Ransom, and Bartimaeus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Walking ahead (vv. 32–34). Mark gives us a picture worth stopping over: a road going up to Jerusalem, Jesus striding out in front, and behind him a group that is amazed and a crowd that is frightened. Then he tells them, for the third and most detailed time, exactly what is waiting — handed over, condemned, given to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed, raised.

The request (vv. 35–45). And immediately James and John ask for the two best seats. The other ten are furious, which is not righteous indignation but competition. So Jesus lays down the law of his kingdom — the great one is the servant, the first is the slave — and grounds it in himself: he came to give his life as a ransom for many.

Jericho (vv. 46–52). The last miracle before Jerusalem. A blind beggar shouts a messianic title that none of the disciples has yet used, is told to be quiet by the crowd, shouts louder, throws away the only thing he owns, and follows Jesus up the road to the cross.

The chapter opened with a rich man who would not follow and closes with a beggar who did.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mark 10:45 is the theological centre of this Gospel, and every word repays weighing.

A ransom — lytron — was the price paid to set a captive free: the sum laid down to buy a slave out of bondage or a prisoner off the block. Jesus says his own life is that price.

And a ransom is a substitute — one thing given instead of another. He does not merely die for our benefit; he dies in our stead, the many going free because the One is handed over.

Behind it stands Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many, and by his knowledge shall the righteous one, my servant, make many to be accounted righteous (Isa. 53:11–12). That word many rings through the prophecy, and Jesus claims it as his own errand.

And to whom is the price paid? Not, as some early teachers imagined, to the devil, as though Satan held a rightful claim. The debt is owed to the justice of God — and God, in the person of his Son, pays it himself.

Here, then, is why he came. Not first to teach, or to heal, or even to model servanthood, though he did all three. To die in the room of sinners who could never buy themselves back. Nineteen verses earlier the disciples asked then who can be saved? and were told with man it is impossible, but not with God. This is how.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the same question — What do you want me to do for you? — asked twice in fifteen verses.

It is put to James and John in verse 36 and to a blind beggar in verse 51. Mark has done that deliberately, and the two answers are the whole chapter.

James and John ask for glory. They open with a blank cheque — we want you to do for us whatever we ask — and then name the two best seats in the kingdom. They get a redirection and a warning.

Bartimaeus asks for mercy, and then for sight. He gets exactly what he asks for, immediately.

Now: the question is still being asked, and most of us answer it more like the brothers than the beggar. The blank-cheque prayer — do what I have decided — dressed up religiously. The request framed around position, comfort, and being noticed.

And notice what makes Bartimaeus's answer better. It is not humility as a technique. He asked for the thing he actually needed, from someone he had correctly identified, having first asked for mercy rather than a favour. He had no credentials, no standing, and no way of repaying anybody — which is precisely the child of verse 15, arriving at the other end of the chapter with nothing in his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid. And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were on the road, going up to Jerusalem.

Going up is literal as well as idiomatic — Jerusalem stands more than three thousand feet above Jericho, and the road climbs steeply through the wilderness. But every Jew said up to Jerusalem regardless of the compass, because the city was up whatever the map said.

And Jesus was walking ahead of them.

Stop on that, because it is one of the great pictures in the Gospel and Mark has painted it in seven words.

He is out in front. Not being led, not being carried along by events, not swept toward Jerusalem by a movement that has got out of hand. He is setting the pace, and everybody else is behind.

Luke says the same thing with a different image: he set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51). Isaiah had said it centuries earlier in the Servant's own voice: I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame (Isa. 50:7).

Whatever else is true of the cross, it was not something that happened to him. He walked to it, faster than the men who were following.

And they were amazed, and those who followed were afraid.

Two groups and two reactions, and Mark distinguishes them.

They were amazed — the twelve. Something in the way he was walking frightened them. They had never seen him like this.
