And those who followed were afraid — the wider group of pilgrims and hangers-on, further back, and plainly picking up the atmosphere without understanding it.

So this is the shape of the procession: one man striding ahead with a set face, a cluster of disciples staring after him in alarm, and a straggle of frightened people behind them.

It is worth sitting with as a picture of the Christian life, because it is often exactly like this. There are stretches where following Christ means going in a direction that plainly costs something, where you do not understand what is happening, and where the honest description of your own state is amazed and afraid.

And the one thing the picture gives you is the one thing that helps: he is in front. Not waiting at the destination, not sending instructions from a distance. On the road, ahead, going first — and there is nothing coming that he has not already walked into.

And taking the twelve again, he began to tell them what was to happen to him.

He takes them aside — the third time he has done this — and tells them again. They have not understood the first two attempts, and he tries a third, in more detail than ever.

He is not going to let them arrive in Jerusalem without having been told.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem stands high in the hills; one always went “up” to it.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, "See, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death and deliver him over to the Gentiles. And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him. And after three days he will rise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
See, we are going up to Jerusalem.

The third passion prediction, and it is by a distance the most specific. The first (8:31) named the rejecting parties. The second (9:31) added the handing over. This one gives the sequence step by step, and there are eight items in it.

The Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the scribes. Handed over — that word again (9:31).

And they will condemn him to death. A verdict from the Jewish authorities.

And deliver him over to the Gentiles. Handed over a second time, and this is new. He has not said this before, and it is a shocking thing to say to Jewish men: the leaders of Israel will pass their own Messiah to the pagans.

It also explains what kind of death is coming. The Sanhedrin's own penalty was stoning; only Rome crucified. When he says Gentiles, he is saying cross, without using the word.

And they will mock him and spit on him, and flog him and kill him.

Four verbs, and every one of them is fulfilled in Mark 15 — the soldiers' purple robe and crown of thorns, the spitting, the scourging, the crucifixion (15:15–20).

The mocking and the spitting are worth noticing, because they are not necessary to an execution. Rome could have killed him efficiently. The contempt is gratuitous, and he names it in advance — which means he walked toward it knowing not only that he would die but that he would be humiliated first.

And it is written down centuries earlier in the Servant's own words: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isa. 50:6).

And after three days he will rise.

The eighth item, and it is on the end of every one of the three predictions. He has never once mentioned the death without the resurrection, and the disciples have never once mentioned the resurrection.

Now put the whole speech beside what happens next, because Mark has arranged it and it is devastating.

He has just described, in eight stages, being condemned, handed to pagans, mocked, spat on, whipped and executed. And the response of two of his closest friends — the next verse, with no interval — is to ask for the best seats.

They heard the word glory and nothing else. It is the third time he has told them and the third time they have taken from it only what they wanted.

Before that is condemned too quickly, it is worth admitting how familiar the mechanism is. We do the same with Scripture constantly — the promise received, the cost skipped over; the comfort taken, the command left; a sermon about the cross followed by a conversation about lunch. The disciples are not a different species. They are us, with better excuses, because at least they had never seen a resurrection.
verseByVerse.note: This third prediction is the fullest, naming the Gentiles, mocking, spitting and flogging.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.quote: And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him and said to him, "Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you." And he said to them, "What do you want me to do for you?" And they said to him, "Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came up to him.

Two of the three. These are the men who were on the mountain of transfiguration, who were in the room when the little girl was raised, and who are about to be taken further into Gethsemane than anybody else.

They are also the Sons of Thunder (3:17), and it shows.

Matthew, telling the same story, says their mother made the request (Matt. 20:20). Both are presumably true — she asked, they were standing there, and Mark, whose source is Peter, puts the responsibility exactly where the other ten put it in verse 41. Nobody was fooled about whose idea it was.

Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.

Look at the shape of that before you look at the content, because the form of the request is as revealing as the substance.

They do not ask a question. They ask him to agree to a question before they put it. It is a blank cheque, signed in advance — and it is exactly how a child approaches a parent when he already knows the answer will be no.

And it is worth holding this up against our praying, because the same move is available in more respectable clothing. There is a way of praying that is not asking but informing — a decision already taken, brought to God for endorsement rather than judgement. Lord, bless what I have determined to do. The words are reverent; the transaction is a blank cheque.

And he said to them, What do you want me to do for you?

He does not agree to the blank cheque. He asks them to say it out loud.

And mark this question, because Mark is going to ask it again in fifteen verses, of a blind beggar on the Jericho road (v. 51). The same words, to two very different people, and the two answers are the whole point of the chapter.

Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your glory.

Now the request, and it is worse than mere ambition.

The right and left hand of a king were the two places of highest honour in the realm — the prime minister and the second-in-command, the men who share the throne room. They are not asking to be useful. They are asking for the top two positions in the government of the universe, and they are asking for both, which means they have already worked out that the other ten are not getting them.

There is something almost admirable buried in it, and it should be said. They believe him. He has just told them he is going to be spat on and killed, and they are still asking about his glory — which means that somewhere in those thick heads is a genuine conviction that this man is going to reign. That is more than the crowd had.

But it sits on top of a deafness so complete it is hard to credit. He named eight stages of his own execution, and the sentence they took away was after three days he will rise, and the plan they made was about seating.

And notice where he is standing while they ask. On a road, going up, walking ahead of them, toward the day when there will in fact be a man on his right and a man on his left in his glory — and they will be two thieves, and the glory will be a cross (15:27).
verseByVerse.note: To sit at a king’s right and left was the place of highest honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?" And they said to him, "We are able." And Jesus said to them, "The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized, but to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You do not know what you are asking.

Not you should not have asked. Not how dare you. He tells them, gently, that they have no idea what they have just requested.

Which is the first mercy in the passage and it is one we should want. God does not grant our prayers according to our understanding of them. If he did, most of us would have been destroyed years ago by things we asked for confidently. There is a great deal to be thankful for in the prayers he has declined.

Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?

Two images, and both are heavier than they sound.

The cup, in the Old Testament, is regularly the cup of God's wrath — in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine... all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Ps. 75:8; cf. Isa. 51:17; Jer. 25:15). And it is the word Jesus will use in Gethsemane, on his face in the dirt: remove this cup from me (14:36).

The baptism is not water. It is being overwhelmed — and the Psalms use exactly that picture of catastrophe: all your breakers and your waves have gone over me (Ps. 42:7).

So he is asking them: can you be drowned in what is about to drown me? Can you drink what I am going to drink?

And they said to him, We are able.

Instantly, and with no idea what they have agreed to.

It is easy to laugh at, and Peter will do the same thing at the last supper (14:31). But do not miss what is right in it: they mean it. These men are not cynics. They think they can, and they want to, and their loyalty at that moment is genuine — it is just standing on nothing.

The cup that I drink you will drink, and with the baptism with which I am baptized, you will be baptized.

And here is the astonishing reply, and it is not sarcasm. It is a prophecy, and it came true.

James was the first of the Twelve to be killed. Herod Agrippa had him put to the sword in Jerusalem, in one verse, about a decade later (Acts 12:2).

John outlived every one of them, and was exiled to a penal island for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus (Rev. 1:9), writing the last book of the Bible as an old man in trouble.

They asked for thrones and were promised suffering, and they got the suffering, and they did not fall away when it came. Whatever else this exchange says about them, it does not end badly.

But to sit at my right hand or at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared.

Two things in that sentence.

It is not a denial that he is God. This is the Son speaking of the ordered work of the Trinity, in which allotting places in the kingdom belongs to the Father — the same submission he shows in Gethsemane and on the cross. He does not say the seats do not exist, or that no one assigns them. He says it is not his to hand out on request.

And the places are prepared. There is a divine allocation, already made, and it is not open to lobbying. You cannot secure a place in the kingdom of God by asking for it, deserving it, arriving early, or knowing the right person — and there is enormous relief in that for anyone who has ever felt they were losing a race they did not want to be running.
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is the Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out; “baptism” pictures being overwhelmed by suffering. James was later killed by Herod Agrippa.

parallels.desc: the waters have come up to my neck
I have a baptism to be baptized with

verseByVerse.quote: And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John. And Jesus called them to him and said to them, "You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the ten heard it, they began to be indignant at James and John.

The word is the one used of Jesus when the children were turned away (v. 14), and here it means exactly what it looks like: they were furious.

And Mark, characteristically, does not tell you why — because he does not need to. The ten are not upset on theological grounds. Nobody says how could you speak like that when he has just told us he will be killed? They are angry because two men made a move for something all twelve wanted, and got there first.

They had already argued about this on a road in chapter 9 and been given a child and a lesson. Nothing has taken. The ambition simply went underground and has now surfaced as outrage at somebody else's ambition — which is the usual way it appears in religious company. Almost nobody says I want to be the greatest. A great many people are quietly annoyed when somebody else is treated as though they were.

And Jesus called them to him. All twelve. He does not deal with James and John separately or take the ten's side. The disease is general and the treatment is given to the whole group.

You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.

He points at the world they can see. Rome is the model — a system in which authority runs downward as pressure, and greatness is measured by how many people have to do what you say.

And there is a barb in those who are considered rulers. Their eminence is a matter of general opinion; it is what everybody agrees to call them.

But it shall not be so among you.

Eight words, and they are among the most disobeyed in the New Testament.

It is not advice. It is a flat prohibition on importing the world's model of authority into the church — and church history is very largely the story of ignoring it, in cathedrals and in small congregations alike, wherever a man has discovered that a position in the things of God can be used to make other people smaller.

Whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be slave of all.

Two rungs, and the second is lower than the first.

Servant is diakonos — the man who waited at table. A servant has a role and can, at the end of the day, go home.

Slave is doulos, and there is no going home. A slave has no time of his own, no rights, and no choice about whom he serves.

And once again the ambition is not forbidden — whoever would be great, whoever would be first. He does not say stop wanting to matter. He redirects the wanting and gives it a road, and the road runs downwards.

Which makes this measurable rather than merely admirable. You cannot be a servant in general. Serving happens to particular people at particular times, and it shows up in a diary and a bank statement. And slave of all removes the last escape, which is choosing whom to serve — the interesting, the grateful, the influential, the ones who will notice.

All. Including the ten who are furious with you, and the two who went behind your back.

verseByVerse.quote: For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.

This is the summit of Mark's Gospel, and it arrives as a because. He has just told them to go to the bottom, and this is the reason: not a principle, but a Person, and what that Person is walking toward.

Take it clause by clause.

Even the Son of Man. That title is not a modest one. It comes from Daniel 7, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven and is given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him (Dan. 7:13–14).

Read that last phrase again. In Daniel, the whole world serves him. And he says he came not to be served.

The one figure in Scripture entitled to universal service arrived and declined it.

But to serve. Which he did, visibly, all the way through this Gospel — but the word here has a specific weight, because he is about to say what the serving cost.

And to give his life as a ransom.

The word is lytron, and it belongs to the marketplace, not the temple. A ransom was the price paid to set a captive free: the sum laid down to buy a slave out of bondage or a prisoner off the block.

So a price is being named, and the currency is his life.

For many. And this is the sharpest word in the verse, because the Greek is anti, which does not mean on behalf of in a vague way. It means in the place of — one thing given instead of another, the way a substitute steps into a queue.

He does not merely die for our benefit. He dies in our stead. The many go free because the One is handed over.

Does for many mean that Christ died only for some? The phrase comes from Isaiah 53, where the servant bore the sin of many, the great number set against the one. Many Christians read it as meaning simply “all”; Reformed Christians read it as the definite people for whom his death actually paid. The more likely reading is the second, since a ransom paid sets the captive free. But his death is sufficient for all and offered to all, and no one who comes to him is turned away.

And behind the whole sentence stands Isaiah 53, which every Jew there had heard read aloud: he poured out his soul to death... he bore the sin of many, and makes intercession for the transgressors (Isa. 53:12). That word many tolls through the prophecy, and Jesus picks it up and claims it as his own errand.

And to whom is the ransom paid? Some early teachers imagined it was paid to the devil, as though Satan held a rightful claim over us that God had to buy out. He does not. He is a thief with stolen goods (3:27), and God owes him nothing. The debt is owed to the justice of God himself — and God, in the person of his Son, pays it himself.

Which means there is no drama here between an angry Father and a reluctant Son. It is one God, resolving in himself what could not be resolved any other way.

So here is why he came. Not first to teach, though he taught as no one ever has. Not first to heal, though he emptied whole villages of illness. Not even to model servanthood, though he has just done that.

He came to die in the room of sinners who could never buy themselves back.

Nineteen verses ago the disciples asked then who can be saved? and he told them it was impossible with man and possible with God. This is how. Not by a lowering of the requirement — by a payment.

And notice, last, where this sentence is placed. It is not in a sermon on the atonement. It is the closing argument in a squabble about who gets the best seats. Twelve men are jostling for position, and he settles it by telling them that he is going to be sold for their freedom.

Everything in the Christian life that is asked of you is asked on the basis of that. You are not told to serve because service is noble. You are told to serve because the one who owned everything went to the bottom, and stayed there, until it killed him — and bought you on the way down.
verseByVerse.note: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jericho. And as he was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a great crowd, Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside. And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out and say, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent. But he cried out all the more, "Son of David, have mercy on me!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they came to Jericho. The last city before the climb. From here it is fifteen miles up through the wilderness to Jerusalem, and Passover is days away, so the road is thick with pilgrims.

Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, the son of Timaeus, was sitting by the roadside.

Mark gives us his name, and that is unusual enough to be worth noticing. Almost nobody healed in this Gospel is named — not the leper, not the paralytic, not the man among the tombs, not the woman with the bleeding. This man is named twice over, in Aramaic and in translation, along with his father.

The likeliest reason is the best one: the church knew him. Bartimaeus was still around when Mark wrote, or well enough remembered that people could say yes, we know him. Which makes this a signed piece of testimony.

Matthew mentions two blind men, and Luke places the healing as Jesus drew near to Jericho (Luke 18:35). Mark names the one the church knew; he does not say there was only one. And in Jesus’ day there were two Jerichos, the old site and Herod’s new town nearby, so one could be leaving one and approaching the other. The accounts do not contradict each other.

And his position is the whole of his life in one phrase: sitting by the roadside. Not going anywhere. Beside the road while everybody else walks up it.

And when he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out.

He cannot see anything. All he has is the noise of a crowd and a name passed down the line — and he acts on it instantly.

Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!

Now stop, because this is one of the most theologically significant sentences anyone speaks in the whole of Mark.

Son of David is a messianic title. It is the promise to David that God would establish his son's throne forever (2 Sam. 7:12–16), the shoot from the stump of Jesse, the king who is coming. And it has not been used once in this Gospel. Not by the crowds, who thought he was Elijah or a prophet. Not by the Pharisees. Not by the twelve — Peter said you are the Christ and was told to keep quiet about it.

A blind beggar on a roadside shouts it in public, in the hearing of hundreds, days before Passover.

Everyone in this chapter who can see has misunderstood him. The rich man called him Good Teacher and went home. James and John asked for thrones. And the man who cannot see anything at all names him correctly on the first attempt.

Have mercy on me. And look at what he asks for. Not heal me, not yet. Mercy — which is what you ask for when you have no claim of any kind, and the only ground of the request is the character of the person you are asking.

The rich man asked what he must do. James and John asked for what they thought they had earned. The beggar asks for mercy, and he is the only one in the chapter who gets exactly what he came for.

And many rebuked him, telling him to be silent.

The crowd turns on him. That word rebuked again — the disciples used it on the parents with children in verse 13.

Why? Because he is an embarrassment. There is a distinguished rabbi passing with a following, on a solemn pilgrimage road, and a beggar is bawling at him. Somebody should keep him quiet.

But he cried out all the more, Son of David, have mercy on me!

He does not stop. He gets louder, and he says the same thing again.

He has nothing to lose and he knows it. He is blind, destitute, sitting in the dust, and this is the one chance he will ever have — and being disapproved of by respectable people is not a price he is troubled by.

Which is worth putting to anyone who has been quietly discouraged out of coming to Christ: by a family that finds it excessive, by a church that made them feel they did not fit, by the sense that they are too much, too messy, too late. The crowd told this man to be quiet, and the crowd was wrong, and Jesus stopped for the shouting.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 15 miles north-east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. Bartimaeus means “son of Timaeus.” “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stopped and said, "Call him." And they called the blind man, saying to him, "Take heart. Get up; he is calling you." And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus stopped.

Three words, and they may be the loveliest in the chapter.

Consider the scene they interrupt. This is the road to Jerusalem. He has been walking ahead of everybody with a set face (v. 32). He has three times told his disciples what is waiting at the top of that hill — the mocking, the spitting, the flogging, the killing. There is a crowd around him, a Passover ahead of him, and a cross at the end of the week.

And he stops, in the road, because a blind man is shouting.

The Son of God on his way to die halts the whole procession for one beggar whom everybody else was trying to silence. Nothing in his life was ever too urgent for a person.

And said, Call him.

And notice how he does it. He does not go over. He tells the people who have been telling the man to shut up to go and fetch him.

That is not laziness; it is deliberate. The crowd that hindered is made to be the crowd that brings.

And they called the blind man, saying to him, Take heart. Get up; he is calling you.

And listen to the change in their voices. Thirty seconds ago they were telling him to be quiet. Now they are encouraging him: Take heart. Get up.

It is the same people. Nothing has changed except that Jesus stopped — and the moment he took an interest, so did they.

There is a small, true observation about human nature in that, and a warning for anybody in a church: the person you find embarrassing, inconvenient, too loud, too needy, may be the one Christ is calling. It is worth being careful whom you shush.

And throwing off his cloak, he sprang up and came to Jesus.

Mark's details are so specific here that they strongly suggest an eyewitness account, and the cloak is the one to stop on.

A beggar's outer cloak was not a garment. It was his equipment. He spread it on the ground in front of him to catch the coins people threw; it was his bed at night and his shelter from cold; in a legal sense it was the one possession the Law protected, because a cloak taken in pledge had to be returned by sundown (Ex. 22:26–27).

It was, quite literally, everything he owned.

And he throws it off — flings it aside, in the road, blind, with no idea where it will land or whether he will ever find it again.

Now set that against the man at the start of this chapter. A rich man was asked to give up his possessions for Christ and went away sorrowful, because he had a great many. A blind beggar, asked for nothing at all, threw away the only thing he had because it might slow him down.

Mark has put them at the two ends of the same chapter. One had much and would not let go of any of it. One had one thing and did not think about it twice.

He sprang up. The verb means to leap. A blind man, jumping to his feet and moving toward a voice.

He does not know how far it is. He does not know what is in the way. He heard he is calling you, and that was enough.
verseByVerse.note: A beggar’s cloak was spread to collect coins and was also his covering at night.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to him, "What do you want me to do for you?" And the blind man said to him, "Rabbi, let me recover my sight." And Jesus said to him, "Go your way; your faith has made you well." And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus said to him, What do you want me to do for you?

The same question, word for word, that he asked James and John fifteen verses ago (v. 36). Mark has done this deliberately, and everything he wants to say about this chapter is in the two answers.

They opened with a blank cheque and asked for the two best seats in the kingdom. This man is asked the identical question, and the difference is total.

It is also worth noticing that Jesus asks at all. It could hardly be more obvious what a blind beggar wants. But he will not do things to people over their heads; he asks the man to say it, out loud, in his own words — which is a dignity nobody had shown him in years.

And the blind man said to him, Rabbi, let me recover my sight.

He asks for the one thing he actually needs, in one clause, with no preamble.

And Mark keeps the word he used: Rabbouni — a heightened form, more personal than the ordinary Rabbi, something like my Master. It appears twice in the New Testament: here, and on the lips of Mary Magdalene in the garden when she recognises the risen Christ (John 20:16).

Note also what he does not ask for. Not money, which is what he had been asking passers-by for all his life and which would have solved his immediate problem. Not compensation, not a place, not a position. Sight — which, once given, would end his livelihood and require him to start again at whatever age he was.

He asks for the thing that will cost him his old life.

And Jesus said to him, Go your way; your faith has made you well.

No touch. No spittle, no fingers, no clay — and no second attempt, unlike the man at Bethsaida (8:22–25). Just a sentence.

Your faith has made you well — the same thing he said to the woman who touched his cloak (5:34). Something more than eyesight has happened here.

And note where the faith was located: not in the quality of his theology, though he got the title right, and not in his persistence, though he had plenty. Faith saves because of who it takes hold of, and this man took hold of the Son of David with both hands and would not be shouted down.

Go your way. He is released. He is free to do exactly as he likes — to go home, to find his cloak, to start a life, to tell Jericho what happened.

And immediately he recovered his sight and followed him on the way.

And he does not go his way. He goes Christ's.

Given his freedom and his eyes in the same breath, the first thing he does with both is get on the road to Jerusalem behind the man who healed him — and Mark's phrase is on the way, which in this Gospel is never merely geography. The way is the road to the cross, and it is the road the disciples have been walking amazed and afraid.

He is the last person healed in Mark before the passion. And he is the only one who is named, who names Jesus correctly, who throws away everything he owns, and who ends the account walking up the hill with him.

So the chapter closes where it could not have been predicted to close. It began with a wealthy, moral, eager man who asked the right question, was looked at and loved, and went home with everything he came with.

It ends with a blind beggar in the dust, with one cloak to his name, who shouted until he was heard, threw the cloak away, asked for mercy, and followed Jesus to Jerusalem.

That is what the kingdom of God looks like from the inside — and it is exactly what he said in verse 15, when he picked a child up off the road: the ones who get in are the ones who come with nothing and simply receive.

parallels.desc: the eyes of the blind opened

10.theology:
Divorce, and what Mark leaves out. Matthew twice records an exception — except for sexual immorality (Matt. 5:32; 19:9) — and Mark records none, while adding, for his Roman readers, the case of a wife who divorces her husband. Not a contradiction but a difference of purpose: Mark gives the principle in its unguarded, creation-order form, the way a thing is stated when you want its full weight felt; Matthew, writing where the rabbis argued endlessly over grounds, records the one qualification Jesus allowed. Paul adds a second — the believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is not enslaved (1 Cor. 7:15). So the Reformed churches have long recognised two grounds on which the bond may be broken and the innocent party freed: adultery and desertion, and no others. Mark's silence is not denial but a refusal to lead with the exception — because the moment the exception becomes the headline, hardness of heart starts hunting for a way in.

"Why do you call me good?" is not a denial that Jesus is good or that he is God, and he never withdraws the word or corrects the man for using it. He holds it up to the light. Good Teacher was easy flattery; Jesus stops him and asks whether he knows what he is saying. Either the word should not have been used — or it is right, and the man must reckon with who is standing in front of him. A door held open, not a door shut.

And v. 45 is the theological centre of Mark. A ransom (lytron) is the price paid to buy a captive out of bondage. The word rendered for is anti — in the place of, one thing given instead of another — so he does not merely die for our benefit but in our stead. Behind it stands Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa. 53:12), that word many tolling through the prophecy and claimed here by Jesus as his own errand. And the price is not paid to the devil, as some early teachers imagined — he is a thief with stolen goods (3:27) and God owes him nothing. The debt is owed to the justice of God, and God in the person of his Son pays it himself.
10.examples:
Then: the same question asked twice, fifteen verses apart. What do you want me to do for you? — to James and John (v. 36), and to a blind beggar (v. 51).

The brothers open with a blank cheque — we want you to do for us whatever we ask — and name the two best seats in the kingdom. Bartimaeus asks for mercy, and then for sight.

Now: most of us pray more like the brothers than the beggar. The blank cheque dressed up religiously — a decision already taken, brought to God for endorsement rather than judgement. The request framed around position, comfort, and being noticed.

And note what actually makes Bartimaeus's answer better. Not humility as a technique. He had correctly identified who was passing — Son of David, a messianic title not one of the disciples had yet used out loud — and he asked for mercy, which is what you ask for when you have no claim of any kind and the only ground of the request is the character of the one you are asking.

And then there is the cloak (v. 50). A beggar's outer cloak was his equipment: spread on the ground to catch coins, his bed at night, his shelter, and the one possession the Law protected (Ex. 22:26–27). It was everything he owned. He flung it aside, blind, with no idea where it landed, because it might slow him down by four seconds.

Set that against the man at the start of the chapter, asked to give up his possessions and going away sorrowful because he had a great many. One had much and would not let go of any of it; one had a single thing and did not think about it twice. Mark put them at opposite ends of the same chapter on purpose.

11.title: Leaves Without Fruit
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples <sup>2</sup>and said to them, “Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. <sup>3</sup>If anyone says to you, ‘Why are you doing this?’ say, ‘The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.’” <sup>4</sup>And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. <sup>5</sup>And some of those standing there said to them, “What are you doing, untying the colt?” <sup>6</sup>And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go. <sup>7</sup>And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. <sup>8</sup>And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields. <sup>9</sup>And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! <sup>10</sup>Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!” <sup>11</sup>And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve. <sup>12</sup>On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. <sup>13</sup>And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. <sup>14</sup>And he said to it, “May no one ever eat fruit from you again.” And his disciples heard it. <sup>15</sup>And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. <sup>16</sup>And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple. <sup>17</sup>And he was teaching them and saying to them, “Is it not written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations’? But you have made it a den of robbers.” <sup>18</sup>And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. <sup>19</sup>And when evening came they went out of the city. <sup>20</sup>As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. <sup>21</sup>And Peter remembered and said to him, “Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered.” <sup>22</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God. <sup>23</sup>Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. <sup>24</sup>Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours. <sup>25</sup>And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses.” <sup>27</sup>And they came again to Jerusalem. And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him, <sup>28</sup>and they said to him, “By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?” <sup>29</sup>Jesus said to them, “I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>30</sup>Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me.” <sup>31</sup>And they discussed it with one another, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ <sup>32</sup>But shall we say, ‘From man’?”—they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. <sup>33</sup>So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And Jesus said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.”
11.overview:
After ten chapters of hushing everyone who worked out who he was, Jesus stages a public claim to the throne — and does it on a borrowed donkey's foal, exactly as Zechariah said the king would come. The crowd throws down cloaks as they did for Jehu, spreads leafy branches cut from the fields, and shouts the Passover psalm at him: Hosanna — save now. They are right about who he is and wrong about what he came to do, and by Friday the road is empty.

Then he goes into the temple, looks around at everything, and leaves, because it is late.

What he does the next morning is therefore not a loss of temper. He had seen all of it the night before, slept on it, and walked two miles back. And Mark wraps the temple inside a fig tree to tell you what it means: a tree in full leaf and no fruit, cursed on the way in; the tables overturned; and on the third morning the tree dead to its roots. Israel's worship that week was magnificent from a distance. He came near, and found leaves.

Out of the dead tree comes the great teaching on faith, prayer and forgiveness. And the chapter ends with the Sanhedrin asking the right question — by what authority? — and being handed one question in return that would have led them home, and spending it instead on a calculation about the crowd.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — The Entry, the Fig Tree, and the Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The entry (vv. 1–11). After nine chapters of silencing everyone who worked out who he was, Jesus stages a public claim to be king — and does it on a borrowed donkey's foal, exactly as Zechariah said. The crowd sings the Passover psalm at him. Then he walks into the temple, looks around at everything, and goes out to Bethany because it is late.

The tree (vv. 12–14). The next morning, hungry, he goes to a fig tree in full leaf and finds nothing on it — and Mark adds the detail that makes the whole thing intelligible: it was not the season for figs. He curses it, and the disciples hear him.

The temple (vv. 15–19). And then he does to the temple what he has just done to the tree. Tables over, seats over, the traffic stopped — and two verses of Scripture that between them tell the leadership exactly what their house has become.

The lesson (vv. 20–26). Next morning the tree is dead to the roots, and out of that comes the great passage on faith, prayer and forgiveness.

Mark has wrapped the temple inside the fig tree deliberately. The tree is the temple: leaves and no fruit, an advertisement with nothing behind it, and it is finished.
verseByVerse.theology:
Was it fair to curse a tree for having no figs out of season? The objection is old and it deserves a proper answer, and the answer turns on the leaves.

A Palestinian fig produces its fruit before or alongside its leaves, not after. In early spring the branches put out small green knobs — the paggim — which are edible, and a hungry traveller ate them. The leaves follow. So a tree standing in full leaf is making a claim: there is fruit here.

The main harvest was months away, which is exactly why Mark tells us it was not the season for figs. He is not embarrassed by the detail; he supplies it, so that no reader can mistake this for agricultural pique. Nobody was owed a crop. What the tree owed was consistency with its own appearance, and it had none.

And then look where Mark has put it. He splits the story in two and wedges the temple between the halves — curse (vv. 12–14), temple (vv. 15–19), withered (vv. 20–21). It is his habitual sandwich, and it is never accidental. The tree interprets the temple.

Israel's worship at that moment was in full leaf: the courts crowded, the sacrifices running, the festival packed, the money changing hands. From a distance it looked like the healthiest religion in the world. He came near, looked around at everything (v. 11), found nothing, and the next morning both the tree and the temple were under sentence.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a den of robbers — the phrase everybody quotes and almost nobody reads properly.

A robbers' den is not where the robbery happens. It is the cave they retreat to afterwards, where they divide the takings and feel perfectly safe. That is the charge, and Jeremiah, whom Jesus is quoting, spells it out: Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely... and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!' (Jer. 7:9–11).

Now: the accusation is not primarily about commerce in church buildings. It is about using religion as a safe house — going out into the week, doing what you do, and coming back on Sunday to feel delivered.

That is a test anyone can run. Does your churchgoing make you more uncomfortable about the way you conduct your business, or less? If a man can hold a grudge for eleven years, cut corners at work, be cold at home — and find that an hour on Sunday settles his conscience without changing any of it, then he has not been worshipping. He has been using the den.

And note where the tables were standing. The trading filled the Court of the Gentiles, the one place a non-Jew was permitted to pray — which is why Mark alone keeps Isaiah's full phrase, for all the nations. The arrangement that made the insiders comfortable had physically evicted the outsiders, and nobody had noticed.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the village in front of you, and immediately as you enter it you will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat. Untie it and bring it. If anyone says to you, 'Why are you doing this?' say, 'The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they drew near to Jerusalem, to Bethphage and Bethany, at the Mount of Olives.

Mark gives the geography carefully, and one item in it is loaded.

The Mount of Olives is the ridge east of the city, across the Kidron valley, and from the top you look straight down onto the temple platform. It is also where Zechariah says the LORD will stand on the day he comes to fight for his people: on that day his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives (Zech. 14:4).

He is approaching from the one direction the prophets had marked.

Jesus sent two of his disciples and said to them, Go into the village in front of you.

Now the arrangements, and they are extremely deliberate. For ten chapters this man has walked everywhere. He has been to Jerusalem before. And on this one occasion he sends ahead for transport.

Everything about the entry is staged, and that is the point: after nine chapters of silencing demons, hushing the healed and telling his disciples to say nothing, he now makes a public, unmistakable, prophetic claim in front of a Passover crowd.

The secret is over. He has decided the hour.

You will find a colt tied, on which no one has ever sat.

Two things in that clause.

First, the animal is a colt — a young donkey. And every Jew present knew the text: Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey (Zech. 9:9).

The verse after it has the LORD promising to cut off the chariot and the war horse. A conqueror rode a horse. A king coming in peace rode a donkey; Solomon rode his father's mule to his coronation (1 Kgs. 1:33). So the choice of animal is a sermon: he is claiming the throne and telling the crowd what kind of king he is, in the same gesture. They will get the first half and miss the second.

Second, no one has ever sat on it. That is not incidental either. Under the Law, an animal put to sacred use had to be one that had never been worked — the red heifer on which a yoke has never come (Num. 19:2), the cart that carried the ark drawn by cows that had never been yoked (1 Sam. 6:7).

This colt is being set apart for holy use, and Mark expects you to know it.

Matthew mentions a donkey and her colt (Matt 21:2). Mark and Luke mention only the colt, the animal Jesus rode. Matthew adds the mother because Zechariah’s prophecy names both (Zech 9:9). To mention more is not to contradict.

Say, The Lord has need of it and will send it back here immediately.

Was this foreknowledge or a prior arrangement? Mark does not say, and either fits — he has shown us Jesus knowing men's thoughts (2:8) and he has shown us practical planning (3:9). What is certain is that the two disciples are given a password and told it will work.

And the password is the striking thing: the Lord has need of it.

Sit with the phrase, because there is something in it for anyone who owns anything. The Lord of glory, who made the animal, asks for the use of it — and promises to send it back. He does not seize it; he requests it, and he returns it.

That is how he deals with what is yours. The money, the house, the car, the spare room, the evenings. He has every right to take, and he asks — and nothing lent to him has ever failed to come back larger than it went.
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem. An animal never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose.

parallels.desc: a heifer on which a yoke has never come

verseByVerse.quote: And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it. And some of those standing there said to them, "What are you doing, untying the colt?" And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they went away and found a colt tied at a door outside in the street, and they untied it.

Exactly as he said. Mark gives the confirmation in the flattest possible language, which is his way of underlining it: they went, they found, they untied.

And the detail is very precise — tied at a door outside in the street. Somebody was standing there afterwards telling this to Peter, and they remembered where the animal was standing.

And some of those standing there said to them, What are you doing, untying the colt?

Which is a fair question to ask two strangers untying your donkey.

Mark's report is almost comic in its restraint, and it is entirely believable. Nobody in a village stands by while their livestock walks off.

And they told them what Jesus had said, and they let them go.

That is all. They repeated the sentence they had been given, and the objection evaporated.

Two small things worth taking from this.

First, the disciples had nothing but the word. They had no documentation, no owner's permission that they could produce, and no explanation that would satisfy anybody. They had a sentence they had been told to say, and they said it, and it was enough. That is a fair picture of a great deal of Christian obedience: you go with the word you were given, into a situation you cannot control, and you find that it holds.

Second, somebody let their animal go. Mark does not name them and probably nobody knew who they were. They are the people who, on the most significant morning of that year, handed over a piece of property to two strangers on the strength of a sentence — and the King of the world rode into his city on it.

There is a whole class of person like that in this Gospel, and they are all anonymous. The man who lent the upper room. The owner of the boat. Whoever gave the demoniac a cloak. Somebody's five loaves and two fish.

None of them are named, and every one of them is in the story because something they owned was asked for and they did not say no.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it. And many spread their cloaks on the road, and others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they brought the colt to Jesus and threw their cloaks on it, and he sat on it.

There is no saddle, so the disciples improvise with their outer cloaks — which is, incidentally, the second time in two chapters that a cloak has been thrown down in front of him (10:50).

And there is an unremarked miracle in the sentence. This is an animal that has never been ridden, in a noisy crowd, on a festival road, with a man on its back for the first time in its life. Anyone who has been near an unbroken young donkey knows what usually happens. Nothing happens. It carries him.

The one creature in Jerusalem that week that did exactly what he wanted was a donkey.

And many spread their cloaks on the road.

This is not enthusiasm; it is protocol, and everyone present knew what it meant. When Jehu was proclaimed king, every man of them took his garment and put it under him on the bare steps, and they blew the trumpet and proclaimed, Jehu is king (2 Kgs. 9:13).

Putting your cloak in the dirt for a man to ride over is a coronation gesture. It says: this is my king, and I will spend something to say so. And a cloak was not a cheap item — it was the garment the Law protected, a man's covering and often his bedding.

They are laying down what they own for him to walk on.

And others spread leafy branches that they had cut from the fields.

Branches likewise. John tells us they were palm branches (John 12:13), which is where Palm Sunday gets its name — and palm branches had been a national symbol since the Maccabees drove out the Greeks two centuries earlier; they later appeared on the coins of the Jewish revolts against Rome.

So the crowd is doing something very precise, and it is political. Cloaks for a king; palms for a liberator.

And here is the ache under the whole scene. They are right about who he is and wrong about what he came to do. The man they are welcoming as the liberator of Israel is riding toward an execution, and within five days a crowd in this city will be shouting for it.

Which is worth a moment's honest self-examination, because it is not only first-century enthusiasm. It is possible to be genuinely thrilled about Jesus, to sing loudly, to spend something on him, and to be expecting an entirely different Christ from the one who is actually coming — a Christ who will sort out your circumstances, vindicate your side, and deliver you from the things you want delivering from.

The cloaks were sincere. Nobody was pretending. And by Friday the road was empty.
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey

verseByVerse.quote: And those who went before and those who followed were shouting, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And those who went before and those who followed were shouting.

Mark places them front and back: a column with him in the middle, and noise from both ends. This is a procession.

Hosanna!

The word is Hebrew and it is not, as we tend to use it, a general shout of praise. Hoshia-na means save now — it is a cry for help, a plea, an imperative addressed to God.

And it comes from a specific place: Psalm 118, the last of the Hallel psalms sung at Passover. Every pilgrim on that road had been singing it all week.

Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!

Psalm 118:26, and the very next line of the psalm they are quoting from.

In its original setting it was the greeting called out to pilgrims arriving at the temple gates. Now it is being sung at one man riding a donkey, and the meaning has shifted under their feet: he who comes had become a title for the Messiah. It is what John the Baptist's messengers asked from prison: are you the one who is to come? (Matt. 11:3).

And Jesus will quote this same psalm back at the temple authorities within a day or two — the stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone, which is Psalm 118:22 (12:10). He is listening to what they are singing.

Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David!

Here the crowd goes beyond the psalm and says what it means. This is not a general blessing. They are announcing the restoration of the Davidic monarchy — a real throne, in this city, under Roman occupation, at Passover, when the population of Jerusalem swelled to several times its size and the governor came up from Caesarea with extra troops precisely because this was the week riots started.

It is an enormously dangerous thing to shout.

Hosanna in the highest!

Save now — in the highest places. Let heaven itself hear it.

And that is the terrible irony of the whole scene, and it is worth stating plainly. They were shouting the right word. Save now was exactly the right request, made to exactly the right person, at exactly the right hour.

They simply had no idea what they were asking for. They wanted saving from Rome, and he had come to save them from something worse, and the salvation they were shouting for was going to be accomplished by Friday afternoon in a manner that would empty this road.

He heard the prayer. He answered it. And almost nobody who prayed it recognised the answer when it came.
verseByVerse.note: “Hosanna” means “save, we pray,” and had become a shout of praise.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple. And when he had looked around at everything, as it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he entered Jerusalem and went into the temple.

This is where the procession has been heading all along. Not the palace, not the fortress, not the governor's residence. The temple.

And it is precisely what Malachi had said would happen: the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple... But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire (Mal. 3:1–2).

And when he had looked around at everything.

Now the verse that nobody expects, and it is one of the most quietly ominous sentences in the Gospel.

He walked about the courts and inspected them.

Everything. The traders. The tables. The coins. The birds in cages. The traffic across the Court of the Gentiles. The whole arrangement, seen by the one person present who knew what the building was for.

And he did not say a word.

As it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve.

He goes home for the night.

Take the measure of that ending, because it is a deliberate anticlimax and Mark has built it. The crowd has just called him king. The palms are on the road. The city is full. Every expectation in that procession says that something is about to happen.

And he looks round the temple, notices the time, and leaves for supper in a village two miles away.

Two things follow.

First, what he does the next day is not a loss of temper. He had seen all of it the night before. He walked out, slept on it, walked two miles back in the morning, and then overturned the tables. That is not a man provoked beyond endurance. It is a considered act, decided in advance, executed deliberately — which is what makes it judgement rather than temper.

Second, the inspection itself is the warning. There is a whole Old Testament pattern behind it: before God acts, God looks. He came down to see the city and the tower at Babel (Gen. 11:5); he went down to see whether Sodom was as bad as the outcry (Gen. 18:21). And in the last book of the Bible, the risen Christ walks among the lampstands saying to church after church: I know your works (Rev. 2–3).

He still does this. He walks round and looks at everything — the church, and the man reading this. Not a glance. A survey.

And what he does about it is decided quietly, and never in a temper.
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was about two miles east of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry. And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it. When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs. And he said to it, "May no one ever eat fruit from you again." And his disciples heard it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the following day, when they came from Bethany, he was hungry.

Three words that are easy to skim: he was hungry. The Son of God, walking two miles into the city before breakfast, wanting something to eat. Mark keeps giving us this — asleep on a cushion in a storm, hungry on a road.

And seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to see if he could find anything on it.

He sees it from a way off, and what he sees is leaves. That is the whole of the story, and the objection people raise dissolves once you know how a fig tree works.

A Palestinian fig puts out its fruit before or alongside its leaves, not after. In early spring the branches produce small green knobs, called paggim, which are edible if unremarkable, and a hungry traveller ate them. The leaves come with them. So a tree in full leaf, visible from a distance, is making a claim: there is something here.

When he came to it, he found nothing but leaves, for it was not the season for figs.

And there is Mark's own explanatory clause, and it is the key to the passage rather than an embarrassment in it. He puts it there so that no reader can mistake this for pique over a missed breakfast.

Nobody was owed a crop. The main harvest was months off, and Jesus knew that better than we do. What the tree owed was consistency with its own advertisement — and it had none. It was the only tree on that road claiming to have something, and it was the only tree with nothing.

Did Jesus not know there would be no fruit? He went to the tree as a man looking for fruit, and that was the point of the acted parable: he came to Israel looking for fruit and found only leaves. It was a deliberate sign, not a mistake.

And he said to it, May no one ever eat fruit from you again.

The only destructive miracle in the Gospels, and it is performed on a tree — which should tell us it is a sign rather than a punishment. Jesus does not blast people; the man who healed on a hundred roads curses a plant, once, in front of witnesses, for a reason.

And his disciples heard it.

Mark adds that on purpose. This was said out loud, deliberately, in their hearing. It was meant to be remembered — and in seven verses Peter will remember it.

Now look at where Mark has placed the story, because that is the interpretation.

He splits it in half and wedges the temple into the gap: the curse (vv. 12–14), the temple (vv. 15–19), the withered tree (vv. 20–21). It is his habitual sandwich, and he never does it by accident. The two halves interpret each other.

The tree is the temple.

Israel's worship that week was in magnificent leaf. Herod's temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world; the courts were packed for Passover; the sacrifices ran from dawn; the priesthood was busy; the money moved. From a distance, on the road, it looked like the healthiest religion on earth.

He came near — looked around at everything (v. 11) — and found nothing but leaves.

And the fig tree was Israel's own image for itself. Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel; like the first fruit on the fig tree in its first season, I saw your fathers (Hos. 9:10). When I would gather them, declares the LORD, there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree (Jer. 8:13).

So this is a prophet's acted parable, of the kind Jeremiah and Ezekiel performed constantly — and the sentence it pronounces will be carried out on the building forty years later, when not one stone was left on another (13:2).

And the test it leaves is a personal one, and it is uncomfortable. The tree was not condemned for being fruitless in season. It was condemned for advertising. Leaves are what other people can see: the attendance, the vocabulary, the reputation for soundness, the Bible on the table. Fruit is what is actually there.

He is not in the distance any more. He comes near, and looks.
verseByVerse.note: Leaves on a fig tree normally promise early fruit. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: no figs on the fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they came to Jerusalem. And he entered the temple and began to drive out those who sold and those who bought in the temple.

Now the acted parable in the building itself, and it is worth being clear about what he attacks and what he does not.

He does not attack the sacrificial system. The animals being sold were needed; God had commanded the sacrifices. Pilgrims came from Egypt, Babylon, Rome and Asia Minor, and it was plainly impractical to drive a lamb a thousand miles — so animals were provided. That is not the offence.

And he does not attack the money-changers as such. The temple tax had to be paid in Tyrian coinage, which was the reliable silver of the region; Roman coins carried the emperor's image and a divine title. Somebody had to change money. That is not the offence either.

The offence is where all of it was happening, and what it had become.

The trading filled the Court of the Gentiles — the vast outer court, the one part of the temple complex a non-Jew was permitted to enter. Beyond it stood a low barrier with notices in Greek and Latin warning that any foreigner who passed it had only himself to blame for his death.

So the one square yard of the house of God available to the nations of the world had been turned into a livestock market and a bureau de change. If a God-fearing Greek or an Ethiopian came to Jerusalem to pray, this is where he had to stand: among the cattle pens, the coin tables and the pigeon cages, in the noise.

John puts a cleansing of the temple at the start of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–22); Mark puts this one in the last week. Some think John moved the event for theological reasons. But the two accounts differ in what Jesus says and in what follows, and the abuse was the kind that would have returned. The more likely reading is that there were two cleansings, one at the beginning and one at the end.

And he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons.

He goes through the court putting things on the floor.

And note which stall Mark singles out. Pigeons — because pigeons were the poor person's sacrifice. If he cannot afford a lamb, then he shall bring... two turtledoves or two pigeons (Lev. 5:7; 12:8). It was the offering Mary and Joseph brought when they presented Jesus in this very building (Luke 2:24).

These were the tables where the poorest worshippers were being handled, and the mark-up was reportedly outrageous. It is those seats that go over.

And he would not allow anyone to carry anything through the temple.

A detail only Mark records, and it is remarkable. He stopped the traffic.

The great court was, apparently, being used as a short cut — the quickest way across that quarter of the city was straight through the temple, and people carried their goods across it. The rabbis themselves later forbade it; nobody was to enter the Mount with a staff, a purse, or dust on his feet, or to use it as a thoroughfare.

So for some part of that day, one man stood in the outer court of the temple of God and would not let a single person walk through it carrying anything.

Everything stops. No trading, no changing, no carrying, no short cuts — and, for the first time in years, a Gentile could have stood in that court and prayed.

He has cleared the room for the people nobody thought about.
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax.

parallels.desc: pigeons for those who cannot afford a lamb

verseByVerse.quote: And he was teaching them and saying to them, "Is it not written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations'? But you have made it a den of robbers." And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him, for they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching. And when evening came they went out of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he was teaching them and saying to them.

Note that Mark's word is teaching. The tables are on the floor and the birds are loose, and what he is doing is a lesson — and he grounds it, as always, in two texts.

Is it not written, My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations?

That is Isaiah 56:7, and it is worth reading the whole context, because it decides everything.

Isaiah 56 is God's promise about the outsider. It concerns the foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD and the eunuch — the two categories explicitly excluded from the assembly under the old arrangements (Deut. 23:1–8) — and God says he will bring them to his holy mountain and make them joyful in my house of prayer, and their offerings will be accepted, for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples.

And here is a detail worth having: Matthew and Luke both quote this verse and both stop before the final phrase. Mark keeps it. For all the nations. The Gospel written for Gentiles in Rome preserves the clause about the Gentiles — and it is the clause that condemns what the court had been turned into.

The commercial arrangement had not merely cluttered the temple. It had evicted precisely the people the verse was about.

But you have made it a den of robbers.

Jeremiah 7:11, and this phrase is quoted constantly and almost always misunderstood.

A robbers' den is not where the robbery happens. Nobody is robbed in a cave in the hills. The den is where the thieves retreat afterwards — where they count it out, sleep soundly, and feel safe.

And Jeremiah's context makes the charge explicit. Standing at the temple gate he says: Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, make offerings to Baal... and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!' — only to go on doing all these abominations? Has this house... become a den of robbers in your eyes? (Jer. 7:9–11).

That is the accusation. Not that they were doing business in church. That they were using the house of God as a safe house — living as they pleased and coming here to feel delivered.

And it is a test anybody can run, because the mechanism has not changed. Does your churchgoing make you more uncomfortable about how you conduct the rest of your week, or less? A man who can hold a grudge for eleven years, sharpen his invoices, be cold to his wife — and find that an hour on Sunday settles his conscience without altering any of it — has not been worshipping. He has been using the den.

And the chief priests and the scribes heard it and were seeking a way to destroy him.

They had decided this long ago (3:6). But now it is urgent, because he has touched the temple, and the temple was their institution, their authority and their income.

For they feared him, because all the crowd was astonished at his teaching.

And there is the reason they cannot simply arrest him, and it is a mixture of the political and the spiritual. They were afraid of him — and the whole crowd was hanging on his teaching, which made a public arrest impossible. They will have to do it at night, and they will need somebody on the inside.

And when evening came they went out of the city. He leaves again, as he did the night before. He will not sleep in Jerusalem this week until the night they come for him.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark keeps “for all the nations” from Isaiah’s words.

parallels.desc: a house of prayer for all peoples

verseByVerse.quote: As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots. And Peter remembered and said to him, "Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered." And Jesus answered them, "Have faith in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As they passed by in the morning, they saw the fig tree withered away to its roots.

The third morning of this chapter, on the same road, and the tree is dead.

Note the phrase: withered away to its roots. Not wilted, not dropping leaves. Killed from the bottom up, in under twenty-four hours, from the part nobody can see.

Matthew, compressing, says it withered at once (Matt. 21:19). Mark, who is following the days as they came, gives us the two mornings — which means the disciples walked past this tree twice, and the second time it was a dead stick.

And they had heard him say it. That is what makes it unforgettable: they were standing there when he spoke, and now they are standing here.

And Peter remembered and said to him, Rabbi, look! The fig tree that you cursed has withered.

You can hear the man's voice. There is no theological reflection in it at all — just Rabbi, look! Peter has spotted it and is pointing.

And it is worth pausing on the fact that Peter is the one who noticed, in a Gospel that comes from Peter's preaching. He is telling this against himself as usual: I saw a dead tree and got excited about the tree.

Because he has entirely missed what it was for. The withering is not the point. The temple is the point, and he has walked past that twice as well.

And Jesus answered them, Have faith in God.

Which is, at first glance, one of the more surprising replies in the Gospel. Peter says the tree is dead, and Jesus says have faith in God.

He does not explain the sign. He does not say and that is what will happen to this nation, though it is, and though he will spell it out in two chapters (13:2). He turns instead to what the disciples are to do with what they have just seen.

And the connection, once you see it, is this. They have watched a word spoken to a tree, and the tree obeyed. They are about to be sent into a world where they will need to speak, and pray, and be up against things far more immovable than a fig. So: have faith in God.

The Greek is literally have faith of God, and the sense is faith whose object is God. Not faith in faith. Not faith in the power of your own believing, which is a modern superstition and a cruel one. Faith in God — a Person, who hears, and decides, and is good.

That distinction is going to matter enormously in the next two verses, because they are among the most abused sentences in the Bible, and this one governs them.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, Be taken up and thrown into the sea, and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him.

Start with this mountain, because they were standing somewhere specific.

The road from Bethany runs over the Mount of Olives, and from it you look across at the temple mount — and beyond, on a clear day, down toward the Dead Sea. This mountain may well have been the very hill the temple stood on, which he had just pronounced fruitless; and the sea was in view.

And moving a mountain was a proverb. The rabbis called a great teacher who could solve impossible problems an uprooter of mountains. Everyone understood the figure: the immovable obstacle, shifted.

Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.

And now the promise that has been made to carry a weight it was never meant to bear, and which has done real damage to real people. So it must be handled carefully and honestly.

What it plainly does say. Do not soften it first. Jesus means his people to pray with enormous boldness, to ask for things far beyond their resources, and to expect God to act. Most of us are not in danger of presumption; we are in danger of praying for nothing much, in case nothing happens. The whole point of the mountain is that it is too big, and he tells them to say so out loud.

What it does not say. It is not a mechanism by which sufficient certainty compels God to act. That reading turns prayer into a technique and God into a force — and it is refuted by the rest of the Bible, and most decisively by the man saying it.

Because within a few days, in a garden a few hundred yards from here, this same Jesus will fall on the ground and ask his Father to remove the cup — and will add, yet not what I will, but what you will (14:36). And the cup does not pass.

If unqualified confidence always secured the request, that prayer is unintelligible. He did not lack faith. He trusted his Father enough to leave the answer with him.

And Paul asked three times about his thorn and was told no, and given something better instead (2 Cor. 12:8–9). And John, who heard this saying, wrote the qualifier into his own letter: if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 Jn. 5:14).

So to the reader who asked and did not receive — and this is written for you, because you are the person this passage most often wounds — your faith was very likely not the problem, and heaping blame on it only adds a second grief to the first.

Prayer that moves mountains is real, and you should ask for mountains to move. But it is prayer offered to a Father, not an incantation aimed at a force. A good Father sometimes gives what we did not ask because it is better than what we did, and sometimes withholds what we begged for because his love can see the whole of a story we can see only the middle of.

Believe boldly. Ask for great things. And trust him enough to want his will more than your own, knowing that his no, when it comes, is as wise and as kind as the yes you were hoping for.

parallels.desc: faith like a grain of mustard seed
ask in faith, with no doubting

verseByVerse.quote: And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone.

And now, having said that a believing man can move a mountain, he names the thing that will stop him.

The join is the most practical thing in the chapter, and it is easily missed because we treat these as two separate subjects. They are not. Jesus goes straight from whatever you ask in prayer to forgive, without a pause. Unforgiveness is presented as the great obstruction in the pipe.

Whenever you stand praying. Standing was the ordinary Jewish posture for prayer — so this is not a special occasion but the daily one. Every time you pray.

Forgive, if you have anything against anyone.

Take the scope of that seriously, because every word widens it. Anything — not only the large injuries; the slight, the exclusion, the remark, the thing said about you at work. Against anyone — no exceptions for family, for the person who has never apologised, for the one who does not know they did it, for the dead.

And notice that the initiative is entirely yours. There is no clause here about them repenting first, or acknowledging it, or being sorry. You stand up to pray; you find something in your hand; you put it down.

So that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses.

This must be stated carefully, because it can be read as though pardon were earned by pardoning, which would overturn the gospel.

It is not that. Nobody is forgiven because they forgive; we are forgiven because a ransom was paid (10:45). But the New Testament is entirely consistent that the two cannot be separated in practice — forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you (Eph. 4:32), and the servant in the parable who was released from ten thousand talents and then took a colleague by the throat over a few pounds (Matt. 18:23–35).

A man who has genuinely grasped what he has been let off does not hold small debts against other people. If he does, the question is not whether he has forfeited his forgiveness. The question is whether he ever understood it.

And a plain, concrete word, because this is where a great many prayer lives quietly die. There is a name.
