You thought of it while reading this paragraph — the person you would rather not pray for, the situation you have decided is unresolvable, the grudge that has been carried so long it has become part of the furniture and no longer feels like sin.

Jesus's instruction is not that you should feel differently about them. It is that you should let it go, in prayer, deliberately, now — and go on doing it whenever it comes back, because it will.

But Jesus also says, if he repents, forgive him (Luke 17:3). Both are true, because forgiveness has two parts. The first is in your heart before God: letting go of the grudge and the wish for revenge, and handing the case to him. That is commanded here, whether or not the other person repents. The second is the restored relationship, and that waits for repentance, as God’s own reconciliation with us does. So a believer wronged by someone unrepentant, even an abuser, must not nurse bitterness, but is not required to pretend nothing happened, to trust where trust has not been earned, or to return to danger.

And a note on the verse your Bible skips. The numbers here run 25, then 27. Many older Bibles print a verse 26 — But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your trespasses — and modern ones leave it as a footnote.

Those words are not in the earliest manuscripts of Mark. A scribe seems to have written them in the margin from Matthew 6:15, where they certainly belong, and a later copyist took the margin for the text. Nothing has been lost: the truth stands plainly in verse 25, and Jesus does teach it in Matthew — only its home is there and not here.
verseByVerse.note: Jews commonly prayed standing. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 26: “But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in heaven forgive your trespasses.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The challenge. They come back into the city and the full weight of the establishment is waiting: chief priests, scribes and elders — the three constituencies of the Sanhedrin, which is to say the supreme court of Judaism has sent a delegation to meet him in the temple courts.

Their question is the right one and the only one: by what authority are you doing these things? A man has stopped the temple trade, halted the traffic across the courts, and is now teaching daily on the premises. Somebody has to ask who authorised it.

The counter-question. Jesus offers to answer if they will answer one of his: was John's baptism from heaven or from man?

It is not evasion, and it is not a debating trick. John's commission was the same kind as his own — direct from God, without institutional sanction — so anyone who can assess the one can assess the other.

The calculation. And Mark lets us listen in while they work out what to say, which is the most damning thing in the chapter: they weigh both answers by what each will cost them, and the question of what is actually true never comes up.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why does Jesus refuse to answer? It looks at first like a rabbinic sparring move, and it is much more than that.

He is not withholding truth from honest enquiry — he has never once done that in this Gospel. He explained the parables privately to anyone who stayed and asked (4:10, 34); he answered a scribe who asked about the greatest commandment and told him he was not far from the kingdom (12:34); he answered the rich man who ran and knelt (10:17-22).

What he refuses is to give an answer to men who have already demonstrated they will not deal honestly with an answer. They have John's case in front of them — a prophet the entire nation recognised — and they cannot bring themselves to say publicly what they think about him, because both possible verdicts are expensive.

And that is a settled principle, not a mood: do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs (Matt. 7:6). He will stand silent in front of Herod, who wanted a miracle for entertainment (Luke 23:9), and largely silent before Pilate.

So the withdrawal of light is itself a judgement — and a merciful one, because more truth given to a man determined to reject it only deepens the guilt of the rejecting.

And note what their answer costs them. We do not know is a lie, spoken publicly by the highest religious authority in Israel, about the most famous prophet of their own generation. To protect their position they declared themselves incompetent — and having done so, they had no ground left from which to judge anybody's authority, including his.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: If we say, "From heaven," he will say, "Why then did you not believe him?" But shall we say, "From man"? — and they were afraid of the people.

Read the deliberation again and notice what is missing from it. Two options are weighed. Each is assessed for consequences. And at no point does anybody in that huddle ask: which of these is true?

That question is simply absent. These are the most religiously educated men in the nation, standing in the temple, discussing a prophet's commission — and truth is not one of the factors.

Now: the mechanism is not first-century and it is not confined to unbelievers. It is the standing temptation of any institution, church or person with more to lose from the truth than from avoiding it.

It is the doctrine quietly not preached because of who would leave. The sin not named because of who is in the family. The question about your own life you have never taken to God because you already know roughly what the answer costs.

And it ends the way it ended here: not in a lie you tell somebody else, but in we do not know — a shrug that feels like humility and is in fact a decision. They walked away with their positions intact and no answer at all, and it is the last conversation they have with him before they arrest him.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came again to Jerusalem. And as he was walking in the temple, the chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him, and they said to him, "By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they came again to Jerusalem. The third entry into the city in three days. He keeps coming back to the building he has just judged.

And as he was walking in the temple.

Note where he is. Not outside making speeches about the temple — inside it, walking about, teaching daily, entirely at home.

He overturned the tables yesterday and he is back this morning, in the same courts, behaving as though the place belonged to him. Which, as he has already said, it does: my house (v. 17).

The chief priests and the scribes and the elders came to him.

The three groups named together are the Sanhedrin — the chief priests (the Sadducean temple aristocracy), the scribes (the legal experts, largely Pharisaic), and the elders (the lay heads of the leading families). This is the full composition of the supreme court of Israel.

So this is not a heckler. It is an official delegation, and Mark names all three parties to make sure we understand that.

And they said to him, By what authority are you doing these things, or who gave you this authority to do them?

Two questions, and both are entirely reasonable.

He has interfered with the operation of the national temple, halted a licensed trade, stopped the public thoroughfare and is now teaching in the courts. Somebody in that position should be asked who authorised him. It is the correct institutional response, and if a stranger did the same thing in any church today, the elders would be right to ask the same question.

Note the second half in particular: who gave you this authority? That is the real question, and it reveals how they think. In their world, authority came through channels. A man was ordained, trained, appointed, licensed. The question assumes there must be a name — a school, a rabbi, a body that stands behind him.

And the answer, of course, is that nobody gave it to him.

That has been the issue since the first chapter of this Gospel, when the crowd at Capernaum said he taught as one who had authority, and not as the scribes (1:22). The scribes had authority the way a barrister has it — derived, cited, borrowed from a higher court. His is not derived from anything.

Which means the delegation is asking a question that has no answer in the terms they have framed it. There is no name to give them but one, and if he says it plainly here, in the temple, three days before Passover, the week ends immediately.

So he does not answer. He asks.
verseByVerse.note: The chief priests, scribes and elders together made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things. Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to them, I will ask you one question; answer me, and I will tell you by what authority I do these things.

This was an entirely normal way to conduct a rabbinic dispute — answering a question with a question was not rudeness but method — and he offers a fair bargain. One question, and he will give them what they came for.

He is not dodging. He means it. If they answer honestly, they will have answered their own question, which is exactly why they will not.

Was the baptism of John from heaven or from man? Answer me.

Two phrases in that sentence do the work.

From heaven is a reverent Jewish way of saying from God without saying the name. So the question is stark and admits of no third option: was John's commission divine, or was he a man acting on his own initiative?

Answer me. He presses them. He will not let it be treated as a rhetorical flourish.

And now see why the question is not a trick but a genuine parallel.

John had no institutional standing whatever. He held no office, belonged to no school, had no ordination and was not attached to the temple — though, as a priest's son (Luke 1:5), he could have been. He appeared in the desert, preached, baptised, and was recognised by an entire nation as a prophet. His authority came directly from God, without a single human channel.

Which is precisely the kind of authority Jesus has, and precisely what the delegation is refusing to consider.

So the question is this: you have already had one case exactly like mine. What did you conclude about it? If they can assess John, they can assess him. And if they cannot assess John — a man dead a year or two, whose ministry the whole country witnessed — then they have disqualified themselves as judges of anybody's commission.

There is more in it than logic, though. There is mercy.

John's entire ministry was pointing at Jesus. He said it in the plainest words available: after me comes he who is mightier than I (1:7), and, in John's Gospel, behold, the Lamb of God. Anyone who honestly settled the question of John's authority would have been carried straight to the answer about Christ's.

Jesus has handed them the one question in the world that would have led them home, and they are about to spend it on a calculation about crowd management.
verseByVerse.note: “From heaven” means from God.

verseByVerse.quote: And they discussed it with one another, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But shall we say, 'From man'?"—they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet. So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And Jesus said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they discussed it with one another.

And now Mark does something extraordinary: he lets us stand inside the huddle and listen. This is the supreme court of Israel, in the temple, working out what to say — and it is the most damning paragraph in the chapter.

If we say, From heaven, he will say, Why then did you not believe him?

Note that they see it instantly. There is no confusion about what John's ministry meant; they know perfectly well that if they concede he was sent by God, they are condemned out of their own mouths for having ignored him.

Which means they had already made a decision about John and knew it was indefensible. They are not weighing evidence. They are managing an exposure.

But shall we say, From man? — they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John really was a prophet.

Mark does not even finish their sentence. He breaks off mid-question to give the reason, as though the calculation were too naked to write out.

They cannot say it. Not because they think it is false, but because the crowd around them would turn — and Josephus confirms how deeply John was revered, and that Antipas was widely blamed for his death.

So both roads are closed. One costs them their credibility. The other costs them their safety.

And here is what is missing from the whole deliberation, and it is the point of the passage.

Read their words again. Two options are considered. Each is assessed for consequences. And at no moment does anyone in that circle ask: which of these is actually true?

The question does not appear. These are the most religiously trained men in the nation, standing in the house of God, discussing whether a prophet was sent by God — and truth is not a factor in the discussion.

That is what institutional self-preservation does to a mind, and it is not a first-century disease. It is the standing temptation of any church, any board, any person with more to lose from the truth than from avoiding it: the doctrine quietly not preached because of who would leave; the sin not named because of whose family it is in; the question about your own life you have never once put to God, because you already know roughly what the answer would cost.

So they answered Jesus, We do not know.

Four words, and they are a lie, told publicly, by the highest religious authority in Israel, about the most famous prophet of their own generation.

And it is the perfect lie, because it sounds like humility. We do not know is what a careful man says. It is also, here, a confession of incompetence — and having declared themselves unable to judge John's commission, they have destroyed their own standing to judge his.

There are still people who use that sentence exactly this way. Agnosticism is sometimes an honest condition and God is patient with it. But it can also be a position taken because it is the cheapest one available — a way of never having to say yes and never having to say no, and of keeping every door open by walking through none of them.

And Jesus said to them, Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things.

He keeps his word exactly. The bargain was one question for one question; they refused, and so does he.

And this is not petulance. It is judgement, and it is the most sobering thing in the chapter — because the withdrawal of light from a man who has decided against it is itself a mercy of a terrible kind. More truth given to someone determined to reject it would only deepen the guilt of the rejecting.

So they walk away with their positions intact and no answer at all. It is the last real conversation the Sanhedrin has with Jesus before they arrest him — and the next time they ask him a direct question about who he is, at night, in the high priest's house, he will answer it in full, and they will tear their clothes and condemn him for it (14:61–64).

He was never unwilling to tell them. He was waiting for the hour when the answer could not be turned into anything else — and that hour was a cross.

11.theology:
Was it fair to curse a tree out of season? The answer turns on the leaves. A Palestinian fig produces its fruit before or alongside its leaves, not after — in spring the branches put out small edible knobs, the paggim, and a hungry traveller ate them. So a tree in full leaf is making a claim. Mark's clause it was not the season for figs is not an embarrassment but the key: he supplies it so no reader mistakes this for pique over a missed breakfast. Nobody was owed a crop. What the tree owed was consistency with its own advertisement, and it had none.

And the placement is the interpretation. Mark splits the story and wedges the temple into the gap — curse, temple, withered — his habitual sandwich, never accidental. The fig tree was Israel's own image for itself (Hos. 9:10; Jer. 8:13), and the sentence pronounced here is carried out on the building in 13:2.

A den of robbers (Jer. 7:11) is the most misquoted phrase in the chapter. A robbers' den is not where the robbery happens; it is the cave they retreat to afterwards, where they feel safe. Jeremiah spells it out at the temple gate: Will you steal, murder, commit adultery... and then come and stand before me in this house, which is called by my name, and say, 'We are delivered!' The charge is not commerce in church. It is using religion as a safe house.

And v. 17 keeps a clause the other Gospels drop. Matthew and Luke both quote Isaiah 56:7 and stop before the final phrase; Mark keeps for all the nations — the Gospel written for Gentiles preserving the clause about Gentiles. Isaiah 56 is God's promise about the foreigner and the eunuch, the two categories explicitly excluded under the old arrangements; and the trading filled the Court of the Gentiles, the one place a non-Jew could stand. The arrangement had physically evicted the very people the verse was about.
11.examples:
Then: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours — a promise that has been made to carry a weight it was never meant to bear.

What it does say: pray with enormous boldness, ask for what is far beyond your resources, expect God to act. Most of us are not in danger of presumption. We are in danger of praying for nothing much in case nothing happens, and the whole point of the mountain is that it is too big.

What it does not say: that sufficient certainty compels God. That reading makes prayer a technique and God a force, and it is refuted most decisively by the man saying it — within days, in a garden a few hundred yards away, he asks his Father to remove the cup and adds yet not what I will, but what you will (14:36), and the cup does not pass. If unqualified confidence always secured the request, that prayer is unintelligible. Paul asked three times about the thorn and was told no (2 Cor. 12:8–9); John, who heard this saying, wrote in the qualifier himself — if we ask anything according to his will he hears us (1 Jn. 5:14).

Now: to the reader who asked and did not receive — your faith was very likely not the problem, and blaming it only adds a second grief to the first. Believe boldly, ask for great things, and trust him enough to want his will more than your own, knowing that his no, when it comes, is as wise and as kind as the yes you hoped for.

And note what he says next (v. 25), with no pause: whenever you stand praying, forgive. Having promised that a believing man can move a mountain, he immediately names the thing that blocks the pipe. There is a name — you thought of it while reading this — and the instruction is not to feel differently, but to put it down, deliberately, now, and again whenever it comes back.

12.title: The Beloved Son and the Widow’s Two Coins
12.text: <sup>1</sup>And he began to speak to them in parables. “A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenants and went into another country. <sup>2</sup>When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit of the vineyard. <sup>3</sup>And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. <sup>4</sup>Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. <sup>5</sup>And he sent another, and him they killed. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed. <sup>6</sup>He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ <sup>7</sup>But those tenants said to one another, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ <sup>8</sup>And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard. <sup>9</sup>What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. <sup>10</sup>Have you not read this Scripture: ‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; <sup>11</sup>this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes’?” <sup>12</sup>And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away. <sup>13</sup>And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. <sup>14</sup>And they came and said to him, “Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone’s opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?” <sup>15</sup>But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, “Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it.” <sup>16</sup>And they brought one. And he said to them, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.” <sup>17</sup>Jesus said to them, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” And they marveled at him. <sup>18</sup>And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, <sup>19</sup>“Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. <sup>20</sup>There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. <sup>21</sup>And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. <sup>22</sup>And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. <sup>23</sup>In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife.” <sup>24</sup>Jesus said to them, “Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? <sup>25</sup>For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. <sup>26</sup>And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? <sup>27</sup>He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong.” <sup>28</sup>And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, “Which commandment is the most important of all?” <sup>29</sup>Jesus answered, “The most important is, ‘Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. <sup>30</sup>And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ <sup>31</sup>The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ There is no other commandment greater than these.” <sup>32</sup>And the scribe said to him, “You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. <sup>33</sup>And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.” <sup>34</sup>And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, “You are not far from the kingdom of God.” And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions. <sup>35</sup>And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, “How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? <sup>36</sup>David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet.”’ <sup>37</sup>David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?” And the great throng heard him gladly. <sup>38</sup>And in his teaching he said, “Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces <sup>39</sup>and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, <sup>40</sup>who devour widows’ houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation.” <sup>41</sup>And he sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. <sup>42</sup>And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny. <sup>43</sup>And he called his disciples to him and said to them, “Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. <sup>44</sup>For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.”
12.overview:
This is the last day Jesus ever taught in the temple, and it is one long interrogation. Three delegations come at him in turn, each with a question designed to finish him, and by verse 34 nobody dares ask him anything at all.

He opens by answering the challenge they refused to answer, with a story. A vineyard is planted at great expense, leased out, and the owner sends for his share — and the tenants beat one servant, humiliate another, kill a third, and go on doing it. Then, having nobody else, the owner sends a beloved son, which in this Gospel is a phrase that has twice come out of heaven. They recognise him, kill him, and throw him out of the vineyard. Mark says the leaders understood the parable perfectly — and went away to arrange the arrest.

Then the traps: a coin with Caesar's face on it, and a riddle about a woman with seven husbands. He answers the first in sixteen words that have shaped Christian political thought ever since, and the second from a single present-tense verb in the burning bush.

Then one honest scribe asks a real question and is told he is not far from the kingdom of God. And the chapter ends with Jesus sitting down opposite the treasury, watching people give, and calling his disciples over to look at a widow putting in two of the smallest coins in the empire — everything she had to live on, three days before he did the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — The Tenants, Caesar’s Coin, and the Resurrection
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The parable (vv. 1–12). They asked by what authority he acts, and refused to answer his question. So he tells them a story about a vineyard, and it is the least veiled parable he ever told: an owner, a run of beaten and murdered servants, and finally a beloved son. They understood it perfectly — Mark says so — and went away to arrange the arrest.

The coin (vv. 13–17). Pharisees and Herodians together again, opening with flattery and closing a trap with two jaws: endorse the tax and lose the crowd, oppose it and be reported for sedition. He asks for a coin, asks whose face is on it, and gives an answer nobody has improved on.

The riddle (vv. 18–27). Then the Sadducees, with a seven-husbands puzzle designed to make resurrection look absurd — and he answers them from the one part of the Bible they accepted, out of a single present-tense verb.

Three challenges from three different quarters, all in one day, all of them designed to end him — and by verse 34 nobody dares ask him anything else.
verseByVerse.theology:
Render to Caesar (v. 17) cuts in two directions at once, and both must be held.

On one side, a real obligation. Jesus does not say the tax is illegitimate or that a man of God may treat the government as an enemy to be defied. The coin is Caesar's; give it to him. Paul draws the same line plainly: the governing authority is God's servant for the ordering of society, so pay your taxes, keep the law, honour the office (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17). Christianity is not anarchy, and a faith that despises all earthly authority has not understood this verse.

On the other side, the obligation is bounded. Caesar may claim the coin; he may not claim the soul. The image on the denarius marks what is his; the image of God stamped on the man marks what is God's — and what is God's, Caesar must never be given.

So the same verse that tells you to pay the tax tells you where obedience stops. The moment the state demands what belongs to God alone — worship, or the violation of God's clear command — the Christian renders to God and not to Caesar. We must obey God rather than men, the apostles answered the very Sanhedrin that plotted this trap (Acts 5:29). It is the fault line the martyrs died on: they would pay any tax Rome levied and pray for its emperor, but they would not drop the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord, because that title was God's.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the Sadducees, and the ground Jesus chooses to fight them on.

They were the aristocratic priestly party who ran the temple — wealthy, powerful, politically pragmatic — and they held that only the five books of Moses carried full authority. They also say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit (Acts 23:8).

Which is why Jesus does not answer from the obvious places. He could have quoted Daniel — many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake (Dan. 12:2) — or Isaiah 26:19, and they would simply have waved those books away. Instead he beats them on their own chosen ground, reaching into the Torah, into the burning bush that every priest knew by heart, and finding the resurrection in a present-tense claim: I am the God of Abraham. Not was. Abraham has been dead four hundred years and God speaks of him in the present tense.

Now: he does not merely win the argument. He wins it inside the fence they built themselves, proving that the hope they denied was lying all along in the only Scriptures they would accept.

And note the diagnosis he gives first: you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. Those are the two ways to go wrong, and they are still the two. Some err because they do not know the text; some because they know the text and have quietly decided what God is not able to do.

verseByVerse.quote: And he began to speak to them in parables. "A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower, and leased it to tenants and went into another country. When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit of the vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he began to speak to them in parables.

To them — the delegation of chief priests, scribes and elders who have just refused to answer his question about John (11:33). They would not answer him, so he tells them a story.

And it is the least veiled parable he ever told. Verse 12 says outright that they understood it.

A man planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a pit for the winepress and built a tower.

Stop there, because the first sentence is a quotation and every man listening knew it.

Isaiah 5 is the Song of the Vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. He dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a wine vat in it (Isa. 5:1–2). The fence, the tower, the winepress — Jesus is reciting the details in order.

And Isaiah tells you what it means without any ambiguity: For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his pleasant planting (Isa. 5:7).

So before a single character has acted, the delegation knows exactly what this story is about. It is about them.

Note also what the owner has done. Every one of those details is an investment. A fence to keep out animals; a tower for a watchman to sleep in; a pit cut out of rock for the press. This is not a man who threw seed at some ground. He has spent years and considerable money on a piece of land, and prepared it thoroughly, before anyone else touches it.

And leased it to tenants and went into another country.

Then he leaves — and the arrangement he leaves behind is entirely ordinary. Absentee landlords with Galilean estates were a normal feature of that economy, and share-cropping was the usual arrangement: the tenants worked the land and paid a proportion of the crop as rent.

The tenants own nothing. They have been given the use of something enormously valuable that somebody else built, on the understanding that its fruit is not ultimately theirs.

That is the position of the leadership of Israel, and it is worth saying plainly that it is also the position of everyone who has ever been given anything by God — a church, a family, a gift, a life. None of it is freehold. The whole parable turns on the difference between a tenant and an owner, and on what happens to a man who forgets which he is.

When the season came, he sent a servant to the tenants to get from them some of the fruit.

And note the modesty of the request: some of the fruit. Not all of it. He is asking for the agreed share of what he planted, in the season when it was due.

He has every right, and he asks.
verseByVerse.note: The setting echoes Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, where the vineyard is Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. And he sent another, and him they killed. And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the parable turns, and Mark makes us watch it happen four times over, with the violence escalating each time.

And they took him and beat him and sent him away empty-handed. The first servant is assaulted and returned with nothing — a message as much as an assault. There will be no rent.

Again he sent to them another servant, and they struck him on the head and treated him shamefully. Worse. Struck him on the head is a serious injury, and treated him shamefully means he was publicly humiliated as well as hurt.

And he sent another, and him they killed. And now the line is crossed.

And so with many others: some they beat, and some they killed. Jesus stops counting. The story could go on indefinitely, and the summary is the point: this went on, and on, and the pattern never changed.

Who are the servants? The parable answers itself for anyone who knows the Old Testament, because my servants the prophets is God's own standing phrase for them — it occurs again and again in Jeremiah, in Kings, in Amos: I have persistently sent all my servants the prophets to them, day after day (Jer. 7:25).

And the treatment described is exactly the record. Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks by the temple's chief officer (Jer. 20:2), lowered into a cistern and left in the mud (Jer. 38:6). Zechariah the son of Jehoiada was stoned to death in the court of the house of the LORD, on the king's orders (2 Chr. 24:20–21). Micaiah was struck in the face and imprisoned on bread and water (1 Kgs. 22:24–27). Elijah ran for his life from a queen. John the Baptist, not long before, lost his head to a girl's request at a party (6:27).

Stephen will say the same thing to the same council within a few years, and it will cost him his life: Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? (Acts 7:52).

But look at what the story is really about, because it is not primarily about the tenants.

It is about an owner who keeps sending.

After the first beating, any landlord in that room would have gone to law or gone with force. This one sends another man. And another. And after a murder, more still. The absurdity of the parable — and the tenants must have thought him a fool — is the patience of the owner.

That is the history of God with his people, and it is the history of God with you. The astonishing thing in this chapter is not human wickedness, which is exactly what anyone would predict. It is that after the beating, and the humiliation, and the killing, and the many others, there is still somebody else at the gate.

And the next verse tells you who is left.

parallels.desc: they mocked the messengers of God

verseByVerse.quote: He had still one other, a beloved son. Finally he sent him to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But those tenants said to one another, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.' And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He had still one other, a beloved son.

Read that slowly, because both halves of it are heavy.

He had still one other. The servants are exhausted. There is nobody else to send. The owner has come to the end of everything he had, and what remains is not another employee.

A beloved son. And here the parable stops being a story about somebody else, because that phrase has occurred twice already in this Gospel and both times it came out of heaven.

At the Jordan: You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased (1:11). On the mountain: This is my beloved Son; listen to him (9:7). Now, in the temple courts, in a parable, in front of the men arranging his death: a beloved son.

He is telling them who he is and what they are about to do, in a story, three days before they do it.

Finally he sent him to them, saying, They will respect my son.

The last card. And the owner's expectation is not naive — it is what any reasonable man would think. A servant can be brushed aside; the heir is the owner in person. Surely this settles it.

And there is a cost in the sending that a first-century listener would feel immediately. This man has already lost servants to these tenants. He knows what they do to the people he sends. And he sends his son.

He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom. 8:32).

But those tenants said to one another, This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.

Notice that they recognise him. That is the horror of the parable and the horror of Good Friday. They do not kill the son by mistake, or because they cannot tell who he is. They kill him because they know exactly who he is.

And their reasoning is the reasoning of every human rebellion against God, stated with unusual honesty: the inheritance will be ours. Get rid of the heir and the estate is ours to keep. It is the serpent's offer in a vineyard — you will be like God — and it is the whole logic of sin, which is never finally about pleasure but about ownership.

And they took him and killed him and threw him out of the vineyard.

The bare violence of it, in one sentence, with no adjectives.

And the last clause is not decoration. To throw a body out unburied was the ultimate contempt; but more than that, Mark's readers are meant to see where it happened. He was killed and put outside.

Which is exactly what took place. He was taken outside the city wall to a place called the Skull and executed there, and the letter to the Hebrews makes the connection explicit: Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Heb. 13:12).

He is standing in the temple describing his own murder, in the third person, to the men who will commit it, and they are listening.
verseByVerse.note: “Beloved son” echoes the Father’s voice at the baptism and transfiguration.

verseByVerse.quote: What will the owner of the vineyard do? He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others. Have you not read this Scripture: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What will the owner of the vineyard do?

He asks the question himself and answers it himself, which is not how he usually ends a parable. There is no ambiguity left and none intended.

He will come and destroy the tenants and give the vineyard to others.

Two judgements, and both landed within a generation.

Destroy the tenants. Within forty years Jerusalem was besieged and burned, the temple was destroyed, and the priestly aristocracy that ran it ceased to exist. Jesus will describe it in detail in the next chapter (13:2).

And give the vineyard to others. This is the harder half, and it must be stated carefully, because it has been misused.

It does not mean that God has finished with the Jewish people; Paul spends three chapters denying exactly that inference and insisting God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew (Rom. 11:2). Nor is the parable aimed at a nation — it is aimed at the tenants, the leadership, the men standing in front of him.

What it means is that the stewardship changes hands. The care of God's vineyard passes to others, and the others turn out to include Gentiles from every nation on earth — which is what Peter says to this very council: the stone rejected by you, the builders, has become the cornerstone (Acts 4:11).

And it is a warning to every church that has ever assumed its position is permanent. A lampstand can be removed (Rev. 2:5). Tenancy is not freehold.

Have you not read this Scripture?

Note the sting of the question, put to professional scribes whose entire life was the reading of Scripture.

The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes.

He quotes Psalm 118:22–23 — and it is the same psalm the crowd was singing at him two days ago on the road into the city (11:9). They sang verse 26 at him; now he reads them verse 22.

And the change of image is the whole gospel in one move. The story ended with a dead son thrown out of a vineyard. The psalm ends with a rejected stone holding up a building.

The builders — that is, the professionals, the men whose job is to know which stones are usable — examine a stone and throw it on the spoil heap. And God picks it up and makes it the cornerstone, the stone that sets the line of every wall in the building.

So the parable does not actually end at verse 8. It ends with resurrection, told in the language of masonry, because the rejected stone is not lying on the heap where they threw it. It is holding up the house.

This was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes. The builders were not thwarted by an accident. What they meant as a rejection was the very thing God was doing — and Peter, who was standing there, quotes this verse twice in his own preaching and letters (Acts 4:11; 1 Pet. 2:7).

verseByVerse.quote: And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them. So they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were seeking to arrest him but feared the people, for they perceived that he had told the parable against them.

Mark tells us three things in one sentence, and they belong together.

They perceived. There was no misunderstanding. The parable landed exactly as intended; they knew they were the tenants, they knew who the beloved son was, and they knew what was being said about their future.

Which removes the most convenient excuse anyone has ever offered for rejecting Christ. These men were not confused. Their problem was never information.

They were seeking to arrest him. And here is the most damning thing in the verse. He has just told them a story in which the tenants kill the son — and their response is to start planning how to take him into custody.

They act out the parable within seconds of hearing it. Told they are the men who murder the heir, they go away to arrange the murder of the heir. It is one of the strangest and most chilling things in the Gospel: the warning becomes the occasion of the crime it warns about.

And that is what a hardened heart does with the truth. It does not soften. It uses the light to see by while it does the thing the light exposed.

But feared the people. Not conscience. Not doubt about whether he might be right. Crowd management. The city is full for Passover, the throng hears him gladly (v. 37), and a public arrest would start a riot with the governor in town and extra troops on the walls.

So the timetable is set by fear of the crowd — which is why it eventually happens at night, in a garden, with a guide who knew where he went to pray.

So they left him and went away.

And there is the saddest clause in the chapter.

They were standing in front of the Son of God. He had just told them, plainly enough for them to understand it perfectly, who he was, what they were about to do, and what it would cost them. Every fact they needed was in their hands.

And they left him and went away.

Nobody dragged them off. There was no argument they lost and stormed out of. They simply turned round and walked, and the next time they are in the same room with him it will be at midnight with false witnesses.

It is possible to understand the gospel completely, to know precisely what is being claimed and what it requires, and to walk away — not in rage, not in confusion, but because it costs too much. That is the most ordinary way in the world of being lost, and it is exactly what these men did on a Tuesday afternoon in the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk. And they came and said to him, "Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone's opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?" But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, "Why put me to the test? Bring me a denarius and let me look at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they sent to him some of the Pharisees and some of the Herodians, to trap him in his talk.

The alliance from chapter 3 again (3:6) — the strict separatists and the party of Herod, who agreed on nothing except this. Nothing unites opposites like a shared hatred of the light.

Mark's word for trap is from hunting: to catch with a snare. And it is a delegation — they sent — so this is the Sanhedrin operating through proxies, having found that direct confrontation did not work.

Teacher, we know that you are true and do not care about anyone's opinion. For you are not swayed by appearances, but truly teach the way of God.

And now the flattery, and it is worth stopping on, because it is a technique and everybody has met it.

Notice what they praise him for: independence, fearlessness, indifference to what people think. That is precisely the quality they need him to display in the next thirty seconds. They are not complimenting him; they are winding him up and pointing him at a cliff. You are the sort of man who says what he thinks regardless of consequences — so tell us what you think about the Roman tax, here, in public.

And the terrible thing is that every word of it is true. He is true; he is not swayed by appearances. They have described him accurately for the purpose of destroying him.

Flattery generally works that way. It is rarely a lie. It is a true thing said by somebody who wants something, and the tell is not the content but the timing — it arrives immediately before the request. Anyone in any position of responsibility should learn to feel a cold draught when a conversation opens like this one.

Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Should we pay them, or should we not?

They ask it twice, to shut off any escape into generality. Yes or no.

And the trap has two jaws, and both are lethal.

Say yes, and he loses the crowd. This is the poll tax imposed after Judea became a Roman province in AD 6, and it had provoked an armed revolt under Judas the Galilean — a rising whose survivors became the Zealots. The tax was hated as the badge of occupation. A Messiah who endorsed it was no Messiah.

Say no, and the Herodians in the room have a capital charge to carry straight to Pilate. Sedition. Inciting non-payment of imperial taxes. That is precisely what they will accuse him of at the trial anyway: we found this man... forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar (Luke 23:2).

But, knowing their hypocrisy, he said to them, Why put me to the test?

He names it before he answers it. He is not taken in for a moment, and he says so out loud — which is its own small lesson in dealing with people who come at you sideways. He does not pretend the flattery was sincere.

Bring me a denarius and let me look at it.

And with that sentence he takes control of the exchange. He has no coin himself — he asks them to produce one. And they can. Somebody in that group of scrupulous men has a denarius in his pocket, in the temple, and hands it over.

The trap is already sprung and they have not noticed.
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians supported Herod’s family and so Roman rule; the Pharisees resented Rome. The poll tax was paid directly to Rome and bitterly resented. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And they brought one. And he said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said to him, "Caesar's." Jesus said to them, "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." And they marveled at him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they brought one. And he said to them, Whose likeness and inscription is this?

Take the coin in your hand for a moment, because the whole answer is stamped on it.

A silver denarius of Tiberius carried the emperor's head in profile and, running round the edge, the words: Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus. On the reverse, the title Pontifex Maximus — high priest.

So this is not merely a coin with a portrait. It is a small metal blasphemy: a claim that a living man is the son of a god, and the chief priest of the world. Every devout Jew handling it knew that. The word Mark uses for likeness is eikōn — image — and the second commandment forbade graven images.

And they produce one, in the temple courts, on request.

They said to him, Caesar's.

They answer, because there is only one answer, and by answering they have conceded that they use his currency, benefit from his roads, and live under his protection.

Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.

The word render is not give — it means to pay back, to return what is owed. The coin has his face on it; hand it back to him.

And now the second half, which is where the sentence detonates.

If what bears Caesar's image belongs to Caesar, then what bears God's image belongs to God. And what bears God's image is not a coin. God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him (Gen. 1:27).

So he has answered the tax question in eight words and then, in eight more, put the questioners themselves on the scales. Caesar gets the coinage. God gets the man — all of him, because there is no part of a human being that is not stamped.

And there is a marvellous restraint in it. He does not say how much belongs to Caesar; that will vary with the government you live under. He fixes only the limit, and the limit is everything that is God's.

Which is why this verse has done duty for two thousand years in two opposite directions, and both are legitimate.

It establishes a real obligation. Jesus does not call the tax illegitimate or licence defiance of government. Paul says the same: the authority is God's servant for the ordering of society, so pay your taxes and honour the office (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17). A faith that despises all earthly authority has not read this verse.

And it bounds that obligation absolutely. Caesar may claim the coin. He may not claim the soul. The moment the state reaches for what belongs to God alone — worship, or the violation of God's clear command — the answer is no. We must obey God rather than men, said the apostles to this same council (Acts 5:29).

That is the fault line the martyrs died on. They paid every tax Rome levied, served in its works, prayed for its emperor — and would not drop the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord, because that word was God's.

And they marveled at him. They came to trap him and went away astonished. It is the only recorded outcome of the interview.
verseByVerse.note: The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection. And they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man's brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother. There were seven brothers; the first took a wife, and when he died left no offspring. And the second took her, and died, leaving no offspring. And the third likewise. And the seven left no offspring. Last of all the woman also died. In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection.

Mark stops to explain, which he does for his Roman readers, and the explanation is essential.

The Sadducees were the temple party: the priestly aristocracy, wealthy, conservative, politically pragmatic, and running the establishment Jesus had just disrupted. They held that only the five books of Moses carried full authority — the Prophets and the Writings they did not treat as binding — and they denied the resurrection, angels and spirits alike (Acts 23:8).

They are not the Pharisees. This is a different opponent with a different objection, and it is the only time in Mark they appear.

Teacher, Moses wrote for us. Note where they begin. Moses — because Moses is the only authority they accept. Everything about the question is designed to be argued on their own ground.

If a man's brother dies and leaves a wife, but leaves no child, the man must take the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.

This is the levirate law of Deuteronomy 25:5–6, and it is worth understanding why it existed, because the Sadducees are about to weaponise a piece of genuine kindness.

In a world with no pensions and no property rights for women, a childless widow was destitute and her husband's name and land died with him. The law required his brother to marry her, so that she was provided for and the first son would carry the dead man's name. It is a mercy, not a curiosity — it is the law behind the book of Ruth.

There were seven brothers.

And now the story, and it is not a real case. It is a debating exercise, constructed to make the doctrine of resurrection look ridiculous, and the number seven is chosen for maximum absurdity.

Watch the rhythm of it, because the telling is as revealing as the argument: the first took a wife and died; the second took her and died; the third likewise; and the seven left no offspring.

Last of all the woman also died.

Note how she appears. Seven men are named as taking her. She is the object of every sentence and the subject of none, until she is disposed of in seven words at the end.

There is no suggestion anywhere in their story that she is a person. Seven bereavements. Seven times widowed, childless, and passed along. Nobody in that conversation gives it a thought.

In the resurrection, when they rise again, whose wife will she be? For the seven had her as wife.

And there is the point of the whole construction, and it is not a question. It is a joke — the sort of thing clever men produce to embarrass a doctrine they have already dismissed, and one imagines they had used it before with success.

The logic runs: if the resurrection is real, then heaven contains an insoluble domestic problem, therefore the resurrection is absurd.

And notice the assumption underneath it, because Jesus is about to go straight for it. They are picturing the life to come as this life continued — the same arrangements, the same institutions, the same property law, running on forever.

Which is exactly the mistake made by a great many people who have never heard of a Sadducee.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection. Levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God? For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is this not the reason you are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God?

He answers the joke with a diagnosis, and it is a blunt one delivered to men who were the professional custodians of both.

Two failures, and they are still the only two available.

You do not know the Scriptures. Not that they had not read them — they had them largely by memory. They did not know what was in them, which is a different thing, as verse 26 is about to demonstrate humiliatingly.

Nor the power of God. This is the deeper failure. They had quietly settled, without ever putting it in words, that God could not do a thing they could not imagine. The whole riddle rests on it: they cannot picture a resurrection life that is not this life extended, so they conclude there is none.

That second failure is extremely common among religious people, and it does not announce itself as unbelief. It sounds like realism. It is the settled assumption that God will not act, that this marriage will not change, that this person will not be converted, that nothing much is going to happen — an assumption formed not from Scripture but from experience, and then read back into Scripture.

For when they rise from the dead, they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.

He denies their premise. The age to come is not this age with the same furniture.

And this verse needs handling gently, because a great many people are living inside it. If you have buried a husband or a wife — if the person you were one flesh with for forty years is in a grave, and you have read this sentence and felt something close on your chest — then take it slowly and take the whole of it.

First, notice what he does not say. He does not say we become angels; he says like angels, and the comparison is specific to the matter in hand — those who cannot die do not need to marry and reproduce.

He does not say that love ends. He does not say we will not know one another. Every instinct that the resurrection means less — fewer people, thinner relationships, a vague and impersonal eternity — is precisely the Sadducees' mistake in reverse, and the Bible never once suggests it. Paul expects to recognise the Thessalonians (1 Thess. 2:19); the disciples recognised Moses and Elijah on a mountain, having never met them.

Second, understand why marriage as an institution is finished. Not because it was too small a thing but because it was a signpost, and you take the signpost down when you arrive. Marriage was always a mystery which, Paul says, refers to Christ and the church (Eph. 5:32). What you had was a picture of the union that is about to be consummated in fact, and no one at the wedding stares at the invitation.

So the honest word to a widow or widower is this: nothing good will be lost. Not the years, not the knowledge of each other, not the love. It will be taken up into something so much larger that the thing you are afraid of losing will look, when you are standing in it, like the smaller version of what you have.

And there is the marriage supper of the Lamb still to come, and you will be at it (Rev. 19:9).

verseByVerse.quote: And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush, how God spoke to him, saying, 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living. You are quite wrong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush?

Now he goes on the attack, and the choice of ground is masterly.

He could have quoted Daniel — many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life (Dan. 12:2) — or Isaiah — your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise (Isa. 26:19). Those are the obvious texts, and they are decisive, and the Sadducees would have waved them away, because they did not grant full authority to the Prophets.

So he goes into the Torah, which they do accept. And not merely into the Torah — into Exodus 3, the burning bush, one of the best-known passages in the whole Bible, which every priest in that delegation knew by heart.

Have you not read? is a devastating question to put to men whose profession is reading, and he asks it twice in this chapter (v. 10).

How God spoke to him, saying, I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.

And the whole argument turns on two words: I am.

Moses is standing at the bush somewhere around 1400 BC. Abraham has been dead for several centuries. Isaac and Jacob likewise. Their bones are in a cave at Machpelah, and everyone concerned knows it.

And God does not say I was the God of Abraham. He says I am.

He is not God of the dead, but of the living.

There is the conclusion, and it is not a play on grammar. It rests on what a covenant is.

God had bound himself to Abraham personally — to be God to you and to your offspring after you (Gen. 17:7). And the point is this: a relationship of that kind cannot be terminated by the death of one party without God's own word failing. If Abraham has simply ceased to exist, then God is describing himself by a relationship with nobody. He is the God of a memory.

He is not. I am. Which means Abraham is.

And behind it lies something even better than survival. God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city (Heb. 11:16). He named himself by these men. He put their names into his own title, permanently — and he is not the God of dust.

You are quite wrong.

He began the answer with you are wrong (v. 24) and he ends it with you are quite wrong, which is stronger — utterly, greatly mistaken. Mark has not softened it.

And take away the thing that is bigger than the argument.

The doctrine of the resurrection is not a late addition, invented between the Testaments or imported by the church. It was lying in the first book of the Bible, in the most familiar passage in it, in a present-tense verb — and the men who read that passage every year had never seen it.

Which is worth remembering next time you read a chapter you think you know. He found the resurrection of the dead in I am. There is more in your Bible than you have got out of it.
verseByVerse.note: “The passage about the bush” is how a passage was located before chapter and verse numbers existed. Jesus answers from the books of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–44 — The Great Commandment, David’s Lord, and the Widow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The one honest question (vv. 28–34). After a day of traps, a scribe asks something he actually wants to know — which commandment is the most important. He gets the Shema and Leviticus 19, agrees warmly, and is told he is not far from the kingdom of God. And after that, nobody dares ask anything at all.

The question he asks them (vv. 35–37). So Jesus asks one instead, and it is the deepest thing he says in public. If the Christ is David's son, why does David call him Lord?

The warning (vv. 38–40). Then a warning about the men in the long robes who love the greetings and the best seats, say long prayers for show, and devour widows' houses.

The widow (vv. 41–44). And he goes and sits down opposite the treasury and watches people give — and the last thing he does in this temple before he leaves it forever is point out a woman putting in two of the smallest coins in circulation.

Mark has put her immediately after devour widows' houses, and that is not an accident.
verseByVerse.theology:
Psalm 110 and the deepest disclosure in the Gospel. Jesus takes the most quoted psalm in the New Testament and asks a question nobody could answer.

Everyone agreed the Christ would be David's son — the promise ran through the whole Old Testament (2 Sam. 7:12–16; Isa. 11:1). And in Psalm 110, David writes: The LORD says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand. The first LORD is God; the second is somebody David calls my Lord.

In that culture the point is unanswerable. Honour ran upward from son to father, never downward. A man does not call his own descendant his lord.

So: how can the Christ be David's son and David's Lord at once? Mark records no answer, and the crowd hears him gladly, and nobody says a word.

The answer is that both are true, and it takes the whole New Testament to say it. Concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by his resurrection (Rom. 1:3–4). David's son by birth; David's Lord from eternity.

And notice which verse of the psalm he quotes: sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet. He asks this in the temple, on the Tuesday, surrounded by the men who will have him killed on the Friday. They are the enemies in the sentence, and he quotes it to their faces.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You are not far from the kingdom of God.

The scribe has answered magnificently. He has the doctrine of God right, the summary of the law right, and the priorities right — he even says out loud, as a temple professional, that love of God and neighbour outweighs the whole sacrificial system, which is a remarkable thing for such a man to concede.

And Jesus does not say you are in. He says not far.

Now: that is the most uncomfortable commendation in the Gospel, because not far is still outside, and it is the address of a great many people who have been in church all their lives.

The gap between near and in is not a gap in knowledge. This man's theology was better than the Twelve's. The gap is a Person. He was standing three feet away, and the question was never whether the scribe could give the right answer about the law but whether he would follow the man who was about to keep it for him.

So it is worth asking plainly: could you give the right answers, and never have come? Right doctrine is the beginning and it is not the destination. Being able to describe a door is not the same as walking through it — and Mark never tells us whether this man did.

verseByVerse.quote: And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well, asked him, "Which commandment is the most important of all?" Jesus answered, "The most important is, 'Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.' The second is this: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself.' There is no other commandment greater than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And one of the scribes came up and heard them disputing with one another, and seeing that he answered them well.

At last, somebody honest.

Mark is careful to tell us the man's motive, and it is different from everyone else's in this chapter. He has been listening. He was impressed. He asks because he wants to know — and Matthew's version has a harder edge to it (Matt. 22:35), so this may be a man whose motives improved as the conversation went on. That happens.

Either way, Mark presents him as a man who came to learn, and he is the only one all day.

Which commandment is the most important of all?

It was a live question and not an idle one. The rabbis counted 613 commandments in the Law — 248 positive and 365 negative — and debated endlessly which were heavy and which light. Asking a teacher to name the first was a standard way of finding out how he thought.

The most important is, Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one.

And Jesus begins one line earlier than he needed to.

He was asked for a commandment and he starts with a statement of fact. This is the Shema (Deut. 6:4), the confession every observant Jew recited morning and evening, taught to children as soon as they could speak, and written on the doorposts of the house.

The order matters enormously. He does not begin with what you must do. He begins with who God is. The command to love follows from the declaration, and it could not be issued without it. Because there is one God — not one among many, not a department of life alongside others — the love owed him cannot be partial. A rival would deserve a share. He has none.

And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.

Four faculties, and the point of listing them is not to divide a person into parts but to leave nothing out. Every route to the word all is taken.

Heart — in Hebrew thought, the control room: what you decide, want, and are committed to. Soul — the life itself, the animating self. Mind — which Deuteronomy 6:5 does not list; God is to be loved with the intellect, and lazy thinking about him is not humility. Strength — the body, the energy, the money, the hours.

Which makes it concrete rather than mystical. Loving God with your strength is a question about your diary and your bank statement. Loving him with your mind is a question about whether you have ever taken the trouble to understand what you believe.

And it is worth admitting what everyone knows on reading it: nobody has kept this commandment for a single hour. It is the first commandment and it is the one that convicts everybody, which is why the man who quoted it is on his way to keep it perfectly on our behalf.

The second is this: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.

He was asked for one and gives two, and they cannot be separated. This is Leviticus 19:18 — and it is worth noticing that Jesus lifts it out of a chapter full of extremely practical instructions about wages, harvests, deafness, blindness and honest scales.

As yourself is not a command to love yourself first; it assumes the self-interest everybody already has and makes it the measuring stick. You know how attentively you consider your own comfort, reputation and future. That much, to him.

There is no other commandment greater than these. And John draws the conclusion the hard way: if anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar (1 Jn. 4:20).
verseByVerse.note: “Hear, O Israel” (the Shema) was recited daily by devout Jews.

verseByVerse.quote: And the scribe said to him, "You are right, Teacher. You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him. And to love him with all the heart and with all the understanding and with all the strength, and to love one's neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices." And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, "You are not far from the kingdom of God." And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the scribe said to him, You are right, Teacher.

He does not argue. He agrees, warmly, and then does something unusual: he repeats the answer back in his own words, which is what a man does when something has actually gone in.

You have truly said that he is one, and there is no other besides him.

And he adds a phrase of his own from Deuteronomy 4:35 — there is no other besides him. He is not parroting. He is thinking.

And to love him with all the heart... and to love one's neighbor as oneself, is much more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.

Now stop, because of who is speaking and where he is standing.

This is a scribe, in the temple courts, during Passover week, with the smoke of the altar going up not far away and the whole vast machinery of sacrifice running around him — and he says that loving God and your neighbour matters more than all of it.

That is a remarkable thing for a religious professional to concede, and it is not novel; it is what the prophets had been saying for centuries. I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hos. 6:6). To obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam. 15:22). Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings... as in obeying the voice of the LORD?

The man has read his Bible and believed it, and he is honest enough to say so in the one place where saying it costs something.

And when Jesus saw that he answered wisely, he said to him, You are not far from the kingdom of God.

The only commendation of its kind in the Gospel, and it is one of the most searching sentences in it — because of what it says and what it does not.

It is genuine praise. Jesus does not damn him with faintness. The man has the doctrine of God right, the summary of the law right, and the priorities right, and he is told so.

And not far is still outside.

That is the ache in it. Near the kingdom is not in the kingdom, and there is no other category. The man is standing closer to it than anyone else in this chapter — closer, in some respects, than the disciples, whose theology was worse — and he is on the wrong side of a line.

So what is the gap? It is not information. He knows more than most of the Twelve.

The gap is a Person, and he is three feet away. The whole of this chapter has been asking who Jesus is: the beloved son in the vineyard, the rejected stone, David's Lord. The scribe can recite the greatest commandment; the question is whether he will follow the man who is about to keep it on his behalf and die for the failure of everyone who did not.

Mark never tells us whether he did. The account simply stops, and the man walks out of the Gospel one step from home.

Which leaves the question with the reader, and it should be asked plainly rather than admired at a distance. Could you give the right answers and never have come? A person can hold sound doctrine, love a good sermon, defend the faith competently, be entirely orthodox — and be near. Being able to describe a door is not the same as walking through it.

And after that no one dared to ask him any more questions.

The interrogations are over. Three parties have tried and all three have been dismantled. Mark closes the day's business in a sentence, and the silence is the verdict.

parallels.desc: to obey is better than sacrifice

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, "How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David? David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared, 'The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet."' David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?" And the great throng heard him gladly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as Jesus taught in the temple, he said, How can the scribes say that the Christ is the son of David?

Nobody dares ask him anything, so he asks them.

And note that it is not an attack on the doctrine. The Christ is the son of David — the promise runs through the whole Old Testament (2 Sam. 7:12–16; Isa. 11:1), and blind Bartimaeus shouted it at him on the Jericho road two chapters ago and was commended for it (10:47–48). Jesus is not denying it. He is asking whether it is the whole of it.

David himself, in the Holy Spirit, declared.

Before the quotation, notice the doctrine of Scripture packed into that phrase. David himself — so the psalm is his. In the Holy Spirit — so it is also God's. Two authors, one text, and no tension between them. That is how Jesus read his Bible.

The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet.

Psalm 110:1 — the single most quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament, and the argument turns on the two different words rendered Lord.

The first is the divine name itself, which English Bibles print as the LORD in small capitals. The second is adoni — my master, my lord, a title of superior rank. So David, writing under the Spirit, records God speaking to somebody whom David himself calls my Lord.

David himself calls him Lord. So how is he his son?

And in that culture the difficulty is total. Honour flowed upward — a son honoured his father, a descendant honoured his ancestor, never the reverse. Abraham does not call Isaac my lord. No Jewish father in history addressed his own great-great-grandson as his superior.

Yet the greatest king Israel ever had looks down the centuries at his own descendant and calls him Master.

Mark records no answer. Nobody had one.

And the answer, which it took the church a generation and the whole New Testament to state, is that both are true at once. Concerning his Son, who was descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection from the dead (Rom. 1:3–4).

David's son by birth. David's Lord from eternity. The one who came from David's line existed before David did — which is why he can say elsewhere, before Abraham was, I am (John 8:58).

This is the deepest thing Jesus discloses about himself in public in this Gospel, and he does it as a riddle, three days before the cross, because a claim like that stated flatly in the temple would end the week early.

And notice which line of the psalm he chose. Until I put your enemies under your feet. He is standing in the temple, on the Tuesday, surrounded by the men who have already resolved to kill him — and he quotes, to their faces, a promise about what God will do with the enemies of his Christ.

And the great throng heard him gladly. The professionals have gone silent; the crowd is delighted. It is the last note of his public teaching in this Gospel, and within three days that same city will be shouting for his execution.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110:1 is among the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New.

verseByVerse.quote: And in his teaching he said, "Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes and like greetings in the marketplaces and have the best seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at feasts, who devour widows' houses and for a pretense make long prayers. They will receive the greater condemnation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beware of the scribes.

He has just been asked a good question by a scribe and commended him for it, which is worth remembering: this is not a blanket condemnation of a profession. It is a warning about what religious office does to a man who lets it.

And it is spoken publicly, to the crowd, about the most respected class in the community. The word is beware — watch out, keep your eyes open. He is telling ordinary people to be alert to their own religious leaders.

Four charges, and they build.

Who like to walk around in long robes. The scribe's white linen robe with its tassels was a mark of the scholar. Note the verb: they like to walk around in them. It is not the robe that is condemned but the strolling — the enjoyment of being seen in a garment that says what you are.

And like greetings in the marketplaces. A scribe was addressed with elaborate deference in public; the rabbis themselves ruled that a man should rise for a teacher of the law. Being recognised in the street was one of the perks, and they liked it.
