And have the best seats in the synagogues. The bench in front of the ark, facing the congregation, where the important men sat looking out at everybody else.

And the places of honor at feasts. The couches nearest the host.

Read the four together and a portrait emerges, and it is not of a wicked man. It is of a man who has come to need the deference. None of these things is a sin in itself; a robe is a robe and a seat is a seat. What is being described is an appetite — the quiet, constant, unadmitted pleasure of being thought well of, which grows so slowly that nobody notices it arriving.

And it is entirely available now. It does not require a robe. There is a version of it in whose name gets mentioned, who is asked to pray, who is consulted, who is thanked from the front.

Who devour widows' houses.

And now the charge turns from vanity to something far worse.

Scribes were not paid for teaching the law; it was to be given free. So they lived on gifts, and pious households considered it a privilege to support a scholar — and a widow with a small inheritance and a great respect for holy men was the softest target in the community. Some acted as legal trustees of estates and took their cut. Whatever the exact mechanism, the word Jesus uses is devour: they eat widows' houses.

This is a religious profession being used to strip the assets of the most defenceless people in the country.

And for a pretense make long prayers.

And the two halves belong together, which is the horror of it. The long public prayer is not incidental to the exploitation; it is the instrument of it. It is what persuades the widow that her money is safe with such a man.

They will receive the greater condemnation.

Not merely condemnation — greater. There are degrees, and the aggravating factor is the religious cover. To use the name of God as the tool of a fraud is worse than the fraud.

And James says the same to teachers in general: not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness (Jas. 3:1).

Now hold that sentence in your hand, because the very next thing Jesus does is sit down and watch a widow put her last two coins into the treasury those men administer.
verseByVerse.note: Long robes marked out men of learning and rank.

verseByVerse.quote: And he sat down opposite the treasury and watched the people putting money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large sums. And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he sat down opposite the treasury.

He is finished with the arguments. He crosses the court, sits down, and watches — directly opposite, straight across from it.

The place is the Court of the Women, and the treasury was thirteen chests ranged around it with metal mouths shaped like trumpets, each labelled for a different purpose. There was no privacy in it. You brought your coins to the chest, and — according to the accounts we have — the amount was announced to the attending priest, so it could be heard.

Which means that giving in that court was audible. Silver rattling down a bronze trumpet made a noise, and a great many coins made a great deal of noise.

And watched the people putting money into the offering box.

He sat and watched people give, deliberately, for some length of time.

And that is a sentence to sit with before we reach the widow, because it is the plainest statement in the Bible that Christ watches giving.

Not the accounts. Not the total. He watched the people. He was sitting opposite the chests, looking at faces and hands, on the last day he ever taught in that building.

He still does. There is no anonymous giving; there is only giving that other people cannot see.

Many rich people put in large sums.

Mark does not sneer at them, and neither should we. These were large gifts, genuinely given, to the house of God, and the temple was maintained by them. Nothing here says they were hypocrites.

But they were audible.

And a poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which make a penny.

Three things in that sentence.

She is a widow — which, two verses after who devour widows' houses, is not a coincidence. Mark has laid the two side by side deliberately, and we will have to reckon with it.

Two small copper coins. The Greek is lepta — literally thin ones, the smallest coin in circulation; the two together were worth about a sixty-fourth of a day's wage.

And note that there were two. That detail is the quiet devastation of the whole story. She could have kept one. Nobody would have known, nobody would have blamed her, and half of nearly nothing is still something to a woman with no income. She had the one choice available to a person with two coins, and she gave both.

Which make a penny. Mark converts the sum into Roman money for his readers — a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin there was. He is writing for people in Rome and wants them to feel how little it was.

And in that court, into a bronze trumpet, it would have made almost no sound at all.
verseByVerse.note: The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, with collection chests for offerings. Her two coins were the smallest in circulation, a tiny fraction of a day’s wage.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called his disciples to him and said to them, "Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he called his disciples to him.

He gathers them round, which he does when something matters. They have been at the other end of the court, or watching the rich, or looking at the buildings — in the very next verse one of them will say look, Teacher, what wonderful stones! (13:1).

He calls them over to look at a woman with two of the smallest coins in the empire.

Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box.

The amen-formula, for something that must not be missed — and then a statement that is simply false by every measure the treasury could apply.

She put in a fraction of a penny. They put in large sums. And he says she gave more than all of them, which means more than the total.

He is using a different set of scales, and the next verse gives it.

For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.

There is the measure, and it is not the amount. It is what was left afterwards.

They gave out of surplus — real gifts, honestly given, and nothing in their lives changed on the way home. She gave and had nothing. The last phrase is literally her whole living — the Greek word is bios, life. She put her life in the box.

So the kingdom's arithmetic is settled here, and it is worth stating plainly because it cuts both ways. It means no one can buy standing with God by the size of a gift; the largest cheque in the country is small change if it costs the giver nothing. And it means that the gift you are embarrassed by — the small amount from a pension, the hour given by somebody with almost no hours, the help offered by a person with nothing to spare — is registered by Christ as larger than the endowment.

But now the hard question, and it should not be dodged: is he commending her or lamenting her?

Mark has put this immediately after they devour widows' houses, and in the next verse the temple is condemned to demolition. It is very difficult to believe the placing is accidental.

Both are true, and the passage is stronger for holding them together.

He is lamenting the system. The treasury she is filling is administered by men he has just denounced for eating widows' houses, and the building it maintains has weeks left in God's reckoning and forty years left in fact. Her gift is going into an institution that is finished, run by men who prey on women like her. He does not commend the machinery for taking it.

And he is commending her without reserve. Nothing in his words is qualified. She did not give to a system; she gave to God, in the only way available to her, and he saw it and said so out loud — and because he did, a woman whose name nobody recorded is known to every Christian on earth two thousand years later.

Does this mean the poor should give everything they have? Jesus commends her heart; he does not command the poor to give away their living. Paul says a gift is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have (2 Cor 8:12), and that a believer must provide for his own household (1 Tim 5:8). And this passage stands immediately after Jesus’ warning against those who devour widows’ houses (12:40): no church or ministry may press the poor to give beyond their means.

And there is one more thing here, and it is the reason this scene closes his ministry in the temple.

The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45). He is sitting in that court with three days left, watching a poor woman put in everything she had, all she had to live on — and he is about to do exactly that.

She gave her whole living into the hands of God with nothing held back and no guarantee of tomorrow. He is the only other person in the story who does the same, and he does it on Friday.

Then he gets up and walks out of the temple, and never goes back.

12.theology:
Render to Caesar cuts in two directions and both must be held. It establishes a real obligation — the coin bears his image, so give it to him, and Paul says the same (Rom. 13:1–7; 1 Pet. 2:13–17). Christianity is not anarchy. And it bounds that obligation absolutely: Caesar may claim the coin, but what bears God's image belongs to God, and man bears it (Gen. 1:27). So the same verse that tells you to pay the tax tells you where obedience stops. We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29) was said to this same council. The martyrs paid every tax Rome levied and would not drop the pinch of incense that called Caesar Lord.

The Sadducees and the ground he chose. They were the priestly aristocracy who accepted only the five books of Moses and denied resurrection, angels and spirits alike (Acts 23:8). So Jesus does not quote Daniel 12:2 or Isaiah 26:19; they would have waved those away. He goes into the Torah, into the burning bush every priest knew by heart, and finds the resurrection in two words: I am the God of Abraham — spoken centuries after Abraham died. A covenant of that kind cannot be ended by the death of one party without God's own word failing. He wins the argument inside the fence they built themselves.

David's son and David's Lord. In Psalm 110:1 the first LORD is the divine name and the second is my lord, a title of superior rank. In that culture honour ran upward only; no man called his own descendant his master. So how is the Christ both? Mark records no answer, and the whole New Testament is the answer: descended from David according to the flesh and was declared to be the Son of God in power... by his resurrection from the dead (Rom. 1:3–4). David's son by birth; David's Lord from eternity. And note the line he quotes — until I put your enemies under your feet — spoken in the temple to the men who would kill him on Friday.
12.examples:
Then: two lepta, the thinnest coins in circulation, dropped into a bronze trumpet-mouthed chest that made almost no sound.

And the detail that undoes you is that there were two. She could have kept one. Nobody would have known and nobody would have blamed her, and half of nearly nothing is still something to a woman with no income. She had the one choice available to a person with two coins, and she gave both.

Now: the measure is not the amount but what is left afterwards. The rich gave real gifts, honestly, and nothing in their lives changed on the way home. She gave and had nothing — all she had to live on.

That cuts both ways. No one buys standing with God by the size of a gift; the largest cheque in the country is small change if it costs the giver nothing. And the gift you are embarrassed by — the small amount from a pension, an hour from someone who has almost no hours — is registered by Christ as larger than the endowment.

Is he commending her or lamenting her? Both, and the passage is stronger for holding them together. He has just denounced the men who devour widows' houses, two verses earlier, and the building her money maintains has forty years left. He does not commend the machinery for taking it. And he commends her without a single qualification — she gave to God in the only way available to her, and because he said so out loud, a woman whose name nobody recorded is known to every Christian on earth.

And note where he was sitting. The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45), and he spent one of his last hours in that temple watching a woman put in everything she had to live on. She is the only other person in the story who does what he is about to do on Friday.

13.title: Stay Awake
13.text: <sup>1</sup>And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!” <sup>2</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.” <sup>3</sup>And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, <sup>4</sup>“Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?” <sup>5</sup>And Jesus began to say to them, “See that no one leads you astray. <sup>6</sup>Many will come in my name, saying, ‘I am he!’ and they will lead many astray. <sup>7</sup>And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. <sup>8</sup>For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains. <sup>9</sup>But be on your guard. For they will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. <sup>10</sup>And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. <sup>11</sup>And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. <sup>12</sup>And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. <sup>13</sup>And you will be hated by all for my name’s sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved. <sup>14</sup>But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. <sup>15</sup>Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out, <sup>16</sup>and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak. <sup>17</sup>And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! <sup>18</sup>Pray that it may not happen in winter. <sup>19</sup>For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. <sup>20</sup>And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days. <sup>21</sup>And then if anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ!’ or ‘Look, there he is!’ do not believe it. <sup>22</sup>For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. <sup>23</sup>But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand. <sup>24</sup>But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, <sup>25</sup>and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken. <sup>26</sup>And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. <sup>27</sup>And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven. <sup>28</sup>“From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. <sup>29</sup>So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates. <sup>30</sup>Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. <sup>31</sup>Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. <sup>32</sup>“But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father. <sup>33</sup>Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. <sup>34</sup>It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake. <sup>35</sup>Therefore stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning— <sup>36</sup>lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. <sup>37</sup>And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake.”
13.overview:
They come out of the temple and a disciple points at the stonework — and he was right to. Herod's platform covers thirty-five acres; the largest block still visible weighs several hundred tons; Josephus says the gold front was too bright to look at in the morning sun. Building had been going on for some forty-six years when Jesus first spoke of it (John 2:20), and it was not finished until AD 63.

Jesus says not one stone will be left on another, and seven years after the last workman went home it was gone.

Four disciples take him aside on the Mount of Olives, looking straight across at the building, and ask when and how they will know. What follows is the longest teaching in Mark before the passion, and its most striking feature is what it refuses to give. He describes signs and then says they do not mean what people will say they mean — the end is not yet. He describes the fall of Jerusalem in detail, and the flight, and the unequalled distress, and sets it inside a generation. And then, at v. 32, the discourse turns a corner: of his own coming there is no sign, no timetable, and no one knows the day — not the angels, not even the Son.

What is left, four times over, is a command. Stay awake — which the parable at the end defines not as scanning the horizon but as being found at your post, doing the work you were left. And in the next two chapters Mark walks his reader through all four watches of the night, and the disciples fail at every one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Signs, Perseverance, and the Abomination
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The stones (vv. 1–4). They come out of the temple and a disciple points at the masonry, and Jesus says that not one of those stones will be left standing on another. Four of them come to him privately on the Mount of Olives, looking straight across at the building, and ask when.

The age (vv. 5–13). His answer begins by taking away the thing they wanted. Deceivers will come; wars will come; earthquakes and famines will come — and none of it means what people will say it means. The end is not yet. The church will be beaten in synagogues and hauled before governors, betrayed by brothers and fathers and children, hated by everyone. And in the middle of the list, one line that is not a disaster at all: the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations.

The crisis (vv. 14–23). Then something specific: an abomination standing where it ought not to be, and instructions so urgent that a man on his roof is not to go downstairs for his belongings. Forty years later, Roman legions came up the valley.

Notice what the discourse never gives them: a date. It gives signs that will be misread, warnings that will be needed, and one command repeated four times — stay awake.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two questions, two answers, one discourse. The key to Mark 13 is that the disciples asked about the temple (v. 4), and Jesus answers about the temple and about his own coming, and the seam between them is visible if you look for it.

Everything down to v. 30 is hedged with signs and set inside a timeframe: false messiahs, wars, the abomination in the holy place, the flight from Judea, unequalled distress — and this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Every one of those things did happen, in the horror of AD 70, some forty years on. That is why the fig tree can say the season is near, at the very gates.

Then look at the hinge in v. 32: But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows. The but turns a corner. From here Jesus says the opposite of everything before — no sign, no timetable, nobody knows, it arrives like a householder in the night.

So the discourse deliberately holds two comings apart: the near judgement on Jerusalem, marked with signs and dated inside a generation, and the far return of the Son of Man, without sign or date. Read this way — and it is the reading the seams of the text ask for — Jesus was not mistaken by a single day. He said the temple would fall in their lifetime, and it did. He said his own coming would be unmarked and unknown, and it remains so.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations (v. 10) — one bright, forward-driving line dropped into the middle of a catalogue of disasters.

It is the only item in the list that is not something to be endured but something to be done, and the little word first makes it a milestone: history will not close until the good news has reached every people.

Now: that turns the whole grim catalogue inside out. The wars and betrayals and floggings are not the church waiting helplessly for the end. They are the conditions under which the gospel travels — and often it travels furthest precisely by way of those dragged before governors and kings (v. 9). Paul reached Caesar's household because he was arrested. The persecution is not an interruption of the mission; it is one of its engines.

So the age between the resurrection and the coming has a task, and not merely a fear. Every tribe that hears is the clock of the world moving one turn closer to the dawn — which is why a Christian reading the news is not simply watching the world fall apart. He is watching the field in which the seed is being sown.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he came out of the temple, one of his disciples said to him, "Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!" And Jesus said to him, "Do you see these great buildings? There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as he came out of the temple.

He has just watched a widow put her last two coins into the treasury (12:41–44), and now he walks out of the building for the last time. He will never enter it again.

One of his disciples said to him, Look, Teacher, what wonderful stones and what wonderful buildings!

And you cannot blame him. Herod's temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world, and a Galilean fisherman standing under it would have had nothing to compare it with.

The platform Herod built covers thirty-five acres — it is still there, and you can walk on it. The retaining walls were made of dressed limestone blocks so precisely cut that they needed no mortar; the largest of them, still visible in the Western Wall tunnels, is about forty feet long and weighs several hundred tons. Nobody has satisfactorily explained how they were moved. The sanctuary itself was faced with white marble and gold, and Josephus says that at sunrise it was too bright to look at directly — from a distance the mountain looked like a snow-covered peak.

Work had begun around 20 BC and was still going on. It was finished in AD 63.

And Jesus said to him, Do you see these great buildings?

Not a dismissal. He grants the premise — yes, look at them.

There will not be left here one stone upon another that will not be thrown down.

Seven years after the last workman went home, it was gone.

Josephus, who was there, describes the destruction of AD 70: the sanctuary burned, and the gold in it melted and ran down into the joints between the stones, and the soldiers pulled the stones apart to get at it. So the demolition was not symbolic vandalism but systematic dismantling, done by men with a financial motive to leave nothing standing on anything else.

The prediction is as exact as a prediction gets.

Why, then, does the Western Wall still stand? It is part of the retaining wall Herod built around the temple platform, not part of the temple itself. Jesus spoke of these great buildings, the sanctuary and its courts, and of them not one stone was left on another.

And now take the sentence as it was spoken, because we hear it as history and they heard it as blasphemy.

This was not merely a large building. It was the house of God, the place where atonement was made, the centre of the religious life of every Jew on earth, the guarantee of the covenant. To say it would be levelled was to say something about God's dealings with his people that no one could hear calmly. Jeremiah nearly died for saying less (Jer. 26:8–9), and a false version of this very saying will be produced at Jesus's trial in two days' time (14:58).

And there is a plainer thing in it for us, standing where that disciple stood.

He was admiring the most permanent-looking thing in his world — the biggest, the most expensive, the most obviously here-to-stay — and it had forty years left. What survived that generation was not the masonry. It was twelve men, most of them poor, and a message.

Everything you can point at and call impressive is on a clock. Ask what you are actually building with, because the stones are always the wrong answer, and they always look like the right one.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great had rebuilt the temple on a vast scale, with some stones many yards long. The Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple, Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately, "Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as he sat on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple.

Mark's geography is doing work again. The Mount of Olives is the ridge across the Kidron valley, and from it you look straight down onto the temple platform — the whole thirty-five acres laid out in front of you, the gold catching the light.

So this entire discourse is delivered with the building in view. He is not describing an abstraction. He is sitting on a hillside, looking at it, telling four men what will happen to what they can see.

And the location carries a prophecy of its own. Ezekiel watched the glory of the LORD depart from a defiled temple, and it stood on the mountain that is on the east side of the city (Ezek. 11:23) — this hill. Zechariah says that on the day of the LORD, his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives (Zech. 14:4).

The glory left the temple and stopped on this ridge. And here he sits.

Peter and James and John and Andrew asked him privately.

The inner three, and Andrew — the same four who were called from their nets in chapter 1 (1:16–20), named together again here, as at the house in Capernaum (1:29).

Privately. The great crowd that heard him gladly in the temple (12:37) is gone. This is the last extended teaching in Mark before the passion, and it is given to four men on a hillside.

Tell us, when will these things be, and what will be the sign when all these things are about to be accomplished?

Two questions, and everything about how you read this chapter depends on noticing them.

When will these things be? — a date.

And what will be the sign? — a warning, a marker, something visible in advance.

And notice what they are asking about. Not the end of the world; Mark's version has no such phrase. They are asking about these things — the stones. He said the temple would be flattened, and they want to know when, and how they will see it coming.

It is exactly what any of us would ask, and it is exactly the question the discourse refuses to answer in the form it was put.

He will give them signs, and then tell them the signs do not mean what they will be tempted to think. He will give them a timeframe for the temple, and then say that of his own coming nobody knows the day or the hour — not the angels, not even the Son. And having declined to supply a date four times over, he will end by telling them the only thing they actually need: stay awake.

Which is a fair warning to bring to the whole chapter. People come to Mark 13 wanting what these four wanted, and the chapter was built to withhold it — not out of secrecy, but because a man who knows the date will prepare on the last afternoon, and a man who does not must live ready every day. The refusal is the pastoral care.
verseByVerse.note: The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus began to say to them, "See that no one leads you astray. Many will come in my name, saying, 'I am he!' and they will lead many astray. And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. This must take place, but the end is not yet. For nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom. There will be earthquakes in various places; there will be famines. These are but the beginning of the birth pains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See that no one leads you astray.

They asked when; his first word is watch out. Before a single sign is described, the danger is named — and it is not the wars or the earthquakes. It is being deceived, and he will return to it three more times (vv. 6, 22, 23).

Many will come in my name, saying, I am he! and they will lead many astray.

And it happened almost immediately. Josephus is full of them: Theudas, who promised to divide the Jordan; the Egyptian who led thousands out to the Mount of Olives promising the walls of Jerusalem would fall down; and in the final revolt, Simon bar Giora and others who took messianic titles. Gamaliel names two of them in Acts (Acts 5:36–37).

The pattern has never stopped. And note the exact shape of it: they come in my name. Not opposing Christ but claiming him — which is why the danger is to the church and not to the world.

And when you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed.

Now the instruction that most needs hearing, and it is the opposite of what religious people usually do with the news.

Do not be alarmed. He is not saying the wars will be small; he is telling his people how to receive the reports.

This must take place, but the end is not yet.

Two clauses that between them dismantle a whole industry.

This must take place. The must is the word of divine necessity, the same one used of his own suffering (8:31). History is not out of hand. What is coming is not a sign that God has lost control of the century.

But the end is not yet. And there is the correction, stated flatly. These things are not the countdown. He is deliberately disconnecting the calamities from the calendar.

For nation will rise against nation... earthquakes... famines.

He lists them, and every generation since has had all three, and every generation has produced people certain that theirs was the last.

These are but the beginning of the birth pains.

The image is exact and it is not merely about pain. Labour pains are real agony, and they mean that something is coming — and the early ones tell you almost nothing about how long it will be.

It is Paul's picture too: the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now (Rom. 8:22). The world is not simply decaying; it is in labour.

So here is the practical use of this paragraph, and it is worth taking seriously in an age of continuous news.

When the next catastrophe arrives — and it will — two responses are available and both are wrong. One is panic, the anxious scanning of events for the pattern. The other is the calculating excitement that treats disaster as a timetable, which has produced a long line of confident predictions and an equally long line of quiet retractions.

Jesus forbids both in one sentence. Do not be alarmed... the end is not yet. Read the news as a man who has been told in advance what the age would look like, and get on with the work he actually gave you — which is in the very next paragraph.
verseByVerse.note: Birth pains are a prophetic image for the troubles before God’s new age.

verseByVerse.quote: But be on your guard. For they will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake, to bear witness before them. And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations. And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say, but say whatever is given you in that hour, for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But be on your guard. The same warning again, and now with a specific content: what is coming is coming to you.

They will deliver you over to councils, and you will be beaten in synagogues, and you will stand before governors and kings for my sake.

Read Acts with this verse open and it is a table of contents. Councils — Peter and John before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4–5). Beaten in synagogues — Paul took the thirty-nine lashes five times (2 Cor. 11:24). Governors — Felix and Festus (Acts 24–25). Kings — Agrippa (Acts 26), and finally Caesar himself.

Note also where the first blows land: in synagogues. The persecution begins at home, among their own people, in the buildings they grew up in. It usually does.

To bear witness before them.

And there is the turn. The purpose clause is not to suffer but to bear witness. The dock is a pulpit. Every one of those trials put the gospel in front of an audience it would never otherwise have reached — which is exactly what Paul says from prison: what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Phil. 1:12).

And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all nations.

One bright line dropped into the middle of a catalogue of disasters, and it must not be missed.

It is the only item in the list that is not something to be endured but something to be done. And the little word first makes it a milestone: history will not close until the good news has reached every people. Note the same must as verse 7 — the wars are a divine necessity, and so is this.

Which turns the whole grim catalogue inside out. The persecution is not an interruption of the mission; it is one of its engines. The gospel travelled furthest along the roads that arrested men were dragged down.

So the age between the resurrection and the coming has a task, and not merely a fear. A Christian reading the news is not watching the world fall apart. He is watching the field in which the seed is being sown.

Has this already happened? In one sense, yes: Paul could say before AD 70 that the gospel had been proclaimed in all creation under heaven (Col 1:23). In its fullest sense it goes on until the end. But Christ’s return is not triggered by our success, as though the church could finish a list and bring him back. The day is fixed by the Father (v. 32). Our part is to be faithful in the task.

And when they bring you to trial and deliver you over, do not be anxious beforehand what you are to say.

And now a promise that needs its edges kept sharp, because it is widely misapplied.

What it is. It is a promise for the dock. When a believer is dragged before a hostile court with no lawyer, no preparation and no idea what the charge will be, God undertakes to supply the words in the moment. Stephen's face and Stephen's speech are the fulfilment (Acts 6:15; 7). So is the boldness of two uneducated fishermen that astonished the council (Acts 4:13).

What it is not. It is not a licence for the preacher who has not opened his Bible all week to climb into a pulpit expecting the Spirit to make up the difference. Nothing in Scripture supports that. Paul told Timothy to do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth (2 Tim. 2:15), and asked for his books and parchments from prison (2 Tim. 4:13).

The unprepared sermon is not faith. It is presumption wearing faith's coat, and this verse was never about it.

For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit.

And that is the ground of the comfort. The believer standing in that courtroom is not alone and is not, finally, the one on trial. Somebody else is doing the speaking.
verseByVerse.note: The councils were local Jewish courts; synagogues had the authority to flog.

parallels.desc: Peter and John before the council

verseByVerse.quote: And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death. And you will be hated by all for my name's sake. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And brother will deliver brother over to death, and the father his child, and children will rise against parents and have them put to death.

Deliver over is what he has said will be done to him (10:33). Now it is done to his people, by their own.

Take the sentence slowly, because we read it as a general statement about hard times and it is not general at all. It names the closest bonds human beings have, in order.

Brother — the person you grew up beside. Father — and note the direction: a father hands over his child. Children — who rise against parents and have them executed.

Nothing about this is hypothetical. It is Micah's picture of a society in total moral collapse — for the son treats the father with contempt... a man's enemies are the men of his own house (Mic. 7:6) — and Jesus echoes it because it is precisely what following him will cost some of his people.

And it has cost exactly that, in every century, and does now. There are believers today whose families reported them.

If your own family regards your faith as a betrayal — if you have lost a brother's respect or a father's welcome over it — then hear that your Lord said this would happen, said it in advance, and knew it from the inside. His own family came to take him away by force, believing he was out of his mind (3:21).

And you will be hated by all for my name's sake.

Not for being difficult, or rude, or politically inconvenient. For my name's sake — and it is worth being honest that Christians sometimes attract dislike for other reasons entirely and then claim this verse. The promise is for hatred earned by belonging to him.

But the one who endures to the end will be saved.

And now the sentence that has kept anxious believers awake, so let it be answered straight.

It is not salvation by stamina. Nothing in the New Testament allows that reading. We are saved by grace through faith, and not by the strength of our own grip.

It is a description of what real faith does. Endurance is not the price of salvation; it is the evidence of it. The rocky ground in chapter 4 also received the word with joy, and had no root, and fell away when the heat came (4:16–17). The falling away did not cancel a genuine faith; it revealed a shallow one.

And the guarantee is in this very chapter. If you are reading that verse and asking will I hold on? — which is the right question and a healthy one — then read on seven verses. For the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days (v. 20). And read on to verse 27, where the Son of Man sends out his angels and gathers his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.

He does not lose them. The shepherd who counts them at the beginning counts them at the end, and the number is the same: no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28).

So the command is real and so is the promise, and they are not in competition. Endure is what you are told to do. For the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days is why you will.

parallels.desc: a man’s enemies are the men of his own house

verseByVerse.quote: But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains. Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out, and let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when you see the abomination of desolation standing where he ought not to be.

Now the discourse turns from the general to the specific, and this is the sign they asked for in verse 4.

The phrase comes from Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11), where it means a desecration so vile that it drives God out and leaves his sanctuary desolate — the word behind abomination is the standard Old Testament term for an idol.

And Daniel's words had already seen one fulfilment, centuries after he wrote them. In 167 BC the Greek tyrant Antiochus IV Epiphanes erected an altar to Zeus on the altar of burnt offering in the temple and sacrificed a pig on it. That is what the phrase meant to every Jew who heard it: the worst thing that has ever happened, happening again.

And note the grammar, because Mark's Greek is deliberately odd. Standing where he ought not to be — the participle is masculine, though abomination is neuter. Mark has broken the agreement on purpose. This is not merely a thing set up in the holy place. It is somebody.

(Let the reader understand.)

An aside from Mark to whoever is reading this aloud in a congregation — and it is a nudge, not a puzzle. It says: this is coded, and you will need to be alert, and when it happens you must not stand about discussing it.

A generation later, Roman legions came up the valley carrying their standards — which were objects of worship, with the emperor's image on them, and were saluted with sacrifice. When the temple fell, Josephus records that the soldiers brought those standards into the temple court and sacrificed to them there.

Is this fulfilled in AD 70, or by a future Antichrist? Many Christians, especially dispensationalists, expect a future ruler to set himself up in a rebuilt temple (2 Thess 2:3–4; Rev 13). But Luke gives Jesus’ words in a form his Gentile readers could not miss: when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, then know that its desolation has come near (Luke 21:20). The more likely reading is that this is AD 70, and the masculine “he” points to the Roman commander and his army. Paul’s man of lawlessness shows that a final rebellion against God is still to come; but that is not what Jesus warns of here, where the remedy is to flee to the mountains.

Then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.

Not fight. Not defend the holy city. Every nationalist instinct in that country said the opposite, and the Zealots acted on it, and it destroyed them.

And Eusebius records that it worked: the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by this prophecy, left the city before the siege closed and crossed the Jordan to Pella — and survived. A church took its Lord's tactical advice literally and lived.

Let the one who is on the housetop not go down, nor enter his house, to take anything out.

Palestinian houses had flat roofs with an outside stair, used for sleeping, drying figs and praying. The instruction is: when you see it, go down the outside steps and keep going. Do not step inside for anything.

And let the one who is in the field not turn back to take his cloak.

A man working in a field took off his outer cloak and left it at the edge. The cloak was expensive, it was his blanket at night, and the Law protected it from creditors precisely because a poor man could not do without it (Ex. 22:26–27).

Leave it.

And the picture behind all this is unmistakable to anyone who knows Genesis. There was another family told to get out of a doomed city and not look back, and one of them turned round (Gen. 19:17, 26). Jesus makes the connection explicit in Luke's version: Remember Lot's wife (Luke 17:32).

So the passage is tactical advice for a specific crisis in AD 70 — and it is also a permanent picture of what judgement does to the value of possessions. There comes a moment when the cloak is not worth the four seconds, and everything you own is exactly that cloak.
verseByVerse.note: Daniel foresaw an idolatrous desecration of the temple; it was foreshadowed in 167 BC, when Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar there. Luke speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies. Roofs were flat and reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days! Pray that it may not happen in winter. For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be. And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved. But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And alas for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing infants in those days!

He has just told them to run without stopping for a coat, and now he thinks about who cannot run.

That is the tenderness in the middle of the terror, and it is easy to read past. The Son of God, describing the fall of a city forty years away, pauses over the women who will be nine months pregnant that week and the mothers with a baby at the breast. He is not delivering a strategic assessment. He is imagining particular people, and it costs him something — the word is not a curse but a cry of grief.

Pray that it may not happen in winter.

And then something more remarkable still. He tells them to pray about the timing.

Winter in Judea means swollen wadis, impassable tracks, cold nights in the open. So: ask God to arrange the date of a judgement he has already determined, so that the flight will be survivable.

Which is worth stopping on, because it settles something about prayer. A thing can be fixed in the purpose of God and still be a proper subject of prayer, and God's sovereignty over an event is not a reason to stop asking about the details of it. Jesus tells them to pray about the weather during the fall of Jerusalem. Nothing is too settled to pray about, and nothing is too small.

For in those days there will be such tribulation as has not been from the beginning of the creation that God created until now, and never will be.

The language is deliberately absolute, and it is the language of the prophets for a catastrophe beyond comparison (cf. Dan. 12:1; Joel 2:2).

What happened in AD 70 is hard to overstate. Josephus, an eyewitness, describes famine so complete that people ate leather; a mother who killed and ate her own child; crucifixions outside the walls at a rate of five hundred a day until there was no more wood; and, at the end, the city burned and the population destroyed or enslaved. He puts the dead at over a million, and even a heavily discounted figure is a horror.

And if the Lord had not cut short the days, no human being would be saved.

Read that as it stands. Left to run its course, the thing would have consumed everybody. Nothing in human resistance was going to stop it.

But for the sake of the elect, whom he chose, he shortened the days.

And there is the sentence that should stop every reader, because it is the pastoral heart of the whole discourse.

The tribulation is bounded. Not by the exhaustion of evil, not by military intervention, not by the strength of the church. God shortens it. The days have an end because he set one.

And the reason he set one is not general benevolence. It is for the sake of the elect, whom he chose — and Mark says it twice over in the same breath, the elect, and then whom he chose, as though determined that we should not miss the deliberateness of it.

Notice what this does and does not promise. It does not promise that God's people are exempt from the tribulation; they were in Jerusalem, and Christians have been in every horror since. It promises something better than exemption: they are the reason it stops.

History is not a machine running until it wears out. Somewhere behind the worst of it there is a hand on the clock, and the setting of that clock is determined by love for particular named people.

So when you cannot see how a thing can go on and anyone survive it — the persecution in that country, the sickness in this house, the years that have been taken — the promise is not that you will be lifted out. It is that there is a limit, that the limit was fixed before it started, and that it was fixed for your sake.
verseByVerse.note: Winter rains made roads and river crossings hard.

parallels.desc: a time of trouble such as never has been

verseByVerse.quote: And then if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ!' or 'Look, there he is!' do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, the elect. But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then if anyone says to you, Look, here is the Christ! or Look, there he is! do not believe it.

He returns to the danger he opened with (v. 5), and it is significant that he ends the section here rather than with the tribulation. The worst thing in this passage is not the siege. It is deception.

Note the specific form it takes: here and there. A location. Somebody has him, somewhere, and you must go and see. That is the mark of the counterfeit, and Matthew's version spells out why it cannot be true: the real coming will be like lightning from east to west (Matt. 24:27) — nobody will need to be told where to look.

For false christs and false prophets will arise and perform signs and wonders.

And here is the thing that must be said plainly, because it cuts against an instinct many Christians have.

The signs will work.

Jesus does not say they will be tricks or that the wonders will be faked. He says they will perform signs and wonders, and the Bible is entirely consistent about this. Pharaoh's magicians duplicated the first plagues (Ex. 7:22). Deuteronomy legislates for exactly this case: if a prophet gives you a sign and it comes to pass, and then says let us go after other gods, you shall not listen, for the LORD your God is testing you (Deut. 13:1–3). Paul warns of a coming lawlessness with all power and false signs and wonders (2 Thess. 2:9).

So the supernatural is not self-authenticating. A thing can be genuinely inexplicable and not be from God — which means that it works is never, by itself, a reason to follow anybody.

The test is never the power. It is the doctrine underneath it. Does this lead people to the Christ who came in the flesh and died on a cross, or away from him? Deuteronomy's test is the same one John gives (1 Jn. 4:2–3), and it is the only one that holds.

To lead astray, if possible, the elect.

Two things in that clause, and they hold together.

The elect are the target. Not the world, which needs no deceiving. The deception is aimed at the church, by people using Christ's name.

If possible — and the phrase is a quiet reassurance without being a licence for carelessness. The attempt will be made and it will be formidable, and God's people are not finally lost. But the way they are kept is not by magic; it is by remembering what they were told, which is exactly the next verse.

But be on guard; I have told you all things beforehand.

The fourth warning in the chapter, and the reason given is a mercy: I have told you beforehand.

That is how God protects his people from deception — not by making them incapable of being fooled, but by telling them in advance and expecting them to remember. Which puts a plain duty on a Christian who wants to be safe: know your Bible well enough that a false thing sounds wrong when you hear it.

The forewarning is only a defence to somebody who has read it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–37 — The Coming of the Son of Man and the Call to Watchfulness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The coming (vv. 24–27). Sun darkened, moon gone out, stars falling, the powers shaken — and then the Son of Man, coming in clouds with great power and glory, sending out angels to gather his people from the four winds. It is Daniel 7 arriving, spoken by a man three days from a public execution.

The fig tree (vv. 28–31). A lesson in reading signs, and the most argued-over verse in the chapter: this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. And then a claim no creature could make — heaven and earth will go, and his words will not.

The hinge (v. 32). But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows — not the angels, not the Son. Everything before this verse had signs. Nothing after it does.

The command (vv. 33–37). A householder goes away, leaves each servant a job, tells the doorkeeper to stay awake — and might come back at any of the four watches of the night. Stay awake, four times over, and the last words are addressed past the four men on the hillside to everybody.

And Mark's reader is about to walk through all four watches in the next two chapters, with the disciples failing at every one.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not even the Son (v. 32) is the verse most often used against the deity of Christ. Arius built on it in the fourth century; it is still reached for today. If Jesus did not know the day, the argument runs, he cannot be God.

The answer the church has always given is not a dodge but the heart of who Christ is: the one person, the eternal Son, took to himself a complete human nature without ceasing to be fully God, so that from the incarnation there are two natures in the one Lord. According to his divine nature he is omniscient, upholding the universe; according to his human nature he learned to speak, grew tired, and — as Luke says plainly — increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52), which a mind that already knew everything could not do. So the single person can truly say I do not know as a man, while as God he knows the hour perfectly.

It is no more a contradiction than that the same Jesus could sleep in the stern of a boat and then stand up and silence the storm with a word (4:38–39). The one he did as a weary man; the other as the Lord of creation.

And Mark has set the proof of it one verse earlier, for anyone with eyes. In v. 31 this same speaker says heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away — a claim no creature could dare make, setting his own words above the entire created order. In v. 32 the same mouth says he does not know the day.

The starkest claim to deity and the starkest confession of human limitation, one breath apart, both true. That is not a prophet who overreached in v. 31, nor a mere man who was honest in v. 32. It is God become man — and this verse, far from disproving his deity, is one of the clearest windows in the Gospel onto the two natures in the one Christ.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a householder goes away and leaves his servants each with his work, and tells the doorkeeper to stay awake.

Notice how the parable defines watchfulness, because it is not what the word suggests. The servants are not told to sit at the window scanning the road. They are given jobs. Watching, in this parable, is doing what you were left to do — and the doorkeeper's post is itself a task.

Now: which corrects both of the standard mistakes about the Lord's return.

One is the anxious calculation that treats every crisis as a countdown and produces confident predictions and quiet retractions. The other is the practical forgetting that lives as though he is not coming at all.

Jesus rules out both with one image. The man who is ready is not the man who worked out the date; it is the man found at his post, doing his work, whenever the door opens. Blessed is that servant whom his master will find so doing when he comes (Matt. 24:46).

So the honest question is not when? — he has refused that four times. It is: what did he leave me to do, and am I doing it? If he came back this evening, would he find you at the post or asleep in it? That is a question about this week's ordinary duties, and it is the only question this chapter finally asks.

verseByVerse.quote: But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in those days, after that tribulation.

A marker in the text. Something else is now in view — after what has just been described.

The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will be falling from heaven, and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.

Every phrase echoes the prophets, and a Jewish hearer would have recognised all of them.

The sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light — Isaiah 13:10, from the oracle against Babylon. All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll — Isaiah 34:4, against Edom. The sun and the moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their shining — Joel 2:10.

So this is not fresh invention. It is the settled prophetic vocabulary for the day when God acts in judgement, and it is worth knowing that the prophets used it for events inside history — the fall of Babylon, the ruin of Edom — as well as for the last day.

Which means readers divide here, and the division is honest. Some take this as the collapse of the old order symbolised by its lights — the end of the temple age, the world of Judaism as it had stood since Sinai, going dark. Others take it of the literal end. The language will bear both, and it is very likely doing both at once, the way prophecy so often speaks of a near event in terms that only the final one exhausts.

But do not let the argument obscure what the imagery is actually saying, because that is not in dispute.

The sun, moon and stars were the fixed points. They are what you steer by, plant by, and set your calendar by; they had not failed once since the fourth day of creation. To say the lights go out is to say that the last reliable things are not reliable.

And the powers in the heavens will be shaken goes further still. Whatever holds the machinery in place — and the ancient world thought of these as ruling powers, angelic or otherwise — is not exempt either.

So: everything you thought was permanent, shaken. The building was going to fall (v. 2); now the sky.

Which is exactly the point of the chapter, and it is a strange comfort rather than a terror. He has spent thirty verses removing everything a person might lean on — the temple, the nation, the family, the possessions, and now the stars — and in six verses' time he will tell you the one thing that is not going anywhere: my words will not pass away.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: the stars will not give their light

verseByVerse.quote: And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory. And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds with great power and glory.

This is Daniel 7:13–14, and Jesus draws on it directly: behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man... and to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him.

Three things are packed into it.

The clouds. In the Old Testament, cloud is where God is — the pillar in the wilderness, the cloud that filled the tabernacle, the cloud on Sinai, the cloud on the mountain of transfiguration (9:7). To come with the clouds is not a description of weather. It is a claim to deity, and the high priest will understand it perfectly when Jesus says it under oath at his trial, and will tear his robes (14:62).

They will see. The whole of this Gospel has been about people not seeing — the blind man who saw walking trees, the disciples with eyes who did not see. That ends here. Nobody will need to be told where to look.

With great power and glory. And now hold this against the calendar. He says this on the Tuesday. On Friday he will be nailed up naked outside the city with a mocking placard over his head, and the same men who arranged it will stand underneath telling him to come down.

The one who says great power and glory is three days from the most public humiliation the ancient world could devise. Both are true. The second is how the first arrives.

Is this the second coming or the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70? Some, reading Daniel 7 carefully, note that there the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive the kingdom, and take these verses as Christ’s vindication shown in the temple’s fall. The more likely reading is that here the far horizon breaks through. People will see him; the elect are gathered from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven; and Jesus speaks of his final coming in the same terms elsewhere (8:38; 14:62). As in the prophets, the near judgment and the final one appear in one view, and these verses are where the final one shows.

And then he will send out the angels and gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven.

And now, after thirty verses of warnings, the end of the story — and it is not a courtroom scene. Mark's version says nothing here about judgement, thrones or separation. The one thing the Son of Man does when he comes is collect his people.

The language is the old promise of the regathering, and it comes straight out of the prophets: I will gather you from the peoples and assemble you out of the countries where you have been scattered (Ezek. 11:17); he will assemble the banished of Israel, and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth (Isa. 11:12).

And the reach of it is total. From the four winds — every direction there is. From the ends of the earth to the ends of heaven — Mark piles the phrases up, and the effect is that there is nowhere a believer can have been put that is outside the sweep of it.

Take that where it belongs. Christians have been scattered by every means the world has: exile, slavery, war, famine, prison, the sea. They have died in places nobody recorded and been buried where nobody knows. There are graves in every country on earth with no name on them.

He sends angels, and gathers his elect — his own, chosen, named — from the four winds, and does not leave one of them behind.

That is what he is coming for. He is coming to collect what is his.

Is this gathering the rapture? Many Christians believe that Christ will first come secretly to take the church away before a great tribulation, and later return in glory. But here the gathering comes after that tribulation (v. 24), it is public, for they will see, and Paul describes the same event with the same trumpet and the same meeting in the air (1 Thess 4:16–17). The more likely reading is that there is one return of Christ, visible to all, at which he gathers all his people. The church is not promised escape from trouble, but keeping through it (v. 13).

parallels.desc: one like a son of man with the clouds

verseByVerse.quote: "From the fig tree learn its lesson: as soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near. So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the fig tree learn its lesson.

The last time a fig tree appeared in this Gospel it was in full leaf and had nothing on it, and he cursed it, and it was an acted parable of the temple (11:13–21). Now the same tree teaches something positive.

As soon as its branch becomes tender and puts out its leaves, you know that summer is near.

And it is worth knowing why the fig in particular. Most trees in that country are evergreen — the olive, the carob, the pine — so they tell you nothing about the season. The fig is bare all winter and one of the last to bud. When the fig breaks, spring is genuinely over and the hot season is coming.

Nobody needs training to read it. A child could. That is the point of the image: the sign is unmistakable and requires no expertise, and it does not give you a date. It gives you a season.

So also, when you see these things taking place, you know that he is near, at the very gates.

The application, and everything turns on how much these things covers.

The phrase points back to what he has just described — the false messiahs, the wars, the abomination in the holy place, the flight from Judea, the unequalled distress. Those are the buds on the branch. When they appear, you know the season has turned.

At the very gates is a striking image and it prepares for the parable that ends the chapter: somebody is standing at the door, about to come in. In five verses there will be a householder returning to a house where a doorkeeper is supposed to be awake.

And here is the practical lesson, which is what he actually asks for.

The right response to a budding fig tree is not to calculate the exact date of midsummer. It is to get ready for hot weather.

The signs in this chapter were never given so that anyone could work out a timetable — he has said the end is not yet (v. 7) and will say no one knows (v. 32). They were given so that when the world goes dark his people would not panic, and would recognise the season, and would keep working.

Which is a rebuke to a whole industry of date-setting, and equally to the opposite error. A man who ignores the tree entirely is caught out by the summer just as surely as the man who publishes a date for it and is wrong.
verseByVerse.note: Unlike many trees in Israel, the fig loses its leaves in winter; its new leaves mark the coming of summer.

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I say to you, this generation will not pass away until all these things take place.

This must be met head on, because it is the verse sceptics reach for first. Here, they say, Jesus plainly promised his return within his hearers' lifetime — and the lifetime passed, and he did not come. If that were the meaning, it would be a failed prophecy, and a plain one.

It is not the meaning, and the discourse itself shows why.

Watch the two questions the whole chapter is answering. Back at the start the disciples asked about the temple — when will these things be? (v. 4) — and most of what has followed answers exactly that: the false messiahs, the wars, the abomination standing in the holy place, the flight from Judea, the unequalled distress.

Every one of those things took place within that generation, in the horror of AD 70, some forty years on. That is why the fig tree can say the season is near, at the very gates. The temple's fall was near, and it came, exactly as he said, down to the last stone.

Then look at the hinge in the very next breath. But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows (v. 32). The word but turns a corner. From there Jesus speaks of his final coming, and of it he says the opposite of everything before — no sign, no timetable, nobody knows the day, it arrives while the house is asleep.

So the discourse deliberately holds two comings apart: the near judgement on Jerusalem, hedged with signs and set squarely inside this generation; and the far return of the Son of Man, without sign or date.

Read this way — and it is the reading the seams of the text ask for — Jesus was not mistaken by a single day. He told them the temple would fall in their lifetime, and it did. He told them his own coming would be unmarked and unknown, and it remains so.

But what of vv. 24–27? Some Christians take this generation to mean the Jewish race, which will survive until the end, or the generation alive when the final signs appear. But everywhere else in Mark this generation means Jesus’ contemporaries (8:12, 38; 9:19). The answer lies in the question the disciples asked: when will these things be? (v. 4). These things are the signs Jesus has described, the false messiahs, wars, persecution, the desolation and the flight (vv. 5–23); in v. 29 they are what you see before he is near, not his coming itself. The coming of vv. 26–27 is the event those signs point toward, and of its day no one knows (v. 32).

Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away.

And over both stands this, which is one of the most extraordinary sentences in the Bible and is easy to skate over because it sounds like a familiar piece of piety.

He has just spent the chapter dismantling every permanence. The temple: gone. The nation: scattered. The family: divided. The possessions: not worth turning back for. The sun and moon and stars: put out.

Now he adds heaven and earth to the list — the whole created order, the thing all the others were made of — and says it will pass away.

And then sets his own words above it.

Consider who is speaking and where. A Galilean carpenter sitting on a hillside with four fishermen, two days from arrest, with no writings, no institution and no army. And he says that when the universe has gone, the sentences he has been speaking this afternoon will still be standing.

No prophet ever said such a thing. They said thus says the LORD and put the permanence where it belonged: the grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isa. 40:8). Jesus says my words.

That is a claim to deity as clear as any in the Gospel, and it is worth noticing that it stands one verse before the sentence people use to deny his deity.

And it is the comfort the chapter has been driving at. Everything you can see is temporary; he has taken thirty verses to prove it. What he has said to you is not.

parallels.desc: the word of our God will stand forever

verseByVerse.quote: "But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.

Two things are here, and both matter enormously.

First, the hinge. The but turns a corner in the discourse. Everything before this had signs and a timeframe. Everything after it has neither. That day is the Old Testament's own phrase for the day of the LORD, and of it there is no sign, no marker, no calculation — a fact that ought to have retired the date-setting business permanently, and never has.

Notice the descending scale: not men, not angels, not the Son. He goes as high as it is possible to go before stopping at the Father, and the effect is to slam the door. If the angels of heaven do not know it, no conference speaker with a chart does.

Second, the difficulty — and no verse in Mark is wielded more often against the deity of Christ.

Arius built on it in the fourth century, and it is still reached for today: if Jesus did not know the day, he cannot be God, since God knows everything.

The answer the church has always given is not a dodge but the very heart of who Christ is. The one person, the eternal Son, took to himself a complete human nature without ceasing to be fully God, so that from the incarnation on there are two natures in the one Lord. According to his divine nature he is omniscient, upholding the universe and knowing all things. According to his human nature he learned to speak, grew tired, and — as Luke says plainly — increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52), which a mind that already knew everything could not do.

So the single person can truly say I do not know as a man, while as God he knows the hour perfectly.

That is no more a contradiction than that the same Jesus could sleep in the stern of a boat because he was exhausted, and then stand up and silence a hurricane with a word (4:38–39). The one he did as a weary man; the other as the Lord of creation. Nobody finds that verse a problem, and it is the identical structure.

And Mark has set the proof of it one verse back, for anyone with eyes to see.

In verse 31 this same speaker says heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away — a claim no creature could dare to make, setting his own sentences above the entire created order.

In verse 32 the same mouth says he does not know the day.

Put them side by side: the starkest claim to deity in the Gospel and the starkest confession of human limitation, one breath apart, both true, both from Jesus. That is not the profile of a prophet who overreached in verse 31, nor of a mere man who was honest in verse 32. It is the profile of God become man.

So this verse, far from disproving his deity, turns out to be one of the clearest windows in the whole Gospel onto the mystery of the two natures in the one Christ — and it is a guarantee of his honesty as well. He is not withholding a date from them. In his incarnate human knowledge he genuinely does not have it, and he says so, to four men who would have given anything for it.

parallels.desc: not for you to know times or seasons

verseByVerse.quote: Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come. It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be on guard, keep awake. For you do not know when the time will come.

Two commands, and the reason given is the ignorance he has just confessed. Because nobody knows — therefore watch. The uncertainty is not a problem to be solved but the very ground of the instruction.

It is like a man going on a journey, when he leaves home and puts his servants in charge, each with his work, and commands the doorkeeper to stay awake.

A short parable, and every clause is load-bearing.

A man going on a journey. The master is genuinely absent. Not pretending, not watching from around the corner. He has gone, and the house runs without him for an indefinite period — which is exactly the situation of the church between the ascension and the return, and it is worth admitting that it feels like absence, because the parable says it is.

Puts his servants in charge. He does not leave a caretaker or lock the doors. He hands over the running of the house to the people who work in it. Real authority, real responsibility, real trust — and no supervision.

Each with his work.

Stop there, because this is the phrase that defines what watchfulness means in this chapter, and it is not what the word suggests to us.

Every servant has a job, and it is his job — specific, assigned, different from the next man's. And that means the servants in this parable are not standing at the window scanning the road. They are working. Watching, here, is doing the thing you were left to do.

And commands the doorkeeper to stay awake.

One man has a post at the door, and his job happens to be the watching — which is the one occupation in the household that produces nothing visible and looks, to anyone passing, like doing nothing at all. It is still work, and he was told to do it.

So take the correction, because it cuts against both of the standard mistakes.

One is anxious calculation — the reading of every crisis as a countdown, the charts, the confident dates and the quiet retractions. That is not what any servant in this parable is doing.

The other is practical forgetting: living as though he is not coming back, because he has not come back yet.

The parable rules out both with one image. The man who is ready is not the man who worked out the date. He is the man found at his post when the door opens.

Which turns the whole chapter into a question you can actually answer this week. Not when? — he has refused that four times now. But: what did he leave me to do, and am I doing it? The children in your house. The work you are paid for. The person you were asked to visit. The gift you have not used in three years. Each with his work.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore stay awake—for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning— lest he come suddenly and find you asleep. And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore stay awake — for you do not know when the master of the house will come, in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning.

He lists the four watches of the Roman night: evening, midnight, cockcrow, morning — six to nine, nine to twelve, twelve to three, three to six. The whole of the dark, divided up, and he could come in any of them.

And now look at what Mark does with those four watches in the next two chapters, because it is one of the most remarkable things in this Gospel and it is easy to miss.

In the evening — and when it was evening, he came with the twelve (14:17), and they sat down to the supper.

At midnight — Gethsemane, where he asks them to watch with him, and comes back and finds them sleeping. Three times. And says to Peter: could you not watch one hour? (14:37).

When the rooster crows — the courtyard, and Peter's third denial, and immediately the rooster crowed a second time (14:72).

In the morning — and as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation and delivered him to Pilate (15:1).

All four watches, in order, in the space of a single night. Mark has written the parable into the passion narrative.

Lest he come suddenly and find you asleep.

And that is exactly what happens. He came to them in the garden, at his hour of greatest need, and found them asleep — and the words Mark uses are the words of this parable. Stay awake is the same verb, three times in Gethsemane.

So the disciples were told this on Tuesday and failed it on Thursday, and Mark makes sure his reader sees it.

Which is a mercy, not merely an indictment. Because the men who failed the test in the garden are the men Christ went to the cross for, and restored on a beach, and sent to the ends of the earth. Failing to watch is not the end of a disciple. But do not imagine, reading this comfortably, that you would have stayed awake. They loved him and they were exhausted and they meant it, and they could not manage an hour.

And what I say to you I say to all: Stay awake.

The last words of the discourse, and they are addressed past the four men on the hillside.

He has been talking privately to Peter, James, John and Andrew, about a temple that fell nineteen centuries ago. And with his final sentence he turns and speaks to everyone who would ever read this — I say to all — which includes, quite deliberately, the person holding this book.
