So the chapter that began with a question about dates ends without one, and with a command instead. Not calculate. Not be afraid. Stay awake: at your post, doing your work, in a house whose master is coming back.

And then he gets up off that hillside and walks down into the four watches of his own night — the evening, the midnight, the cockcrow and the morning — awake through every one of them, while everybody who loved him slept.
verseByVerse.note: These are the four Roman watches of the night, roughly from 6 p.m. to 6 a.m.

13.theology:
Two questions, two answers, one discourse. The key to Mark 13 is that the disciples asked about the temple (v. 4), and the seam between the two answers is visible if you look for it. Everything down to v. 30 carries signs and a timeframe — false messiahs, wars, the abomination in the holy place, the flight from Judea — and this generation will not pass away until all these things take place. Every one of them did happen, in AD 70. Then v. 32 turns the corner: But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows. From there, the opposite of everything before — no sign, no date, nobody knows. Read this way, Jesus was not mistaken by a day: the temple fell in their lifetime as he said, and his own coming remains unmarked as he said.

Not even the Son (v. 32) is the verse most often used against Christ's deity, from Arius onwards. The answer is not a dodge but the heart of the incarnation: the one person, the eternal Son, took a complete human nature without ceasing to be fully God. As God he knows the hour; as man he increased in wisdom (Luke 2:52), which a mind that already knew everything could not do. It is the same structure as sleeping in a boat from exhaustion and then silencing the storm with a word (4:38–39) — the one as a weary man, the other as Lord of creation.

And Mark set the proof one verse earlier. In v. 31 the same speaker says heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away — a claim no creature could dare make, setting his own sentences above the created order. In v. 32 the same mouth says he does not know the day. The starkest claim to deity and the starkest confession of human limitation, one breath apart, both true. This verse is not a problem for his deity; it is one of the clearest windows in the Gospel onto the two natures in the one Christ.

And the signs will work (v. 22). Jesus does not say the wonders will be faked. Pharaoh's magicians duplicated the plagues (Ex. 7:22); Deuteronomy legislates for a prophet whose sign comes to pass and who then leads you to other gods (Deut. 13:1–3). The supernatural is not self-authenticating. It works is never by itself a reason to follow anybody; the test is always the doctrine underneath (1 Jn. 4:2–3).
13.examples:
Then: in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning — the four watches of the Roman night, listed as the hours at which the master might come home.

And Mark writes all four into the next two chapters, in order. When it was evening, he came with the twelve (14:17). At midnight, Gethsemane — where he asks them to watch, comes back and finds them sleeping, three times, and says could you not watch one hour? (14:37). At cockcrow, the courtyard, and immediately the rooster crowed a second time (14:72). And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests delivered him to Pilate (15:1).

The parable's own words are the passion narrative's words. Lest he come suddenly and find you asleep — and he came to them in the garden at his hour of greatest need and found them asleep.

Now: do not read that as an indictment only. The men who failed it in the garden are the men he died for, restored on a beach, and sent to the ends of the earth. But do not imagine you would have stayed awake either. They loved him, they meant it, they were exhausted — and they could not manage an hour.

And note how the closing parable defines watchfulness: the servants are given jobs, each with his work. Not scanning the road; working. The man who is ready is not the one who calculated the date but the one found at his post when the door opens. So the question this chapter finally asks is answerable this week: what did he leave me to do, and am I doing it?

14.title: The Cup, the Kiss, and the Fire
14.text: <sup>1</sup>It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him, <sup>2</sup>for they said, “Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people.” <sup>3</sup>And while he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he was reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly, and she broke the flask and poured it over his head. <sup>4</sup>There were some who said to themselves indignantly, “Why was the ointment wasted like that? <sup>5</sup>For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.” And they scolded her. <sup>6</sup>But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. <sup>7</sup>For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. <sup>8</sup>She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. <sup>9</sup>And truly, I say to you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her.” <sup>10</sup>Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. <sup>11</sup>And when they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he sought an opportunity to betray him. <sup>12</sup>And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him, “Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?” <sup>13</sup>And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, “Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him, <sup>14</sup>and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, ‘The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ <sup>15</sup>And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us.” <sup>16</sup>And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>17</sup>And when it was evening, he came with the twelve. <sup>18</sup>And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me.” <sup>19</sup>They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, “Is it I?” <sup>20</sup>He said to them, “It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. <sup>21</sup>For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” <sup>22</sup>And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, “Take; this is my body.” <sup>23</sup>And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. <sup>24</sup>And he said to them, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many. <sup>25</sup>Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.” <sup>26</sup>And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. <sup>27</sup>And Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ <sup>28</sup>But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.” <sup>29</sup>Peter said to him, “Even though they all fall away, I will not.” <sup>30</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” <sup>31</sup>But he said emphatically, “If I must die with you, I will not deny you.” And they all said the same. <sup>32</sup>And they went to a place called Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, “Sit here while I pray.” <sup>33</sup>And he took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. <sup>34</sup>And he said to them, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch.” <sup>35</sup>And going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. <sup>36</sup>And he said, “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will.” <sup>37</sup>And he came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, “Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? <sup>38</sup>Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” <sup>39</sup>And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. <sup>40</sup>And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him. <sup>41</sup>And he came the third time and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. <sup>42</sup>Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.” <sup>43</sup>And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. <sup>44</sup>Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, “The one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard.” <sup>45</sup>And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, “Rabbi!” And he kissed him. <sup>46</sup>And they laid hands on him and seized him. <sup>47</sup>But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. <sup>48</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? <sup>49</sup>Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled.” <sup>50</sup>And they all left him and fled. <sup>51</sup>And a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, <sup>52</sup>but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked. <sup>53</sup>And they led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. <sup>54</sup>And Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire. <sup>55</sup>Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. <sup>56</sup>For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree. <sup>57</sup>And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, <sup>58</sup>“We heard him say, ‘I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.’” <sup>59</sup>Yet even about this their testimony did not agree. <sup>60</sup>And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, “Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?” <sup>61</sup>But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him, “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?” <sup>62</sup>And Jesus said, “I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.” <sup>63</sup>And the high priest tore his garments and said, “What further witnesses do we need? <sup>64</sup>You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision?” And they all condemned him as deserving death. <sup>65</sup>And some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, “Prophesy!” And the guards received him with blows. <sup>66</sup>And as Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came, <sup>67</sup>and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, “You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus.” <sup>68</sup>But he denied it, saying, “I neither know nor understand what you mean.” And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed. <sup>69</sup>And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, “This man is one of them.” <sup>70</sup>But again he denied it. And after a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, “Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean.” <sup>71</sup>But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, “I do not know this man of whom you speak.” <sup>72</sup>And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, “Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.” And he broke down and wept.
14.overview:
The longest chapter in Mark, and the clock runs in hours. Two days before Passover the chief priests decide to take him quietly — not during the feast — and are overruled by their own accomplice, so that the Lamb dies at Passover after all.

Mark wraps that plot around a woman in Bethany who breaks a flask of nard worth a year's wages over his head. The room calls it waste; he calls it beautiful, and says she has anointed him for burial. Then Judas goes out and sells him for less than the perfume cost.

In a borrowed upper room he takes the Passover bread — the meal that had looked backwards to Egypt for fourteen centuries — and turns it round: this is my body, and this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many. Then they sing the Hallel and walk out into the dark.

What follows is the most exposed scene in the Gospels. In an olive grove, appalled and shaking, he asks his Father to take away the cup — the Old Testament's cup of wrath — and adds the words that hold the world together: yet not what I will, but what you will. Three times he comes back to friends who cannot stay awake for an hour.

Then a kiss, an armed crowd, and every one of them running. Upstairs in the high priest's house he answers the direct question at last — I am — and is condemned for it. Downstairs, at a charcoal fire, Peter says, in effect, "I am not", three times, and a bird calls.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Anointing, Betrayal, and the Last Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The plot and the perfume (vv. 1–11). Two days before Passover the chief priests are looking for a way to take him quietly. Mark then interrupts them with a woman in a house in Bethany breaking a flask of nard over his head — and closes the sandwich with Judas going to the priests for money. The plot frames the anointing, and the anointing interprets the plot: while men calculate the price of his death, a woman prepares his body for burial.

The upper room (vv. 12–21). Two disciples are sent into the city with a sign — a man carrying a water jar — and find everything as he said. And at the table, with the twelve reclining round him, he says that one of them will hand him over, and none of them looks at Judas.

The Supper (vv. 22–26). He takes the bread of the Passover, the meal that had commemorated the exodus for fourteen centuries, and says this is my body. He takes the cup and says this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

Then they sing, and go out into the night.
verseByVerse.theology:
He is not attending the Passover. He is the Passover.

For fourteen hundred years Israel had killed a lamb, put its blood where the destroyer would see it, and eaten a meal standing up, ready to leave — and told their children that this was the night God brought them out. Every element of that meal pointed backwards.

Jesus takes it and turns it round. The bread is his body. The cup is my blood of the covenant — which is Moses's phrase at Sinai, where he threw blood over the people and said behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you (Ex. 24:8), and it is Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant written on hearts, with sins remembered no more (Jer. 31:31–34).

So there is a new exodus, and he is the lamb of it, and the blood goes not on a doorframe but into a cup that is handed round a table and drunk.

And poured out for many is Isaiah 53 — the Servant who poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa. 53:12) — and it is his own word from 10:45, where the Son of Man gives his life as a ransom for many. Not a tragedy that overtook him. A ransom, deliberately paid, for a definite number of people whom he knew by name.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a woman breaks a flask worth a year's wages over his head, and the room objects that it could have been sold for the poor.

The objection is not stupid. Three hundred denarii would have fed a great many families, and the New Testament is fierce about the poor. But Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 15:11 at them — you always have the poor with you — and it is worth knowing that the verse he is quoting goes on: therefore I command you, You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land. He is not excusing anyone from generosity. He is saying that this particular week will not come again.

Now: and then the sentence for everyone who has ever felt they had nothing worth giving: she has done what she could.

Not what she should have. Not what somebody more capable would have. What she could — which was one thing, and she did it, and he called it beautiful and said it would be told wherever the gospel went. It has been, for two thousand years, and Mark does not even record her name.

That is the measure. Not the scale of the service but whether it was the whole of what you had.

verseByVerse.quote: It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread. And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him, for they said, "Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was now two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread.

Mark starts the clock. From here to the end of the chapter, time is measured in hours.

And the setting is not incidental. Passover was the feast of deliverance — the night God brought Israel out of Egypt behind the blood of a lamb — and the city was full. Josephus gives figures that are surely inflated, but every account agrees that the population swelled several times over; hundreds of thousands of pilgrims camped on the hillsides. Lambs were being counted into the temple by the thousand for slaughter.

And the chief priests and the scribes were seeking how to arrest him by stealth and kill him.

They have wanted this since chapter 3, when Pharisees and Herodians walked out of a synagogue together to plan it (3:6). What has changed is that it is now an operational question. Not whether but how.

By stealth — by cunning, by a trick. They need him away from the crowd, in the dark, with no witnesses.

For they said, Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar from the people.

And here is a sentence worth stopping on, because of what happened to it.

This is a decision of policy, taken by the highest religious authority in Israel, on grounds of crowd control. Their considered judgement was: not this week. Wait until the pilgrims have gone home and the city is quiet, and then take him.

And he died on the Friday of that very feast.

They did not change their minds because they were persuaded. They changed them because an opportunity arrived they had not counted on — a man from the inside, offering to do it quietly, that night. And so the timetable of the crucifixion was set not by the Sanhedrin's plan but against it.

Which matters more than it might seem, because the date was not negotiable. The lamb had to die at Passover. Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Cor. 5:7) — and every element of the timing had been fixed since Exodus 12, fourteen centuries earlier.

So watch what happens in this chapter. The most powerful men in Jerusalem make a plan and are overruled by their own accomplice. Judas thinks he is arranging a transaction. The priests think they are managing a public order problem. Pilate will think he is settling a provincial dispute.

Every one of them is a free agent doing exactly what he wants, and every one of them is running to a schedule that was set before the world was made — this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23).

Both halves of that sentence are true, and Mark holds them together without embarrassment from here to the end.
verseByVerse.note: Passover recalled Israel’s rescue from Egypt; Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that followed it. Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims.

parallels.desc: the council resolves to kill him

verseByVerse.quote: And while he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he was reclining at table, a woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly, and she broke the flask and poured it over his head. There were some who said to themselves indignantly, "Why was the ointment wasted like that?
verseByVerse.commentary:
And while he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper.

Mark drops the scene into the middle of the plot, and the first thing to notice is the address.

Bethany is the village over the ridge from Jerusalem where he has been sleeping all week (11:11). And the house belongs to Simon the leper — a man who is plainly not a leper any longer, since he is hosting a dinner party and people are reclining at his table. A leper could not do either; he lived outside the town and shouted a warning at anyone who came near (Lev. 13:45–46).

So somebody healed him, and the nickname stuck, and now the man who used to shout unclean at strangers has the Son of God at his table two days before the cross.

Mark does not tell us the story. He does not need to. Chapter 1 told us that a leper knelt in front of Jesus and said if you will, you can make me clean, and Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him (1:40–42). Whether or not this is the same man, this is the same kind of house — and it is where the Lord chose to spend one of his last evenings.

A woman came with an alabaster flask of ointment of pure nard, very costly.

Every word is doing work.

Alabaster — a soft translucent stone, carved into small sealed flasks for perfume. There was no stopper; the neck was sealed and had to be snapped off.

Pure nard — an oil pressed from the root of a plant that grows in the Himalayas. It came overland, thousands of miles, and its price reflected the journey. Mark's word for pure may mean unadulterated, which is the point: this is not the diluted version.

Very costly — and verse 5 gives the figure. Three hundred denarii. A denarius was a day's wage for a labourer, so this flask represents about a year of a working man's income. In modern terms, a household's annual earnings, in a bottle.

It was very likely her security. Perfume was a way of storing wealth in a portable form, and for a woman with no property rights, a sealed flask of nard might be everything she had against old age.

And she broke the flask and poured it over his head.

She snaps the neck. And once it is broken it cannot be resealed, which means there is no possibility of using half and keeping half. The breaking is a decision that all of it is going somewhere.

And then she pours it over his head — which is not what you do with perfume. A drop on the wrist is the normal use. This is the whole flask, running down his hair and his beard and onto his clothes and the floor, until the room could smell nothing else.

It is also, though nobody in that house says so, how you anoint a king (1 Sam. 10:1; 2 Kgs. 9:6).

There were some who said to themselves indignantly, Why was the ointment wasted like that?

And the room turns on her.

Wasted. That is their verdict, and it is the only verdict available to a calculating mind. Something valuable has been destroyed and there is nothing to show for it.
verseByVerse.note: John names the woman as Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus. Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. Alabaster was a soft stone used for perfume flasks.

verseByVerse.quote: For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor." And they scolded her.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii and given to the poor.

And here is the objection stated in full, and it must be taken seriously rather than brushed aside, because it is a good objection.

Three hundred denarii is a year's wages. It would have fed a great many families in a city where the poor were everywhere and the safety net was nothing but almsgiving. And giving to the poor was a particular duty at Passover — it was customary to remember the destitute at the feast.

Moreover, the New Testament is fierce about this. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction (Jas. 1:27). Jesus himself told a rich man to sell everything and give it to the poor, four chapters ago (10:21).

So this is not a stupid objection, and it is not obviously a wicked one. It is the objection any sensible, socially concerned, morally serious person would make.

Which is exactly why the passage is so searching.

And they scolded her.

They did not merely disapprove. They went at her.

Picture what that was like. She has just done the most extravagant thing she will ever do, in public, in a roomful of men, on an impulse she probably could not have explained — and the room rounds on her and tells her she is a fool and has wasted money that should have gone to the hungry.

She says nothing. Mark records not one word from her in the whole account.

John tells us who started it, and it changes the flavour entirely: Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said, "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?" He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it (John 12:4–6).

So the objection about the poor came, in the first instance, from a man stealing from the fund for the poor. And the rest of the room agreed with him, because it was a reasonable thing to say.

And that is worth carrying, because the mechanism has not aged. A perfectly sound principle can be used as cover, and the people repeating it need not be insincere — most of the men in that room were not. It is very easy to criticise somebody else's costly devotion in the name of a good cause, and to feel morally serious while doing it, and to give nothing yourself.

Within two days, Judas will have his thirty pieces of silver, and this woman will have nothing left. And Mark has put them side by side on purpose: one person in this chapter turns Jesus into money, and one turns money into worship.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages. John says the complaint came from Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus said, "Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them. But you will not always have me. She has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for burial. And truly, I say to you, wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leave her alone. Why do you trouble her?

He defends her before he explains her, which is worth noticing. The first thing out of his mouth is not theology but protection: get off her.

And why do you trouble her is tender — they are giving her a hard time, making trouble for her. He has seen what the room is doing to a woman who cannot answer back.

She has done a beautiful thing to me.

The word is kalos — good, fine, lovely. Not merely permissible; beautiful.

And that word is the whole answer to waste. The disciples were applying the only category they had, which is usefulness: what did it achieve, what could have been bought, what was the return. Jesus introduces another category altogether, and it is one that a purely practical religion has no room for.

There is a place for the beautiful and useless. Worship is precisely that. Nobody is fed by it and nothing is produced, and God calls it lovely — which is why he commanded gold and blue and scarlet and fine twined linen for a tent in a desert, and why the church has always spent something on what could have been done more cheaply.

For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want, you can do good for them.

This sentence has been misused for centuries as a shrug — the poor are a permanent feature, so do not exert yourself — and it must be rescued, because it is a quotation and the original settles it.

He is quoting Deuteronomy 15:11, and here is the whole verse: For there will never cease to be poor in the land. Therefore I command you, You shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor, in your land.

The permanence of poverty is stated as the reason for open-handedness, not as an excuse from it. Every Jew in that room knew the verse and knew how it ended. Jesus is not releasing anybody from anything — note his own clause, whenever you want, you can do good for them, which assumes they will and should.

But you will not always have me.

There is the point. This is not a general principle about extravagance versus charity. It is a statement about a week that will not come again.

He has two days left. The opportunity to do anything at all for the physical body of Jesus of Nazareth is closing, and this woman is the only person in Jerusalem who appears to have noticed.

She has done what she could.

And there is one of the loveliest sentences in the Gospel, and it should be laid up by anyone who has ever felt that what they have to offer is not worth offering.

Not what she should have done. Not what a more capable person would have managed. Not a great work. What she could — which was one thing, done once, with everything she had, and he called it beautiful.

That is the measure, and it is a mercy. The question is never the scale of the service. It is whether it was the whole of what you had. Two small coins from a widow outweighed the treasury (12:44); a flask from a woman with nothing else outweighed the criticism of twelve apostles.

She has anointed my body beforehand for burial.

And now he tells them what she has actually done, and it is more than she knew.

Bodies were anointed for burial — the women will come to the tomb on Sunday morning to do exactly this, and will find it empty and never get the chance (16:1). This woman is the only person who managed it, and she managed it while he was still alive.

Whether she understood that is doubtful. She came to honour him; he tells her she has buried him.

Wherever the gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in memory of her.

A prophecy, and it has been kept for two thousand years on every continent.

And here is the last touch, and it is exquisite: Mark does not tell us her name. (John identifies her as Mary of Bethany; Mark leaves her anonymous.) So the promise is fulfilled in a strange way — the whole world knows what she did, and the Gospel that promises she will be remembered does not say who she was.

Which is perhaps the most encouraging thing in the passage. She is not famous. The deed is. And the one who noticed it, and valued it, and made sure it was written down, is the same one who watched a widow put in two coins nobody heard.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them. And when they heard it, they were glad and promised to give him money. And he sought an opportunity to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Judas Iscariot, who was one of the twelve, went to the chief priests in order to betray him to them.

The sandwich closes. Plot — anointing — plot, and Mark's arrangement makes the contrast unavoidable: a woman pours out a year's wages on him, and a man goes out to sell him.

Who was one of the twelve. Mark says it here, and Jesus will say it at the table (v. 20), and Mark will say it again when the mob arrives (v. 43). Three times in one chapter, as though he cannot stop.

It is the thing that will not go away. Not a follower, not a sympathiser. One of the twelve — appointed on the mountain (3:19), sent out two by two with authority over unclean spirits, present at every private explanation, and about to have his feet washed.

And when they heard it, they were glad.

They were glad. That is the word, and it is chilling in its ordinariness. The men who had just decided not during the feast are delighted, because the problem they could not solve has just walked through the door and offered to solve itself.

And promised to give him money.

Mark does not give the figure; Matthew does — thirty pieces of silver (Matt. 26:15), which is the compensation the Law fixed for a slave gored by an ox (Ex. 21:32), and the wage thrown to the rejected shepherd in Zechariah with the LORD's own dry comment: the lordly price at which I was priced by them (Zech. 11:12–13).

Set the two halves of this passage against each other and the arithmetic is unbearable. The perfume was three hundred denarii. Thirty pieces of silver is roughly a hundred and twenty. A woman spent more on his head than the priests paid for his life.

And he sought an opportunity to betray him.

Mark's word is eukairōs — a good moment, a convenient time. It is the same root as the opportunity Herodias was waiting for before the birthday party (6:21).

So it does not happen at once. Judas goes back to the group and waits, and eats with them, and watches for a gap. He sat through the supper knowing. He heard one of you will betray me and said is it I? with the rest.

And why? The Gospels do not give a full account, and it is worth resisting the urge to supply one.

John names the greed and the pilfering (John 12:6), and money is plainly in it. Some have suggested he was trying to force Jesus's hand — to put him in a position where he would have to act and declare himself. Luke and John both say Satan entered him (Luke 22:3; John 13:27).

What Mark gives us is not a motive but a mechanism, and it is more useful. The betrayal of Jesus works by an opportune time: privately, quietly, when nobody is watching and the cost of loyalty has suddenly become visible and a reasonable-looking alternative has appeared.

That is how it always works. Almost nobody decides to abandon Christ. A moment simply arrives in which it is very much easier not to be associated with him, and there is a way out that can be explained to yourself, and it is taken.

Judas found his gap in a garden after dark. Peter will find his beside a fire in a courtyard within hours. The difference between them is not the failure. It is verse 72.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says the price was thirty pieces of silver.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb, his disciples said to him, "Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?" And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, "Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And on the first day of Unleavened Bread, when they sacrificed the Passover lamb.

The Thursday. And Mark's clause is worth pausing over: when they sacrificed the Passover lamb.

That afternoon, in the temple, the slaughter went on for hours. The lambs were brought by household heads, killed in the court, the blood caught in basins and passed along a line of priests to be poured at the base of the altar, and the carcass taken home to be roasted whole. Josephus's figures for the number of lambs are enormous. The noise and the smell of it filled the city.

And while that was happening, the Lamb of God was arranging where he would eat.

John seems to set the Passover a day later: on Friday morning the leaders would not enter Pilate’s house so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover (John 18:28), and Friday is the day of Preparation of the Passover (John 19:14). Several solutions have been offered: that different groups followed different calendars that year; that Jesus held a Passover meal a day early; or that in John “the Passover” means the whole week-long feast and its sacrifices, and “Preparation” means the day before the Sabbath of Passover week (cf. Mark 15:42). The last is the most likely. The Supper was a Passover meal, as Matthew, Mark and Luke all say, and John’s words refer to the meals of the feast that followed.

His disciples said to him, Where will you have us go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?

A practical question, and a real problem. The Passover had to be eaten inside the walls of Jerusalem, and the city was heaving. Every room in every house was spoken for. Finding a space for thirteen men on the afternoon of the feast was not a small matter.

And he sent two of his disciples and said to them, Go into the city, and a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him.

The instruction is almost comically thin. No address, no name, no directions. Go into a city of several hundred thousand people and look for a man with a jug.

And it works, because the sign is not as vague as it sounds. Carrying water in a jar was women's work. Men carried water in skins; a man with a water pot on his shoulder would stand out in that street the way a man in a ballgown would stand out in ours. Luke's account has the same detail, and it is exactly the kind of thing that would be visible in a crowd from fifty yards.

So it is either arranged in advance with a signal, or it is foreknowledge, and Mark does not say which. He told them where to find a colt the same way (11:2), and that worked too.

And why the secrecy? This is the part that repays thinking about.

Judas has already been to the priests and is waiting for his opportunity. If the location of the meal were announced in the morning, the arrest could happen in the middle of it — and the last supper would never have taken place.

So Jesus arranges a rendezvous that even his own disciples cannot disclose, because they do not know it. Two men are sent, and they will not be able to tell anybody where they are going until they get there.

He is buying an evening. He has something to say to those eleven men that has to be said before the arrest, and he takes precise practical measures to make sure he gets the time.

Nothing in this chapter happens to him by accident. He knows what Judas has done, he knows what the priests want, and he plans around them — which is a very different thing from being caught.
verseByVerse.note: The lambs were sacrificed at the temple on the afternoon before the Passover meal. Carrying water was usually women’s work, so a man with a jar would stand out.

verseByVerse.quote: and wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, 'The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?' And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us." And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And wherever he enters, say to the master of the house, The Teacher says, Where is my guest room, where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?

The password again, as with the colt (11:3). The Teacher says — and apparently that is enough.

Which means there is a man in Jerusalem who knows exactly who the Teacher is, and has a room ready, and asks no questions. Another of the anonymous people in this Gospel whose property was requested and who did not say no.

Note also the confidence of the phrase my guest room. Not a room. He speaks as a man with an arrangement.

And he will show you a large upper room furnished and ready; there prepare for us.

Two details, and both are Mark's own eye.

Large. Big enough for thirteen men to recline. Passover was eaten reclining — that was the point of it, a deliberate contrast with the first Passover eaten standing with sandals on, because a free man reclines at table and a slave does not.

Furnished and ready — spread with cushions and couches. It is done. Somebody has prepared it already.

And it is very likely that this room turns up again. In Acts, when the eleven return from the Mount of Olives after the ascension, they go to the upper room where they were staying, and it holds about a hundred and twenty people (Acts 1:13–15). Whether or not it is the same house, the church's first address in Jerusalem was an upstairs room lent by somebody nobody bothered to name.

And the disciples set out and went to the city and found it just as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover.

Just as he had told them. It is the pattern of the colt (11:4–6). The pattern is deliberate: in the last week, the things Jesus predicts keep turning out to be exactly right, in small matters and large.

He said there would be a colt; there was. He said there would be a man with a jar; there was. He said the room would be ready; it was.

And in a few hours he will say one of you will betray me, and you will all fall away, and before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times — and those will turn out to be exactly right too.

And they prepared the Passover. Which meant work: taking a lamb to the temple, waiting in the queue, holding it while its throat was cut, carrying it back, roasting it whole, and setting out the unleavened bread, the bitter herbs, the sauce and the wine.

Two disciples spent that afternoon preparing a lamb for the man who was about to become one.
verseByVerse.note: Larger houses had an upper room reached by an outside stair.

verseByVerse.quote: And when it was evening, he came with the twelve. And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, "Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me." They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, "Is it I?" He said to them, "It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me. For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when it was evening, he came with the twelve.

The first of the four watches from the parable two nights ago — in the evening, or at midnight, or when the rooster crows, or in the morning (13:35). Mark's reader is meant to feel the clock start.

And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me.

The meal is under way. And he does not open with an accusation; he opens with the amen-formula, which in this Gospel introduces the things that must not be missed.

One who is eating with me. That clause is not there for identification — it does not narrow anything, since all twelve are eating with him. It is there for the weight of it.

In that culture, sharing a meal was a covenant. To eat a man's bread was to be bound to him; to eat his bread and then harm him was the deepest treachery available. And the phrase is a quotation: Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps. 41:9) — a psalm Jesus quotes explicitly in John's account of this evening (John 13:18).

They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, Is it I?

And here is one of the most instructive moments in the Gospel, and it goes by in a line.

Nobody looks at Judas.

Eleven men have spent three years with him. They have walked hundreds of miles with him, eaten every meal with him, slept in the same fields. He has held the money bag, which means they trusted him with it. And when the Lord says one of them is a traitor, not one of them turns his head.

Which tells you that Judas was not obviously a Judas. There was no tell. He had preached, cast out demons, and passed for a disciple in the company of disciples for three years.

And it tells you something about them, too. Their question is not who is it? It is is it I? — and the Greek expects the answer no, so it is not a confession but a fearful hope. Still: every one of them, hearing that a betrayer was in the room, looked first at himself.

That instinct is the healthiest thing in the chapter and the exact opposite of Peter's mistake ten verses later. The men who say surely not I will all run away within hours; the man who says even though they all fall away, I will not will deny him with oaths.

Self-suspicion is not morbid. It is sanity. Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Cor. 10:12).

It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me.

He does not name him. Matthew and John record a further exchange that identifies him to those close enough to hear; Mark leaves it as a description that fits everyone at the table.

Which means Judas is given every chance, up to the last minute, to stop. The warning is public and the identification is private. Nobody drags him out. He could have got up.

For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed!

And here, in one sentence, the two truths Mark refuses to separate.

The Son of Man goes as it is written. This is not an accident. It was written — in Isaiah 53, in Psalm 41, in Zechariah. The cross is not the failure of the plan; it is the plan.

But woe to that man. And the man who does it is fully answerable. The determination of God does not make Judas a puppet or excuse him by an inch.

Scripture holds both without apology and never resolves them into a formula. Delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and, in the same breath, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23).

It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.

The most terrible sentence Jesus ever spoke about anybody, and it should not be softened. It means that non-existence would have been preferable to what Judas has coming — which is a plain statement that there is something worse than never having lived.

And notice that it is said in his hearing, at the table, while he could still have moved. It is not a verdict pronounced afterwards. It is a last warning delivered to a man's face, which is what makes it mercy as well as judgement.
verseByVerse.note: Dipping bread in a shared dish was a mark of close fellowship.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, "Take; this is my body." And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it. And he said to them, "This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them.

Four verbs, and by now the reader of this Gospel knows them: he took, he blessed, he broke, he gave. He did the same on a hillside with five loaves (6:41) and again with seven (8:6). What he did for the hungry he now does for the twelve, and this time the bread is himself.

Understand what he is interrupting. The Passover meal had a fixed liturgy and every element had a script. The head of the household took the unleavened bread and explained it: this is the bread of affliction which our fathers ate in the land of Egypt. Every man at that table had heard that sentence at every Passover of his life.

And Jesus takes the bread at the appointed moment and says something else.

Take; this is my body.

Four words, and the church has divided over them.

So let it be said plainly and without heat, because a reader is entitled to know what is at stake and what is not.

What all Christians agree on. That this meal is commanded, that it is central, that it is not a bare memory exercise, and that Christ is really given to faith in it. Nobody who takes Scripture seriously thinks this is nothing.

Where they differ is in what is means. Rome teaches transubstantiation — that the bread's substance becomes the body of Christ. Lutherans hold that the body is present in and with the bread. The Reformed churches — Calvin most carefully — hold that the bread remains bread and signifies the body, and that the risen Christ, bodily in heaven, is truly given to the believer by the Holy Spirit as he eats, so that the communion is real without the bread ceasing to be bread.

Two things in the text itself support that last reading. He was holding his body while he said it. The disciples were looking at him; nobody in that room can have thought the loaf had become the man in front of them. And he speaks this way constantly — I am the door, I am the vine — without anyone taking him to be timber or a plant.

But do not let the argument cost you the thing itself. The point of the sentence is not metaphysics. It is that he gave it to them, and told them to take it and eat it. Whatever else the Supper is, it is Christ given, and given to be received — not looked at, not admired, not discussed. Taken.

And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it.

They all drank of it. Mark notes it, and it is worth noting, because Judas was at that table.

This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.

Now the cup, and every phrase in it is quarried out of the Old Testament.

My blood of the covenant. That is Moses's sentence at Sinai. Having read the law to the people, he took the blood of the sacrifices and threw it over them and said: Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you (Ex. 24:8). It is the one place in the Law where the phrase occurs, and every man at that table would have caught it.

So a covenant is being cut, and it is new — Luke and Paul both preserve the word (Luke 22:20; 1 Cor. 11:25) — which takes us to Jeremiah: Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant... I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts... and I will remember their sin no more (Jer. 31:31–34).

At Sinai the blood was thrown over the people from outside. Here it is put into a cup and handed round to be drunk.

Poured out for many. This is Isaiah 53, where the Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isa. 53:12); and it is his own word from 10:45, where the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many.

Not a death that happened to him. A death poured out, deliberately, on purpose, for people.

And for many is not a limitation grudgingly admitted but a promise gladly made: there is a great multitude that no man can number whose sins were actually and effectively dealt with that Friday — not made dealable-with, but dealt with — and if you are trusting him tonight, you are one of the many he had in mind while he was holding that cup.

Many Christians read for many as a Hebrew way of saying “all”, the multitude set against the one (cf. Rom 5:15–19), and so as a death for every person. The reading given here is the Reformed one: Christ’s blood was poured out for his people, and actually secured their forgiveness. But both readings agree that his death is sufficient for all, offered to all, and that no one who comes is turned away.
verseByVerse.note: At the Passover meal the head of the household explained the bread and cups; Jesus gives them a new meaning. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert “new” before “covenant.”

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God." And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.

The last thing he says at the table, and it is not about his death. It is about a party.

Take the two halves of it.

I will not drink again. He is telling them that this is the last meal. He knows he will not eat with them again on this side of it, and there is a real renunciation in the sentence — a man giving up the ordinary comfort of wine and company because tomorrow is what it is.

Until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.

And there is the turn, and it is one of the great turns in the Gospel. On the last night of his life, hours from Gethsemane, he looks past the cross entirely — past the arrest, the flogging, the nails, the grave — and speaks with complete confidence about a future meal at which he will be present and drinking.

He is not hoping. There is no if in the sentence.

And that meal is a real appointment. The Old Testament had promised it: On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine... he will swallow up death forever (Isa. 25:6–8). Revelation names it: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9).

So every time the church takes this cup it is doing two things at once — looking back to a death and forward to a dinner. As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes (1 Cor. 11:26).

He said he would be there. He has never yet failed to keep a table booking.

And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.

And now the detail that closes the section, and it is easily read past — but if you know what they sang, it will not leave you alone.

The Passover liturgy ended with the second half of the Hallel: Psalms 115 to 118. Those were the words. There was no choosing.

So the last thing Jesus of Nazareth sang before Gethsemane included these lines:

The snares of death encompassed me... then I called on the name of the LORD. (Ps. 116:3–4)

Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints. (Ps. 116:15)

The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. (Ps. 118:22 — the very verse he had thrown at the chief priests two days earlier, 12:10)

Bind the festal sacrifice with cords, up to the horns of the altar. (Ps. 118:27)

And the last line of the last psalm, the final words he sang before he walked out into the dark:

Oh give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; for his steadfast love endures forever. (Ps. 118:29)

He sang that. On the way to Gethsemane, in a voice that would be praying in agony within the hour, he sang that God is good and his love does not stop.
verseByVerse.note: The hymn was probably from the Hallel psalms (Pss 113–118), sung at Passover.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The warning (vv. 27–31). On the walk out he tells them they will all fall away — and in the same breath tells them where to meet him afterwards. Peter says he will not, and says it twice, and the rest say the same.

The garden (vv. 32–42). Then the most exposed scene in the Gospels. He takes three men further in, tells them his soul is sorrowful to the point of death, falls on the ground and asks his Father to take the cup away — and adds the words that hold the world together. Three times he comes back and finds them asleep.

The arrest (vv. 43–52). Judas arrives with a crowd carrying swords and clubs, and identifies him with a kiss. A sword is drawn, an ear comes off, and Jesus asks whether they think he is a robber. Then everybody runs — including a young man who gets away leaving his only garment in a soldier's hand.

And in three of the four watches of the parable he preached two nights ago (13:35), the disciples are asleep or running, and he is awake.
verseByVerse.theology:
What is the cup? Everything in Gethsemane depends on it, and the answer is not the general dread of dying.

Men far less brave than Jesus have gone to horrible deaths singing — including thousands of his own martyrs, many of them under torture, some of them within living memory of this night. If the cup were merely execution, the Christian would have the awkward position of a Lord less composed at the prospect than his servants.

The cup is an Old Testament image, and it is fixed. In the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and he pours out from it, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Ps. 75:8). Wake yourself, wake yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath (Isa. 51:17). Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it (Jer. 25:15).

The cup is the wrath of God against sin. That is what is set in front of him in that garden, and it is why a man who had faced hurricanes and legions without a flicker is on the ground shaking.

And he drank it. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21). Which means there is nothing left in that cup for anyone who is in him — the reason a Christian can face death more calmly than Christ did in the garden is precisely that Christ was not calm in the garden.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: You will all fall away (v. 27) — and then, before Peter has said a word, but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (v. 28).

Read those two verses in the order he said them, because the order is the gospel. He announces the restoration before the failure has happened. Not after they repent. Not on condition of anything. He tells eleven men who are about to abandon him where to meet him afterwards.

And the word he uses is a shepherd's word — I will go before you, the way a shepherd walks ahead of the flock. He has just quoted Zechariah about the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered (Zech. 13:7); now he says he will gather them again himself.

Now: and the angel at the empty tomb repeats it, with one addition that has comforted more failing Christians than almost any other line in Scripture: go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee (16:7).

The one who was named in the failure is named in the restoration. If you have failed him badly and are wondering whether there is a road back, notice that the road was mapped and announced before you ever took the wrong turn.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "You will all fall away, for it is written, 'I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.' But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will all fall away.

Not some. Not one. All of them, and he says it walking down the hill with them in the dark.

The verb is skandalizō — to be tripped up, to stumble over something. It is the same word used of the seed on rocky ground that falls away when the heat comes (4:17), and of the offence people took at him in Nazareth (6:3).

For it is written, I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.

He quotes Zechariah 13:7, and the striking thing about the quotation is who does the striking.

Zechariah has God saying: Awake, O sword, against my shepherd, against the man who stands next to me... Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered. And Jesus takes it over in the first person singular: I will strike the shepherd.

So the hand behind tomorrow is not Judas's, or Caiaphas's, or Pilate's. Those men will all act freely and be answerable for it. But behind them, and over them, is the settled purpose of the Father — it was the will of the LORD to crush him (Isa. 53:10).

And note what that means for the disciples' failure. Their scattering is not an unforeseen embarrassment. It was written down centuries before, in the same sentence as the striking of the shepherd, and he tells them so before it happens.

But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.

And now the sentence that changes everything, and the whole force of it is in where it stands.

He says this before the failure, not after it.

Peter has not yet boasted. Nobody has run. The garden has not happened, the courtyard has not happened, the fire has not been lit. And into that moment — having just told eleven men that every one of them will abandon him within hours — he tells them where he will meet them afterwards.

There is no condition attached. He does not say if you repent, or if you come back, or if you prove yourselves. He says: after I am raised, I will go on ahead, and I will see you in Galilee.

The word for go before is a shepherd's word — to lead out in front of the flock, walking ahead so they can follow. He has just quoted a prophecy about a struck shepherd and scattered sheep, and in the next breath he says he will be out in front of them again.

Galilee, of all places. Not Jerusalem, where it all went wrong — home, where they were called off their boats.

And this promise is repeated by an angel in an empty tomb on Sunday morning, with one addition that has done more for failing Christians than almost any other line in the Bible: go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you (16:7).

So if you have failed him — really failed him, not a slip but the kind that makes you wonder whether there is any road back — take this in the order Mark gives it. The restoration was announced before the betrayal happened. The meeting place was fixed while they were still swearing they would never need it.

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered
he is going before you to Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Even though they all fall away, I will not." And Jesus said to him, "Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." But he said emphatically, "If I must die with you, I will not deny you." And they all said the same.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter said to him, Even though they all fall away, I will not.

You can hear him. It is entirely characteristic and it is meant well — and every word of it is wrong.

Even though they all. Look at what he has done in four words. He has accepted the prophecy for the other ten and exempted himself, and he has done it in front of them. That is not merely presumption about himself; it is a low estimate of his brothers said out loud in their hearing.

The man who thinks he alone will stand has already begun to fall, because he has stopped needing anybody.

And Jesus said to him, Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.

The answer is not a rebuke but a specification, and Mark's version is the most precise of the four — this very night, twice, three times.

Note the detail. It is the kind of thing only the man it happened to would remember with that exactness, and this Gospel is Peter's preaching. He has written down the sentence that broke him, with the numbers in it.

Matthew, Luke and John say before the rooster crows; only Mark says twice. The others give the general warning, before the cock-crow at dawn; Mark, from Peter’s own memory, gives the precise form, with a first crowing that Peter ignored and a second that broke him. There is no contradiction; one account is simply more detailed.

But he said emphatically, If I must die with you, I will not deny you.

Peter is not making a considered statement; he is protesting.

And he means it. That is the thing to hold on to, because it is what makes this passage useful rather than merely a story about a boastful man. Peter was not lying. He loved him. He will draw a sword in a few hours against an armed crowd, which is more than the other ten manage. Whatever else he was, he was not a coward.

He simply did not know himself.

And they all said the same.

Mark will not let Peter carry it alone. Every one of them said it, and every one of them ran.

So take the practical lesson, because it is aimed straight at anyone who feels reasonably safe.

The danger is not that you might one day decide to abandon Christ. Nobody in this room decided anything. The danger is confidence in a strength that has never been tested — the quiet assumption that you would hold, that you would speak up, that you would not do what those people did.

Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Cor. 10:12).

And notice what Jesus does not say. He does not say then you were never mine. He does not withdraw the promise of verse 28. He tells Peter exactly what he will do, and then takes him into the garden anyway, and dies for him on the Friday, and has him specifically named by an angel on the Sunday.

The boast was hollow. The love behind it was not, and Christ knew the difference — which is why the man who swore he would never deny him, and did, is the man whose memories became this Gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark mentions the rooster crowing twice.

verseByVerse.quote: And they went to a place called Gethsemane. And he said to his disciples, "Sit here while I pray." And he took with him Peter and James and John, and began to be greatly distressed and troubled. And he said to them, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death. Remain here and watch."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they went to a place called Gethsemane.

An olive grove on the lower slope of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron valley.

And he said to his disciples, Sit here while I pray. Eight are left at the gate.

And he took with him Peter and James and John.

The same three who were taken into Jairus's house to see a dead girl raised (5:37), and up the mountain to see him transfigured (9:2). They have seen him at his most glorious. Now they are taken to see him at his lowest, and it is the same three men, and that is not an accident. Nobody is qualified to speak about the glory who has not also seen the garden.

And began to be greatly distressed and troubled.

Mark reaches for two of the strongest words available — greatly distressed, and troubled — and it is still not enough. Appalled, shuddering, in the sort of distress that has no bottom to it.

Something has begun that was not there an hour ago. He began — this is not a settled sorrow he has carried all week. It falls on him in that garden.

My soul is very sorrowful, even to death.

He tells them, in words, what is happening to him — and it is worth stopping to notice that he does. The Son of God, in the worst hour of his life, turns to three friends and says how bad it is.

There is a kind of piety that regards that as weakness. It is not in this Gospel. He asked for company and he told them the truth about his state.

The phrase itself is a quotation. Three times in the Psalms the sufferer says Why are you cast down, O my soul? (Ps. 42:5, 11; 43:5) — and the word Mark uses is the same one the Greek Old Testament uses there. He is praying the Psalms, in the dark, in his own agony, using words that were given to him.

Even to death means the sorrow is of a weight that could kill a man. Luke, the physician, records what it did to his body: sweat like great drops of blood falling to the ground (Luke 22:44).

How can the Son of God be so distressed, and ask for the cup to be taken away? Because he is truly man as well as God. His human soul shrank from the cup of God’s wrath, as any holy man would, and he said so. But his will was never set against the Father’s; he asked, and then submitted: not what I will, but what you will (v. 36). This is not a crack in the Trinity. It is the obedience of the Son, learned with loud cries and tears (Heb 5:7).

Remain here and watch.

And there is the word from the parable — stay awake, grēgoreite, the same verb he used three times two nights ago (13:34, 35, 37).

He is not asking them to pray for him, and he is not asking them to do anything. He is asking them to stay awake near him.

Which is the plainest description of what friendship costs in somebody else's grief. You cannot fix it. You are not asked to. You are asked not to go to sleep.

And take away this, before anything else in the garden: whatever you are carrying, he is not looking at it from a distance. There is a night in the record when the Son of God was appalled, and shaking, and told his friends that the sorrow was killing him — and he is the one you are bringing it to.
verseByVerse.note: Gethsemane (the name means “oil press”) was an olive grove on the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley.

parallels.desc: why are you cast down, O my soul?

verseByVerse.quote: And going a little farther, he fell on the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him. And he said, "Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And going a little farther, he fell on the ground.

Not knelt. Fell. Matthew says on his face.

This is the man who slept through a hurricane, faced down a legion, and walked into the temple and turned the tables over. He is on the ground in the dirt among the olive roots.

And prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass from him.

Mark gives us the substance first and then the words. And note the conditional: if it were possible. He is not demanding. He is asking whether there is another way, and the asking is real.

And he said, Abba, Father.

Mark keeps the Aramaic, as he did with Talitha cumi and Ephphatha — and this time it is by far the most significant, because this is the actual sound of Jesus praying.

Abba is the ordinary family word a child used for his father in the home. It has sometimes been over-translated as Daddy, which is too small — grown men used it of their fathers all their lives — but it is unmistakably intimate, domestic, and not the language of formal worship. Jewish prayer very rarely, if ever, addressed God that way.

He prays as a son at home. And in the deepest agony of his life, that is the word he reaches for.

And it did not stay his alone. Twice the New Testament says that the Spirit puts this very word into the mouths of ordinary Christians: you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, Abba! Father! (Rom. 8:15; also Gal. 4:6). The name he used in Gethsemane is the name he handed over.

All things are possible for you.

Before the request, the confession. He does not begin by asking whether God is able. He states that God is able, and then asks — which is the right order, and the reverse of how most of us pray in a crisis.

Remove this cup from me.

And here is the request, and everything depends on what the cup is.

It is not simply death. That has to be said, because the reading that makes Gethsemane a fear of dying leaves the Christian with a Lord less composed at execution than thousands of his own martyrs, many of whom went to far worse deaths singing.

The cup is a fixed Old Testament image, and it means the wrath of God. In the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine, well mixed, and he pours out from it, and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Ps. 75:8). you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath (Isa. 51:17). Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath (Jer. 25:15).

That is what is standing in front of him in the dark: not the nails, but the undiluted anger of God against every sin ever committed by everyone he came to save — and he is to drink it to the dregs.

Which explains everything about this scene that is otherwise inexplicable. He is not afraid of pain. He is looking into the cup.

Yet not what I will, but what you will.

Nine words, and they hold the world together.

Notice that he does not withdraw the request. He asks, honestly, for the thing he wants — and then submits. Both are prayer. The asking is not unbelief and the submitting is not resignation.

And this is the exact reversal of Eden. In a garden, a man was told what the Father's will was and said, in effect, "not your will but mine", and the world broke. In a garden, a man who could have had anything said not what I will, but what you will, and it was mended.

So when you are praying about something God has not taken away, this is your model and your permission. Ask plainly for what you want; he did. And then hand it over; he did that too — and the cup did not pass, and he drank it, and that is why there is nothing left in it for you.
verseByVerse.note: “Abba” is Aramaic for “father,” the word a child used at home. The “cup” pictures God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came and found them sleeping, and he said to Peter, "Simon, are you asleep? Could you not watch one hour? Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he came and found them sleeping.

He gets up off the ground, walks back through the trees, and they are asleep.

And this is the moment Mark's reader has been prepared for. Two nights ago, on a hillside overlooking this valley, he told them a parable about a master who comes home in the night — lest he come suddenly and find you asleep (13:36).

He came. They were asleep. The parable is being acted out on the men it was told to, within forty-eight hours.

And he said to Peter, Simon, are you asleep?

He speaks to Peter, and he uses the old name.

Simon. Not Peter, the rock. Simon, the name he had when he was pulling nets out of the lake, before any of this. It is the only time in Mark that Jesus addresses him as Simon, and the choice is deliberate and gentle — and devastating.

The man who two hours ago said even though they all fall away, I will not cannot stay awake.

Could you not watch one hour?

One hour. Not the night; an hour. It is the smallest possible request, made by a man who is dying of grief thirty yards away, and it was too much.

Before that is used against them, be honest about the circumstances. It was late, they had eaten a heavy meal with four cups of wine, they had walked, and Luke — kindly — records that they were sleeping for sorrow (Luke 22:45). Grief exhausts people. They were not indifferent; they were shattered.

Which does not remove the failure but does explain it, and Jesus explains it too.

Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation.

Two commands, and they belong together: stay awake, and pray. And the reason given is preventative — that you may not enter into temptation. He is not scolding them for missing something; he is telling them that in about twenty minutes they are going to be tested, and this hour is the preparation for it.

They slept through the preparation, and failed the test.

Take that as the plainest practical lesson in the chapter. The battle is lost or won before the moment of temptation arrives. The man who has not prayed does not fall in the moment; he fell in the hours before it, when nothing seemed to be happening and there was no obvious reason to be on his knees. Gethsemane is where the courtyard was decided.

The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.

And then, having named their failure, he excuses it — or rather, he explains it with a sympathy that is almost unbearable given who is speaking and what is coming.

The spirit indeed is willing. He grants it. Their intentions were real; Peter meant every word of his boast. There is nothing false in these men's love.

But the flesh is weak. The word for flesh means human nature in its frailty — not wickedness, but weakness. He is not saying they are hypocrites. He is saying they are men.

And notice who is diagnosing it: somebody who at that moment is on the ground with his own flesh failing under a weight none of them can imagine. He knows exactly how weak it is. He is finding out.

Which is why this is a comfort as well as a warning. He knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust (Ps. 103:14). Your Lord is not surprised by your weakness and does not despise it — he has been more tired, more frightened and more alone than you have ever been, and he stayed awake for you.

verseByVerse.quote: And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words. And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy, and they did not know what to answer him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And again he went away and prayed, saying the same words.

He goes back and prays it again. The same words.

Do not hurry past that, because it says something important about prayer that a great many Christians have never been told.

There is a way of thinking that treats repetition as a failure of faith — as though asking twice showed you had not believed the first time, or as though prayer required fresh and eloquent phrasing to be genuine. Jesus prayed the same sentence three times in one hour, in the most important prayer meeting in the history of the world.

Paul did the same about his thorn: three times I pleaded with the Lord about this (2 Cor. 12:8). And when there are no words left, the Spirit himself intercedes with groanings too deep for words (Rom. 8:26).

So if all you can do tonight is say the same desperate sentence over and over, you are not praying badly. You are praying in Gethsemane.

And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were very heavy.

The same again. And Mark adds a small human detail — their eyes were very heavy — which is exactly the phrase you would use of yourself at two in the morning.

And they did not know what to answer him.

And this is the saddest clause in the paragraph, and it is unmistakably Peter's own memory.

They woke up, and he was standing over them, and there was nothing to say. No excuse would work. They had been asked for one hour, twice, and had failed twice, and the silence in that grove must have been terrible.

Mark has recorded exactly this before, and it is worth putting the two together. Coming down from the mountain of transfiguration, the three kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean — and at the transfiguration itself, Peter blurted out a suggestion about tents for he did not know what to say, for they were terrified (9:6).

The same three men, in the two moments when they saw most clearly who he was, both times with nothing to say.

That is honest reporting, and it is one of the reasons this Gospel reads like testimony rather than legend. Nobody inventing a founding narrative writes down that the leaders slept through the crisis and had no answer when they were caught.

Peter told it against himself for the rest of his life. And there is a mercy in that too, because the church has therefore never been able to pretend that its first leaders were made of better material than the rest of us.

verseByVerse.quote: And he came the third time and said to them, "Are you still sleeping and taking your rest? It is enough; the hour has come. The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand."
