verseByVerse.commentary:
And he came the third time and said to them, Are you still sleeping and taking your rest?

Three times he prayed; three times he came back; three times they were asleep. And within hours Peter will deny him three times. Mark's numbers are not accidental.

The sentence can be read as a question or as a resigned statement — sleep on now, take your rest — and the Greek allows either. Either way the tone has changed. He is no longer asking them for anything.

Something has happened in that third prayer. He went into the grove appalled and shaking; he comes out of it settled, and every sentence from here to the cross has the same steadiness in it.

The struggle was real and it is over. He asked, he submitted, and the answer was no — and he takes the no and gets up.

It is enough; the hour has come.

The hour — the same word he used on the ground, praying that the hour might pass from him (v. 35). It has not passed. It has arrived.

And Mark has been building to this word since chapter 1. The hour is what the whole Gospel has been walking toward, and it does not sneak up on him. He announces it.

The Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.

He has said this three times before, in three passion predictions (8:31; 9:31; 10:33). This is the fourth, and the tense has changed. It is no longer will be. It is happening.

Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.

And here is one of the most extraordinary sentences in the Gospel, and everything depends on the direction he is facing when he says it.

Rise, let us be going. It sounds, for half a second, like an escape — get up, we are leaving. It is the opposite. Torches are coming up the path from the Kidron valley and he can see them, and he is walking towards them.

The disciples are asleep. Judas is arriving with an armed crowd. And the man who has spent the last hour on the ground begging for another way stands up and says: come on, let us go and meet him.

Nobody takes him. He goes.

No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18).

And notice the pronoun in the last clause: my betrayer. Not the betrayer. He still owns him — the man is still, in some terrible sense, his.

So Gethsemane ends with the sleeping disciples woken by the sound of their Lord walking toward the men who have come to kill him, having settled the matter in prayer while they slept.

verseByVerse.quote: And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders. Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, "The one I will kiss is the man. Seize him and lead him away under guard." And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, "Rabbi!" And he kissed him. And they laid hands on him and seized him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And immediately, while he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve.

Mark says it again — one of the twelve. The third time in the chapter. He cannot leave it alone, and neither should we.

And with him a crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the scribes and the elders.

An armed party sent by the Sanhedrin — temple police, probably, and John adds a detachment of Roman soldiers with lanterns and torches (John 18:3). Swords for the professionals, clubs for the rest.

They have come at night, into a garden, mob-handed, to arrest an unarmed teacher who has been standing in the temple courts all week in broad daylight.

Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, The one I will kiss is the man.

And here is a detail worth pausing on: they needed a sign.

Which means the men sent to arrest him could not reliably pick him out — at night, by torchlight, among a dozen Galileans dressed alike. That is a small, entirely believable piece of realism, and it also tells you that Jesus did not look like anything in particular. No halo. Nothing to distinguish the Son of God from the fishermen standing next to him.

Seize him and lead him away under guard.

The last clause is the professional detail — under guard, securely. Judas knows what this man has done to crowds and storms, and he is taking no chances.

And when he came, he went up to him at once and said, Rabbi! And he kissed him.

The kiss.

It was the ordinary greeting of a disciple to his teacher — respect, affection, belonging. And Mark's verb here is emphatic: not simply kissed but kissed him warmly, repeatedly, the intensified form of the word.

So the sign chosen to identify him for execution was the sign of love, and it was performed thoroughly.

There is nothing in human wickedness worse than this, and the Bible knows it. Even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps. 41:9). Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy (Prov. 27:6).

And Rabbi — my teacher. That is what he calls him. Not Lord. It is the last word Judas speaks in this Gospel, and it is a title of respect emptied of everything that made it mean anything.

Matthew records the answer, and it is almost unbearable: Friend, do what you came to do (Matt. 26:50). Luke records another: Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss? (Luke 22:48).

He let him do it. He did not turn his face away or step back. He received the kiss.

And they laid hands on him and seized him.

Eight words, and the Gospel turns. From this moment until the resurrection, Jesus of Nazareth is in custody. Everything from here is done to him — he is led, handed over, questioned, struck, flogged, carried out, nailed up.

The one who could not be bound by a legion of demons, or a hurricane, or a fever, or death itself, lets a temple guard put its hands on him in the dark and take him away.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. And Jesus said to them, "Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But let the Scriptures be fulfilled." And they all left him and fled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But one of those who stood by drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear.

Mark does not name him. John, writing much later when everyone involved was dead, says it was Peter, and that the man's name was Malchus (John 18:10) — which is the kind of detail you only get from somebody who was there and knew the household.

And it is worth being fair to Peter for a moment. Eleven men are about to run, and one of them draws a weapon against an armed party sent by the Sanhedrin. He was not a coward, and whatever else he got wrong tonight, he got it wrong bravely.

He also got it entirely wrong. Aiming at a head and taking an ear suggests a wild swing rather than a swordsman's stroke; the man was a servant, not a soldier; and Luke, the physician, records the last healing miracle of Jesus's ministry — he touched the ear and healed him (Luke 22:51).

The final act of his freedom was to repair the damage his own disciple had done to the man who came to arrest him.

Does this forbid Christians to use force? Matthew records Jesus’ rebuke, all who take the sword will perish by the sword (Matt 26:52), and John his reason, My kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36). Jesus forbids the sword to defend his kingdom or to stop the cross. He does not abolish the state’s sword (Rom 13:4), nor the defence of life (Exod 22:2). Christians may protect themselves and others; they may never advance Christ’s cause by force.

And Jesus said to them, Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me?

He addresses the arresting party, and the question is a rebuke about their method.

The word for robber is lēstēs — not a pickpocket but a bandit, an armed insurrectionist. It is the word Josephus uses for the Zealot guerrillas, and it is the word used of the two men crucified beside him (15:27).

So: you have turned out in force, at night, armed, as though I were a terrorist. And the pointed part follows.

Day after day I was with you in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me.

He has been standing in their own building, in public, all week. They could have arrested him at any hour of any day. They did not, because of the crowd (12:12; 14:2) — and so the whole apparatus of swords and torches and a midnight raid is not a security precaution. It is a confession.

Men who take a prisoner in the dark are telling you what they think of their own case.

But let the Scriptures be fulfilled.

And with that he stops arguing. He breaks off the rebuke and submits.

Not this is a miscarriage of justice, though it is. Not my Father will vindicate me, though he will. Simply: this is what was written, and it is happening, and I am not going to stop it.

And they all left him and fled.

Seven words, and Mark does not soften them by a syllable.

All. The eleven who had said, an hour ago, that they would die with him. The three who could not stay awake. Peter, who had just drawn a sword.

Left him. The verb is the one used of abandoning something — and it is the same word Mark used in chapter 1 when they left their nets and followed him (1:18). They left everything to follow him; now they leave him.

And you will all fall away (v. 27) is fulfilled within the hour, exactly as he said, and he had told them where to meet him afterwards before they did it.

From here he is alone. There is not a friendly face in the rest of this chapter.
verseByVerse.note: John names the swordsman as Peter and the servant as Malchus; Luke adds that Jesus healed the ear.

verseByVerse.quote: And a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked.

Two verses found in no other Gospel, and they have puzzled readers for nineteen centuries, because on the face of it they are pointless. A person nobody has heard of loses his clothes and runs. Nothing depends on it. The narrative would not miss it.

Which is precisely why most readers have concluded that this is Mark himself.

The reasoning is simple and hard to get round. It is far too specific and far too embarrassing to be invented; nobody puts an anonymous humiliation into a Gospel for the sake of it. It is the classic signature of an eyewitness who wants to be in the record without being named — a small, undignified detail that only he would know and only he would tell.

And there is a candidate. The house with the upper room is thought by many to have belonged to Mark's family; the church in Jerusalem later met at his mother's house (Acts 12:12), and it was to that house that Peter went when the angel let him out of prison. If the supper was eaten there, a young man in that household might well have heard where they had gone, got up in the night with a linen sheet round him, and followed at a distance.

He was there. He was in his nightclothes. And when they grabbed him he twisted out of the sheet and ran into the dark with nothing on.

And there is more here than an author's initials.

Look at what Mark has just told us. They all left him and fled (v. 50). And now the desertion is given a face — one specific person, caught in the torchlight, who would rather lose everything he was wearing than be taken with Jesus.

That is what the abandonment looked like from the inside. Not a decision; a bolt.

And now watch the linen. The young man's garment is a linen cloth — and in the next chapter Joseph of Arimathea bought a linen shroud, took the body down, wrapped him in the linen shroud, and laid him in a tomb (15:46).

A young man abandons his linen cloth and runs away naked, so that his Lord can be wrapped in one.

And there is a last bracket, and it is the loveliest thing here. The word for young man is neaniskos, and it occurs exactly twice in Mark. Here — running away naked in the dark. And on the first morning of the week, when the women come to the tomb and find the stone rolled back: they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed (16:5).

Whatever else that means, Mark has bracketed the passion with two young men: one who fled from Christ stripped and ashamed, and one seated inside an empty tomb, clothed in white, telling the women that he has risen.

That is the gospel in two pictures, and if the young man is Mark himself, as many have thought, the man who wrote it put himself in the first one.
verseByVerse.note: Only Mark records the young man. Many have guessed he was Mark himself, but the text does not say.

parallels.desc: he who is stout of heart shall flee away naked in that day

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 53–72 — The Trial and the Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The council (vv. 53–65). He is taken to the high priest's house and the whole Sanhedrin assembles in the middle of the night. They look for evidence to justify a verdict they have already reached, and cannot find any that holds — the witnesses contradict each other, even about the temple saying. He says nothing at all. Then the high priest puts the direct question, under oath, and he answers it in full for the first time in this Gospel: I am — and adds Daniel 7 and Psalm 110 to it. The robes are torn, the sentence is passed, and men begin to spit at him.

The courtyard (vv. 66–72). And Mark cuts, in the same building, to the one disciple who followed. A servant girl looks at Peter across a fire; a second challenge comes; then the bystanders place his accent. Three times, escalating — a denial, a denial, and finally oaths and a curse.

Then a bird calls, and he remembers, and the strongest of the twelve goes to pieces.

Mark has interleaved the two scenes deliberately: upstairs, Christ confesses and is condemned for it; downstairs, Peter denies and is safe.
verseByVerse.theology:
The trial was illegal, and the record shows it. By the standards later codified in the Mishnah, capital cases were to be tried in daytime, in the temple's own hall, never begun on the eve of a Sabbath or a festival, and a conviction could not be handed down on the same day as the trial — an acquittal could, but a death sentence required a night to pass first. This proceeding breaks all of it. It is held at night, in the high priest's residence, at Passover, with sentence passed at once.

How much of that code was in force in AD 30 is genuinely debated. But Mark's own account convicts them without any of it, in one sentence: the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death (v. 55). That is not a court. A court seeks the truth and then decides the penalty; this one had the penalty and went looking for grounds.

And I am is the fullest confession in the Gospel. Nine chapters of demons silenced and healed men hushed, and now, under oath, with nothing left to protect, he answers plainly. Egō eimi — the words of the burning bush (Ex. 3:14) — and then two texts fused: seated at the right hand of Power (Ps. 110:1), which he had put to them as a riddle two days earlier (12:36), and coming with the clouds of heaven (Dan. 7:13).

He tells the court that the man in the dock will be their judge, and they understand him perfectly.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the high priest tears his garments (v. 63) — the formal gesture required of a judge on hearing blasphemy.

And it is worth knowing what the Law said about that particular man's clothes. The high priest was under a standing prohibition: he shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes (Lev. 21:10). The office was not permitted the ordinary signs of mourning.

So on the night the Sanhedrin condemned Jesus for blasphemy, the high priest of Israel broke the Law of Moses to do it. Every man in that room was more concerned with the letter of the law than anybody alive, and the one they killed for breaking it was the only one in the building keeping it.

Now: and then they spat at him and covered his face and hit him and said Prophesy! — a game, apparently, of making the blindfolded man name who struck him.

They did not know that he had prophesied, that afternoon and the night before, with total accuracy: that one of the twelve would betray him, that all of them would run, and that Peter would deny him three times before the cock crowed twice.

While they were demanding a prophecy, the last of those predictions was coming true below them, in the courtyard, in the hearing of a servant girl.

verseByVerse.quote: And they led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together. And Peter had followed him at a distance, right into the courtyard of the high priest. And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they led Jesus to the high priest. And all the chief priests and the elders and the scribes came together.

The full council, assembled in the middle of the night. That takes organisation — messengers sent round the city, seventy-odd men roused from their beds and brought to one house at an hour when nobody meets.

Which tells you the arrangements were made in advance. They were waiting for Judas's signal, and the moment it came the machinery started.

John tells us they took him first to Annas, the former high priest and the power behind the office (John 18:13). The man Mark calls the high priest is Caiaphas — his son-in-law, and the man who had already said that it is better for you that one man should die for the people (John 11:50).

And Peter had followed him at a distance.

And now Mark begins the second thread, and he does it here — before the trial, so that the two run side by side in the reader's mind.

At a distance. Three words, and they are the saddest description of discipleship in the New Testament.

He has not fled, and that is worth saying loudly, because Peter is easy to despise and he does not deserve it. Ten men are somewhere in the dark on the far side of the Kidron. One followed.

But he followed at a distance — close enough to see, far enough not to be associated. And that is the most dangerous place in the world to stand: near enough to keep your conscience quiet, far enough to keep your safety. Nobody stays there long. It resolves, one way or the other, within hours.

Right into the courtyard of the high priest.

He gets inside. John says another disciple, known to the household, got him through the gate (John 18:15–16).

And he was sitting with the guards and warming himself at the fire.

Every word of that is deliberate, and Mark will repeat it in verse 67 so that we cannot miss it.

Sitting with the guards. Not standing at the edge. He has sat down among the men who arrested his Lord an hour ago, in the courtyard of the man who is trying him.

Warming himself at the fire. It was a cold April night in the Judean hills, and there was a charcoal fire in the middle of the yard, and Peter is at it with his hands out.

Picture the geometry, because Mark has built it. Upstairs, Jesus is standing in front of the Sanhedrin being spat at. Downstairs, in the same building, Peter is comfortable and warm, sitting with the men who did it.

He has not denied anything yet. He has simply taken a place at the enemy's fire because it was cold and he wanted to see what would happen — and the next thing that happens is that the firelight falls on his face.

There is a version of that fire in every Christian's life: the place where you can be near Christ and comfortable at the same time, sitting with people who have no time for him and saying nothing, because it is warm and going home would cost something. Nobody has ever been asked a hard question at a safe distance. They get asked at the fire.
verseByVerse.note: John records a first hearing before Annas, the former high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death, but they found none. For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking testimony against Jesus to put him to death.

Read that sentence slowly, because Mark has convicted the court in one line and he has done it without any appeal to procedural rules.

They are not seeking testimony. They are seeking testimony against him, to put him to death. The verdict is fixed and the evidence is being recruited to fit it.

That is the precise inversion of what a court is. A court establishes what happened and then determines the consequence. This body has the consequence and is shopping for the happening.

And it is worth adding what the later Jewish law code says about capital trials, even granting that we cannot be certain how much of it was in force in AD 30. Capital cases were to be heard in daylight; in the temple's own hall of hewn stone; never begun on the eve of a Sabbath or a feast; and a guilty verdict could not be returned on the same day as the trial — an acquittal could be given at once, but a condemnation had to wait overnight, so that the judges slept on it.

This trial is held at night, in a private residence, at Passover, and the sentence is passed within the hour.

But notice that Mark does not lean on any of that. His indictment is simpler and it is in verse 55.

But they found none.

And here is something quietly extraordinary that is very easy to read past.

The supreme court of Israel, with every motive in the world and the whole night to work in, and presumably the resources to find and prompt willing witnesses, could not assemble a credible case against him.

Three years of public ministry. Thousands of hours of teaching, most of it in the open air, much of it in front of hostile professionals taking notes. Enemies who had been following him from town to town since chapter 2, precisely in order to catch him out.

And they could not find two men who could agree on anything he had done wrong.

That is not a small piece of evidence for the sinlessness of Jesus of Nazareth. It is the testimony of a hostile prosecution that had every reason to produce something and could not.

For many bore false witness against him, but their testimony did not agree.

They had witnesses; the witnesses were lying; and the lies did not match.

Which was fatal to the prosecution under the Law, and every man in that room knew it: a single witness shall not suffice against a person for any crime... only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established (Deut. 19:15). And the penalty for a false witness in a capital case was the death he had sought to inflict (Deut. 19:18–19).

Nobody in that room is charged with anything.
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin. The law required two agreeing witnesses.

parallels.desc: false witnesses have risen against me

verseByVerse.quote: And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, "We heard him say, 'I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.'" Yet even about this their testimony did not agree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And some stood up and bore false witness against him, saying, We heard him say, I will destroy this temple that is made with hands, and in three days I will build another, not made with hands.

This is the best they can manage, and it is worth taking apart, because it is a lie built out of something true — which is how the most effective lies are made.

He did say something like it. John records it, at the first cleansing of the temple, three years earlier: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. And John adds the explanation the witnesses have conveniently lost: he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 2:19–21).

Now count the alterations.

The imperative becomes a threat. He said destroy this temple — addressed to them, a challenge. They report I will destroy this temple — a stated intention, which turns a saying about his own death into a plot against the national sanctuary.

And the metaphor is flattened into masonry. He was speaking of his body. They present it as a claim about the building — which, in a week when the city was full of pilgrims and the temple was the heart of the nation, was as inflammatory a charge as could be devised. Jeremiah nearly lost his life for prophesying against this building (Jer. 26:8–11), and Stephen will lose his for the same accusation within a few years (Acts 6:13–14).

So the technique is: take his real words, change the person of one verb, and remove the interpretation. Nothing is invented. Everything is turned.

That is worth recognising, because it is still the commonest way Christ and his people are misrepresented. Not fabrication — selective reporting with the key removed. A sentence lifted out, the context deleted, the qualifier dropped, and the thing said is technically traceable to something he actually said.

Yet even about this their testimony did not agree.

And it collapses anyway. Even the best lie in the room could not survive two men telling it.

Mark's little word even carries the exasperation of the prosecution. They had one usable charge and could not get it into evidence.

And here is the thing to hold on to, because the whole passion turns on it.

He is not convicted of this. He is not convicted of anything the witnesses said, because none of it stood up. The charge that finally kills him will come out of his own mouth in three verses' time, when the high priest asks him a direct question and he tells the truth.

They could not find a crime. So they asked him who he was, and he told them — and that was enough.

And there is one more turn in it. The thing they mocked as a lie was the one thing in the whole trial that was about to come true. In three days there would be a temple not made with hands, and it would be his risen body, and the church has been built on it ever since — in whom the whole structure, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord (Eph. 2:21).

The false witnesses were accidentally right, and nobody in the room noticed.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, "Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?" But he remained silent and made no answer. Again the high priest asked him, "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?" And Jesus said, "I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus, Have you no answer to make?

The case has collapsed and Caiaphas stands up — physically moves into the middle of the room — because the trial is failing and he has to rescue it.

And his first move is to try to get the prisoner talking. Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?

But he remained silent and made no answer.

Mark says it twice over, in two ways, because the silence is the point.

He does not defend himself. He does not point out that the witnesses contradict each other, which would have ended the proceeding. He does not explain what he actually said about the temple, which would have taken thirty seconds and was completely defensible.

He says nothing.

And it is a quotation. He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth (Isa. 53:7).

Take the measure of that silence. Every instinct in a wronged man is to explain. He is standing in front of a court that has already decided, having been arrested by a mob, accused by liars, on the strength of a friend's kiss — and he will not say a word in his own defence, because saying it would have worked.

Again the high priest asked him, Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?

And now the direct question, and it is the question the whole Gospel has been asking since 1:1.

The Blessed is a reverent Jewish substitute for the divine name — Caiaphas will not say God out loud. So he is asking: are you the Messiah, the Son of God?

Matthew adds that he put him under oath (Matt. 26:63).

And Jesus said, I am.

Two words.

Nine chapters of demons silenced, healed men hushed, disciples told to say nothing to anybody. The whole strategy of secrecy, sustained from the first synagogue in Capernaum, held for three years — because the title would have been misunderstood, because a crowd would have crowned him, because the cross had to define it.

Now there is nothing left to protect. He is in chains, the crowd cannot reach him, and a crown is not on offer. And the moment it can only cost him his life, he says it plainly.

And the words themselves are egō eimi — I am. The same two words he spoke on the water in the dark (6:50), and they may echo the words God gave Moses at the bush (Ex. 3:14).

And you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven.

He does not stop at the answer. He adds a sentence that fuses two texts, and he chooses them with care.

Seated at the right hand of Power is Psalm 110:1 — the psalm he had put to these very men as an unanswerable riddle two days ago (12:36).

Coming with the clouds of heaven is Daniel 7:13 — the one like a son of man who is given dominion and glory and a kingdom, and all peoples serve him.

Put them together and this is what a bound prisoner says to the court that is about to sentence him: you will see me on the throne, and you will see me coming as judge.

And you will see it. The men in that room are told they will witness it themselves.

When would they see this? Some take it as the vindication of Christ after his death, in his resurrection, ascension and the judgment on Jerusalem, since in Daniel the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to receive his kingdom. Others take it as the final coming, when every eye will see him, even those who pierced him (Rev 1:7). The more likely reading holds both together. From his resurrection Jesus is enthroned at God’s right hand, and those who condemned him saw the signs of it; the coming with the clouds will be seen by all at his return, when these judges stand before their Judge.

The dock and the bench are about to change places, and everyone present understood him perfectly. That is why the next verse happens.
verseByVerse.note: “The Blessed” is a reverent way of saying “God.” Jesus’ “I am” is his plainest claim in Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: And the high priest tore his garments and said, "What further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy. What is your decision?" And they all condemned him as deserving death. And some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, "Prophesy!" And the guards received him with blows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the high priest tore his garments.

The formal judicial gesture on hearing blasphemy — an act of mourning, performed so the court can see that the words have been recognised for what they are.

And there is something here that ought to be better known. The Law placed a standing prohibition on this particular man's clothes: The priest who is chief among his brothers... shall not let the hair of his head hang loose nor tear his clothes (Lev. 21:10). The high priest was forbidden the ordinary signs of grief, even for his own father and mother.

So on the night the Sanhedrin condemned Jesus for blasphemy, the high priest of Israel did, at the very least, something the Law forbade him as a sign of mourning. The most scrupulous men alive, in a room full of experts on the letter of the law — and the only person in the building keeping it was the one they were about to kill for breaking it.

What further witnesses do we need? You have heard his blasphemy.

And this is the one honest sentence anybody speaks all night, though not in the way Caiaphas intends.

He is right that no further witnesses are needed. The case is settled out of the prisoner's own mouth. The false testimony has been abandoned; the charge is what Jesus said about himself.

And he is right about the logic, too. If Jesus is not who he said he was, this is blasphemy — a man claiming the throne of God and the judgement of the world. Caiaphas is not being unreasonable. He is being consistent, and he has reached the only conclusion available to someone who has already decided the claim is false.

There were never more than two options in that room, and there are never more than two now. Either the man in the dock is God's Son, or he said the most blasphemous thing a human being has ever said. Nobody who has read this trial can go on calling him a fine moral teacher.

What is your decision? And they all condemned him as deserving death.

All. Mark says it flatly. Whether every member was present is another question — Joseph of Arimathea was a member and had not consented (Luke 23:51) — but the verdict was unanimous among those who voted.

And some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to strike him, saying to him, Prophesy!

And now the court, having passed sentence, does this.

Spitting was the deepest contempt available in that culture — the Law used it as the mark of public disgrace (Num. 12:14; Deut. 25:9). And Isaiah said the Servant would receive it: I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isa. 50:6).

Covering his face and striking him is a game. They blindfold him and hit him and demand that he name who did it — Luke spells it out (Luke 22:64). Grown men, the religious leadership of Israel, playing a guessing game with a bound prisoner in the middle of the night.

Prophesy!

And that is the cruellest word in the chapter, and the most ironic.

Because he had prophesied — that very evening, with total accuracy. He said one of the twelve would betray him, and one had. He said they would all fall away, and they had. He said the temple would come down, and it would.

And he said one more thing, which was at that exact moment coming true, two floors below them, in the courtyard, in the hearing of a servant girl warming her hands at the same fire.
verseByVerse.note: Tearing one’s garments was a sign of horror or grief.

parallels.desc: I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting

verseByVerse.quote: And as Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the servant girls of the high priest came, and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said, "You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus." But he denied it, saying, "I neither know nor understand what you mean." And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as Peter was below in the courtyard.

Below. Mark gives us the architecture, and it is the whole point of the arrangement.

Upstairs: Christ, on trial, confessing who he is, and being struck for it. Downstairs, in the same house, in the open yard: Peter, at the fire, about to be asked the same question.

Two men, one building, one night, and the same question put to both — are you the Christ? and you also were with him. One says I am and it costs him his life. The other says, in effect, "I am not", and it costs him everything else.

One of the servant girls of the high priest came.

And look at who breaks him.

Not a soldier. Not a member of the council. Not the temple police who arrested him and had seen him draw a sword three hours ago. A servant girl — the lowest-status person in the household, a girl on the gate, whose opinion could not have hurt him and who had no power over him whatsoever.

The man who swore he would die with him is undone by a domestic.

And seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him.

She looked at him — fixed her eyes on him, stared. Mark used the same words when Jesus looked at the rich young man and loved him (10:21).

She is peering across a charcoal fire in the dark, and the light is on his face, and she is working out where she has seen him before.

And it is precisely because he sat down at that fire that she can see him at all. In the shadows at the edge of the yard, nobody asks you anything.

You also were with the Nazarene, Jesus.

Note what the accusation actually is. Not you are a disciple, not you believe his teaching. You were with him. Association. That is all.

And the Nazarene is faintly contemptuous — the man from that village, that provincial nobody.

But he denied it, saying, I neither know nor understand what you mean.

The first denial, and it is not a flat lie so much as a fog. I neither know nor understand what you mean. It is the answer of a man buying time, and it is the sort of thing everybody has said.

Which is worth being honest about, because we imagine Peter's denial as something dramatic and unlike us. It begins as an evasion at a fire. Not I renounce Christ — just I neither know nor understand what you mean, said to somebody unimportant, to make a moment go away.

And he went out into the gateway and the rooster crowed.

He moves. He gets up and goes out to the entrance passage — nearer the door, further from the light, closer to escape.

And a bird calls somewhere in the city, and he does not hear it.

That is the mercy in this account and almost nobody notices it. The first crow was a warning, delivered exactly when Jesus said it would be, in the middle of the night, to a man who had been told what it meant three hours earlier. There was still time. Two denials had not yet happened.

He heard a cock crow and it meant nothing to him at all.

verseByVerse.quote: And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, "This man is one of them." But again he denied it. And after a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, "Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the servant girl saw him and began again to say to the bystanders, This man is one of them.

She has not let it go, and now she is talking to other people about him. The pressure is widening: the first challenge was private, this one is public.

One of them. The wording has hardened. Not you were with him but he is one of them — a category, a group, a party.

But again he denied it.

Mark does not even record the words this time. Just the fact. The second lie is easier, and it needs less said.

That is how it works, and it is the most practically useful thing in this passage. The first denial makes the second one cheap. Having said I neither know nor understand what you mean, he now has to defend the first statement as well as himself, and the only way to defend it is to say it again with more force.

A man who tells one lie has taken out a loan. Every subsequent lie is interest.

And after a little while the bystanders again said to Peter, Certainly you are one of them, for you are a Galilean.

Third challenge, and now it is not one girl but a group of them, and they have evidence.

You are a Galilean. It is his accent. Galilean Aramaic was noticeably different from the Judean speech of Jerusalem — the rabbis joked about Galileans swallowing their consonants and confusing their gutturals. Matthew makes it explicit: certainly you too are one of them, for your accent betrays you (Matt. 26:73).

So Peter is trapped by the way he says words. He can deny knowing Jesus; he cannot deny the sound of his own mouth. Every sentence he speaks to defend himself proves the case against him.

And there is something in that worth carrying home.

He was recognisable. Not by a badge or a confession, but by what he could not help — where he came from, how he spoke, the marks of three years in that company. Something about him gave him away before he opened his mouth to lie, and kept giving him away every time he did.

That is what following Christ does to a person over time, and it is a mercy even when it is inconvenient. There ought to be something about a Christian that does not switch off — a way of speaking, a way of handling money, a way of treating people — that people notice before anything is said.

Peter's accent was more faithful than Peter was.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable regional accent.

verseByVerse.quote: But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, "I do not know this man of whom you speak." And immediately the rooster crowed a second time. And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, "Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times." And he broke down and wept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear.

And now the bottom.

This is not swearing in the modern sense. Two things are happening, and both are formal and terrible.

He invokes a curse. The word means to call down a curse — on himself, in the standard oath formula of that world: may God do so to me and more also if I am lying.

And he swears. He takes an oath, calling God to witness the truth of what he is saying.

So Peter calls God as his witness, and calls down God's curse on his own head, to guarantee a lie about God's Son.

And this is the same man who three hours ago said if I must die with you, I will not deny you, and who six chapters before that was told get behind me, Satan for trying to keep him from the cross. He has always been in earnest. That is the horror of it.

I do not know this man of whom you speak.

Notice that he will not say the name. Not Jesus, not the Nazarene — this man. He puts as much distance into the sentence as the grammar will allow.

And the words are, in the most literal sense, the exact opposite of the truth. He knew him better than almost anyone alive. He had watched him raise a dead girl, still a storm, feed five thousand, and shine on a mountain. He had said, at Caesarea Philippi, you are the Christ.

Upstairs, at that moment, Jesus is saying I am. Downstairs, Peter is saying, in effect, "I am not".

And immediately the rooster crowed a second time.

A bird, in a city, before dawn.

God did not send an angel or a thunderclap. He used the most ordinary sound in the world, the one that had been part of every morning of Peter's life, and timed it to the second.

And Peter remembered how Jesus had said to him, Before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.

The remembering is the turn, and it is everything.

Luke adds the detail that finishes a person: and the Lord turned and looked at Peter (Luke 22:61). If the prisoner was being moved across the courtyard at that moment, then the two men's eyes met at the exact instant the bird called.

And he broke down and wept.

Mark's phrase is difficult to translate — the ESV margin offers when he had thought about it, he wept. Whatever the precise sense, the strongest of the twelve went completely to pieces in a courtyard in the dark.

And here is where the chapter leaves us, and everything depends on it.

Two men betrayed Jesus that night. Both were of the twelve. Both had been warned to their faces. Both did exactly what he said they would.

One went out and hanged himself. One went out and wept.

The difference is not the size of the sin — denying him three times with oaths is not obviously better than selling him for silver. The difference is what each man did with the wreckage. Judas felt remorse, and it drove him away from Christ, to a rope. Peter felt grief, and it drove him back — and on the third morning an angel in an empty tomb will say: go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee (16:7).

Named. Specifically. The one who denied him is the one singled out to be told.

So if you have failed him badly, do not read this chapter and despair. Read what he said before any of it happened: you will all fall away — but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.

But Jesus said, whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father (Matt 10:33), and Paul, if we deny him, he also will deny us (2 Tim 2:12). Those words describe a final, settled denial, the denial of someone who will not come back. Peter’s was a terrible fall, but not a final one. Jesus had prayed that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:32), and it did not. A believer can fall badly; Christ keeps him from falling away for good.

The tears in that courtyard are not the end of Peter. They are the beginning of the man who preached at Pentecost, and wrote two letters about standing firm, and died on a cross of his own — and who told this story, against himself, with the numbers in it, for the rest of his life, so that everyone who has ever warmed their hands at the wrong fire would know there is a way back.

14.theology:
What is the cup? Everything in Gethsemane turns on it, and it is not the general dread of dying. Thousands of his own martyrs have gone to worse deaths singing; if the cup were merely execution, the Christian would have a Lord less composed than his servants.

The cup is a fixed Old Testament image and it means the wrath of God: in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine... and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs (Ps. 75:8); you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath (Isa. 51:17); take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath (Jer. 25:15). That is what stands in front of him in the dark, and it is why a man who slept through a hurricane is on the ground shaking. And he drank it — for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21) — which is precisely why there is nothing left in it for anyone who is in him.

And Gethsemane reverses Eden. In a garden a man was told the Father's will and said, in effect, "not your will but mine", and the world broke. In a garden a man who could have had anything said not what I will, but what you will, and it was mended.

Abba (v. 36) is one of the Aramaic words Mark preserves, and the most significant: the ordinary family word a child used for his father at home. Jewish prayer very rarely, if ever, addressed God that way. And it did not stay his — twice the New Testament says the Spirit puts this very word into the mouths of ordinary Christians (Rom. 8:15; Gal. 4:6). The name he used in Gethsemane is the name he handed over.

And I am (v. 62) is the fullest confession in the Gospel. Nine chapters of silencing demons and hushing healed men — and now, under oath, in chains, when it can only cost him his life, he answers plainly, in the words of the burning bush, and fuses Psalm 110:1 to Daniel 7:13. He tells the court that the man in the dock will be their judge, and they understand him perfectly.
14.examples:
Then: You will all fall away (v. 27) — and then, before Peter has opened his mouth, but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (v. 28).

Read those in the order he said them, because the order is the gospel. He announces the restoration before the failure happens. No condition attached — not if you repent, not if you come back. He tells eleven men who are about to abandon him where to meet him afterwards, and the word he uses is a shepherd's word: I will go before you, out in front, the way a shepherd leads. And not Jerusalem, where it all went wrong — Galilee, where they were called off their boats.

Now: the angel at the empty tomb repeats it with one addition — go, tell his disciples and Peter (16:7). The one named in the failure is named in the restoration.

And the chapter ends with two men who betrayed him. Both of the twelve, both warned to their faces, both doing exactly what he said they would. One went out and hanged himself; one went out and wept.

The difference is not the size of the sin — denying him three times with oaths is not obviously better than selling him for silver. It is what each did with the wreckage. Remorse drove Judas away from Christ, to a rope. Grief drove Peter back.

So if you have failed him badly, notice where Peter was standing when it started: at a distance (v. 54), and then warming himself at the fire — near enough to keep his conscience quiet, far enough to keep his safety. Nobody stays there long. And notice that the man who told this story against himself, with the numbers in it, for the rest of his life, is the man whose memories became this Gospel.

15.title: Truly This Man Was the Son of God
15.text: <sup>1</sup>And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. <sup>2</sup>And Pilate asked him, “Are you the King of the Jews?” And he answered him, “You have said so.” <sup>3</sup>And the chief priests accused him of many things. <sup>4</sup>And Pilate again asked him, “Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you.” <sup>5</sup>But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed. <sup>6</sup>Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. <sup>7</sup>And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. <sup>8</sup>And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. <sup>9</sup>And he answered them, saying, “Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?” <sup>10</sup>For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up. <sup>11</sup>But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead. <sup>12</sup>And Pilate again said to them, “Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?” <sup>13</sup>And they cried out again, “Crucify him.” <sup>14</sup>And Pilate said to them, “Why? What evil has he done?” But they shouted all the more, “Crucify him.” <sup>15</sup>So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified. <sup>16</sup>And the soldiers led him away inside the palace (that is, the governor’s headquarters), and they called together the whole battalion. <sup>17</sup>And they clothed him in a purple cloak, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him. <sup>18</sup>And they began to salute him, “Hail, King of the Jews!” <sup>19</sup>And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. <sup>20</sup>And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him. <sup>21</sup>And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. <sup>22</sup>And they brought him to the place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull). <sup>23</sup>And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. <sup>24</sup>And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take. <sup>25</sup>And it was the third hour when they crucified him. <sup>26</sup>And the inscription of the charge against him read, “The King of the Jews.” <sup>27</sup>And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left. <sup>29</sup>And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, “Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, <sup>30</sup>save yourself, and come down from the cross!” <sup>31</sup>So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying, “He saved others; he cannot save himself. <sup>32</sup>Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe.” Those who were crucified with him also reviled him. <sup>33</sup>And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. <sup>34</sup>And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” <sup>35</sup>And some of the bystanders hearing it said, “Behold, he is calling Elijah.” <sup>36</sup>And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, “Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.” <sup>37</sup>And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last. <sup>38</sup>And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. <sup>39</sup>And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” <sup>40</sup>There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. <sup>41</sup>When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem. <sup>42</sup>And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, <sup>43</sup>Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. <sup>44</sup>Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. <sup>45</sup>And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph. <sup>46</sup>And Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. <sup>47</sup>Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
15.overview:
Fifteen hours from the garden to the grave, and Mark tells it almost without adjectives.

At first light the council reconvenes to make the night's verdict look regular and hands him to Rome, because they could pass a religious sentence and could not carry one out. Pilate asks one question, gets four words, and then nothing at all — and it astonishes him, because he has never seen a prisoner decline to save himself.

He knows the case is malicious; Mark says so plainly (v. 10). He tries the festival amnesty and the crowd, worked by the chief priests, asks for a murderer instead — a man called Barabbas, guilty of exactly the crime Jesus is falsely charged with. Pilate asks the only honest question of the morning and, getting no answer, hands him over anyway, wishing to satisfy the crowd.

Then a cohort of soldiers stages a coronation as a joke and gets every detail right; a pilgrim from Africa is pressed into carrying the beam and his sons end up in the church at Rome; and Mark records the crucifixion itself in four words.

At noon the light goes out. At three he shouts the first line of Psalm 22 into the dark, and then shouts again and dies — and sixty feet of temple curtain tears from the top down, and a Roman officer who has watched him for six hours says the thing no human being in this Gospel has yet said.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — Before Pilate and the Mocking
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The transfer (vv. 1–5). As soon as it is light the council reconvenes to make the night's verdict look regular, and hands him to Rome — because they could pass a religious sentence and could not carry out an execution. Pilate asks one question and gets four words, and then nothing at all, and it astonishes him.

Barabbas (vv. 6–15). Pilate has read the situation correctly — he perceived that it was out of envy — and tries to release him through a festival custom. The chief priests work the crowd, and the crowd asks for a murderer. Pilate asks the only honest question of the morning, what evil has he done?, gets no answer, and hands him over anyway.

The mockery (vv. 16–20). Then the whole battalion is called together for a game: a purple cloak, a crown twisted out of thorns, a reed, mock salutes and real spitting.

Every element of it is accurate. He is the King; he does receive homage; he will wear purple and a crown. A cohort of Roman soldiers staged a coronation as a joke and got every detail right.
verseByVerse.theology:
Barabbas is the atonement acted out on a platform in Jerusalem.

Mark tells us exactly what he was: a rebel, in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection — guilty of precisely the crime Jesus is falsely charged with, and guilty in fact.

So two men stand before the crowd. One is guilty; the other is the Son of the Father and is innocent. The crowd is offered a choice, chooses the guilty man, and condemns the innocent one — and the innocent one dies in the guilty man's place, on the cross that had been prepared for him.

Nobody in Jerusalem understood what they were watching. But somewhere in that city, by nine o'clock that morning, there was a murderer walking around free, and the only reason he was free is that Jesus of Nazareth was on his cross.

That is the whole gospel, and it happened to one man literally before it happened to anybody else spiritually. Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Pet. 3:18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: What evil has he done? (v. 14) — the right question, asked by the one man in Jerusalem with the authority to act on it, who then did the opposite.

Mark is careful to show that Pilate knew. He perceived that it was out of envy (v. 10). He tried the amnesty. He put the question twice. The Roman governor of Judea conducted a better assessment of the evidence than the Sanhedrin had, and reached the correct conclusion, and signed the order anyway.

Now: and the reason Mark gives is five words long — wishing to satisfy the crowd. Not conviction, not deception, not a legal error. He wanted the noise to stop, and his position was already precarious enough that a riot at Passover could have finished him.

That is the commonest failure of people in authority, and it has never needed a Roman governor to perform it. The doctrine not defended because of who would leave. The wrong not named because of whose son it was. The decision made by counting the room rather than weighing the case.

Pilate did not decide that Jesus was guilty. He decided that being right was more expensive than being popular — which is a different sin, and a far more available one.

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as it was morning, the chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council. And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate. And Pilate asked him, "Are you the King of the Jews?" And he answered him, "You have said so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as soon as it was morning.

The fourth watch of the parable (13:35), and the last of the four. Evening at the supper, midnight in the garden, cockcrow in the courtyard, and now morning — and the disciples have slept or run through every one of them.

The chief priests held a consultation with the elders and scribes and the whole council.

They meet again at first light, and the reason is almost certainly procedural. A capital verdict reached at night was irregular even by their own standards; a daylight session could be recorded as the proper trial.

So this is a formality performed to make an illegality look regular — and Mark, who has already told us they had the sentence before they had the evidence (14:55), lets the reader draw the conclusion.

And they bound Jesus and led him away and delivered him over to Pilate.

Bound. He was already in custody; the binding is for the transfer, and it is how you move a man through the streets.

Delivered him over — paradidōmi, the word Mark has been using since chapter 1. It is the word for Judas's betrayal (14:10), for what the Son of Man must undergo (9:31), and it will be used of Pilate handing him to the soldiers (15:15). Everyone in this chapter is handing him on to somebody else. Nobody wants to be the last pair of hands.

And why Pilate at all? Because the council could pass a religious sentence and could not execute one. Rome reserved capital punishment to itself in the provinces, and John records the council saying so plainly: it is not lawful for us to put anyone to death (John 18:31).

Which is why the charge has to change on the way. Blasphemy will not interest a Roman court for a second. So the accusation is translated into something Rome must act on — a man claiming to be a king.

And Pilate asked him, Are you the King of the Jews?

Note that this is the first thing out of his mouth, before any evidence is heard, which tells you what he had been told in advance.

And it is the only charge Rome cares about. Judea was a difficult province with a history of messianic risings; a claimant to a throne was a security matter. Pilate is not asking a theological question. He is asking an operational one: is this man a threat?

And he answered him, You have said so.

Four words, and they are neither a yes nor a no.

It is not evasion. It is a refusal to accept the frame. King of the Jews is Pilate's phrase, loaded with everything Rome feared — insurrection, a rival throne, tax revolt. Jesus will not deny the kingship, because he is the King. He will not affirm it in Pilate's terms, because in Pilate's terms it means something he has never claimed.

John gives the fuller exchange, and it is the same distinction: My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting (John 18:36).

And this is his last recorded answer to a question in this Gospel. From here, almost nothing — until a cry at three in the afternoon.
verseByVerse.note: Under Roman rule the council could not carry out a death sentence. Pontius Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea from AD 26 to 36.

verseByVerse.quote: And the chief priests accused him of many things. And Pilate again asked him, "Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you." But Jesus made no further answer, so that Pilate was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the chief priests accused him of many things.

Mark does not itemise them, and Luke does: we found this man misleading our nation and forbidding us to give tribute to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king (Luke 23:2).

Every one of those is false or twisted. He had told them explicitly to pay the tax (12:17) — the very men accusing him were in the room when he said it, and had marvelled at the answer.

Many things. The strategy is volume. If no single charge will hold, pile them up and hope the weight does the work.

And Pilate again asked him, Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you.

And here is something worth noticing about Pilate: he is trying to help.

That is what this question is. A governor who wanted a conviction would let the accusations stand unanswered and move to sentence. Pilate is prompting the prisoner — say something, they are burying you — because he can see the case is thin and he would rather not do this.

Matthew adds that his wife sent word about a dream and told him to have nothing to do with this righteous man (Matt. 27:19). Pilate is not a man in the grip of conviction. He is a man looking for an exit.

But Jesus made no further answer.

And he will not take the exit he is offered.

Take the measure of this, because a single sentence would have done it. He could have said: I told them to pay the tax; ask them. He could have said: my kingdom is not of this world, and here are eleven witnesses that I have never armed a man. The case against him was so weak that a competent defence would have collapsed it in two minutes, and everyone in the room knew it.

He says nothing.

And it is a fulfilment, deliberately. He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth; like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth (Isa. 53:7).

So that Pilate was amazed.

He marvelled; he was astonished.

Consider what it takes to astonish a Roman governor at a criminal hearing. This man had presided over years of provincial justice. He had seen every kind of defendant: the pleaders, the bribers, the weepers, the men who cursed him, the men who invented alibis. Every single one of them fought.

He had never seen a man decline to save himself.

And that is the thing to carry out of this scene. The silence was not resignation and it was not despair. It was the most deliberate act in the room. He could have talked his way out — and the whole point was that he would not, because talking his way out was the one thing that would have left us where we were.

He kept his mouth shut so that ours could be opened.

parallels.desc: like a sheep that before its shearers is silent

verseByVerse.quote: Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked. And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas. And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them. And he answered them, saying, "Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?" For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now at the feast he used to release for them one prisoner for whom they asked.

A goodwill custom at Passover — the feast of liberation, so a prisoner is set free. It is attested nowhere outside the Gospels, which some have made an objection; but Roman governors did grant such amnesties, and a local custom in one province for one feast is exactly the sort of thing that leaves no other trace.

And among the rebels in prison, who had committed murder in the insurrection, there was a man called Barabbas.

Mark is precise, and every detail matters.

Among the rebels. Not a common criminal — a political prisoner, one of a group.

Who had committed murder in the insurrection. Mark says the insurrection, as though his readers knew which one. So there had been a recent rising, and Barabbas had killed somebody in it.

He is, in other words, guilty of exactly what Jesus is falsely accused of — sedition against Rome, a claim to overthrow the order. One of these two men actually did what the other is charged with.

And the name. Bar-abbas is Aramaic and it means son of the father. Some manuscripts of Matthew even give his first name as Jesus — Jesus Barabbas (Matt. 27:16–17).

So the choice put to the crowd, in the plainest possible terms, is between two men called son of the father. One is a murderer. The other is the Son of the Father.

And the crowd came up and began to ask Pilate to do as he usually did for them.

Note that the crowd initiates it. They have come for their prisoner, and they have somebody in mind.

And note also who this crowd is. It is not necessarily the crowd from Sunday. Those pilgrims are camped on the hillsides; this is early Friday morning, at the governor's residence, and the people present are those who could be assembled at short notice by men with influence. Verse 11 tells us who assembled them.

And he answered them, saying, Do you want me to release for you the King of the Jews?

Pilate makes his move, and it is a shrewd one. He offers the amnesty in a way that puts his preferred outcome first.

He is also, in that phrase, needling the priests. The King of the Jews is his title for him throughout — he uses it here, again in verse 12, and he will have it nailed to the cross in three languages, and refuse to change it (John 19:22).

For he perceived that it was out of envy that the chief priests had delivered him up.

And Mark tells us plainly what Pilate had worked out, which settles the question of his culpability.

Envy. Not concern for public order. Not theological outrage. The priests wanted him dead because the crowds hung on his teaching (11:18; 12:37), because his authority made theirs look like what it was, and because he had walked into their temple and turned the tables over.

A Roman politician recognised professional jealousy when he saw it, because he had seen a great deal of it.

So Pilate knows the charge is malicious, knows the man is innocent, and knows exactly why he is standing there. Everything that happens next happens with that knowledge in the room.
verseByVerse.note: Barabbas means “son of the father.” The “insurrection” was one of many uprisings against Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead. And Pilate again said to them, "Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?" And they cried out again, "Crucify him." And Pilate said to them, "Why? What evil has he done?" But they shouted all the more, "Crucify him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release for them Barabbas instead.

They agitated the crowd, the way you shake a jar.

And this is the single most important sentence for understanding the next hour, because it tells you the crowd is being worked.

They did not arrive with a view about Barabbas. Somebody moved among them and gave them one. Matthew says the same: the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd (Matt. 27:20).

And that is worth stopping on, because crowds are still made this way and it is one of the most frightening things in the Bible.

Some of the people shouting in that courtyard may well have been on the Bethphage road five days earlier with their cloaks in the dust. Nobody in Jerusalem had changed their mind about Jesus on the evidence. There was no new fact.

What happened was that the people with authority and access told them what to think, and they thought it, and within minutes they were shouting for a man's execution.

A crowd is not a mind. It is an amplifier, and whoever gets to it first decides what it amplifies. Which is why you shall not fall in with the many to do evil (Ex. 23:2) is in the Law, and why a Christian who finds himself agreeing with a roomful of people should always check whether he has examined the thing or merely caught it.

And Pilate again said to them, Then what shall I do with the man you call the King of the Jews?

Again. Mark keeps the count. This is Pilate's second attempt, and there will be a third.

And notice the question he has just made public. What shall I do with him? — put to a crowd, out loud, as though it were theirs to answer.

It is the question every person eventually has to answer, and the tragedy of Pilate is that he asked it in the one way that guaranteed the wrong answer. He asked the room instead of deciding himself.

And they cried out again, Crucify him.

Two words. No argument, no charge, no reasoning. A demand for a specific method of execution — and it is worth noting that crucifixion was a Roman punishment, not a Jewish one. The crowd is asking a pagan governor to do to their own countryman the thing reserved for slaves and rebels.

And Pilate said to them, Why? What evil has he done?

The third attempt, and the only honest question of the morning.

It is a fair question and it has an answer: nothing. And Mark records no reply, because there was none. Nobody in that courtyard could name a crime, and the silence where the answer should be is the verdict of history on the whole proceeding.

But they shouted all the more, Crucify him.

Louder. That is the reply. When a case cannot be made, volume does the work — and it worked.

verseByVerse.quote: So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd, released for them Barabbas, and having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Pilate, wishing to satisfy the crowd.

Mark gives the motive in one phrase, and it is not a legal judgement. To give them what would content them.

He knows the man is innocent. He has all but said so in his own questions. He has tried the amnesty and the direct question. And he folds, because the noise is rising and his position cannot take a riot at Passover.

Pilate's record was already poor. He had provoked riots by bringing military standards bearing the emperor's image into Jerusalem, and by raiding the temple treasury to build an aqueduct; Philo records a rebuke from Tiberius himself. He was one incident away from recall, and he knew it. In the end he was recalled anyway, a few years later, for a massacre in Samaria.

So a man weighed an innocent life against his own career and chose the career — and lost it in any case, which is very often how that trade turns out.

Released for them Barabbas.

Somewhere in Jerusalem, before nine o'clock that morning, a convicted murderer walked out into the street a free man and did not know why.

He is the first person in history to have Jesus die in his place, and he is the picture of every one since. He did not repent, or ask, or understand. He did not even know it was happening. Somebody else's name was called instead of his, and the cross that had his name on it took another man.

Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Pet. 3:18).

And having scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified.

Mark gives it in a subordinate clause of three words, and it should not be hurried past, because the reticence of the Gospels here is deliberate and total. Not one of the four describes the physical suffering. They report the facts and leave them.

The Roman flagellum was a short whip of several leather thongs, weighted with pieces of bone and metal. The prisoner was stripped and tied to a post; there was no fixed number of strokes as there was under Jewish law, and the beating was administered by soldiers until the officer stopped it. Eusebius, writing of martyrs, says the victims' veins and organs were sometimes laid bare. Men died under it.

This was the routine preliminary to crucifixion — partly punishment, partly to shorten the ordeal by weakening the man.

So when he is brought out to the soldiers in the next verse, and when Simon of Cyrene is pressed into carrying the beam in verse 21, this is why.

But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed (Isa. 53:5).
verseByVerse.note: Roman scourging used a whip weighted with bone or metal; it could itself kill.

parallels.desc: with his wounds we are healed

verseByVerse.quote: And the soldiers led him away inside the palace (that is, the governor's headquarters), and they called together the whole battalion. And they clothed him in a purple cloak, and twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him. And they began to salute him, "Hail, King of the Jews!" And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him. And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the soldiers led him away inside the palace, and they called together the whole battalion.

The word is speira — a cohort, nominally six hundred men, though the detachment in Jerusalem would have been smaller. Whatever the number, Mark's point is that this was not two bored guards. They called everybody in.

Understand who these men were. Auxiliaries, mostly recruited from Samaria and Syria, garrisoned in a province they despised, on riot duty at a festival they did not understand. They loathed the Jews and the feeling was returned. And here is a Jew who has been handed to them as a king.

This is entertainment.

And they clothed him in a purple cloak.

Purple was the imperial colour — expensive, restricted, the mark of royalty. What they had to hand was probably a soldier's red cloak, which passed for purple in a joke.

And twisting together a crown of thorns, they put it on him.

Not a circlet resting on the head but a wreath, twisted like the laurel of a Caesar's portrait.

And thorns are not incidental to the Bible. They arrive in Genesis 3 as part of the curse on the ground: thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you (Gen. 3:18). The first visible mark of a world under judgement is pressed onto the head of the man who came to lift it.

And they began to salute him, Hail, King of the Jews!

It is the imperial greeting — Ave, Caesar — with the name changed. They are performing an accession, and the joke is that this bleeding provincial is being given the honours of an emperor.

And they were striking his head with a reed and spitting on him and kneeling down in homage to him.

Striking, spitting, kneeling — and it went on.

The reed is the sceptre — Matthew says they first put it in his right hand (Matt. 27:29) — and then they take it and hit him on the head with it, which drives the thorns in.

And kneeling down in homage is the verb for worship, the same word used of the demoniac falling at his feet (5:6) and the wise men before the child (Matt. 2:11). They are bowing the knee to the Son of God as a joke.

And now see what Mark has quietly done, because there is not a word of comment in it.

Every single element of that mockery is true.

He is the King of the Jews — Pilate will nail the words over his head within the hour and refuse to take them down. He will wear a crown, and a robe, and receive the homage of the nations. And at the name of Jesus every knee should bow (Phil. 2:10) — including, one day, every knee in that room.

A cohort of Roman soldiers staged a coronation as a joke, and got the costume, the crown, the sceptre, the acclamation and the kneeling exactly right. They were the only people in Jerusalem that morning conducting the correct ceremony.

They simply thought it was funny.

And when they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple cloak and put his own clothes on him. And they led him out to crucify him.

The game ends. The robe comes off, because it belongs to somebody and will be wanted back — and in a few verses they will gamble for the clothes he is standing in.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. The ESV notes that a battalion (cohort) was a tenth of a Roman legion. Purple was the colour of royalty.

parallels.desc: I gave my back to those who strike

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The road and the cross (vv. 21–27). A man on his way in from the country is pressed into carrying the beam, and Mark names his sons, probably because his readers knew them. At Golgotha he refuses the drugged wine, the soldiers gamble for his clothes, and Mark records the crucifixion itself in four words: and they crucified him.

The mockery (vv. 29–32). Three groups take their turn — passers-by, the chief priests, and the two men dying beside him. The taunt is always the same, and it is the wilderness temptation for the third time: come down; save yourself.

The darkness (vv. 33–37). At noon the light goes out for three hours. And at three o'clock he cries out in Aramaic the opening line of Psalm 22, and Mark preserves the sound of it. Then a loud cry, and he is dead.

What the death did (vv. 38–41). Sixty feet of temple curtain tears from the top down. A Roman officer says the thing no human being in this Gospel has yet said. And the women who have been there all along are named.
verseByVerse.theology:
