The cry of dereliction (v. 34) is the sentence a suffering reader stops at, and two errors must be kept off it.

The first would soften it — as though Jesus were merely reciting a comforting psalm and was not truly forsaken. He was. The abandonment was real; he was bearing sin, and God's holiness turned from the sin-bearer.

The second would break God in two — as though the Trinity were torn apart, the Father ceasing to love the Son, the Son ceasing to be God. That did not happen and could not. The Son remained the beloved Son and remained God through every moment of the darkness; what he lost was not his Father's love or his own deity but the felt light of the Father's face, borne in our place.

Both are true at once: he entered a real forsakenness, and he entered it still holding on — for notice the word he uses. He does not cry God, why have you abandoned me, but my God, my God: twice claiming as his own the very One he could no longer feel. That is faith stripped of every comfort and still gripping in the dark.

And that is the word for the believer who has prayed into silence. The blackest hour a soul can know — real God-forsakenness, the full weight of it — has already been entered by the Son, so that it would never fall on you. I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb. 13:5) is bought with this cry. If you must pray in the dark, pray as he did — my God — to the God you cannot feel, and know that he prayed it first, and prayed it there, so that you would never have to pray it alone.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: He saved others; he cannot save himself (v. 31) — the chief priests, standing at the foot of the cross, jeering.

And they have stated the gospel with complete accuracy without meaning a word of it.

Every clause is true. He did save others — a leper, a paralytic, a legion, a dead girl, a boy with a spirit. And he could not save himself — not because the power was gone, since he could have called twelve legions of angels (Matt. 26:53), but because saving himself and saving others were the two things that could not both be done.

Now: the mockers thought they had found a contradiction. They had found the mechanism. The one who saves others cannot save himself; that is not a failure of power but the shape of substitution, and it is why there is a gospel at all.

And notice the demand attached: come down now from the cross that we may see and believe (v. 32). They had the order exactly backwards, and it is the standing human demand — show me and I will trust you.

He did not come down, and that is why anyone believes. Had he come down they would have seen a miracle and gone home unforgiven. He stayed up, and by three o'clock a Roman officer who had asked for no sign at all was saying truly this man was the Son of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, the father of Alexander and Rufus, to carry his cross. And they brought him to the place called Golgotha (which means Place of a Skull).
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they compelled a passerby, Simon of Cyrene.

The condemned man carried the crossbeam — the patibulum, perhaps eighty or a hundred pounds — to the place of execution, through the streets, as part of the punishment.

He cannot carry it. That is what this verse is telling us without saying it. After a night of interrogation, a scourging with the flagellum, and a cohort's entertainment, he is physically finished, and a Roman execution detail does not stop for compassion. They needed the prisoner alive at Golgotha.

They compelled. The verb is a Persian loan-word that had passed into Greek as a technical term for military requisition — the right of a soldier to press a civilian into service. It is the word behind if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two (Matt. 5:41).

So Simon does not volunteer. A soldier taps him and he has no choice.

Who was coming in from the country. He is walking into the city, probably for the feast, minding his own business. Cyrene is in North Africa — modern Libya — with a large Jewish community, so this is a pilgrim who has travelled a very long way to keep the Passover.

He has planned this trip for months. And a soldier picks him out of the crowd, and the day is not his any more.

The father of Alexander and Rufus.

And here is a detail that only Mark has, and it is one of the most quietly moving things in the Gospel.

Why name the sons? Mark does not tell us who Simon's wife was, or how old he was, or what became of him. He names two men — and the only possible reason is that his readers knew them.

This Gospel was written for the church at Rome. And in Paul's letter to that church there is a line in the closing greetings: Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, also his mother, who has been a mother to me as well (Rom. 16:13).

It cannot be proved, and it does not need to be, because the shape of the thing is clear either way. Mark expects his readers to nod at those names — yes, Rufus, we know him — which means the family of the man pressed into carrying the cross ended up in the church.

So think what that morning did. A pilgrim from Africa is dragged out of a crowd against his will, humiliated in a public street, made to carry a condemned criminal's cross for a man he had never met — and it is the making of his household. His sons are named in a Gospel. His widow, perhaps, mothered the apostle Paul.

Nobody has ever been pressed into carrying something for Christ and been the poorer for it, though it very rarely feels like that at the time. Simon did not choose that cross and would have given anything to avoid it, and it is why we know his name.

And they brought him to the place called Golgotha, which means Place of a Skull.

Mark translates the Aramaic for his Roman readers, as he does throughout. The Latin for skull is calvaria, which is where Calvary comes from.

Why the name? Possibly the shape of a rock outcrop; possibly simply what a public execution ground was called. It was outside the city wall — Jesus also suffered outside the gate (Heb. 13:12) — and beside a road, because the whole point of crucifixion was that people passing should see it.
verseByVerse.note: Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.” Rufus may be the man Paul greets in Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it. And they crucified him and divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they offered him wine mixed with myrrh, but he did not take it.

The drink was a rough anaesthetic. Wine with myrrh dulled the senses, and there is a tradition that women of Jerusalem provided it as an act of mercy to the condemned, on the strength of Proverbs 31:6 — give strong drink to the one who is perishing.

Even the Romans allowed it. It cost nothing and made the prisoner easier to handle.

He did not take it.

Five words, and they are a decision.

He is about to be nailed to a piece of wood and left there for six hours, and he is offered the one thing available in the ancient world that would take the edge off it — and he refuses.

Why? Because he had said, the night before, that he would not drink wine again until he drank it new in the kingdom (14:25). And more than that: because the cup he had been given in Gethsemane was to be drunk to the bottom, undiluted, with a clear mind.

Everything that follows — the mockery, the darkness, the cry — he goes through fully conscious, having deliberately declined the mercy that would have blurred it.

He would not be half-present at his own crucifixion.

And they crucified him.

Four words.

That is all Mark says. No description of the nails, the raising, the position of the body, the first hours. Neither he nor Matthew nor Luke nor John describes the physical process at all, and the restraint is universal and deliberate.

Part of the reason is that nobody in the first century needed it explained. Crucifixion was a public fact of life in the Roman world; Cicero called it the most cruel and disgusting penalty and said the very word should be kept far from the ears of Roman citizens. Everyone knew what it looked like and what it did.

But there is more to it than that. The Gospels are not trying to move you by the horror. They are telling you what happened and what it accomplished — and a reader who is overwhelmed by the physical agony can miss the darkness at noon and the cry at three, which are the things that actually killed him.

And divided his garments among them, casting lots for them, to decide what each should take.

The executioner's perquisite: the condemned man's clothes went to the detail. Which means he was stripped, and that the shame of it was total and public.

And four soldiers sat down in the dirt a few feet away and gambled.

That is one of the most terrible details in the passion, and it is not the cruelty that makes it so. It is the ordinariness. The Son of God is dying above their heads, and the men closest to him at that moment are playing dice for a coat, because it is a working day.

Mark does not point out that this is a quotation. He does not have to, because anyone who knew the Psalter would already have gone cold: they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots (Ps. 22:18).

And that is the first line of Psalm 22 to surface in this chapter. There will be more. Mark is laying them in quietly, one at a time, until the man on the cross says the first line out loud.
verseByVerse.note: Wine mixed with myrrh was a drugged drink to dull pain; Jesus refused it. The clothes of the condemned went to the execution squad.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: And it was the third hour when they crucified him. And the inscription of the charge against him read, "The King of the Jews." And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it was the third hour when they crucified him.

Nine in the morning, counting from sunrise, which is how Mark counts throughout — the sixth hour is noon (v. 33) and the ninth is three in the afternoon (v. 34).

So the timetable is: arrested around midnight, condemned by the council before dawn, before Pilate at first light, crucified at nine, dark at noon, dead by three. Roughly fifteen hours from the garden to the grave.

And a difficulty worth naming honestly, because a reader with John open will find one. John says Pilate's judgement was about the sixth hour (John 19:14) — which on Mark's reckoning would be noon, three hours after Mark has him already crucified.

Two answers are usually given and both are reasonable. Some hold that John is using Roman civil reckoning from midnight, which would put the judgement at six in the morning and fit perfectly. Others point out that both writers work in three-hour blocks — third, sixth, ninth — with no clocks and no minute hands, and that John's about is doing real work; ancient time-telling rounded heavily, and a modern reader's expectation of precision is anachronistic.

What is not in doubt is that Mark's own account is internally consistent to the hour, and that all four Gospels agree on the day, the place, the manner and the outcome. A difference over the reckoning of a morning is not a difference about what happened.

And the inscription of the charge against him read, The King of the Jews.

Roman practice: the titulus, a board with the crime written on it, carried before the prisoner or hung round his neck and then fixed to the cross, so that everyone passing could see what this had been done for.

Which makes this the only crime in history for which the charge, posted publicly by the state, was the plain truth.

John adds that it was written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek — the language of religion, the language of power, and the language of culture — and that when the chief priests asked Pilate to change it to this man said, I am King of the Jews, he refused: what I have written I have written (John 19:19–22).

The one decisive thing Pilate did all day was to leave a true sentence standing.

And with him they crucified two robbers, one on his right and one on his left.

Robbers — bandits, insurrectionists, the same word Jesus used of the arresting party's assumption about him (14:48). Whether these two were Barabbas's associates we are not told; but Jesus hangs where Barabbas would have hung, in his place.

One on his right and one on his left. And five chapters ago, James and John came asking to sit at his right hand and his left in his glory, and he asked whether they could drink his cup, and told them the places were not his to give (10:37–40).

These are the men who got them.

And a word about the verse your Bible skips. The numbers run 27, then 29. Some older Bibles print a verse 28 — And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, He was numbered with the transgressors — and modern ones put it in a footnote.

Those words are not in the earliest manuscripts of Mark. They are a genuine quotation of Isaiah 53:12, and Luke records Jesus applying it to himself (Luke 22:37); a scribe evidently wrote the reference in the margin here, where it fits so beautifully, and a later copyist took the margin for the text.

Nothing is lost. The thing the verse says is true, is Scripture, and is being fulfilled in front of us — a man numbered with criminals, one on each side. It simply belongs in Isaiah and Luke rather than here.
verseByVerse.note: The third hour was about 9 a.m. The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 28: “And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘He was numbered with the transgressors.’”

verseByVerse.quote: And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads and saying, "Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself, and come down from the cross!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads.

The first of three groups to mock, and this one is the general public — people on the road, going in and out of the city, because Golgotha was beside a thoroughfare and that was the point of it.

Wagging their heads. A gesture of contempt, and another quotation. All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads (Ps. 22:7). That is now the second line of Psalm 22 in this chapter, and Mark has still not named the psalm.

The same gesture appears in Lamentations, over the ruins of Jerusalem: all who pass along the way clap their hands at you; they hiss and wag their heads (Lam. 2:15).

Aha! You who would destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days.

They are throwing the trial's charge back at him — the false witness from last night (14:58), which even the court could not get two men to agree on. It has evidently got out and become the street version of what he said.

And of all the things they might have mocked, they chose the one that was about to come true. In three days there would be a temple raised that was not made with hands, and it would be his body, and the church has been built on it ever since.

Save yourself, and come down from the cross!

And here is the taunt, and it is worth recognising the voice.

This is the third time. In a wilderness, at the very beginning, Satan offered him the kingdoms of the world without a cross (Matt. 4:8-9; cf. Mark 1:13). At Caesarea Philippi, Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, and was told Get behind me, Satan! (8:32-33). And now, from the ground, at the foot of the cross itself: come down.

Same offer, three times, in three voices — an enemy, a friend, and a crowd. And it is always the same offer: be the Christ without the cross.

The tragedy of the people saying it is that they are asking for the one thing that would have damned them. If he had come down, they would have had a spectacle and no salvation. The only way he could save the men jeering at him was to stay where he was and let them go on jeering.

And here is the thing to take home from it, because it is not a first-century taunt.

The pressure to come down is the standing temptation of every Christian — to have the crown without the cross, the benefits of Christ without the death of self, a faith that costs nothing. It is offered constantly, and it always sounds reasonable, and it is always the voice from the wilderness.

He did not come down. That is the whole reason there is anything to say.

verseByVerse.quote: So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another, saying, "He saved others; he cannot save himself. Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe." Those who were crucified with him also reviled him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So also the chief priests with the scribes mocked him to one another.

The second group, and the worst.

These are not passers-by shouting. This is the religious leadership of Israel, standing at a public execution, talking to one another — sharing the joke among themselves, in front of a dying man, with the satisfaction of people whose problem has been solved.

They are the most educated men in the country, in their own holy city, at Passover, at the foot of a cross.

He saved others; he cannot save himself.

And with those seven words they state the gospel more accurately than anyone else in the Gospel of Mark, and do not believe a syllable of it.

Take the two halves.

He saved others. This is a concession, made in mockery, by his enemies, at the moment they have nothing to gain by it — and it is therefore about as good a piece of hostile testimony as exists. They are not disputing the miracles. They never did (3:22). Standing at his execution, the official opposition grants that this man rescued people.

He cannot save himself. And that is true too, and it is the most important sentence in the chapter.

Not because the power was gone. He could have called twelve legions of angels (Matt. 26:53); he had stilled a hurricane with a word and emptied a grave with another.

He could not save himself because saving himself and saving others were the two things that could not both be done. That was the whole choice, and it had been the choice since the wilderness. If he comes down, he is safe and we are lost. If he stays, we are saved and he is not.

The priests thought they had found a contradiction. They had found the mechanism of the atonement, and they said it out loud in the one place where it was being performed.

Let the Christ, the King of Israel, come down now from the cross that we may see and believe.

And the offer of belief, on their terms, with the order reversed.

That we may see and believe. Show us and we will trust you. It is the demand for a sign all over again, from the same men who demanded one at Dalmanutha and were refused (8:11–12).

And it is a lie, and they had already proved it. They had seen. They had seen a withered hand restored in their own synagogue and gone out to plan a murder (3:5–6). Within days they will hear that the tomb is empty and pay soldiers to say the body was stolen.

He did not come down, and that is why anyone believes at all. Had he come down, the crowd would have seen a miracle and gone home exactly as they came — impressed, and unforgiven. He stayed up; and within three hours, a Roman officer who had asked for no sign whatever was saying truly this man was the Son of God.

Those who were crucified with him also reviled him.

The third group, and Mark leaves it there without comment.

Two men in the same agony, six feet away, dying the same death — and they join in. There is no solidarity at Golgotha.

Luke tells us what happened to one of them before the afternoon was out: he stopped, and rebuked the other, and said Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom — and was told today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:39–43).

So one of the men reviling him in this verse died a few hours later with a promise from Christ in his ears. Which is worth remembering about anyone you have given up on, including yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour. And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, "Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?" which means, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the sixth hour had come, there was darkness over the whole land until the ninth hour.

Noon until three. The three brightest hours of a Middle Eastern spring day, and the light goes out.

It is not an eclipse; Passover falls at full moon, when a solar eclipse is astronomically impossible, and no eclipse lasts three hours. Mark offers no explanation and no mechanism. He simply reports that the sun failed over the land for three hours while the Son of God was dying, and leaves it.

And a reader who knows the prophets will hear something. And on that day, declares the Lord GOD, I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight. I will turn your feasts into mourning... I will make it like the mourning for an only son (Amos 8:9–10).

Darkness at noon, at a feast, mourning for an only son. Amos said it eight hundred years earlier.

And there was another darkness once, in Egypt, on the eve of the first Passover — a darkness to be felt, three days of it, and then the night the firstborn died (Ex. 10:21–23). At the first Passover the darkness came before the firstborn was struck. It does so again.

In the Bible darkness at midday is never atmosphere. It is judgement, and it means the day of the LORD has come.

For three hours, nobody sees anything. The mockery in the previous verses stops — Mark records no voice at all during the darkness. Whatever was happening between the Father and the Son in those hours happened where nobody could watch.

And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?

And out of the dark comes the loudest sound of the day.

Mark keeps the Aramaic, as he did with Talitha cumi to a dead girl, Ephphatha to a deaf man, and Abba in the garden. All of them are moments of extremity, and all of them are the actual sound of his voice.

Note that it is with a loud voice. A crucified man's death is a slow asphyxiation; the chest is fixed and every word costs an agonising push up on the nails. This is shouted.

Which means, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?

It is Psalm 22:1 — and now the psalm that has been surfacing all chapter is named out loud by the man it was written about. The clothes, the lots, the wagging heads, the mockery, the pierced hands and feet: all of it is in that psalm, and he begins to recite it.

Two errors have to be kept off this verse.

The first would soften it — as though he were merely quoting a psalm that ends in triumph, and was not truly forsaken. He was. The abandonment was real. He was bearing sin, and God's holiness turned from the sin-bearer. He made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Cor. 5:21); Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal. 3:13).

The second would break God in two — as though the Trinity were torn, the Father ceasing to love the Son, the Son ceasing to be God. That did not happen and could not. He remained the beloved Son and remained God through every moment of the dark. What he lost was not his Father's love or his own deity, but the felt light of the Father's face — borne in our place.

Both are true at once. And notice the word he uses. He does not cry God, why have you abandoned me. He cries my God, my God — twice claiming as his own the very One he can no longer feel.

That is faith stripped of every comfort and still holding on in the dark, and it is the only place in the Gospels where he addresses his Father as anything other than Father.

And this is the word for the believer who has prayed into silence and wondered whether the darkness proves God has finally let go. It does not. The blackest hour a soul can know — real God-forsakenness, the full weight of it — has already been entered by the Son, so that it would never fall on you. I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb. 13:5) was bought with this cry.

If you must pray in the dark, pray as he did: my God — to the God you cannot feel. He prayed it first, and prayed it there, so that you would never have to pray it alone.
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m. Jesus cries out in Aramaic the opening words of Psalm 22.

parallels.desc: my God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
I will make the sun go down at noon

verseByVerse.quote: And some of the bystanders hearing it said, "Behold, he is calling Elijah." And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink, saying, "Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And some of the bystanders hearing it said, Behold, he is calling Elijah.

They mishear. Eloi and Eliyahu are close enough in Aramaic that a shouted word from a dying man could be taken either way — and there was a popular belief that Elijah came to the aid of the righteous in extremity.

So the deepest sentence ever spoken on this earth is misheard as a superstition.

And that is worth a moment, because it is exactly what has been happening all through this Gospel. The crowd hears the words and gets the meaning wrong. They thought he was John the Baptist, or Elijah, or one of the prophets (8:28). The demons knew who he was and the crowds never did.

He is quoting Scripture in his agony, and they think he is calling for a folk-hero.

And someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine, put it on a reed and gave it to him to drink.

The sour wine is posca — cheap vinegary wine cut with water, the standard drink of a Roman soldier on duty. There would have been a jar of it at the execution site because the detail had to stand there all day.

And note what this is not. It is not the drugged wine of verse 23, which he refused. That was myrrhed wine, an anaesthetic. This is a mouthful of liquid to a man dying of thirst, and there is no reason to think it was cruelty — somebody ran.

It is also Psalm 69:21: for my thirst they gave me sour wine to drink. Another psalm, another line fulfilled by a man who thought he was being kind.

Saying, Wait, let us see whether Elijah will come to take him down.

And there is the reason given, and it turns the kindness into something else: keep him going a little longer, so we can see whether anything happens.

The whole crowd has become an audience waiting for an ending.

And now consider what nobody at Golgotha knew.

Elijah had already come. Jesus had said so, plainly, on the way down from the mountain: I tell you that Elijah has come, and they did to him whatever they pleased (9:13) — meaning John the Baptist, who had preached in the wilderness in Elijah's spirit, and had lost his head to a girl's request at a party.

So they stand under the cross wondering whether Elijah will come and rescue him. Elijah had come, and had been beheaded in a cellar for telling a king the truth, and nobody had rescued him either.

There was never going to be a rescue. That was the entire point, and it is why he is on the cross rather than in the crowd.
verseByVerse.note: Sour wine was the cheap wine soldiers drank.

parallels.desc: for my thirst they gave me sour wine

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus uttered a loud cry and breathed his last.

Ten words. Mark says nothing else.

And two things in that short sentence are extraordinary, and both are the observations of people who were standing there.

A loud cry.

This is not how crucified men die, and the centurion in the next verse knows it better than we do. Crucifixion kills by exhaustion and asphyxiation. The body hangs, the chest cannot empty, and every breath requires the man to push himself up on the nails through his feet. Death comes when he has no strength left to do it — and it takes days, and the end is a slow suffocation in which speech has long since become impossible.

Men in the last minutes of crucifixion could not shout. They could barely whisper.

He shouted. Twice in four verses Mark records a loud voice, and the second is at the very moment of death. John tells us what he said: It is finished (John 19:30).

That is not a man dying of exhaustion. It is a man finishing something.

He breathed his last.

Mark's verb is exepneusen — literally, he breathed out. And it is worth setting beside a sentence he wrote a long way back in this Gospel: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45).

To give. Nobody took it.

No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord. I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again (John 10:18).

So the death of Jesus of Nazareth is not the moment the Romans finally overcame him. It is the last act of his freedom — a shout, and then a decision, at three o'clock in the afternoon, in Passover week, a few hundred yards from the temple where the lambs had been killed.

He was in complete command of his own dying, and he chose the hour.

And in the same instant, in that temple, something happened that nobody outside the building could have seen.

verseByVerse.quote: And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom.

One sentence, and it may be the most important sentence in the book.

What the curtain was. The veil that hung before the Most Holy Place — the innermost room of the temple, where God had said he would dwell. Josephus describes it as enormous: embroidered in blue, purple and scarlet, and later Jewish sources give it a height of about sixty feet and a thickness of a handbreadth.

What it was for. It was a locked door made of cloth. Behind it, no one went — ever — except the high priest, once a year, on the Day of Atonement, and never without blood (Lev. 16:2; Heb. 9:7). The curtain existed to say one thing, and it said it for fifteen centuries: you cannot come in.

It was the standing announcement that sin has separated a holy God from unholy people, and that the separation is not negotiable.

And it tore.

Note the moment. Mark puts it in the same breath as the death — the shout, the last breath, the curtain. Not three days later at the resurrection. The instant he died.

And note the direction: from top to bottom.

Sixty feet of heavy woven fabric does not tear. And if it did, and if men had done it, they would have started at the bottom, because that is where hands reach.

This one opened from the top, which is beyond human reach — and it is Mark's way of telling you whose hands did it. The way into the presence of God was not forced open from our side. It was torn open from his.

It is the second time in this Gospel that something has been torn from above. At the Jordan, at his baptism, the heavens being torn open (1:10) — the same violent verb, schizō, which Mark uses exactly twice, at the beginning and at the end. Heaven ripped open at the start, and the veil ripped open at the finish, and between them the whole ministry.

What it means, put plainly. The barrier is gone. Not lowered, not made easier to negotiate — destroyed, by God, from his side, at the moment his Son died.

The letter to the Hebrews spells out what the church made of it: we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19–20).

Through the curtain, that is, through his flesh. The veil was his body, and his body was torn so the veil could be.

So when you pray tonight — an ordinary person, in an ordinary room, with an ordinary week's failures behind you — understand what you are walking through. There is no queue, no annual appointment, no priest to send in on your behalf, and no basin of blood to carry, because the blood has been shed and the door is off its hinges.

The most exclusive room in the world was opened to everybody at three o'clock on a Friday afternoon, and the man who opened it did it by dying.
verseByVerse.note: The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from the rest of the temple; only the high priest entered, once a year.

parallels.desc: a new and living way through the curtain

verseByVerse.quote: And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, "Truly this man was the Son of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, Truly this man was the Son of God!

And here is the sentence the whole Gospel has been travelling toward.

Weigh what Mark has done, because the architecture is exact.

He opened his book with these words: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God (1:1). Since then the title has been spoken twice by the Father — at the Jordan and on the mountain — and shrieked by demons who knew perfectly well what he was (3:11; 5:7).

And no human being in fifteen chapters has said it. Peter got as far as you are the Christ and then took him aside to argue about the cross. The disciples asked each other who then is this? and never answered. The crowds said John the Baptist, or Elijah, or a prophet.

The first person in this Gospel to look at Jesus of Nazareth and call him the Son of God is a Roman execution officer.

Could a pagan soldier have meant only “a son of God”, a hero or divine man? The Greek has no article, so the words could mean that, and the centurion may have understood less than he said. But Mark records the words as the confession his whole book has been building toward (1:1). Whatever the man meant, he said more than he knew, and he said it at the cross.

Consider the man. A centurion commanded eighty to a hundred men and had risen through the ranks; he was a professional soldier, probably twenty years in, and he was in charge of this detail. He had supervised executions before — very likely many. He was a pagan. He had spent the morning watching his own men gamble for the prisoner's clothes.

And he is standing facing him. Mark gives us the position: not off to one side, not in the crowd. Directly in front of the cross, close enough to see a man's face, for six hours.

And what converted him was not a miracle. It was the way this man died.

Mark says it precisely: he saw that in this way he breathed his last. Not that he saw a wonder. He saw how he died — the refusal of the drugged wine, the silence under mockery, the absence of cursing, the prayer in the dark, and finally a shout from a man who should not have had the breath for a whisper.

He had watched men die for twenty years and he had never seen anything like it.

And that is the answer to the question the Gospel keeps asking. You learn who Jesus is by watching him die. Not by the healings — the crowds saw those and stayed baffled. Not by the teaching — the scribes heard it and planned a murder. At the cross, where he looks least like the Son of God, is the one place a human being finally sees it.

And there is a last thing, and it is Mark's quiet announcement of everything that is coming.

The confession does not come from Israel. It comes from a Gentile — a foreigner, an occupier, a man with no covenant, no Scriptures and no synagogue, who had almost certainly never heard the name of Jesus before that morning.

At the very hour when the chief priests of Israel are standing in the same place jeering, a soldier of the empire that killed him becomes the first man to confess him.

The gospel has already leapt the wall. The nations are coming in, and the first of them is standing in front of a cross with blood on his boots.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him, and there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were also women looking on from a distance.

Mark has said nothing about them for fifteen chapters, and now, when everyone else has gone, he tells you they were there.

From a distance — nearly the phrase he used of Peter in the courtyard: Peter had followed him at a distance (14:54).

The difference is that Peter's distance was chosen and theirs was imposed. Women did not stand at the foot of a Roman execution among the soldiers. As near as they were permitted, they were.

They watched him die. Nobody made them, and there was nothing they could do, and they stayed for six hours.

Among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome.

Mark names three of them, and naming matters — these are witnesses, and named witnesses could be found and questioned by anyone in the early church who wanted to check the story.

Mary Magdalene — from Magdala on the lake. Luke says seven demons had come out of her (Luke 8:2), which means she is one of the great trophies of his ministry, and she will be the first person on earth to see him alive.

Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses — identified by her sons, presumably because the church knew them.

Salome — probably the mother of James and John (compare Matt. 27:56), which means the woman who once asked for the best two seats in the kingdom (Matt. 20:20–21; cf. Mark 10:35–37) is standing here watching what those seats actually cost, with two robbers occupying them.

When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him.

Two verbs, and both are large.

They followed him. That is the word for discipleship in this Gospel, the word used of the fishermen leaving their nets (1:18). Mark applies it to women without comment, in a world where a rabbi did not have female disciples.

And ministered to him. The verb is diakoneō — to serve, to wait on. And it is one of the great words of this book. It is what the angels did for him in the wilderness (1:13); it is what Peter's mother-in-law got up and did the moment she was healed (1:31); and it is the word in the sentence that defines his whole mission: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (10:45).

Luke adds the practical detail: they provided for him out of their means (Luke 8:3). Somebody paid for the food. For three years, a group of women funded and fed the ministry of Jesus of Nazareth, and nobody wrote down what it cost them.

And there were also many other women who came up with him to Jerusalem.

Many others. Not three; a company.

And now hold the two halves of this chapter together, because Mark has arranged them.

The twelve men who swore they would die with him are not in this chapter. One sold him, one denied him with oaths, and the rest ran in the dark and are hiding somewhere in the city.

The women stayed. They watched him die (v. 40), they watched where he was buried (v. 47), and they will be at the tomb at dawn on Sunday with spices they had no idea they would not need (16:1).

The chain of eyewitness runs unbroken from the cross to the empty tomb, and every link in it is a woman — in a culture where a woman's testimony carried little weight in court, which is precisely why no one inventing a story would have built it this way.
verseByVerse.note: Salome may be the mother of James and John, named in Matthew as “the mother of the sons of Zebedee.”

parallels.desc: the women who provided for him

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The request (vv. 42–43). Evening is coming and with it the Sabbath, and a body left on a cross overnight would defile the land under the Law. And a member of the very council that condemned him goes to the governor and asks for the corpse.

Mark says he took courage, and he needed it. Joseph of Arimathea is a man of standing who has kept his hopes to himself, and he chooses the moment when Jesus is a convicted criminal and every one of his friends has run — to go public.

The verification (vv. 44–45). Pilate is surprised that he is dead already and sends for the officer in charge to confirm it. So the death of Jesus of Nazareth is certified by a professional executioner and reported to a Roman governor before the body is released.

The tomb (vv. 46–47). A linen shroud, a grave cut in rock, a stone rolled across — and two women sitting where they can see, memorising the address.
verseByVerse.theology:
The burial is not a postscript. It is evidence, and Mark reports it like a man building a case.

Four facts are established in six verses, and every one of them closes off an objection that would be raised later.

He was really dead. Pilate was surprised, because crucifixion normally took two or three days — so he summoned the centurion and asked. A professional soldier who had stood facing him for six hours confirmed it to the governor before the body was signed over. Any theory that Jesus survived the cross has to get past a Roman execution officer's report to his prefect.

He was really buried, in a known place. Not a common grave, which is where crucified bodies usually went, but a rock-cut tomb belonging to a named man of the council — a man the authorities could have produced and questioned.

The tomb was sealed. A stone rolled across the entrance.

And the location was witnessed. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid — Mark's last sentence of the chapter, and it exists to say that the women who go to the tomb on Sunday morning went to the right one.

There is no room in this account for a mistaken address, a swoon, or a grave nobody could find.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council... took courage and went to Pilate.

John tells us he had been a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38), and Luke that he had not consented to the council's decision (Luke 23:51). So here is a man who had believed quietly for some time and had never said so.

And of all the moments to come out, he chooses this one.

Not the Sunday, when the tomb is empty and there is something to be glad about. Not the triumphal entry, when the crowds were shouting and it would have cost him nothing. He declares himself on the Friday afternoon, when Jesus is a convicted blasphemer executed by Rome, when the movement is finished, when every one of the twelve has vanished — and he does it by walking into the governor's residence and asking, as a member of the Sanhedrin, for the body of the man his own colleagues had just killed.

Now: he had everything to lose and nothing to gain. There was no upside. Association with a crucified criminal ended a career in that city, and he must have known it.

Which is worth putting to any Christian who has been quiet for a long time and is waiting for an easier moment to speak. The easier moment does not come, and it is not supposed to. Joseph's courage arrived on the worst possible day, and it is why he is in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council, who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God, took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when evening had come, since it was the day of Preparation, that is, the day before the Sabbath.

Mark explains the term for his Roman readers, as usual. Friday was the day you got ready — cooking, cleaning, finishing anything that could not be done once the Sabbath began at sunset.

And there is a legal urgency behind the clock. The Law required that an executed man's body be taken down before nightfall: his body shall not remain all night on the tree, but you shall bury him the same day, for a hanged man is cursed by God (Deut. 21:22–23).

Paul quotes that verse about this event: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us — for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Gal. 3:13).

So there are perhaps three hours of daylight left, and a body on a cross, and no one to claim it. Roman practice was to leave the corpses hanging as a deterrent, or throw them into a common pit.

How is Friday to Sunday “three days”? In Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a day, so after three days and on the third day mean the same span (cf. Esth 4:16 with 5:1). Even Jesus’ three days and three nights (Matt 12:40) is a way of saying three days, not a count of seventy-two hours. Some have argued for a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion, but Mark is plain that Jesus died on the day before the Sabbath.

And John calls this Friday the day of Preparation of the Passover (John 19:14). That most likely means the Friday of Passover week, the preparation for that week’s Sabbath, which is exactly how Mark explains the term here (cf. 14:12).

Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the council.

And a man walks out of nowhere into the last hours of the Gospel.

A respected member of the council — the Sanhedrin, the same body that condemned him at midnight — honourable, of good standing. Luke adds that he was a good and righteous man, who had not consented to their decision and action (Luke 23:51).

He is somebody. He has a position, colleagues, a reputation and a rock-cut tomb, which was an expensive thing to own.

Who was also himself looking for the kingdom of God.

Mark's phrase is gentle and it is a believer's description. He had been waiting — like Simeon in the temple, like Anna, like all the quiet people in Israel who had read the prophets and were watching for God to act.

And John tells us what had kept him silent: he was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly, for fear of the Jews (John 19:38).

So he had believed, privately, for some time, and had never said so out loud — because of exactly who his colleagues were.

Took courage and went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.

He had to dare, to steel himself. He had to work up to it.

And consider the timing, because it is the whole point of the man.

He does not come out on Sunday, when the tomb is empty and there is something to be glad about. He does not come out on the day of the entry, when the crowds were shouting and it would have cost him nothing but enthusiasm.

He declares himself on the Friday afternoon — when Jesus is a dead criminal, the movement is over, the twelve have vanished into the city, and the only thing to be gained from association is ruin.

He walks into the residence of the governor who has just executed the man, identifies himself as a member of the court that requested it, and asks for the corpse. Every person in that building will now know where he stands, and so will every colleague on the council by morning.

Nothing about it is calculated. There was no upside.

Which is worth putting to anybody who has been a quiet Christian for a long time and is waiting for a better moment to say so. The better moment does not arrive, and it is not meant to. Joseph's courage came on the worst possible day of the worst possible week — and it is the reason a man from a village nobody can now locate is named in all four Gospels.
verseByVerse.note: The day of Preparation was Friday, the day before the Sabbath. Arimathea was a town of Judea. Bodies of the crucified were often left unburied.

parallels.desc: not left on the tree overnight

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died. And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead. And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate was surprised to hear that he should have already died.

And this is one of the most useful verses in the chapter, though it looks like an administrative detail.

Pilate's surprise is professional. Crucifixion was designed to be slow — that was the point of it, as a deterrent. Victims commonly lasted two or three days; there are accounts of men surviving longer. It was so slow that the soldiers sometimes broke the legs to hasten it, which is exactly what they had just done to the two men beside him (John 19:32).

Jesus was on the cross for six hours. To a Roman governor who had signed a great many of these orders, that was fast enough to be worth checking.

And summoning the centurion, he asked him whether he was already dead.

So Pilate does not take Joseph's word for it, and he does not guess. He sends for the officer commanding the execution detail — very probably the same man who has just said truly this man was the Son of God — and puts the question to him directly.

And when he learned from the centurion that he was dead, he granted the corpse to Joseph.

The body is not released until a professional soldier has confirmed the death to the governor's face.

And now notice what Mark has built, without any appearance of arguing.

He is writing thirty-odd years after the event, for a church whose central claim was that this man came out of that grave alive. The obvious objection — then and now — is that he never actually died: that he fainted, was taken down early, revived in the cool of the tomb, and walked out.

Mark closes that door with a bolt, and he does it by simply reporting the paperwork.

The death was doubted by the governor, examined on his instruction, and certified by the officer who had stood facing him for six hours and had watched hundreds of men die. Only then was the body handed over.

Any theory that Jesus survived the cross has to get past a Roman execution officer's report to a Roman prefect — and then has to explain how a man scourged with the flagellum, crucified, and sealed in a rock tomb for thirty-six hours without food, water or medical care, rolled away a stone from the inside and convinced eleven terrified men that he was the risen Lord of life.

And there is one more word here, and it is the word Mark chooses in verse 45.

Everywhere else in these verses the body is called a body. Here, in the sentence where Pilate signs it over, Mark uses ptōma — a corpse. It is the blunt word, the one you would use of a carcass, and Mark uses it exactly once more in this Gospel, of John the Baptist's body being collected by his disciples (6:29).

He is not being callous. He is being exact, because everything depends on it.

What Joseph of Arimathea carried down off that cross and into a garden was a dead man. Not a swoon, not a coma, not a rumour. A corpse — with a Roman officer's word on it, and a governor's signature.

Which is precisely why what happens on Sunday morning matters.
verseByVerse.note: Crucified men often lingered for days; a death within hours surprised Pilate.

parallels.desc: the soldiers find him already dead

verseByVerse.quote: And Joseph bought a linen shroud, and taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud and laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock. And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Joseph bought a linen shroud.

He goes and buys it — on the afternoon before a Sabbath, at short notice, with his own money. There is nothing prepared about any of this. A man who woke up that morning a secret disciple is now shopping for grave clothes for an executed criminal.

And the word is sindōn. It has appeared once before in this Gospel, a chapter ago: a young man who followed Jesus into the garden with nothing but a linen cloth about his body, and when they seized him he left the linen cloth and ran away naked (14:51–52).

One man abandoned his linen cloth to get away from Christ. Another bought one to wrap him in.

And taking him down, wrapped him in the linen shroud.

Somebody had to do it. Somebody had to get the nails out, take the weight of the body, carry it, and wrap it — and it was a member of the Sanhedrin, in his good clothes, on the eve of the Sabbath, making himself ceremonially unclean for a week by handling a corpse (Num. 19:11) in the middle of the feast.

John adds that Nicodemus came too, with seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (John 19:39). Two members of the council that condemned him are the only men in Jerusalem attending to his body.

And laid him in a tomb that had been cut out of the rock.

Matthew tells us it was Joseph's own, newly cut and never used (Matt. 27:60).

A rock-cut tomb was for the wealthy — an expensive, permanent thing, prepared for a man and his family. Joseph gives away his own grave.

And the prophecy is exact and strange: of the Servant, they made his grave with the wicked and with a rich man in his death (Isa. 53:9). Executed among criminals; buried in a rich man's tomb. Both halves happened on the same afternoon.

And he rolled a stone against the entrance of the tomb.

A heavy disc of stone, set in a channel, rolled across the doorway. It took several men to move, which is why the women will be worrying about it on Sunday morning (16:3).

And that is the last thing anybody does for Jesus of Nazareth. A stone across a door, and then everyone goes home because the sun is going down.

Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw where he was laid.

The last sentence of the chapter, and it is doing a specific job.

They are still there. Everyone else has gone; the men who buried him are hurrying to get home before the Sabbath. Two women stay behind in the fading light and watch which tomb it is.

Mark records it because it matters. These two are named at the cross (v. 40), named at the burial (v. 47), and named at the tomb on Sunday morning (16:1). The chain of witness is unbroken and the address is confirmed. Nobody went to the wrong grave.

And so the chapter ends in the worst silence in the Bible.

The King of the Jews is dead. The body is in a borrowed grave with a stone across it. The disciples are hiding. The women are walking home in the dark with nothing to do until the Sabbath is over.

Every single person who loved him believed, that night, that it was finished — and they were right, and they had no idea what the word meant.

He had told them three times that he would rise again after three days. Not one of them remembered it. And this is Friday.
verseByVerse.note: Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, often disc-shaped, rolled into a groove.

15.theology:
The cry of dereliction (v. 34) has two errors to be kept off it. The first would soften it, as though he were merely reciting a psalm and not truly forsaken — he was; he was bearing sin, and God's holiness turned from the sin-bearer (2 Cor. 5:21; Gal. 3:13). The second would break God in two, as though the Trinity were torn and the Father ceased to love the Son — that did not happen and could not. He remained the beloved Son and remained God through every moment; what he lost was the felt light of his Father's face, borne in our place.

And notice the word he uses. Not God, why have you abandoned me, but my God, my God — twice claiming as his own the very One he could no longer feel. That is faith stripped of every comfort and still gripping in the dark, and it is the only place in the Gospels where he addresses the Father as anything but Father.

The curtain (v. 38) may be the most important sentence in the book. Sixty feet of woven fabric, a handbreadth thick, whose entire purpose for fifteen centuries was to say you cannot come in — torn at the instant he died, and torn from the top, which is beyond human reach. The way in was not forced from our side; it was opened from his. And it is the second thing in Mark torn from above: the heavens being torn open at the baptism (1:10), the same violent word, at the beginning and the end. We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh (Heb. 10:19–20).

And the burial is evidence, not postscript. Pilate was surprised he had died so soon — crucifixion normally took days — so he summoned the centurion and asked. The death was doubted by the governor, examined on his order, and certified by the officer who had stood facing him for six hours, before the body was released. Mark even switches words in v. 45 to ptōma, corpse. Any theory that he survived the cross has to get past a Roman execution officer's report to his prefect.
15.examples:
Then: He saved others; he cannot save himself (v. 31) — the chief priests, jeering at the foot of the cross, stating the gospel with complete accuracy and believing none of it.

Both halves are true. He did save others, and his enemies concede it at the moment they have nothing to gain by conceding anything. And he could not save himself — not for lack of power, since he could have called twelve legions of angels (Matt. 26:53), but because saving himself and saving others were the two things that could not both be done. They thought they had found a contradiction; they had found the mechanism of the atonement.

Now: and the demand attached to it — come down now from the cross that we may see and believe — has the order exactly backwards, and it is the standing human demand. Show me and I will trust you.

He did not come down, and that is why anyone believes at all. Had he come down, the crowd would have seen a miracle and gone home impressed and unforgiven. He stayed up; and within three hours a Roman officer who had asked for no sign whatever was saying truly this man was the Son of God.

And notice what converted that officer. Not a wonder — Mark is precise: he saw that in this way he breathed his last. He saw how he died. That is the answer to the question this Gospel keeps asking. You learn who Jesus is by watching him die. The crowds saw the healings and stayed baffled; the scribes heard the teaching and planned a murder; and at the cross, where he looks least like the Son of God, a pagan finally sees it — and he is the first human being in fifteen chapters to say the words Mark opened his book with (1:1).

16.title: He Has Risen; He Is Not Here
16.text: <sup>1</sup>When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. <sup>2</sup>And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb. <sup>3</sup>And they were saying to one another, “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” <sup>4</sup>And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large. <sup>5</sup>And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed. <sup>6</sup>And he said to them, “Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. <sup>7</sup>But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.” <sup>8</sup>And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and astonishment had seized them, and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. <sup>9</sup>Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. <sup>10</sup>She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept. <sup>11</sup>But when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they would not believe it. <sup>12</sup>After these things he appeared in another form to two of them, as they were walking into the country. <sup>13</sup>And they went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them. <sup>14</sup>Afterward he appeared to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him after he had risen. <sup>15</sup>And he said to them, “Go into all the world and proclaim the gospel to the whole creation. <sup>16</sup>Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned. <sup>17</sup>And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; <sup>18</sup>they will pick up serpents with their hands; and if they drink any deadly poison, it will not hurt them; they will lay their hands on the sick, and they will recover.” <sup>19</sup>So then the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. <sup>20</sup>And they went out and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by accompanying signs.
16.overview:
Three women buy spices when the shops reopen on Saturday evening, and set out at first light to finish a burial. Not one of them expects a resurrection — he had told them three times and it had gone in nowhere. They are carrying ointment for a corpse, and the only thing on their minds is a stone they cannot move.

They arrive and find it moved, and a young man in white sitting inside, and the most important sentence in the book: He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. Not a symbol and not an experience — an event with an address, and an invitation to inspect the evidence.

Then a message with two extra words in it: tell his disciples and Peter. And they run away and say nothing to anybody, because they are terrified — which is where the oldest manuscripts of this Gospel stop.

The twelve verses that follow are printed in brackets in the ESV and most modern Bibles, and the question they raise is answered here in full rather than buried in a footnote. They summarise appearances recorded elsewhere, give the commission, and end with the Lord Jesus taken up and seated at the right hand of God — exactly as he had told the high priest he would be, on the night they condemned him for saying it.

And the last sentence of Mark is the reversal of verse 8: the people who said nothing went out and preached everywhere.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
The errand (vv. 1–4). The Sabbath ends at sunset on Saturday, the shops open, and three women buy spices. They set out at first light on Sunday to finish a burial, and the only thing worrying them on the road is a practical problem they cannot solve: the stone. They arrive and find it solved.

The announcement (vv. 5–7). Inside the tomb a young man in white is sitting on the right, and what he says is the most important sentence in the book. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him. And then a message with one name added to it that has comforted failing Christians for two thousand years.

The silence (v. 8). And they run, and say nothing to anybody, because they are terrified.

That is where the oldest manuscripts of this Gospel stop — mid-sentence, almost, on the word afraid. Which raises the question this chapter cannot avoid, and which is dealt with plainly below rather than left in a footnote.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why is 16:9–20 in brackets, and can I trust my Bible?

Open the ESV at this page and you will find, before verse 9, a line in square brackets: Some of the earliest manuscripts do not include 16:9–20. That deserves a straight answer, because a reader who meets it for the first time can feel the ground move.

Here are the facts, plainly. The two oldest complete manuscripts of the New Testament we possess — Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both fourth century — end Mark at verse 8. Eusebius and Jerome, writing in the fourth and fifth centuries, both say that the accurate copies known to them ended there. Some manuscripts have a different, shorter ending; a few have both. And the Greek of verses 9–20 does not read like Mark: it uses more than a dozen words found nowhere else in the book, and verse 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as though for the first time, though she has just been named in verse 1.

The honest conclusion is that Mark very probably did not write these twelve verses, and that they were added early — early enough to be widely known and read in churches by the second century.

And here is what that does not mean. It does not mean anything has been smuggled into your Bible. Every substantial thing in the passage is taught plainly elsewhere: the appearance to Mary Magdalene (John 20), the two on the Emmaus road (Luke 24), the commission to all nations (Matt. 28), the ascension and session at God's right hand (Luke 24; Acts 1; Eph. 1:20). No doctrine of the Christian faith stands or falls here.

So take the reassurance the right way round. The reason you know about this is that the church kept the evidence and printed it in the margin instead of quietly tidying it away. A faith that could not survive its own manuscripts would hide them. This one puts the workings at the bottom of the page — which is precisely why the rest of the text can be trusted.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: tell his disciples and Peter (v. 7).

Two extra words, and they are there because somebody in heaven knew exactly which man in Jerusalem was certain he had forfeited his place.

Peter had denied him three times with oaths and a curse, in a courtyard, to a servant girl, and had gone out and wept. As far as he knew, he was finished — not merely ashamed, but out.

And the first message from the other side of the grave has his name in it, added on, as though the general term might not reach him. In effect: tell the disciples, and make sure you tell Peter.

Now: and notice that this is not new. Jesus had promised it before the failure happened: you will all fall away... but after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (14:27–28). The angel repeats his promise, and adds the name.

So if you are a Christian who has failed badly enough to wonder whether there is a road back, the answer is in two words at the empty tomb. The road was mapped before you took the wrong turn, and when the message came, the one who had failed worst was named.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint him. And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Sabbath was past.

Saturday evening, after sunset, when the shops could open again. They had watched him buried on Friday afternoon with the light going (15:47), and then the Sabbath closed down and nothing could be done for twenty-four hours.

That was the longest day in the history of the world, and Mark says nothing about it at all.

Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices.

The same names as at the cross (15:40) and — for two of them — at the burial (15:47). Mark keeps naming them because they are witnesses, and a named witness could be found and questioned.

And they spend money. Somebody's savings went on those spices, and it was the last thing they would ever be able to do for him.

So that they might go and anoint him.

Understand what this errand is, because it decides how you read everything that follows.

They are going to a grave to do the last office for a corpse. The burial on Friday had been done at speed, by two men racing the sunset, and there had been no time for the proper anointing. They are going to finish it.

Which means — and this must be said plainly, because it matters — not one of them expected a resurrection. Nobody in this chapter is going to the tomb to see whether it worked. They are carrying two days of grief and a bag of burial spices to a body they expect to be there and to have begun to decay.

He had told them three times that he would rise after three days (8:31; 9:31; 10:34). It had gone in nowhere.

So whatever else the first Easter morning was, it was not wish-fulfilment. Nobody was hoping. The people closest to him had entirely given up, and the story of the resurrection begins with his friends buying ointment for a dead man.

And very early on the first day of the week, when the sun had risen, they went to the tomb.

Mark's timestamps are typically precise: very early, and yet with the sun up — they set out in the dark and arrived as it came light.

And the first day of the week is a phrase that changed the calendar of the world. All four Gospels use it. Within a generation, Christians were meeting on it (Acts 20:7; 1 Cor. 16:2), and by the end of the century John was calling it the Lord's day (Rev. 1:10).

The Sabbath was the seventh day, the day of rest at the end of creation. The church moved its meeting to the first — the day the new creation started.

Does this mean Sunday is the Christian Sabbath? Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession, hold that it is. The more likely reading is that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17), and that Christians meet on the first day not as a law but because it is the day of the resurrection. The apostles’ churches did so from the beginning (Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 16:2), and it remains a good and wise practice.
verseByVerse.note: The Sabbath ended at sundown on Saturday; the first day of the week is Sunday.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were saying to one another, "Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?" And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back—it was very large.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were saying to one another, Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?

The tense is continuous — they kept saying it, all the way there. This is the conversation on the road.

And it is entirely reasonable. They had watched Joseph roll it across on Friday (15:46). These are women carrying jars, on a path outside the city at dawn, and the one thing standing between them and the errand is a piece of stone they cannot move and have no plan for.

Note that they set out anyway. They had no solution and they went — which is worth something, because a more calculating person stays at home until the problem is solved.

And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled back — it was very large.

Mark puts the size at the end of the sentence, almost as an afterthought, and it is exactly how somebody tells a story afterwards: and it had been moved — and it was enormous.

A blocking stone for a rock-cut tomb was a disc set in a channel, and the archaeology suggests weights of a ton or more. Getting it into place was downhill work for several men. Getting it out again was not.

And here is the first thing the resurrection does in this Gospel, and it is worth taking home.

The problem they had worried about the whole way had already been dealt with before they got there — and not as a favour to them. The stone was not moved so that the women could get in. Matthew is explicit that it was rolled back and sat on by an angel (Matt. 28:2), and the body was long gone by then; a sealed tomb was no obstacle to a risen Christ, who would walk through locked doors that same evening (John 20:19).

The stone was moved so that the world could look in.

But the pastoral point stands, and it is the plainest comfort in the chapter. They spent the walk on a difficulty that had already been settled. God had gone ahead of them in the dark, while they were still asleep and still grieving and still certain that nothing had changed.

Which is very often the shape of it. The thing you are rehearsing at four in the morning — the conversation you cannot see a way through, the obstacle you have no plan for — may well be dealt with before you get to it. It was still worth setting out with no solution. That is what they did, and the stone was already back.

verseByVerse.quote: And entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And entering the tomb.

They go in. A rock-cut tomb of this kind had a low doorway and an antechamber, with a shelf cut into the wall where the body was laid — so they stoop through and stand up inside a room built for the dead.

They saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe.

Mark says a young man. Matthew says plainly that it was an angel (Matt. 28:2–5), and the white robe and the reaction settle it; Mark simply describes what they saw.

Matthew has one angel, Luke two men and John two angels; the women and the times vary too. Each Gospel tells the story selectively, and none says there was only one. The women evidently came in more than one group and at slightly different times. The core is the same in all four: the women came first, the tomb was empty, and the message was that he had risen.

And now the bracket, which is one of the loveliest things in this Gospel and is easy to miss.

That phrase, a young man, occurs exactly twice in Mark.

The first time was in the garden, on the night of the arrest: and a young man followed him, with nothing but a linen cloth about his body. And they seized him, but he left the linen cloth and ran away naked (14:51–52) — perhaps Mark himself, putting his own worst moment into his own book without a name attached.

The second time is here: a young man, sitting down, dressed in a white robe, inside an empty grave, telling women that Christ is risen.

One fled from Christ stripped and ashamed in the dark. One sits in the place of death, clothed in white, with the news. Mark has bracketed the passion between them, and whether or not he intended every echo, the picture is the gospel: that is what happens to people between Friday and Sunday.

Sitting on the right side. A small detail with two things in it.

He is sitting, which is the posture of somebody whose work is finished and who is waiting. There is no urgency in that tomb. The crisis is over; an angel has sat down.

And the right side is the side of honour — the place the sons of Zebedee asked for (10:37), the place where Jesus himself now sits (v. 19).

And they were alarmed.

They came expecting a corpse and found a living stranger sitting where it should have been. Every reaction to the supernatural in this Gospel is the same, and it is never serene: the disciples in the boat (4:41), the crowd at the demoniac's healing (5:15), the three on the mountain (9:6).

Nobody in the Bible meets the power of God and finds it comfortable. Which is why the first word out of the angel's mouth is the one it always is.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Do not be alarmed. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here. See the place where they laid him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be alarmed.

The same word as the last verse, negated. He deals with their terror before he gives them the news, which is how heaven habitually opens a conversation — fear not is the first thing said to Zechariah, to Mary, to the shepherds, and to John on Patmos.

You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified.

Three things in that identification, and every one is nailed down.

Jesus — the personal name. Of Nazareth — the village, the human address, the ordinary provincial origin that made people take offence (6:3). Who was crucified — the manner of death, stated flatly and in the past tense.

There is no ambiguity here about who is meant or what happened to him. The risen one is the crucified one; it is the same man, and he still carries the identity. When he appears to Thomas he will still have the holes in him (John 20:27).

Christianity has never offered a Jesus who got past the cross. It offers a man who went through it and out the other side, and who is known by it forever — a Lamb standing, as though it had been slain (Rev. 5:6).

He has risen; he is not here.

Four words in Greek and they are the hinge of history.

He has risen — and the Greek is a passive: he was raised. Which is how the New Testament almost always puts it. God the Father raised him (Acts 2:24; Rom. 6:4) — the resurrection is the Father's public verdict on the Son, the answer to the cry from the dark, the reversal of the council's sentence. The court of heaven has overturned the court of Caiaphas.

He is not here. And that is the second half, and it is a claim about a physical location on a spring morning. Not his spirit lives on. Not his cause continues. The body is not in the room, and the room is one the women had personally watched him carried into (15:47).

See the place where they laid him.

And now the angel does something no religion has ever done: he offers evidence and invites inspection.

Look. Come here and look at the shelf. There is nothing on it.

The resurrection is not presented in this Gospel as a spiritual experience, a symbol, or a way of speaking about hope surviving death. It is presented as an event with an address, a date and a witness list, and the first thing anybody is told to do about it is to examine the physical evidence.

Paul stakes everything on the same ground: if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins (1 Cor. 15:17). Christianity is the only faith in the world that can be disproved by producing a body — and nobody ever has, though a great many people in Jerusalem that spring had every reason to try.

The tomb was open, the location was known, and the authorities had soldiers. All they had to do was walk in and carry out the evidence.

The place was empty, and it still is.

verseByVerse.quote: But go, tell his disciples and Peter that he is going before you to Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But go, tell his disciples and Peter.

The first commission of the Christian era is given to three women in a graveyard, and it contains two extra words that have done more for failing Christians than almost any other phrase in Scripture.

And Peter.

He was one of the disciples. The word covered him. There was no need to add anything.

Unless somebody in heaven knew exactly which man in Jerusalem was certain that it no longer did.

Peter had denied him three times, in a courtyard, to a servant girl, with oaths and a curse on his own head — and had gone out and broken down (14:71–72). He had spent Saturday somewhere in that city with nothing to think about but that. As far as he knew, he was not merely ashamed; he was out. He had disqualified himself, publicly, in the worst hour of his Master's life, after boasting that he never would.

And the first message sent from the other side of the grave has his name attached to the end of it, as though the general term might not reach him. In effect: tell the disciples, and make sure you tell Peter.

Somebody wanted him to be in no doubt.

That he is going before you to Galilee.

And this is not new information. It is a quotation.

On the walk out to Gethsemane, before anybody had failed, Jesus had said: You will all fall away... But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee (14:27–28). The angel repeats the sentence almost word for word.

Which means the restoration was promised before the betrayal happened, and the meeting place was fixed while they were still swearing they would never need it.

Go before is a shepherd's picture — to walk out in front of the flock. He had quoted Zechariah about the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered, and now the struck shepherd is out in front of them again.
